And I think he was among those who wrote an article, I believe in a newspaper published in al-Sharqiyya, saying that the Noble Qur'an is structured upon the number nineteen, and that everything in it revolves around nineteen; the hundred and fourteenth surah is multiplied by what... that is, one hundred and fourteen is the result of multiplying what by what? I do not know his words on this.
* Student: Perhaps six, nineteen times six.
* The Shaykh: Six times nineteen is one hundred and fourteen; and six times one is six, and five makes one hundred and fourteen by his account: six times nineteen. And likewise he distorted the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Over it are nineteen﴾ [al-Muddaththir 30]. He said: ﴿over it﴾ means upon the correctness of what came in the Qur'an; ﴿nineteen﴾ means nineteen letters, which is the basmalah. Yet the Qur'an says: ﴿Over it are nineteen﴾, meaning what?
* Student: Angels.
* The Shaykh: Over the Fire are angels. But he said: No, upon the correctness of this Qur'an are nineteen letters, which is the basmalah.
* Student: What is the purpose?
* The Shaykh: The purpose, he says, is to argue that this Qur'an could not have been brought by Muhammad, because this number and the Qur'an being structured upon it was only known after the computer came, so it became known.
Is the basmalah nineteen letters?
* Student: This corrupt person is confusing.
* The Shaykh: Yes, very confusing, so much so that he said: ﴿Qaf. By the glorious Qur'an﴾ [Qaf 1]: it begins with the letter qaf, because the total of the qafs in it divides by nineteen and it comes out. The proof that he did not say "and the people of Lot" is that if he had said "and the people of Lot," an extra qaf would have been added and the division would not have worked. So he said: ﴿and the brothers of Lot﴾ [Qaf 13], yes, in order for the division to be complete. In any case, he is clearly a confuser and distorter, without doubt. But we will, God willing, demolish it: we have written a refutation of him in this, and the first thing we can demolish is the matter of the basmalah. The basmalah was not the first thing revealed, so that we could say the Qur'an is structured upon it, is that correct or not?
* Student: Yes, correct.

The Shaykh: What was the first revelation?
Student: "Read in the name of your Lord" (al-'Alaq 1).
The Shaykh: "Read." Second, the basmala, according to his claim, is not nineteen letters: the ba', the sin, the mim, the hamza, the lam, the second lam, the ha', the alif, the ra' repeated, the ha', the mim, the alif, the nun... how many is that for you? Fourteen. The hamza, the ra' repeated, the ha', the ya', the mim, that makes twenty.
Student: (...).
The Shaykh: Twenty. And he says: we count the written form "al-Rahman" as having no alif; if you drop the alif from "al-Rahman" it becomes nineteen.
Student: Keep the lam.
The Shaykh: We say: yes, if you say so, then keep the lam. If you keep the lam, "al-Rahman al-Rahim" (al-Fatihah 1) becomes twenty-one, is that right? Then we also say to him: if you consider the writing, was the Qur'an revealed in written form or revealed as spoken?
Student: Spoken.
The Shaykh: Spoken. If the written system were otherwise, would the letters increase or decrease, or neither increase nor decrease?
Student: They do not decrease.
The Shaykh: No, the letters that are pronounced do not increase; but the written ones do increase. We see that now, in English writing, sometimes the vowel marks may become letters, isn't that so?
Student: Yes.
The Shaykh: And go to the Chinese and their like, how many letters do they have?
Student: Thousands.
The Shaykh: They have thousands in their writing. The point in this is that writing is a craft, it has no bearing on pronunciation, and the Qur'an was revealed in the language, "in clear Arabic tongue" (al-Shu'ara' 195). But they deceive and confuse; they claim they serve the Qur'an by this before these foreigners who know only the material, but if they explained to people the beauty of this religion and what it brought of morals and dealings (...).

﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. The Romans have been defeated, in the nearest land; but they, after their defeat, will overcome, within a few years﴾ (al-Rum 1–4).

His words: "Surat al-Rum is Meccan." What is the Meccan?
Student: It is what was revealed before the Hijrah.
The Shaykh: It is what was revealed before the Hijrah, and the Medinan is what was revealed after it, whether it was revealed in Mecca or not; you know it is Medinan. On this basis, His saying ﴿Today I have perfected your religion for you﴾ (al-Ma'idah 3) was revealed at 'Arafah on the day of the Farewell Pilgrimage.
Student: It would be Medinan.
The Shaykh: It would be Medinan, even though it was revealed in Mecca.
(And it has sixty or fifty-nine verses): If we count "Alif Lam Mim" as an independent verse, it becomes sixty verses; otherwise, fifty-nine.
His words: "Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim": It has passed that the basmala is an independent verse brought at the beginning of surahs, and it is not attached to what follows, neither in al-Fatihah nor elsewhere, contrary to some scholars who say it is a verse of al-Fatihah, so they count al-Fatihah as seven verses including the basmala. The basmala: ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful (1). Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds (2). The Most Gracious, the Most Merciful (3). Master of the Day of Judgment (4). You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help (5). Guide us to the straight path (6). The path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour, not of those who have earned anger, nor of those who are astray (7)﴾ (al-Fatihah 1–7). How many is that for you? Seven, with the basmala.
The correct view is that the basmala is not a verse of al-Fatihah nor of any other surah. The first verse of al-Fatihah is: ﴿Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds﴾. And where is the seventh? Because it is seven verses by agreement; the seventh is His saying ﴿The path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour..﴾. We divide this into two verses: ﴿The path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾ is the sixth, and ﴿not of those who have earned anger, nor of those who are astray (7)﴾ is the seventh. In the Mushaf you find the basmala is a verse in al-Fatihah and not a verse in other surahs, but the correct view is that there is no difference.
Student: How (...), O Shaykh, (...) seven verses without it?
The Shaykh: Without the basmala?
Student: Yes (...) the second.
The Shaykh: Possibly, yes, this is the correct view.

His words: ﴿Alif Lam Mim﴾. The author said: "God knows best what He means by it." Yes, when we do not know something, it is obligatory to say: God knows best what He intended. It has been said this is half of knowledge, because a person is either knowing or ignorant; if he says about what he knows, what he knows, and about what he does not know, "God knows best," that is half of knowledge.

There is no doubt that a person's saying "God knows best" about what he does not know is what is obligatory upon him. Do not say: "By God, I am..." If you say "I do not know," your standing does not diminish among people; rather it increases among people, just as it does not diminish with God, nor among people, because the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever humbles himself for God, God raises him" [Narrated by al-Tabarani in al-Awsat (4894) from 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her)].

This is from the aspect of humility before God: that you say about what you do not know, "I do not know." It is like forgiveness, which increases a person only in honour, and like charity, through which wealth does not decrease. Likewise, "I do not know" does not diminish a person's standing in knowledge but increases it, because when people see that this man is cautious, speaks only of what he knows and refrains from what he does not know, they trust him and recognise that he speaks only what he knows.

So the author's words, "God knows best what He means by it," are what is obligatory upon every person who does not know what God intended. But when we return to His saying: ﴿We have made it an Arabic Qur'an that you may understand﴾ (Yusuf 2), we know that this Qur'an is according to the Arabic language, and that there is not a word in it except that it is understandable; otherwise God would be sending down something whose meaning we do not know. So if we apply these alphabetic letters to this rule, what is the rule? This verse: ﴿We have made it an Arabic Qur'an that you may understand﴾. If we apply the alphabetic letters to this rule, do we find that such a combination in the Arabic language has a meaning or has no meaning?
Student: It has a meaning.
The Shaykh: ﴿Alif Lam Mim﴾ has a meaning?!
Student: No.
The Shaykh: It has no meaning in the Arabic language; it is simply a group of alphabetic letters (alif, lam, mim). That is why you do not pronounce it as "alam" (a word). Rather you say "alif lam mim," isn't that so?
Student: Yes.
The Shaykh: So by the rule of the Arabic tongue in which the Qur'an was revealed, or with which the Qur'an was revealed so that we may understand it, by this Arabic tongue it has no meaning. It is only alphabetic letters with no meaning in themselves. Then we know them, but what does God intend by them? Shaykh al-Islam and many scholars mentioned that their purpose is to show that the Qur'an is inimitable despite being composed of these letters with which people speak.

The alphabetic letters with which people speak, the Qur'an is made of these letters; it did not bring new, strange letters, so that we could say it defeated people by them, because it would have brought letters they neither understand nor pronounce. Rather, they are letters from which their speech is composed. So is the inimitability then in terms of the letters, that it brought new letters, or in terms of the composition, context, and sublime, beneficial meanings? The answer?
Student: The second.
The Shaykh: From the second, the second aspect. And this which Shaykh al-Islam adopted is undoubtedly strong: these alphabetic letters in themselves have no meaning, but they have a purpose and an intent, which is that in the Qur'an, which has defeated all creation, no new letters were brought; rather it is from the letters they speak with.

Some contemporary scholars have said that these letters are like a key to the surah in which they occur, meaning that if you find "Lam Mim" at the head of a surah of the Qur'an, it is only because of the abundance of lam and mim in it, so they are like a key to it; likewise if you find nun, it is because of the abundance of nun in it, and if you find lam and ra', it is because of the abundance of lam and ra'. But this is criticised, and criticised; and were this consistently applied, it would also have some basis.

In any case, we know, by the fact that the Qur'an is in the Arabic tongue so that we may understand it, that these alphabetic letters in themselves are?
Student: They have no meaning.
The Shaykh: They have no meaning.

His words: ("﴿The Romans have been defeated﴾, and they are the People of the Book. Persia defeated them, and they are not People of the Book but worship idols; the disbelievers of Mecca rejoiced at that and said to the Muslims: We shall defeat you just as Persia defeated the Romans.")
﴿The Romans have been defeated﴾: this is a verb in the passive voice, and ﴿the Romans﴾ is the deputy subject. He made the verb feminine, ﴿ghulibat﴾, and did not say "ghuliba al-Rum," even though those who fight are men; but he made it feminine in view of the group. The one who defeated them was Persia. The wisdom, God knows best, in omitting the agent is that this is a greater humiliation for the Persians, and that it is more discreet regarding the Romans' humiliation and abandonment.

I say: the agent was concealed for two reasons:
The first reason: a humiliation of the Persians, that they are not worthy of mention.
Second: making the matter easier for the Romans, because if it is said to a person "you were defeated," it is lighter than if it is said "so-and-so defeated you," because if it is said "so-and-so defeated you," the meaning becomes that he is humbled before that named man.

His words: "The Romans: the People of the Book." It would have been better if the author had said "People of a Book," because the Romans are Christians, and People of the Book includes Jews and Christians, so saying "People of a Book" would have been better.
("Persia defeated them, and they are not People of the Book, but worship idols"): because they are Magians who worship fire.
("The disbelievers of Mecca rejoiced at that and said to the Muslims: We shall defeat you just as Persia defeated the Romans"): meaning that the disbelievers of Mecca took this as an omen and said: if the Romans are People of the Book and Persia defeated them while Persia are idolaters, then this is a key to victory for us: that we should defeat the Muslims, who are People of the Book, while we are idolaters.

He says: (﴿In the nearest land﴾, i.e., the nearest land of the Romans to Persia, in the Jazirah, where the two armies met, and the aggressor was Persia.)
Regarding His saying ﴿in the nearest land﴾, it is said the meaning is the land nearest to Persia, and that Persia transgressed against the Romans, so fighting arose between them.
It is also said: ﴿in the nearest land﴾ means the nearest of them to the land of the Arabs. This refers to history, which determines the location of this battle so that we know the nearest land; but there is no doubt that ﴿adna﴾ means "nearer."

He said: (﴿And they﴾, i.e. the Romans, ﴿after their defeat﴾: the verbal noun is added to its object, i.e., Persia's defeat of them, ﴿will overcome﴾ Persia ﴿within a few years, to God...﴾).
Look at the emphasis of this promise: this promise was emphasised by being introduced with a nominal sentence, ﴿and they, after﴾, because when it begins with a noun it becomes a nominal sentence denoting permanence and constancy. It was emphasised in another respect by its nearness, since the predicate is linked with the particle sa-, which denotes nearness. Then it was emphasised by a third emphasis, His saying: ﴿after their defeat they will overcome﴾, to establish that the victory is certain and that this is a matter that must occur even though they are now defeated; because if ﴿after their defeat﴾ were removed, and it said "and they will overcome," a person might say: "They will overcome even if they were defeated?! Perhaps if they have been defeated they will not overcome." So when He said ﴿after their defeat they will overcome﴾, this affirmed the victory.

Thus the emphasis of these people's victory comes in three aspects, which we were taught. Give me the three emphases showing they will overcome.
Student: The pronoun.
The Shaykh: What is the pronoun?
Student: ﴿Hum﴾.
The Shaykh: What is its aspect of emphasis?
Student: The entry of sa-.
The Shaykh: No, who knows?
Student: The nominal sentence.
The Shaykh: Yes, the aspect of emphasis is that it converted the sentence into a nominal one, which denotes permanence and continuity. Come on, complete the third.
Student: His saying: ﴿after their defeat﴾.
The Shaykh: His saying ﴿after their defeat﴾; what is its aspect? Who knows the aspect?
Student: That He said ﴿after their defeat they will overcome﴾, He said ﴿they will overcome﴾, perhaps (...) they will not overcome.
The Shaykh: Likewise, that they will overcome even in the state of their defeat. Good.

﴿And they, after their defeat, will overcome﴾. But ﴿within a few years﴾ (within a few years) is connected to His saying ﴿will overcome﴾, i.e., within the span of these few years.

(﴿Within a few years﴾: it is between three and nine, or ten): between three and nine, or between three and ten. How many is between three and nine? Fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth: five years. And up to ten?
Student: Six.
The Shaykh: Six years. This "few," is it five years or six years, or not?
If we say between three and ten: four, and what lies between three and ten: four, five, six, seven, eight, nine.
If we say between three and nine: four, five, six, seven, eight: five years. Is three included or not included?
Student: Not included.
The Shaykh: Not included. He did not say from one to ten, or between one and ten; he said "between three and nine."
Student: Does "few" mean more than three up to ten?
The Shaykh: Yes, how many does that make?
Student: It becomes more...
The Shaykh: No, the author's words imply it is not more; if he had said, it includes what exceeds three.
Student: Yes, that is, either four...
The Shaykh: What exceeds three up to ten.
Student: Why (...)?
The Shaykh: Yes? God has a possibility, and this we should understand at first: that "few" is from one to nine or to ten, but the author's wording has a problem.
Student: (...) begins with three (...) this "few" (...) three hundred (...) "few": four, five, six; that is, more than three is counted as "few" up to ten.
The Shaykh: And what is below it is not "few"?
Student: Yes.
The Shaykh: Yes, so it means we say from one to ten, but below three.
Student: Not "few".
The Shaykh: Not included, yes.
Student: (...) includes (...) it may be what follows (...) and what precedes (...).
The Shaykh: Yes, in any case we return to our first understanding: it is from three to nine or to ten; that is, what is below three is not included in "few."
Student: And three.
The Shaykh: As for three, by the author's words, "between three," three is not included, because what lies between a thing and a thing does not include both sides.

He said: ("So the armies met in the seventh year after the first encounter, and the Romans defeated Persia"): ("met") means another war took place between them, and the Romans defeated Persia, so God's promise that they would overcome within a few years was fulfilled, because the matter did not exceed seven years before the Romans gained victory over Persia; God fulfilled His promise that they would overcome within this period. He said: the victory would occur within this period.
Student: (...) victory, meaning it takes a few years (...).
The Shaykh: No, the meaning is that the victory was completed within seven years; it does not mean that the victory continued for seven years.

His saying: (﴿To God belongs the command, before and after﴾ [al-Rum 4], i.e., before the Romans were defeated and after it; the meaning is that Persia's victory first and the Romans' victory second were by God's command, i.e., His will.)
His saying ﴿To God belongs the command﴾: this is a nominal sentence in which the predicate is fronted to indicate exclusivity: to God alone belongs the command. The "al-" here is for totality, meaning all the command; and the "al-" that denotes totality is one that can be replaced by "kull" (all). If it denotes totality of meaning, it denotes totality of meaning; if it denotes totality of individuals, it denotes totality of the genus:
﴿And man was created weak﴾ (al-Nisa' 28): this "al-" denotes totality of the genus, because it is correct to replace it with "kull", saying: "and every man was created weak."

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 30, verses 1–5 (part 3 of 4):**

﴿By time. Indeed, mankind is in loss﴾ [al-'Asr 1, 2]. This "al" (the definite article) is also for comprehensiveness of the genus (istighraq al-jins), meaning every human being. If it is for comprehensiveness of the meaning (istighraq al-ma'na), then it is for comprehensiveness of the meaning. They illustrate this with their saying: "Zayd is the best of men" (zaydun ni'ma al-rajulu), meaning: he is the best person who combines the qualities of manhood.

Here, ﴿al-amr﴾ (the matter/command): is the "al" here for comprehensiveness of the genus?

* Student: For comprehensiveness of the genus.
* Shaykh: Yes, for comprehensiveness of the genus. That is: to Allah belongs every matter.

As for His saying: ﴿To Allah belongs the command﴾, is the intended meaning of "command" here the cosmic command (al-amr al-kawni) or the legislative command (al-amr al-shar'i)? It is the cosmic command, meaning that all affairs return to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, whether they relate to the actions of the servants or to the actions of Allah, glorified and exalted. We have already mentioned in the book of Tawhid that command is divided into two types: cosmic command and legislative command.

An example of the cosmic command is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [Ya-Sin 82].

What is an example of the legislative command?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, that is the will (irada). The legislative command is Allah's legislated commands, such as: "Do this and that," like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So let those who oppose His command beware lest a trial strike them or a painful punishment strike them﴾ [al-Nur 63], meaning: His legislated command.

* Student: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you﴾.
* Shaykh: Yes, His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to their owners﴾ [al-Nisa' 58]. This is a legislative command.

As for His saying: ﴿And when We intend to destroy a city, We command its affluent ones, and they defiantly transgress therein, and the word is justified against it, and We destroy it with complete destruction﴾ [al-Isra' 16]: which of the two commands is it?

* Students: The cosmic.
* Shaykh: It is the cosmic command. This is the necessary interpretation: Allah commands them with a cosmic command to transgress, so they transgress.

As for the one who says that the intended meaning of "command" in the verse is the legislative command, and that Allah commands them so they transgress, meaning He commands them to obey, and they transgress, and then He seizes them with punishment, this view is false. It implies that the meaning is: Allah sends the messengers, commanding people to obey Allah. And for what purpose? So that they transgress and punishment befalls them. This meaning amounts to saying that Allah sent the messengers as a vengeance upon the servants, and this is impossible.

Furthermore, we say: does the legislative command apply only to the affluent? It is general to them and to others. The essential point is that this view is weak and false, and it contradicts the wisdom of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in sending the messengers.

Here, ﴿To Allah belongs the command before and after﴾: we have said that the intended meaning is the cosmic command. As for His saying ﴿before﴾ (min qablu), grammarians may ask: why is it given a dammah even though "min" is a preposition?

* Student: Because there is an omitted element that is not present in pronunciation, meaning: "To Allah belongs the command before everything and after it." It is built on dammah in a position of genitive (mabni 'ala al-damma fi mahall jarr), because the dammah is present in pronunciation and the word is genitive in position.

* Shaykh: Because (qabla and ba'da), when the genitive complement is omitted and its meaning is intended, are built on dammah. This is the reason: when the complement is omitted and its meaning is intended, it is built on dammah. If the complement is present, they become inflected (mu'rabayn), so you say: "I came from before (min qabli) that Zayd came," and you put it in the genitive.

Likewise, if the complement is omitted and neither its wording nor its meaning is intended, the word is inflected, as in the saying of the poet:

*So the drink became palatable to me, and I was before (qablan) nearly choking on the water of the Euphrates.*

Likewise, if the complement is omitted and its wording is intended, the word is inflected but not given tanwin. So for example one says: "I was eager for the lesson, so I came from before (min qabli)," meaning: from before the start of the lesson. Here the complement is omitted and its wording is intended.

How do we know? What tells us whether its wording or its meaning is intended? The inflection itself tells us. If it is built on dammah, we know the complement has been omitted and its meaning is intended. If it is not, we know the complement has been omitted and its wording is intended. If it has tanwin, we know that neither its wording nor its meaning is intended.

* Student: Is it permissible to say of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, that He is "intended" (manwiyy)?

* Shaykh: No. It is appropriate to say "willing" (murid): that Allah wills the complement, because will (irada) indicates intention (niyya).

(﴿And on that day﴾, that is, the day the Romans prevail, ﴿the believers will rejoice in the victory of Allah﴾ [al-Rum 4, 5], over the Persians.)

His saying ﴿And on that day, the believers will rejoice﴾: "day" (yawm) is a time adverb (zarf) related to ﴿will rejoice﴾, and it is annexed to ("idh"), and "idh" has tanwin of compensation (tanwin 'iwad). It is compensation for what?

* Student: For a clause.

* Shaykh: For a clause. That is why it says: "the day the Romans prevail." So what is omitted now is a clause.

﴿And on that day the believers will rejoice in the victory of Allah﴾ [al-Rum 4, 5]. Joy cannot be described by a person; if you asked, "What is the meaning of joy?" one would say: lightness of the soul and delight of the soul. Or we say: joy is known. This is why, in the dictionary (al-Qamus), when such words come up, it writes after them "(m)", meaning it is well known and needs no explanation.

As for His saying ﴿the believers will rejoice﴾, the intended people are the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions.

His saying ﴿in the victory of Allah﴾ is related to ﴿will rejoice﴾. It is a verbal noun (masdar) annexed to its subject, while its object is omitted, and its estimated form is: "in the victory of Allah [the Romans] over the Persians." That is why the author said: "in the victory of Allah over them against Persia."

What is the meaning of victory (nasr)? Victory means assistance and dominance, meaning that Allah helps them until they prevail over their enemies. That is victory: that Allah helps a person until he prevails over his enemy. This is the meaning of victory.

His saying ﴿the victory of Allah﴾ is called "victory" even though it is between disbelievers and disbelievers, because we say that victory is assistance and dominance, and there is no difference whether it is between a believer and a disbeliever or between a disbeliever and a disbeliever. Moreover, the People of the Book are closer to the Persians (sic: the Romans are closer to the believers than the Persians), and this is why they have special rulings that bring them closer to the Muslims.

He said: "They rejoiced in that and knew of it on the day it occurred, the day of Badr, when Gabriel descended with it, along with their joy in their victory over the polytheists in it." That is, the battle between the Persians and the Romans took place at the same time as the battle between the disbelievers and the believers. And when was that? At Badr. On this basis, this verse was revealed before the Hijrah.

* Student: After the Hijrah.

* Shaykh: Before the Hijrah by five years. Because if the period of dominance, meaning the period in which the dominance occurred, was seven years, and Badr was in the second year, then the Persian dominance over the Romans must have been five years before the Hijrah.

* Student: The verse?

* Shaykh: Yes, the revelation of the verse and the Persian dominance.

His saying "along with their joy in their victory over the polytheists in it": so in this period, the victory of the People of the Book over the Magians and the victory of the Muslims over the polytheists came together.

Allah, Exalted is He, said: (﴿He gives victory to whom He wills, and He is the Mighty﴾: the Dominant, ﴿the Merciful﴾ [al-Rum 5], toward the believers).

* Student: Shaykh, the author's statement has a transmitted basis (dalil naqli).

* Shaykh: It appears he followed only history. As for a statement from the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him), there is no evidence for it, but there is a historical report that says this.

His saying: ﴿He gives victory to whom He wills﴾.

* Student: Before this, the author said: "The Persians' dominance first, and the Romans' dominance second, by the command of Allah, that is, His will," we forgot it.

* Shaykh: Yes, we forgot it and passed over it. We should have discussed his saying "by the command of Allah, that is, His will." In reality this is a distortion (tahrif). Rather, the correct view is that it is by His command, that is, by His saying: ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [Ya-Sin 82]. Allah, Exalted, does not decree anything except by speech: ﴿His command, when He intends a thing﴾. "Shay'an" (a thing) is indefinite in the context of a conditional, so it includes everything Allah wills, and He only says to it: "Be," and it is.

So the correct view is that the intended meaning of "command" here is speech. ﴿To Allah belongs the command, cosmic and legislative, before and after﴾. Will is not the same as speech, because will is an attribute that does not necessarily entail speech, since the one who wills may do what he wills or may say it. Speech, however, is more specific than will: every speech includes will, but not every will includes speech.

His saying ﴿He gives victory to whom He wills﴾ [al-Rum 5]: "whom" (man) here is general. It covers whether the one given victory is a disbeliever or a believer, because the matter is in the hand of Allah, Exalted. We have mentioned many times that everything tied to His will includes wisdom, because Allah does not will anything except for a wisdom. So He gives victory to whomever He wills to give victory, for a wisdom that required it.

His saying ﴿and He is the Mighty﴾ [al-Rum 5]. The author said: "the Dominant." This is one meaning of might (al-'izza), because might is divided into three types: might of rank (izzat al-qadr), might of subjugation (izzat al-qahr), and might of inaccessibility (izzat al-imtina').

Might of rank means that He, glorified and exalted, is great in rank, and the more a thing is great in rank, the more it is rare in existence. Allah, glorified and exalted, has no equal.

Might of subjugation means: dominance and supremacy.

As for might of inaccessibility, it means that every deficiency is impossible for Him, glorified and exalted. So He is Mighty in these three respects.

Might of rank: meaning He is great, with no peer in His measure and greatness. The second, might of subjugation: meaning He is the Subduer and Dominant over everything. The third, might of inaccessibility: what is the meaning of might of inaccessibility? It means that every deficiency is impossible for Him. From this meaning comes the saying "a hard land" (ard 'azaz), and we say "ard 'azya" in our dialect. What does "'azaz" mean? It is hard ground in which nothing can have an effect. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is described with might in all these respects.

His saying ﴿the Merciful﴾ [al-Rum 5]: the author said "toward the believers," citing His saying: ﴿and He was merciful to the believers﴾ [al-Ahzab 43].

The correct view is that Allah's mercy is both general and specific. All who are in the heavens and the earth are under His general mercy. If it were not for Allah's mercy toward the disbelievers, would they remain?

* Student: No.

* Shaykh: Certainly they would not remain. That Allah provides them with sustenance, health, vigor, intellect, and the like is without doubt from Allah's mercy. But the mercy by which there is mercy in this world and the next is specific to the believers.

* In these noble verses there are many benefits:

* First: that the speech of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, consists of letters, because ﴿Alif Lam Mim﴾ are letters. This is a refutation of the Ash'arites, who say that the speech of Allah is the meaning subsisting in the self and not the letters, and that these letters are created to express that meaning subsisting in the self.

They also say that this meaning subsisting in the self does not change or vary; it is one whether it is a question, a report, a command, or a prohibition, or the Quran, or the Psalms, or the Torah, or the Gospel. It does not vary. The Torah is the Gospel, it is the Quran, it is the Psalms, it is the scrolls of Abraham and the scrolls of Moses. Do you understand this?

* Students: Yes.

* Shaykh: But imagine it is possible: they say these differ only in expression. If this meaning is expressed in Arabic it becomes the Quran; if in Hebrew it becomes the Torah; if in Syriac it becomes the Gospel; if in the language of David it becomes the Psalms; and so on. This is an unintelligible meaning.

They also say that a question and a report have the same meaning, so if, for example, a question comes from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, it is like a report from Him, because the meaning is the same. Without doubt, merely conceiving this is sufficient to refute and nullify it.

* Among the benefits of the verse: the knowledge of Allah, Exalted, of the unseen. This is the affirmation of Allah's knowledge of the unseen, from His saying: ﴿And they, after their defeat, will overcome, within a few years﴾ [al-Rum 3, 4].

* Among its benefits: the affirmation of the Prophet's (ﷺ) prophethood, because reporting the unseen cannot happen except through revelation.

* Among the benefits of the verse: that Allah, Exalted, has complete authority and governance, from His saying: ﴿To Allah belongs the command before and after﴾.

* Among its benefits also: that all things happen only by the command of Allah, because when He said ﴿And they, after their defeat, will overcome﴾ He said ﴿To Allah belongs the command before and after﴾. So their being defeated was by the command of Allah, and their victory was by the command of Allah. All matters are by the decree and command of Allah, Exalted, all things by His command, glorified and exalted.

* Among its benefits: a refutation of the Qadariyyah, who say that the servant independently originates his own action. They say that the servant is independent in his action, and that Allah has no decree, command, will, or anything else in it. This verse refutes them.

* Among the benefits of the verse: the permissibility of expression that brings fear and sorrow upon the enemy, because His saying ﴿within a few years﴾ (which is from three to ten, or to nine) means that these Persians will remain in terror and fear. Every year that comes, they will say: "This is the year of defeat." Without doubt this increases their terror and fear, because if they were defeated in the first year, the matter would be over; but being threatened with a matter that is not known to occur within a few years is, without doubt, harder on them than a matter that comes and ends.

* Among the benefits of the verse: that in His saying ﴿The Romans have been defeated﴾, it is eloquence to omit the agent, as a way of humiliating him: ﴿The Romans have been defeated﴾, without mentioning the victor, in order to humiliate him. * Likewise the second benefit: kindness toward the Romans.

Then He said: ﴿And on that day the believers will rejoice in the victory of Allah. He gives victory to whom He wills, and He is the Mighty, the Merciful﴾. * Among the benefits of this: the permissibility of the believers' rejoicing at the victory of some disbelievers over others, if that serves the interest of Islam, or not?

* Student: Regarding His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And on that day the believers will rejoice in the victory of Allah﴾.

* Shaykh: ﴿And on that day the believers will rejoice in the victory of Allah﴾. It was not that the Muslims were victorious over the disbelievers; disbelievers were victorious over disbelievers. But this serves the interest of Islam. On this basis, if two states among the states of disbelief fight each other, and one of them is closer to benefiting the Muslims than the other, and we rejoice at its victory, do we say this is forbidden? How can you rejoice at a disbeliever's victory over a disbeliever? Or do we say it is permissible?

* Student: It is permissible.

* Shaykh: We say it is permissible, just as the believers rejoiced at the Romans' victory over the Persians, even though both were disbelievers. But those were People of the Book, so they were closer to the believers than the Magians.

* Among its benefits: the permissibility of calling the victory of disbelievers "victory," because of His saying: ﴿by the victory of Allah﴾.

If someone says: how do you reconcile this verse with His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Allah will surely support those who support Him. Indeed, Allah is Strong and Mighty. [They are] those who, if We give them authority in the land, establish prayer and give zakah and enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong﴾ [al-Hajj 40, 41], given that the Romans do not have these qualities?

The answer: victory is of two kinds. An absolute, lasting victory, which is only for those who support Allah. And a temporary, incidental victory, which may be for them and for others. So Allah's victory for the Romans over the Persians was not a lasting victory. The proof is that afterward Allah gave the believers victory over the Persians and the Romans, and they conquered the kingdoms of Khosrow and the kingdoms of Caesar, so this was not a lasting victory.

* Among the benefits of the verse: the affirmation of will to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, from His saying: ﴿He gives victory to whom He wills﴾.

* Among its benefits also: the affirmation of might to Allah, from His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and He is the Mighty﴾, and the affirmation of mercy in His saying: ﴿the Merciful﴾, and the affirmation of the perfection of His might, since it is joined with mercy. We should know that the Most Beautiful Names indicate perfection; each one of them indicates a perfection on its own, and then when two names are joined together they indicate a combined perfection.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 30, verses 1–5 (part 4 of 4):

Al-'Aziz (the Mighty) indicates perfection, and al-Rahim (the Merciful) indicates perfection. When the two are combined, another perfection is derived from them, above the perfection that each name contains on its own: that His might is accompanied by mercy. The might of others may be devoid of mercy. When a person becomes mighty, whoever is overcome by him is seized with the seizure of one who is mighty and powerful, and he shows no mercy. The might of Allah is different, for it is accompanied by mercy, and it is also accompanied by wisdom.

Let me give you an example. If a man overpowers a people and becomes mighty while they are humbled, this man may be seized by pride in his sin, so he strikes them down and shows them no mercy. But the might of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is not like that. Rather, it is accompanied by mercy, just as it is accompanied by wisdom. For this reason Allah always pairs might with wisdom.

There are other benefits in this as well.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, there is no harm in it. We rejoice when some of them triumph over others if the victor brings benefit to Islam, and then they support the Muslims with money or with weapons, or at the very least he has restrained his evil while the other one would have been evil.
* Student: From where do we take this? From this verse, or...?
* Shaykh: Yes, we take it from this verse.
* Student: The apparent meaning of the verse is that they do not support the Muslims.
* Shaykh: But they are less evil than these others.
* Student: What is the benefit in the Romans' victory over the Persians?
* Shaykh: The benefit is that the Romans are People of the Book, so they are closer to Islam and more considerate of the Muslims than those others. That is the benefit.
* Student: Every name of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, contains an attribute. But is the reverse also true, that every attribute gives rise to a name?
* Shaykh: No, that is not permissible.
* Student: Alright. The will (mashi'ah), how do we know it?
* Shaykh: We do not say that among the names of Allah are "the Willer" (al-Sha'i), "the Desirer" (al-Murid), or "the Speaker" (al-Mutakallim). We do not say: these are among the names of Allah.
* Student: So the attributes are broader than the names?
* Shaykh: Yes, the attributes are broader, without doubt.
* Student: His reports about Himself in the attributes: is the report broader than the attributes?
* Shaykh: Yes. That is, He is described with things, but He is not named by them. However, we do not describe Him with an attribute except where it has been transmitted. It is not the case that we may describe Allah with any attribute we like. So it is not permissible to name Allah, for example, "the Sorrowful," "the Lover," or "the Ardent," or anything similar. In other words, even the attributes are tawqifi (dependent on textual revelation). We do not invent for Him an attribute from ourselves. But the attributes are broader than the names.
* Student: Al-Mun'im (the Bestower of blessings): has al-Mun'im been transmitted?
* Shaykh: No, it is not among the names of Allah.
* Student: No, the attribute al-Mun'im?
* Shaykh: The attribute "bestowing blessing" (an-ni'mah). There is no doubt that Allah bestows blessings: ﴿And remember the favour of Allah﴾ [al-Ma'idah 7].
* Student: So we say that the blessing (ni'mah), meaning He brought it?
* Shaykh: Can there be a blessing without one who bestows it?!
* Student: ﴿The path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾ [al-Fatihah 7].
* Shaykh: Yes. Likewise, from "You have bestowed" (an'amta) the name al-Mun'im is derived. As for al-Muhsin (the Bountiful/Beneficent), it has been transmitted among the names of Allah, based on His saying: "Indeed Allah is Muhsin (Bountiful), He has prescribed excellence (ihsan) for everything. So when you kill, kill well."[[Narrated by Abd al-Razzaq in al-Musannaf (8603) from Shaddad ibn Aws, may Allah be pleased with him, and its wording is: "Indeed Allah is Muhsin, He loves excellence toward everything. So when you kill, kill well, and when you slaughter, slaughter well, and let one of you sharpen his blade and let him spare the animal he slaughters."]]

With this, the objection that arises for many people is resolved. They say: "They name their children Abd al-Muhsin." No, Muhsin is not a problem. Abd al-Muhsin? They say: "How can you attach it to something that is not among the names of Allah?"
* Student: Is Abd al-Mun'im found?
* Shaykh: It is found too.
* Student: What is the ruling on naming with it?
* Shaykh: This naming, if it is established that it is among the names of Allah. Otherwise, someone might say: we may say that it is permissible, because al-Mun'im in the absolute sense is Allah. Every person who has a blessing, it is restricted. Otherwise, blessings even from a human being: ﴿And when you said to the one on whom Allah had bestowed favour and you had bestowed favour upon him﴾ [al-Ahzab 37].
* Student: Abd al-Radi (the Pleased)?
* Shaykh: Abd al-Radi? I do not know.
* Student: Ibn Hazm says it is permissible to name someone Abd al-Muttalib.
* Shaykh: No, that is a mistake. This is an error on his part.
* Student: Humayd.
* Shaykh: Yes, Humayd is among the names of Allah: ﴿And He is the Protecting Friend, the Praiseworthy﴾ [al-Shura 28].
* Student: No, that one of us should be named "Humayd." That is what I mean.
* Shaykh: By Allah (...). But if the attribute is not intended, there is no harm. There was a man named Hakim (the Wise) in the time of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and he did not change it, even though al-Hakim is among the names of Allah. This is because the attribute was not intended to be considered. The names of Allah, Exalted is He, are intended to affirm the attribute along with the name. But I have named my son "Hakim," and he is one of the most foolish of people. Likewise, I name him "Muhsin," and he is one of the most oppressive of people.
* Student: Is it permissible to name someone Abd al-Hakim?
* Shaykh: Unless it contradicts something, yes, it is permissible.
* Student: Pausing at the ends of verses (...).
* Shaykh: This matter was discussed earlier. What did we say?
* Student: What is the question?
* Shaykh: The question is: do we stop at the verses even if what follows is connected to them, or do we continue and observe the meaning?
* Student: We observe the meaning.
* Shaykh: On this there are two opinions among the scholars. Some of them hold that we stop at the verses, and they say: this is what is transmitted from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, that he used to recite the Quran verse by verse. The evidence for this is that Allah made it verses, so we stop at them even if what follows is connected to them. This is common in the Quran: ﴿So woe to those who pray﴾ [al-Ma'un 4]. Is this the end of a verse?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: It is permissible to stop.
﴿So that you may give thought (la'allakum tatafakkarun)﴾ [al-Baqarah 219, 220], "in this world and the Hereafter." ﴿tatafakkarun﴾ is a verse. And this one: ﴿And on that day the believers will rejoice﴾. Is this a verse for you? ﴿the believers will rejoice﴾.
* Student: A verse.
* Shaykh: ﴿in the victory of Allah﴾.

Some scholars have said that you observe the meaning. You stop at the completion of a meaning, and you do not separate a verse from a verse connected to it. Even if the detailed approach were adopted, namely that a person who is reciting stops at every verse, because the speech will not be cut off (...), it connects and the meaning becomes clear.

If you want to speak about the meanings of the verses, you observe the meaning. If this detailed approach were adopted, it would have a basis. But I do not know whether any of the scholars has said it or not. Adopting it according to the rules of the scholars is not objectionable, because originating a third opinion that is formed from the two opinions before it is not objectionable. This is a question discussed in usul al-fiqh (the principles of jurisprudence): if the scholars have agreed on two opinions, is it permissible to originate a third opinion or not?

The correct view is that if the third opinion does not go outside the two, and the most that can be said is that it makes a distinction within it, then it is permissible, because it has not departed from the disagreement. But if it goes outside both, then it is not permissible. For example, if we say here that there is a distinction, has it gone outside the two opinions or not?
* Student: No.
* Shaykh: It has not gone outside them, but it stops at one thing and does not stop at another. Like the one who says: the witr (the odd-numbered night prayer) is obligatory, while others say: witr is not obligatory.

If we say: it is obligatory for one who is in such-and-such a situation, and not obligatory for one who is in such-and-such a situation, as Shaykh al-Islam chose, namely that it is obligatory for the one who has a regular portion (wird) of night prayer that he performs, and not obligatory for anyone else, then this third opinion does not go outside the two, because it agrees with one of the two opinions in one case and with the other opinion in another case.
* Student: The third opinion (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, but it does not go outside them. However, if one person says it is forbidden, and another says it is permissible, and then a third opinion comes saying it is obligatory, this is not possible. If they have agreed on permissibility or prohibition, it is not possible (...) to say it is obligatory, because that does not agree with the two opinions.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 30, verse 1–5 (part 1 of 4):

The Jahmiyyah turned away from them entirely and said: "He is in the earth by His essence, and not in the heaven, and we seek refuge with Allah." Thus they reversed the realities.

Among them is a group who were deceptive and said: "We affirm both proofs. We say that Allah is with us by His essence, and that He is above the Throne by His essence." And they said: "We are happier with the evidence than you, O people of the Sunnah, because we have acted upon two proofs: we said that He is with us by His essence, and that He is upon the Throne by His essence, so His place would be above and below."

These people agreed with the Jahmiyyah and agreed with the people of the Sunnah in one respect. They agreed with the people of the Sunnah in their saying that Allah is upon His Throne by His essence. And they agreed with the Jahmiyyah in their saying that He is in the earth by His essence. And they said: "We have taken up this evidence and that evidence, while the Jahmiyyah took up one evidence and left another, and the people of the Sunnah took up one evidence and left another. What is the answer to this doubt? For this is a great doubt, so what is the answer to this doubt?"

Did I not think that this would be confusing to you? Did you not understand the meaning? The question: these are a group which Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah related from al-Ash'ari in al-Maqalat, the doctrines of the creation (Maqalat al-Khalq). They say: Allah, glorified and exalted, is in the earth by His essence, and He is upon His Throne by His essence. And they say: "We have taken up the two proofs: ﴿He is with you wherever you are﴾ [al-Hadid 4], and He is ﴿upon the Throne﴾ [Taha 5]. So we have taken up this verse and that verse, so we are happier with the evidence than the people of the Sunnah and the community and than the Jahmiyyah, because the people of the Sunnah and the community, according to their claim, took up one proof, and the Jahmiyyah took up one proof. The Jahmiyyah took up what? They took up the texts of association (ma'iyyah) and left the texts of elevation (uluw); they turned away from them entirely. And the people of the Sunnah and the community took up, according to their claim, the texts of elevation and left the texts of association, while they say or claim that they took up all the texts together. So what do you say?"

* Student: We respond to them that Allah, glorified and exalted, is with us by His knowledge.
* The Shaykh: They say: "This is interpretation (ta'wil)." They say, as I told you: ﴿He is with you﴾ means His knowledge is with you, so you have opposed the apparent meaning of the wording.
* The Student: I have a proof against them.
* The Shaykh: What?
* The Student: The saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Do you not see that Allah knows what is in the heavens and what is in the earth?﴾ up to His saying: ﴿except that He is with them wherever they are﴾ [al-Mujadilah 7]. That is, He began with knowledge and ended with association.
* The Shaykh: In reality, they may answer this, saying: "Yes, the One who is with you knows you. We did not say that He is with you and does not know you." We say: ﴿He is with you﴾ [al-Hadid 4]; it follows from His association that He is knowing. So His saying ﴿He is with you﴾ is as if it were a reason for His saying ﴿He knows﴾ [al-Hadid 4]. In al-Mujadilah: ﴿Do you not see that Allah knows what is in the heavens and what is in the earth? There is no private conversation of three but that He is their fourth, nor of five but that He is their sixth, nor less than that nor more but that He is with them wherever they are. Then He will inform them of what they did on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Mujadilah 7].
* Student: We say to them: You have combined two contradictories, for you have declared Allah transcendent above being above in the heaven, and you have made Him in the earth within it (...). So how is that?!
* The Shaykh: Correct, this is the answer: we say, "You have now combined two contradictories. If He is high, as you claim and as is the truth, how can He be in the earth? Is He one god or many?" They say: one god. So if He is above, He cannot be below, because above and below are opposites, such that if one is negated the other is established, and they cannot be combined.

Then we say: if you say that He is in the earth by His essence, then when a person is in the mosque, Allah is in the mosque; and whoever is in the market, Allah is in the market; and whoever is in the desert, Allah is in the desert; and whoever is in the air, Allah is in the air, and so on. This means that we would be saying there are countless gods, so you have now opposed the proof.

Then we say, if they also say: "What do you mean by your saying: He is truly with us and He is truly above the Throne? This cannot be." We say to them: It can be. He, glorified and exalted, is truly with us while He is above the Throne, knowing us, seeing us, hearing us, managing us, and having authority and dominion over us. Whoever is like this is with you even if He is above you. The one who knows you, hears you, sees you, encompasses you, and dominates you in management and authority is with you even if He is above you. If a man is said to be with his wife and has authority over her, if he is in the office and she is in her house, is it not said that he is with her or not?
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: And that is a simple companionship. So how about the Creator, Mighty and Majestic, from whom not an atom's weight is hidden in the heavens or in the earth?! So we say: this is a possible matter, that Allah, glorified and exalted, is with us while He is above His Throne, because we say: with us, what? Encompassing us in knowledge, hearing, sight, power, authority, management, and other meanings of His lordship. And one whose state is this is suitable to be said to be with you while He is above His Throne, or not? It is suitable to be said that He is with you while He is above His Throne.

Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, pointed to an example that brings this closer. He said: the Arabs say, "We kept travelling and the moon was with us," or "the star was with us," or "the Pole Star was with us," for example, while it is in the sky and we are on the earth, even though it is a created thing. So how about the Creator?!

The point is that we say to these confusers (al-mulabbisin) — for this is indeed confusion, which may befall some people who say: "We believe in both proofs, while you, O people of the Sunnah, believe only in one proof" — we say: you have not believed in both proofs. In reality you have now denied both proofs, for Allah does not intend by association that, and it is impossible that by His association, glorified and exalted, He would intend to be in the earth.

And if we said that this is the true meaning of the texts, or their apparent meaning, we would be saying that the apparent meaning of the texts is disbelief, or not? If we said that the apparent meaning of the texts of association is that Allah is in the earth, we would be saying the apparent meaning is disbelief, because the person who believes that Allah is in the earth is a disbeliever who denies the evidences that indicate the elevation of Allah, glorified and exalted, as we have said: rational proofs and transmitted textual proofs.

In sum: what this author followed is correct. If we say that He is with the good-doers in support and help, that is correct. This type of association, the scholars say, is the specific association (al-ma'iyyah al-khassah). Association is of two kinds: general (ʿammah) and specific (khassah). The general is that which includes everyone, and among it is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿nor less than that nor more but that He is with them wherever they are﴾ [al-Mujadilah 7]. This is general association, or not?
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Because it encompasses the believer and the disbeliever, the righteous and the wicked. Its purpose is to show Allah's encompassing of everything. For this reason Ishaq ibn Rahawayh, who was one of the imams of the early generations (salaf), was asked about this verse: ﴿There is no private conversation of three but that He is their fourth﴾ up to the end of the verse [al-Mujadilah 7]: what is the meaning of this statement? He said: its meaning is: wherever you are, He is closer to you than the jugular vein. He interpreted association as nearness, and this does not contradict what others have interpreted it as, that He is with them in knowledge.

General association implies encompassing, and it may also be for warning, as in the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿They hide from the people but they do not hide from Allah, and He is with them when they plot by night what He does not approve of in speech﴾ [al-Nisa 108]. What is the intended meaning of this association?
* Student: Encompassing.
* Another Student: Warning.
* The Shaykh: A warning, that Allah encompasses them, but in order to warn them against this ugly deed: they hide from people but do not hide from Allah, and He, glorified and exalted, encompasses them in knowledge, hearing, sight, and power.

As for the specific association, it is also of two kinds: specific to a person, and specific to an attribute.
The one specific to a person is like what?
* Students: ﴿Indeed, I am with you both; I hear and I see﴾.
* The Shaykh: His saying to Musa and Harun: ﴿Indeed, I am with you both; I hear and I see﴾ [Taha 46], and His saying to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him: ﴿Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us﴾ [al-Tawbah 40].
The one specific to an attribute is like this verse: ﴿Indeed, Allah is with the good-doers﴾ [al-Ankabut 69], ﴿And that Allah is with the believers﴾ [al-Anfal 19], ﴿And be patient; indeed Allah is with the patient﴾ [al-Anfal 46]. And there are many other examples of this.

Know that there is no contradiction in the Book and the Sunnah, nor between the Book and the Sunnah, is that correct or not?
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Because contradiction means that one of two matters is false and the other true, and there is nothing in the Book and the Sunnah like that at all. So if you imagine a contradiction, know that this is due to one of three situations: either the deficiency of your knowledge, or the inadequacy of your understanding, or shortcoming in reflection. When a person imagines something contradictory in the Qur'an or between the Qur'an and the Sunnah, let him know that its cause is one of three matters. What are they?
* Student: Lack of knowledge, lack of understanding, or little reflection.
* The Shaykh: Shortcoming in reflection.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, this fourth category is not an imagining. The one who claims there is a contradiction has a bad intention. The evidence for this is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Do they not reflect upon the Qur'an? Had it been from other than Allah, they would have found in it much difference﴾ [al-Nisa 82]. As for the bad intention that He pointed to in the Qur'an, it is in the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Do they not reflect upon the Qur'an, or are there locks upon their hearts?﴾ [Muhammad 24].

Now, suppose a person reflects upon the Qur'an and then finds two verses and wants to reconcile them but is unable. What is his position? For this always arises: he is unable to reconcile two verses, neither understanding the way of reconciliation nor knowing that one of them abrogates the other. What should he do?
* Student: He stops.
* The Shaykh: He says as those firmly grounded in knowledge say: ﴿We believe in it; all is from our Lord﴾ [Al 'Imran 7], and he pauses. But even so, it is not sufficient for him merely to pause, saying that the matter is unclear to him, that there is a contradiction in the Qur'an. That is not enough; he must pause and know. Know what? That there is no contradiction in the Qur'an, and he must set aside the imagined conflict, leaving it aside and not remaining upon his imagination; for if he remains upon the imagined conflict, he has leaned upon this imagining, and he is in danger.

So it is obligatory to know that there is no contradiction in the Book of Allah, and that there is no contradiction between the Qur'an and the Sunnah at all. And by this we know that the Sunnah is a proof like the Qur'an, contrary to those who say it is not a proof. As for those who say that the Sunnah is not a proof, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, has informed about them, saying: "Let me not find any one of you reclining on his couch, to whom a matter from my command comes, and he says: 'We do not find this in the Book of Allah. Whatever we find in the Book of Allah, we follow.'"[[Recorded by Abu Dawud (4605) from the hadith of Abu Rafi', may Allah be pleased with him, the freed slave of the Prophet ﷺ.]] This matter has now occurred: people have arisen, and we seek refuge with Allah, who say: "We do not accept what is in the Sunnah at all."

The truth is that those who do not accept what is in the Sunnah are in reality disbelievers in the Qur'an itself, because the Qur'an says: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it﴾ [al-Hashr 7]; ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah﴾ [al-Nisa 80]; ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger has certainly strayed into clear error﴾ [al-Ahzab 36]. Whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger: it makes clear that disobeying the Messenger is error. And if the intended meaning were disobedience to the Messenger only in what Allah commanded, the mention of the Messenger would have no purpose. Then we say: Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as clarification for all things﴾ [al-Nahl 89]. ﴿The Book as clarification for all things﴾: has the Qur'an clarified everything?
* Student: In detail, no.
* The Shaykh: In detail, no. Most of the details are found in the Sunnah. So the clarification of the Sunnah is part of the clarification of the Qur'an. The evidences for this, praise be to Allah, are many. But it is strange that there appeared in America, among the wicked people, and we seek refuge with Allah, one called Rashad Khalifa, who had been a teacher at one of the colleges there. He began collecting money, founded a sect called the "Book sect," and began calling to the Qur'an, exalting the Qur'an, and acting by the Qur'an, while greatly denying the Sunnah, and we seek refuge with Allah. He says: those who act by the Sunnah are only madmen, and in some positions: only foolish, brainless people who have no understanding. The Qur'an is the greatest constitution, but as for the Sunnah, no.

He began, and we seek refuge with Allah, calling to this corrupt doctrine. Because he gathered much money and used it for this purpose, he wrote a book on the tafsir of the entire Qur'an, an assault upon the Sunnah and upon those who adhere to the Sunnah and the like. I seek refuge with Allah. This man, in fact, some people from America sent me a copy of his tafsir, but the problem is that, regrettably, I do not know the English language, and I did not benefit from it. I gave it to someone who said he wanted to publicize it and would have people in Jeddah translate it, good translators and so on, but they were on vacation and we gained nothing from this.

My purpose here is that the Book and the Sunnah are both twins; both are from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and both are sources of legislation, by the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿If you disagree over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger, if you believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾ [al-Nisa 59].
* Student: Was he originally a Muslim or (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, he claims he is one of the firmly grounded scholars!
* Student: No, I mean: (...).
* The Shaykh: He was originally a Muslim.
* Student: How?
* The Shaykh: He was originally a Muslim, but this, and we seek refuge with Allah!
* Student: What is his name?
* The Shaykh: His name is Rashad Khalifa.

And I think he was among those who wrote an article, I believe in a newspaper published in al-Sharqiyya, saying that the Noble Qur'an is structured upon the number nineteen, and that everything in it revolves around nineteen; the hundred and fourteenth surah is multiplied by what... that is, one hundred and fourteen is the result of multiplying what by what? I do not know his words on this.
* Student: Perhaps six, nineteen times six.
* The Shaykh: Six times nineteen is one hundred and fourteen; and six times one is six, and five makes one hundred and fourteen by his account: six times nineteen. And likewise he distorted the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Over it are nineteen﴾ [al-Muddaththir 30]. He said: ﴿over it﴾ means upon the correctness of what came in the Qur'an; ﴿nineteen﴾ means nineteen letters, which is the basmalah. Yet the Qur'an says: ﴿Over it are nineteen﴾, meaning what?
* Student: Angels.
* The Shaykh: Over the Fire are angels. But he said: No, upon the correctness of this Qur'an are nineteen letters, which is the basmalah.
* Student: What is the purpose?
* The Shaykh: The purpose, he says, is to argue that this Qur'an could not have been brought by Muhammad, because this number and the Qur'an being structured upon it was only known after the computer came, so it became known.
Is the basmalah nineteen letters?
* Student: This corrupt person is confusing.
* The Shaykh: Yes, very confusing, so much so that he said: ﴿Qaf. By the glorious Qur'an﴾ [Qaf 1]: it begins with the letter qaf, because the total of the qafs in it divides by nineteen and it comes out. The proof that he did not say "and the people of Lot" is that if he had said "and the people of Lot," an extra qaf would have been added and the division would not have worked. So he said: ﴿and the brothers of Lot﴾ [Qaf 13], yes, in order for the division to be complete. In any case, he is clearly a confuser and distorter, without doubt. But we will, God willing, demolish it: we have written a refutation of him in this, and the first thing we can demolish is the matter of the basmalah. The basmalah was not the first thing revealed, so that we could say the Qur'an is structured upon it, is that correct or not?
* Student: Yes, correct.

The Shaykh: What was the first revelation?
Student: "Read in the name of your Lord" (al-'Alaq 1).
The Shaykh: "Read." Second, the basmala, according to his claim, is not nineteen letters: the ba', the sin, the mim, the hamza, the lam, the second lam, the ha', the alif, the ra' repeated, the ha', the mim, the alif, the nun... how many is that for you? Fourteen. The hamza, the ra' repeated, the ha', the ya', the mim, that makes twenty.
Student: (...).
The Shaykh: Twenty. And he says: we count the written form "al-Rahman" as having no alif; if you drop the alif from "al-Rahman" it becomes nineteen.
Student: Keep the lam.
The Shaykh: We say: yes, if you say so, then keep the lam. If you keep the lam, "al-Rahman al-Rahim" (al-Fatihah 1) becomes twenty-one, is that right? Then we also say to him: if you consider the writing, was the Qur'an revealed in written form or revealed as spoken?
Student: Spoken.
The Shaykh: Spoken. If the written system were otherwise, would the letters increase or decrease, or neither increase nor decrease?
Student: They do not decrease.
The Shaykh: No, the letters that are pronounced do not increase; but the written ones do increase. We see that now, in English writing, sometimes the vowel marks may become letters, isn't that so?
Student: Yes.
The Shaykh: And go to the Chinese and their like, how many letters do they have?
Student: Thousands.
The Shaykh: They have thousands in their writing. The point in this is that writing is a craft, it has no bearing on pronunciation, and the Qur'an was revealed in the language, "in clear Arabic tongue" (al-Shu'ara' 195). But they deceive and confuse; they claim they serve the Qur'an by this before these foreigners who know only the material, but if they explained to people the beauty of this religion and what it brought of morals and dealings (...).

﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. The Romans have been defeated, in the nearest land; but they, after their defeat, will overcome, within a few years﴾ (al-Rum 1–4).

His words: "Surat al-Rum is Meccan." What is the Meccan?
Student: It is what was revealed before the Hijrah.
The Shaykh: It is what was revealed before the Hijrah, and the Medinan is what was revealed after it, whether it was revealed in Mecca or not; you know it is Medinan. On this basis, His saying ﴿Today I have perfected your religion for you﴾ (al-Ma'idah 3) was revealed at 'Arafah on the day of the Farewell Pilgrimage.
Student: It would be Medinan.
The Shaykh: It would be Medinan, even though it was revealed in Mecca.
(And it has sixty or fifty-nine verses): If we count "Alif Lam Mim" as an independent verse, it becomes sixty verses; otherwise, fifty-nine.
His words: "Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim": It has passed that the basmala is an independent verse brought at the beginning of surahs, and it is not attached to what follows, neither in al-Fatihah nor elsewhere, contrary to some scholars who say it is a verse of al-Fatihah, so they count al-Fatihah as seven verses including the basmala. The basmala: ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful (1). Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds (2). The Most Gracious, the Most Merciful (3). Master of the Day of Judgment (4). You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help (5). Guide us to the straight path (6). The path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour, not of those who have earned anger, nor of those who are astray (7)﴾ (al-Fatihah 1–7). How many is that for you? Seven, with the basmala.
The correct view is that the basmala is not a verse of al-Fatihah nor of any other surah. The first verse of al-Fatihah is: ﴿Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds﴾. And where is the seventh? Because it is seven verses by agreement; the seventh is His saying ﴿The path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour..﴾. We divide this into two verses: ﴿The path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾ is the sixth, and ﴿not of those who have earned anger, nor of those who are astray (7)﴾ is the seventh. In the Mushaf you find the basmala is a verse in al-Fatihah and not a verse in other surahs, but the correct view is that there is no difference.
Student: How (...), O Shaykh, (...) seven verses without it?
The Shaykh: Without the basmala?
Student: Yes (...) the second.
The Shaykh: Possibly, yes, this is the correct view.

His words: ﴿Alif Lam Mim﴾. The author said: "God knows best what He means by it." Yes, when we do not know something, it is obligatory to say: God knows best what He intended. It has been said this is half of knowledge, because a person is either knowing or ignorant; if he says about what he knows, what he knows, and about what he does not know, "God knows best," that is half of knowledge.

There is no doubt that a person's saying "God knows best" about what he does not know is what is obligatory upon him. Do not say: "By God, I am..." If you say "I do not know," your standing does not diminish among people; rather it increases among people, just as it does not diminish with God, nor among people, because the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever humbles himself for God, God raises him" [Narrated by al-Tabarani in al-Awsat (4894) from 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her)].

This is from the aspect of humility before God: that you say about what you do not know, "I do not know." It is like forgiveness, which increases a person only in honour, and like charity, through which wealth does not decrease. Likewise, "I do not know" does not diminish a person's standing in knowledge but increases it, because when people see that this man is cautious, speaks only of what he knows and refrains from what he does not know, they trust him and recognise that he speaks only what he knows.

So the author's words, "God knows best what He means by it," are what is obligatory upon every person who does not know what God intended. But when we return to His saying: ﴿We have made it an Arabic Qur'an that you may understand﴾ (Yusuf 2), we know that this Qur'an is according to the Arabic language, and that there is not a word in it except that it is understandable; otherwise God would be sending down something whose meaning we do not know. So if we apply these alphabetic letters to this rule, what is the rule? This verse: ﴿We have made it an Arabic Qur'an that you may understand﴾. If we apply the alphabetic letters to this rule, do we find that such a combination in the Arabic language has a meaning or has no meaning?
Student: It has a meaning.
The Shaykh: ﴿Alif Lam Mim﴾ has a meaning?!
Student: No.
The Shaykh: It has no meaning in the Arabic language; it is simply a group of alphabetic letters (alif, lam, mim). That is why you do not pronounce it as "alam" (a word). Rather you say "alif lam mim," isn't that so?
Student: Yes.
The Shaykh: So by the rule of the Arabic tongue in which the Qur'an was revealed, or with which the Qur'an was revealed so that we may understand it, by this Arabic tongue it has no meaning. It is only alphabetic letters with no meaning in themselves. Then we know them, but what does God intend by them? Shaykh al-Islam and many scholars mentioned that their purpose is to show that the Qur'an is inimitable despite being composed of these letters with which people speak.

The alphabetic letters with which people speak, the Qur'an is made of these letters; it did not bring new, strange letters, so that we could say it defeated people by them, because it would have brought letters they neither understand nor pronounce. Rather, they are letters from which their speech is composed. So is the inimitability then in terms of the letters, that it brought new letters, or in terms of the composition, context, and sublime, beneficial meanings? The answer?
Student: The second.
The Shaykh: From the second, the second aspect. And this which Shaykh al-Islam adopted is undoubtedly strong: these alphabetic letters in themselves have no meaning, but they have a purpose and an intent, which is that in the Qur'an, which has defeated all creation, no new letters were brought; rather it is from the letters they speak with.

Some contemporary scholars have said that these letters are like a key to the surah in which they occur, meaning that if you find "Lam Mim" at the head of a surah of the Qur'an, it is only because of the abundance of lam and mim in it, so they are like a key to it; likewise if you find nun, it is because of the abundance of nun in it, and if you find lam and ra', it is because of the abundance of lam and ra'. But this is criticised, and criticised; and were this consistently applied, it would also have some basis.

In any case, we know, by the fact that the Qur'an is in the Arabic tongue so that we may understand it, that these alphabetic letters in themselves are?
Student: They have no meaning.
The Shaykh: They have no meaning.

His words: ("﴿The Romans have been defeated﴾, and they are the People of the Book. Persia defeated them, and they are not People of the Book but worship idols; the disbelievers of Mecca rejoiced at that and said to the Muslims: We shall defeat you just as Persia defeated the Romans.")
﴿The Romans have been defeated﴾: this is a verb in the passive voice, and ﴿the Romans﴾ is the deputy subject. He made the verb feminine, ﴿ghulibat﴾, and did not say "ghuliba al-Rum," even though those who fight are men; but he made it feminine in view of the group. The one who defeated them was Persia. The wisdom, God knows best, in omitting the agent is that this is a greater humiliation for the Persians, and that it is more discreet regarding the Romans' humiliation and abandonment.

I say: the agent was concealed for two reasons:
The first reason: a humiliation of the Persians, that they are not worthy of mention.
Second: making the matter easier for the Romans, because if it is said to a person "you were defeated," it is lighter than if it is said "so-and-so defeated you," because if it is said "so-and-so defeated you," the meaning becomes that he is humbled before that named man.

His words: "The Romans: the People of the Book." It would have been better if the author had said "People of a Book," because the Romans are Christians, and People of the Book includes Jews and Christians, so saying "People of a Book" would have been better.
("Persia defeated them, and they are not People of the Book, but worship idols"): because they are Magians who worship fire.
("The disbelievers of Mecca rejoiced at that and said to the Muslims: We shall defeat you just as Persia defeated the Romans"): meaning that the disbelievers of Mecca took this as an omen and said: if the Romans are People of the Book and Persia defeated them while Persia are idolaters, then this is a key to victory for us: that we should defeat the Muslims, who are People of the Book, while we are idolaters.

He says: (﴿In the nearest land﴾, i.e., the nearest land of the Romans to Persia, in the Jazirah, where the two armies met, and the aggressor was Persia.)
Regarding His saying ﴿in the nearest land﴾, it is said the meaning is the land nearest to Persia, and that Persia transgressed against the Romans, so fighting arose between them.
It is also said: ﴿in the nearest land﴾ means the nearest of them to the land of the Arabs. This refers to history, which determines the location of this battle so that we know the nearest land; but there is no doubt that ﴿adna﴾ means "nearer."

He said: (﴿And they﴾, i.e. the Romans, ﴿after their defeat﴾: the verbal noun is added to its object, i.e., Persia's defeat of them, ﴿will overcome﴾ Persia ﴿within a few years, to God...﴾).
Look at the emphasis of this promise: this promise was emphasised by being introduced with a nominal sentence, ﴿and they, after﴾, because when it begins with a noun it becomes a nominal sentence denoting permanence and constancy. It was emphasised in another respect by its nearness, since the predicate is linked with the particle sa-, which denotes nearness. Then it was emphasised by a third emphasis, His saying: ﴿after their defeat they will overcome﴾, to establish that the victory is certain and that this is a matter that must occur even though they are now defeated; because if ﴿after their defeat﴾ were removed, and it said "and they will overcome," a person might say: "They will overcome even if they were defeated?! Perhaps if they have been defeated they will not overcome." So when He said ﴿after their defeat they will overcome﴾, this affirmed the victory.

Thus the emphasis of these people's victory comes in three aspects, which we were taught. Give me the three emphases showing they will overcome.
Student: The pronoun.
The Shaykh: What is the pronoun?
Student: ﴿Hum﴾.
The Shaykh: What is its aspect of emphasis?
Student: The entry of sa-.
The Shaykh: No, who knows?
Student: The nominal sentence.
The Shaykh: Yes, the aspect of emphasis is that it converted the sentence into a nominal one, which denotes permanence and continuity. Come on, complete the third.
Student: His saying: ﴿after their defeat﴾.
The Shaykh: His saying ﴿after their defeat﴾; what is its aspect? Who knows the aspect?
Student: That He said ﴿after their defeat they will overcome﴾, He said ﴿they will overcome﴾, perhaps (...) they will not overcome.
The Shaykh: Likewise, that they will overcome even in the state of their defeat. Good.

﴿And they, after their defeat, will overcome﴾. But ﴿within a few years﴾ (within a few years) is connected to His saying ﴿will overcome﴾, i.e., within the span of these few years.

(﴿Within a few years﴾: it is between three and nine, or ten): between three and nine, or between three and ten. How many is between three and nine? Fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth: five years. And up to ten?
Student: Six.
The Shaykh: Six years. This "few," is it five years or six years, or not?
If we say between three and ten: four, and what lies between three and ten: four, five, six, seven, eight, nine.
If we say between three and nine: four, five, six, seven, eight: five years. Is three included or not included?
