This is closer to being a masdar whose governing verb is omitted and not a substitute for its governing verb. The meaning is that Allah promised them a promise attributed to Himself, and a promise attributed to Him cannot be broken; therefore He said: ﴿Allah does not fail His promise.﴾

So this sentence, ﴿Allah does not fail His promise﴾, serves as an emphasis for His saying ﴿The promise of Allah﴾, because the promise of Allah, being attributed to Him, can never be broken. Failing to keep a promise arises from either lying or incapacity. If someone promises you and then fails you, he is either a liar or incapable, and lying and incapacity are impossible for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, because of His perfect truthfulness and power. So, does Allah fail His promise? The answer is no: Allah does not fail His promise and it is impossible for Him to do so.

Failing a promise means that a person, or the one promising, acts contrary to what he promised. For example, a man says to you: "I will visit you tomorrow at eight o'clock." Then eight comes and he does not visit you. Has he failed his promise or not?

* Student: He has failed.

* The Shaykh: The reason?

* Student: He did not come at eight.

* The Shaykh: That is not the point; but what is the reason for his failing?

* Student: Either he is incapable or he forgot.

* The Shaykh: Either he is incapable, or he is a liar from the start.

* Student: Or he forgot.

* The Shaykh: Or he forgot; forgetting is also a form of incapacity.

On this basis we say, regarding Allah: He does not fail His promise, because of the perfection of His truthfulness in His report and the perfection of His power in carrying out His promise. He, glorified and exalted, is perfect in power and His speech is perfect in truth; therefore He said: ﴿Allah does not fail His promise﴾ concerning it, that is, concerning victory.

And what is the source of what He promised? ﴿And they, after their defeat, will overcome﴾. There is also another promise in the preceding verses: the joy of the believers, as in His saying: ﴿And on that Day the believers will rejoice﴾ [Ar-Rum 4]. So Allah, glorified and exalted, promised the victory of the Romans over the Persians and the joy of the believers. There is no doubt that joy includes the expansion, delight and gladness of the soul, which is a blessing Allah bestows upon the one who rejoices.

As for His saying: ﴿Allah does not fail His promise, but most of the people do not know﴾ [Ar-Rum 6]: His saying ﴿The promise of Allah﴾ is followed by His saying ﴿but﴾ (wa-lakin). Or it may be understood as conjoined to His saying ﴿Allah does not fail His promise﴾, with ﴿but most of the people﴾.

*Lakinna* (but) puts the noun in the accusative and the predicate in the nominative. Where is its noun? It is ﴿akthara﴾ (most), and its predicate is the clause ﴿do not know﴾.

As for His saying ﴿but most of the people﴾, the author says: (i.e., the disbelievers of Makkah). Restricting this to the disbelievers of Makkah is open to question; the correct view is that it includes the disbelievers of Makkah and others. Everyone who lacks faith does not know what Allah, exalted be He, has ordained of fulfilling the promise, because he is either a denier or a doubter who wavers, and so he does not know.

As for the phrase (﴿do not know﴾ His promise to give them victory), or do they not know that Allah does not fail His promise, or both? Both: they do not know that Allah, glorified and exalted, will bring them victory, either because of their ignorance of what Allah has told them, or because of their doubt in His truthfulness or in God's power to carry it out. And they also do not know that Allah does not fail His promise, in this matter or in any other, due to their doubt about Allah's truthfulness and His power, blessed and exalted, to fulfil His promise.

As for His saying ﴿but most of the people﴾: so then, are the few of the people knowing or not? Yes, they know, because they believe in Allah, glorified and exalted, and in His power and truthfulness of speech.

Then He said: ﴿They know an outward aspect of the worldly life﴾ [Ar-Rum 7]. This ﴿they know﴾ is a second predicate of ﴿lakinna﴾, and the first predicate is ﴿do not know﴾.

It has also been said that it is a substitute (badal) for ﴿do not know﴾. This view has been rejected on the grounds that an affirmative cannot be substituted for a negative because they are contrary; how can you substitute an affirmative ﴿they know﴾ for its opposite ﴿do not know﴾? On this basis we say that the second ﴿they know﴾ is a second predicate of ﴿lakinna﴾, and is it permissible to have multiple predicates? 

* Student: It is permissible.

﴿They know an outward aspect of the worldly life﴾ [Ar-Rum 7]. Note how glorious Allah is: ﴿they know﴾ affirms knowledge for them, but it is a deficient knowledge in two respects:

The first respect: they know only the outward aspect, not the inner: ﴿an outward aspect of the worldly life﴾. How many hidden matters in this life are unknown to those disbelievers?

The proof that the disbelievers do not know every hidden thing in this world is the development of crafts and inventions, because this development is unknown to those before them, and then there will come another development that is unknown to those who exist now.

So they know only an outward aspect of the worldly life, and they do not know everything in the world, whether outward or inward.

Also, He says ﴿an outward aspect of the worldly life﴾ and not "every outward aspect." The difference lies in saying: "They know every outward aspect of the worldly life," or "They know the outward aspect of the worldly life," or "They know an outward aspect of the worldly life" (﴿yaʿlamūna ẓāhiran min al-ḥayāh al-dunyā﴾). The expression can take these forms: they know every outward aspect; they know the outward aspect; ﴿they know an outward aspect of the worldly life﴾. Which is the least?

* Students: The last one.

* The Shaykh: The last one: meaning they do not know every outward aspect, but only an outward aspect of it. And there are other outward aspects they also do not know. Thus it is known that the knowledge of these people is deficient. Regarding Allah, exalted be He, they do not know; they are ignorant. And regarding the world, they know only an outward aspect of the worldly life.

Regarding the Hereafter, He says: ﴿And they, of the Hereafter, are heedless﴾ [Ar-Rum 7]. Note the nominal sentence in which the subject is emphasized. Which is the emphasized element? In ﴿they are, of the Hereafter, they are heedless﴾, the second ﴿they﴾ is an emphasis of the first. If it were removed and it said: "And they, of the Hereafter, are heedless," would the sentence be sound or not?

* Students: It is sound.

* The Shaykh: It is sound, but it was repeated for emphasis. They are, regarding the matters of the Hereafter, heedless, turning away from them and not reflecting on them. You find one of them astonished at his knowledge of worldly affairs, but regarding the matters of the Hereafter he has a heedlessness and does not reflect on them, nor try to exercise his mind and consider this great creation: what will be its end, how was it created, and where does it lead? Heedless.

Allah, exalted be He, said in another verse: ﴿Rather, their hearts are in confusion about this﴾ [Al-Mu'minun 63], meaning about the matter of faith in Allah and His Messenger ﷺ. And what of their other deeds? ﴿And they have deeds other than that, which they are doing﴾ [Al-Mu'minun 63]: they grasp these completely, but regarding faith in Allah and the Last Day, no; their hearts are in confusion. The recompense for this confusion is experienced when it is said to him: ﴿You were certainly in heedlessness of this, but We have removed from you your cover, so your sight today is sharp﴾ [Qaf 22]. And when does this happen? It happens on the Day of Resurrection.

The point is that those who are heedless of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and of the Hereafter have knowledge of the worldly life. Look now at the crafts, and you will find something that dazzles you; but among a people who, regarding the matter of the Hereafter, are unlettered and know nothing, because they, may Allah protect us, have heedlessness. It is astonishing: how they now reach the atmosphere, make airplanes, and make strange machines, and yet they have no knowledge of Allah and the Last Day.

If you asked a Muslim child, he would answer you; if you asked the greatest of their inventors, he would not answer you. That is the bounty of Allah, which He gives to whom He wills.

* Student: The pronoun here, in ﴿they know an outward aspect of the worldly life﴾, should we make it refer to the disbelievers or to others, even to heedless Muslims? Is it not better to generalize it?

* The Shaykh: No. The intention is that these ignorant people, meaning, to emphasize the blame towards them, those who were ignorant of Allah and the truth of His promise. Yet this is not due to a deficiency in them or in their understanding, but to their heedlessness. Even believers know only an outward aspect of the worldly life, not everything; but believers have knowledge of Allah and His names and attributes, and then this is not a defect in them. The point of deficiency is that these people do not know what pertains to faith in Allah, and know only an outward aspect of the worldly life.

* Student: Does it refer only to the disbelievers?

* The Shaykh: Yes, it refers to the disbelievers, because the intention is to emphasize the blame concerning them. Otherwise, even Muslims are included by another proof, from His saying: ﴿And He creates what you do not know﴾ [An-Nahl 8], that even believers know only an outward aspect of the worldly life.

* Student: Some Muslims, a minority, most of them are heedless of it; he prays, but if you ask him about... but in worldly matters he is good.

* The Shaykh: Yes, correct.

* Student: Does this not apply to them?

* The Shaykh: This involves a resemblance to the disbelievers, in that he achieved the affairs of this world and turned away from the affairs of the Hereafter.

* Student: Do the disbelievers deny the existence of Allah, or do they not deny it?

* The Shaykh: They differ: some of them deny the existence of Allah and some do not. But whoever does not deny the existence of Allah, and believes in the existence of Allah, yet then worships other than Him or associates partners with Him, this is contradictory.

* * *
﴿Allah does not fail His promise﴾ [Ar-Rum 6]. The following benefits are derived from this noble verse:
* The victory of the Romans over the Persians, and the believers' joy at it, is a report that contains a promise.
* Among its benefits: the impossibility of Allah failing His promise, from His saying: ﴿Allah does not fail His promise﴾.
* Among its benefits: the affirmation of power and truthfulness for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, derived from His saying: ﴿Allah does not fail His promise﴾, meaning it includes perfect truthfulness and power.
* Among its benefits: that most people do not know what Allah deserves of the attributes of perfection; from His saying: ﴿but most of the people do not know﴾ [Ar-Rum 6].
* Among its benefits: that true knowledge is knowledge of Allah, His names and His attributes, not knowledge of the world; from His saying: ﴿do not know﴾, then He said: ﴿they know an outward aspect﴾. He negated knowledge from them because knowledge of the world is not knowledge in reality. From this it is derived that true knowledge for which a person is praised is knowledge of Allah, His names, His attributes and His rulings.
* Among its benefits: the deficiency of a person's knowledge; from His saying: ﴿they know an outward aspect of the worldly life﴾, not every outward aspect and not the inward, so a person's knowledge is deficient even in worldly matters.
* Among its benefits: the blame of those who rush after worldly sciences while heedless of the Hereafter; from His saying: ﴿they know an outward aspect of the worldly life, and they, of the Hereafter, are heedless﴾ [Ar-Rum 7].
* Among its benefits: that it includes praise of those who turn towards the Hereafter and strive for it even if they miss some worldly matters; since blaming the opposite is praise of its contrary, those who turn to the Hereafter, even if they have only a few worldly sciences, are far more perfect than those who turn to the world and are heedless of the Hereafter. This is what these verses indicate.
* Among its benefits also: that it is not possible for a person to encompass all worldly knowledge either.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 30, verse 6–7:

He said: ﴿The promise of Allah. Allah does not fail His promise, but most of the people do not know.﴾ [Ar-Rum 6] ﴿The promise of Allah.﴾ The author says: (It is a maf'ul mutlaq (absolute object) that replaces the verb with its own verbal form; the original is: "Allah promised them victory").

His saying: ﴿The promise of Allah.﴾ We all know that it is a verbal noun (masdar) and not a verb. ﴿Wa'da Allah﴾ is a masdar annexed to its agent, meaning Allah's promise to them. The author says that it is a substitute for its verb, i.e., one that stands in place of the verb: "Allah promised them."

It has also been said that it is a masdar whose verb is omitted, and it is not a substitute for it. On this view, what is presumed is treated as what is present: "We promised them the promise of Allah." This is closer to being a masdar whose governing verb is omitted and not a substitute for its governing verb. The meaning is that Allah promised them a promise attributed to Himself, and a promise attributed to Him cannot be broken; therefore He said: ﴿Allah does not fail His promise.﴾

So this sentence, ﴿Allah does not fail His promise﴾, serves as an emphasis for His saying ﴿The promise of Allah﴾, because the promise of Allah, being attributed to Him, can never be broken. Failing to keep a promise arises from either lying or incapacity. If someone promises you and then fails you, he is either a liar or incapable, and lying and incapacity are impossible for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, because of His perfect truthfulness and power. So, does Allah fail His promise? The answer is no: Allah does not fail His promise and it is impossible for Him to do so.

Failing a promise means that a person, or the one promising, acts contrary to what he promised. For example, a man says to you: "I will visit you tomorrow at eight o'clock." Then eight comes and he does not visit you. Has he failed his promise or not?

* Student: He has failed.

* The Shaykh: The reason?

* Student: He did not come at eight.

* The Shaykh: That is not the point; but what is the reason for his failing?

* Student: Either he is incapable or he forgot.

* The Shaykh: Either he is incapable, or he is a liar from the start.

* Student: Or he forgot.

* The Shaykh: Or he forgot; forgetting is also a form of incapacity.

On this basis we say, regarding Allah: He does not fail His promise, because of the perfection of His truthfulness in His report and the perfection of His power in carrying out His promise. He, glorified and exalted, is perfect in power and His speech is perfect in truth; therefore He said: ﴿Allah does not fail His promise﴾ concerning it, that is, concerning victory.

And what is the source of what He promised? ﴿And they, after their defeat, will overcome﴾. There is also another promise in the preceding verses: the joy of the believers, as in His saying: ﴿And on that Day the believers will rejoice﴾ [Ar-Rum 4]. So Allah, glorified and exalted, promised the victory of the Romans over the Persians and the joy of the believers. There is no doubt that joy includes the expansion, delight and gladness of the soul, which is a blessing Allah bestows upon the one who rejoices.

As for His saying: ﴿Allah does not fail His promise, but most of the people do not know﴾ [Ar-Rum 6]: His saying ﴿The promise of Allah﴾ is followed by His saying ﴿but﴾ (wa-lakin). Or it may be understood as conjoined to His saying ﴿Allah does not fail His promise﴾, with ﴿but most of the people﴾.

*Lakinna* (but) puts the noun in the accusative and the predicate in the nominative. Where is its noun? It is ﴿akthara﴾ (most), and its predicate is the clause ﴿do not know﴾.

As for His saying ﴿but most of the people﴾, the author says: (i.e., the disbelievers of Makkah). Restricting this to the disbelievers of Makkah is open to question; the correct view is that it includes the disbelievers of Makkah and others. Everyone who lacks faith does not know what Allah, exalted be He, has ordained of fulfilling the promise, because he is either a denier or a doubter who wavers, and so he does not know.

As for the phrase (﴿do not know﴾ His promise to give them victory), or do they not know that Allah does not fail His promise, or both? Both: they do not know that Allah, glorified and exalted, will bring them victory, either because of their ignorance of what Allah has told them, or because of their doubt in His truthfulness or in God's power to carry it out. And they also do not know that Allah does not fail His promise, in this matter or in any other, due to their doubt about Allah's truthfulness and His power, blessed and exalted, to fulfil His promise.

As for His saying ﴿but most of the people﴾: so then, are the few of the people knowing or not? Yes, they know, because they believe in Allah, glorified and exalted, and in His power and truthfulness of speech.

Then He said: ﴿They know an outward aspect of the worldly life﴾ [Ar-Rum 7]. This ﴿they know﴾ is a second predicate of ﴿lakinna﴾, and the first predicate is ﴿do not know﴾.

It has also been said that it is a substitute (badal) for ﴿do not know﴾. This view has been rejected on the grounds that an affirmative cannot be substituted for a negative because they are contrary; how can you substitute an affirmative ﴿they know﴾ for its opposite ﴿do not know﴾? On this basis we say that the second ﴿they know﴾ is a second predicate of ﴿lakinna﴾, and is it permissible to have multiple predicates? 

* Student: It is permissible.

﴿They know an outward aspect of the worldly life﴾ [Ar-Rum 7]. Note how glorious Allah is: ﴿they know﴾ affirms knowledge for them, but it is a deficient knowledge in two respects:

The first respect: they know only the outward aspect, not the inner: ﴿an outward aspect of the worldly life﴾. How many hidden matters in this life are unknown to those disbelievers?

The proof that the disbelievers do not know every hidden thing in this world is the development of crafts and inventions, because this development is unknown to those before them, and then there will come another development that is unknown to those who exist now.

So they know only an outward aspect of the worldly life, and they do not know everything in the world, whether outward or inward.

Also, He says ﴿an outward aspect of the worldly life﴾ and not "every outward aspect." The difference lies in saying: "They know every outward aspect of the worldly life," or "They know the outward aspect of the worldly life," or "They know an outward aspect of the worldly life" (﴿yaʿlamūna ẓāhiran min al-ḥayāh al-dunyā﴾). The expression can take these forms: they know every outward aspect; they know the outward aspect; ﴿they know an outward aspect of the worldly life﴾. Which is the least?

* Students: The last one.

* The Shaykh: The last one: meaning they do not know every outward aspect, but only an outward aspect of it. And there are other outward aspects they also do not know. Thus it is known that the knowledge of these people is deficient. Regarding Allah, exalted be He, they do not know; they are ignorant. And regarding the world, they know only an outward aspect of the worldly life.

Regarding the Hereafter, He says: ﴿And they, of the Hereafter, are heedless﴾ [Ar-Rum 7]. Note the nominal sentence in which the subject is emphasized. Which is the emphasized element? In ﴿they are, of the Hereafter, they are heedless﴾, the second ﴿they﴾ is an emphasis of the first. If it were removed and it said: "And they, of the Hereafter, are heedless," would the sentence be sound or not?

* Students: It is sound.

* The Shaykh: It is sound, but it was repeated for emphasis. They are, regarding the matters of the Hereafter, heedless, turning away from them and not reflecting on them. You find one of them astonished at his knowledge of worldly affairs, but regarding the matters of the Hereafter he has a heedlessness and does not reflect on them, nor try to exercise his mind and consider this great creation: what will be its end, how was it created, and where does it lead? Heedless.

Allah, exalted be He, said in another verse: ﴿Rather, their hearts are in confusion about this﴾ [Al-Mu'minun 63], meaning about the matter of faith in Allah and His Messenger ﷺ. And what of their other deeds? ﴿And they have deeds other than that, which they are doing﴾ [Al-Mu'minun 63]: they grasp these completely, but regarding faith in Allah and the Last Day, no; their hearts are in confusion. The recompense for this confusion is experienced when it is said to him: ﴿You were certainly in heedlessness of this, but We have removed from you your cover, so your sight today is sharp﴾ [Qaf 22]. And when does this happen? It happens on the Day of Resurrection.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 30, verses 8–9 (part 1 of 3):

Then Allah the Exalted said: (﴿Have they not reflected within themselves?﴾ [al-Rum 8]: so that they might turn back from their heedlessness).

His saying: ﴿Have they not reflected﴾. We have previously explained many times how such a construction is parsed (i'rab), and we said that the grammarians have two opinions regarding its parsing:

The first: that the hamza (interrogative particle) is placed before its original position, and that its original form is: (wa-alam yatafakkaru) [and did they not reflect], so that it is a clause conjoined to what precedes it.

The second view: that the hamza enters upon an omitted element which is to be estimated according to the context, and the conjunction that follows it is conjoining that omitted element.

In this verse, the estimate is: "Were they heedless and did they not reflect?" When He said: ﴿and they are heedless of the Hereafter﴾, He said: ﴿Have they not reflected?﴾ The interrogation is for reproach, because a person is commanded to reflect.

His saying: ﴿Have they not reflected within themselves?﴾ Is the phrase ﴿within themselves﴾ the place of reflection or the means of reflection? That is: is the intended meaning of the verse an exhortation to their reflecting upon themselves, as in His saying: ﴿And within yourselves; will you not see?﴾ [al-Dhariyat 21], or an exhortation to reflect upon the creation of the heavens and the earth within themselves?

* Student: Both matters.
* Shaykh: Both? Yes, both, but the closer one is the last; for this reason He said: ﴿what Allah created of the heavens﴾ [al-Rum 8].

So the meaning is: Have they not returned to themselves and reflected with genuine reflection upon this existence, so that they might thereby know the wisdom of Allah the Mighty and Majestic and what it entails of His great attributes?!

His saying: ﴿within themselves: what Allah created of the heavens and the earth and what is between them except with truth﴾ (ma): what is its parsing?
* Student: A relative pronoun.
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: A negation particle.
* Shaykh: A negation particle; the proof is His saying: ﴿except with truth﴾.

﴿What Allah created of the heavens and the earth﴾: (khalaqa) means to bring into existence and to originate, and it is not, for the most part, except with measure and arrangement; for the origin of creation is measuring within the self, as the poet said:
"And indeed you measure what you create, while some people create but do not measure."
That is: what you measured. So creation is origination with measure and arrangement.

His saying: ﴿the heavens﴾ has been discussed before, and that what is meant by them is the layers, and they are seven.

His saying: ﴿and the earth﴾ is singular, and what is meant is the genus, so it includes all the earths. It is conjoined to ﴿the heavens﴾ and is in the accusative; for this reason it is marked with a fatha, unlike ﴿the heavens﴾ [al-samawat], since that is a sound feminine plural.

His saying: ﴿and what is between them﴾ (ma): a relative pronoun conjoined to "the earth" or to "the heavens"?
* Student: To the heavens.
* Shaykh: To the heavens, yes.
The scholars say: when conjoined items are multiple, the conjunction is to the first of them, because it is directly governed by the operator, and what follows it is a branch of it. So the conjunction here is to the heavens.

If you said: "Zayd came, and 'Amr, and Bakr, and Khalid, and Sa'id," then Sa'id is conjoined to Zayd, the first, because he is directly governed and what follows is a branch; a branch is not conjoined to a branch, but to a root.

His saying: ﴿and what is between them﴾: (bayniyyah) implies contiguity; a thing may be between two things without touching either of them. Here, what is between the heavens and the earth does not necessarily touch them, but could it touch? It could, but it is not necessary.

On this basis we say: ﴿what is between them﴾ includes the clouds, the winds, the stars, the sun, the moon, and other great creatures that we do not know.

In specifying what is between the heavens and the earth there is evidence that what lies between them is a great matter, comparable to the heavens and the earth themselves; this is known to the astronomers who observe the great signs in the horizon which indicate the perfection of Allah the Exalted.

His saying: ﴿except with truth﴾: this is the point of benefit: ﴿What Allah created of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, except with truth﴾. It is a restriction, and it is the locus of benefit: that is, this creation is accompanied by truth. So the "ba" is for accompaniment and attendance: His creation, Exalted is He, is attended by truth. Why? Because it includes perfect justice and perfect truthfulness.

Perfect justice: the heavens and the earth stand only by justice, and justice is truth. Does this include that their purpose is true? Yes, it includes it; so it is by truth at the beginning and at the end, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play﴾ [al-Anbiya' 16].

If these heavens and earth were created so that creatures would live upon them, live, and die without recompense, without reckoning, without reward or punishment, then it would be vain and not truth. Therefore these great creatures must have an end, an end which is truth.

On this basis we say: His saying ﴿with truth﴾ includes the beginning and the end.

His saying: ﴿and a specified term﴾ is conjoined to ﴿with truth﴾; that is: He did not create them except also with a specified, determined term. The term (ajal) is the end of a thing, and ﴿specified﴾ [musamma] is from whom?
* Student: From Allah the Exalted.
* Shaykh: From Allah the Exalted; He is the one who determined it.

His saying: (with a term) includes the beginning and the end: its beginning is with a term, and its end is with a term as well, for Allah the Exalted brought these heavens and earth into existence after they were non-existent, and bringing them into existence was by the term determined with Him. Likewise, He will bring the heavens and the earth to an end, and their ending is?
* Student: By the term.
* Shaykh: By the term. So everything with Allah the Mighty and Majestic is decreed, even the events that occur in the heavens and the earth after their creation and origination, all by a term that does not advance or delay. If you reflect a little, you will know through it the perfection of Allah's power, Exalted is He: how these great and numerous affairs are all arranged by a term that neither advances nor delays?!

We are now agreed that the lesson begins at eight o'clock, but when we begin at eight-thirty, or at eight-twenty, and we are late, our affair is not regulated, though it is simple.

Likewise all the affairs of creation: no one can regulate all his works by their specified term, however eager he is, because there may befall him what is beyond his capacity, what he cannot do. But the Lord, Exalted is He, has determined everything by its term, not advancing or delaying, and there is no doubt that this is from the perfection of wisdom and craftsmanship: ﴿The handiwork of Allah, who perfected everything﴾ [al-Naml 88].

If we reflect upon this great existence, with its celestial and terrestrial events, general and specific, we truly take them as clear evidence of the perfect power of the One who arranges this universe, who created it: everything by a term. In another verse: ﴿And everything with Him is by measure﴾ [al-Ra'd 8]: also by a measure which neither increases nor decreases. So by its term and its measure it neither increases nor decreases. Glory be to Allah the Mighty.

His saying: (﴿and a specified term﴾ therefore) is it thus with you?
* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: (It perishes at its end, and after it is the Resurrection). (It perishes): that is, the heavens and the earth and what is between them perish at the end of this term, then the Resurrection comes.

He says: (﴿And indeed many of mankind﴾, that is, the disbelievers of Makkah, ﴿in the meeting with their Lord are disbelievers﴾, that is, they do not believe in the Resurrection after death).

His saying: ﴿many of mankind﴾ [al-Rum 8]: the author restricted it to the people of Makkah, but the correct view is generality: the people of Makkah and others. Many people deny the Resurrection; perhaps we find among others than the people of Makkah those who are even more insistent in denying it. Restricting a general term in the Qur'an is not appropriate unless there is evidence for it, and then it is to be obeyed.

His saying: ﴿in the meeting with their Lord are disbelievers﴾: liqa' means confronting and facing. Every person will meet Allah the Mighty: ﴿O mankind, indeed you are labouring toward your Lord with labour, and you will meet Him﴾ [al-Inshiqaq 6]. Which person? The believer or the disbeliever? Even the disbeliever?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: Yes; because He said ﴿O mankind﴾, which is general. Then He said after ﴿and you will meet Him﴾: ﴿As for he who is given his record in his right hand﴾ [al-Inshiqaq 7], and ﴿As for he who is given his record behind his back﴾ [al-Inshiqaq 10]. This shows that it is general. So everyone will meet Allah the Mighty and He will call him to account. But Allah's reckoning of people differs: the believer is made to acknowledge his sins, and when he acknowledges them, he is forgiven; but the disbeliever, we seek refuge with Allah, is disgraced by them, punished for them, and it is humiliation for him.

It is said: ﴿in the meeting with their Lord are disbelievers﴾: the lam in ﴿la-kafirun﴾ is for what? For emphasis; ﴿kafirun﴾ is the predicate of ﴿inna﴾, and ﴿bi-liqa' rabbihim﴾ is connected to it and was placed before it for the sake of the rhyme (fawasil).

Observing the fawasil in the Noble Qur'an is evident, because when speech has consistent rhyming endings, this is more invigorating to the soul and more desirable for listening to and reciting it.

He said: ﴿in the meeting with their Lord are disbelievers﴾. Kufr linguistically means concealment, and from it the kufrah, which is the sheath of the palm spathe (tal'), is so named because it covers it. The meaning of kufr is: concealing Allah's blessing upon a person, such that he disobeys Him when commanded and denies Him when called to faith.

The types of kufr are many. Among them: the kufr that expels from the religion, and among them: a kufr that is a specific trait of kufr, not absolute kufr; and this is referred to the textual evidences of the Law.

﴿And indeed many of mankind in the meeting with their Lord are disbelievers (8). Have they not travelled in the earth and seen how was the end of those before them﴾ [al-Rum 8–9]: this is conjoined to His saying ﴿Have they not reflected﴾. So there is reflection upon the creation of the heavens and the earth, and travelling in the earth alone; then travelling in the earth is either travelling by foot or travelling by understanding. If it is travelling by understanding, it falls within what preceded.

It may be said that this is more specific than what preceded, because here He said: ﴿and see how was the end of those before them﴾; it is sight of events, not of the creation of the earth. So this verse is separate from the previous one in meaning: the former is reflection, and for this its object came general, concerning the heavens and the earth and what is between them.

And this travelling for a specific matter: what is it? It is: the events; that ﴿they may see how was the end of those before them﴾. It includes travelling by foot and travelling by thought and understanding. On the view that it is travelling by feet, the travelling is sensory; on the second view, it is meaningful; so it includes sensory travel and meaningful travel.

Sensory travel: if someone says: how do you ask a person to travel on foot to places of punishment, when the Prophet ﷺ forbade us to enter places of punishment except while weeping?

We say: there is no contradiction; this is precisely the purpose of traveling to places of punishment: admonition and restraint, and this is achieved through weeping. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ forbade us to enter the dwellings of Thamud except while weeping, and he said: «If you are not weeping, do not enter them»[[Ibn Hisham cited it in al-Sirah (2/522) as a mursal narration from al-Zuhri, with the wording: "Do not enter the dwellings of those who wronged themselves except while you are weeping."]].

Some people go to the dwellings of Thamud for recreation, amusement, and enjoyment of the scenery; for this reason they take photographs of them, out of fear or admiration?
* Students: Admiration.
* Shaykh: Admiration for them. This is from hardness of heart, we seek refuge with Allah, and ignorance of what the Prophet ﷺ brought; for most of those who go to this destination are ignorant. We do not say that all of them have hardness of heart, having deliberately opposed the truth; but we say that they have some ignorance. Otherwise, a person who does not know of himself that, if he goes, he will be affected to the point of weeping, may not enter, because the Prophet ﷺ forbade that.

His saying: ﴿in the earth﴾: ﴿Have they not travelled in the earth﴾. What is the meaning of ﴿fi﴾?
* Student: "On."
* Shaykh: It is said its meaning is "on," because if it were taken in its apparent sense, the travel would be in tunnels beneath the earth. ﴿Fi﴾ denotes container, and the container surrounds the contained from all sides; the earth cannot surround you from all sides unless you are inside the earth in a tunnel, and this is not intended. So here (fi) means (ʿala).

And it is said: (fi) denotes containment in its proper sense and there is no need to interpret it, and the containment of each thing is according to its nature, so ﴿fi al-ard﴾ means: on the surface of the earth. Everyone knows that it is not meant that you pierce the earth and walk beneath it! No one understands this; in any case, the meaning intended is walking on the surface of the earth.

* Student: (...) walking on the surface of the earth (...).
* Shaykh: (fi) does not become (...).
* Student: Except from above.
* Shaykh: No, from right to left; there is no wall. In any case the meaning is clear, even if we say (fi) denotes containment, the container is according to its nature in each place; it is not necessary that it be inside.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿in the earth, then they may see﴾. ﴿Al-ard﴾ is singular and the intended meaning is the genus: that is, the lands upon whose people punishment fell, such as the dwellings of Thamud, and others: al-Ahqaf, and the dwellings of the people of Lut, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And indeed it is on a road that remains﴾ [al-Hijr 76].

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: (...) Yes, as I said: it is ignorance; ignorance predominates over them (...). No one prospers by going to a place which the Messenger ﷺ forbade entering except in a state of weeping, but most of them are ignorant.

He said: ﴿then they may see how was﴾: (yanzuru): is it sight of the eye or sight of insight?
* Student: Insight.
* Another student: The first.
* Shaykh: If the travel is by foot, then the seeing is by the eye; if the travel is by understanding, then the seeing is insight. That is: they may see with the eye of insight or with the eye of sight, according to the travel mentioned earlier.

His saying: ﴿then they may see﴾: the fa' here, is it causal or conjunctive?
* Student: Causal.
* Another student: Conjunctive.
* Shaykh: Both are permissible. It may be conjunctive, and the meaning: "Did they not travel, and so did not see?" And it may be causal, the meaning: "Did they not travel, so that by their travel they might see how was the end of those before them?"

* Student: Shaykh, we said: if one travels on the earth, he sees with the eye of sight; it does not become the eye of insight. If he did not perceive, it would not benefit...
* Shaykh: Yes, it does not contradict that; with the eye of sight which leads to the eye of insight. But the intended meaning is that when you travel on foot, I am not saying that when you reach a place you close your eyes; you look with your eye. But does this sight benefit or not? If there is no insight in it, it does not benefit. Therefore the intended meaning of travel on foot is sight with the eye, so that this leads to sight with insight; otherwise, direct sight while travelling on foot is with the eye.

His saying: ﴿then they may see﴾: (yasiru) and (yanzuru): what is the jussive particle here? They are jussive by what? They are jussive by the deletion of the nun and the waw of the subject, because they are of the five verbs.

His saying: ﴿how was the end of those before them﴾: ﴿kayfa﴾ is an interrogative noun, the predicate of (kana) placed first, and ﴿'aqibah﴾ is its subject in its place. ''Aqibah'' is a verbal noun in the sense of ''uqba'', and the ''aqibah'' of a thing is what follows it and comes after it. So His saying: ﴿the end of those before them﴾ means: what followed their denial of the messengers.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 30, verses 8–9 (part 2 of 3):

And His saying: (﴿Those before them﴾, from the nations, and it is their destruction because of their denial of their messengers.) What was the end of Thamud? Destruction and annihilation. The end of 'Ad, who were arrogant in the land and said, "Who is stronger than us?", no one was stronger than them. Their end was that they were destroyed by a matter of the most subtle things, which is the wind. The wind is subtle, a body that is not seen. These great, mighty-bodied people with powerful strength were destroyed by this subtle wind that cannot be seen, so that the weakness of man would become clear, and that however great he may be, Allah the Mighty and Majestic is stronger than him, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Do they not see that Allah, who created them, is greater than them in strength?﴾ [Fussilat 15].

And likewise the towns of the people of Lut, who were given luxury and became corrupt, may Allah protect us, they were given luxury and pampering, until they reached such an extreme of luxury, may Allah protect us, that they turned away from what Allah had created for them of their wives to having intercourse with males. We ask Allah for well-being.

He said: ﴿How was the end of those before them, who were greater than them in strength?﴾ The phrase ﴿كَانُوا﴾ ("they were") is a resumptive (istinafiyya) clause, intended to explain the condition of those earlier peoples.

(﴿Greater than them in strength﴾, like 'Ad and Thamud.) There is no doubt that they were stronger than the Quraysh. The strength of 'Ad is well known: ﴿of the lofty pillars, the like of which had never been created in the lands﴾ [al-Fajr 7–8].

As for Thamud, they were the ones who hewed out houses from the mountains, ﴿splendid houses﴾, secure houses, lofty and towering, out of the rocks of the mountains, and this indicates strength. And from the plains they took for themselves palaces, ﴿you take from its plains palaces﴾ [al-A'raf 74], great and magnificent palaces. This is what happened to the people of Makkah, and yet Allah the Mighty destroyed them because of their disbelief and denial.

﴿They were greater than them in strength and they plowed the earth﴾, and ﴿they plowed the earth﴾ is conjoined (ma'tufa) to ﴿they were﴾ (kānū), not to the predicate of kāna, nor to kāna itself. The end of those before them: they plowed the earth. It is not conjoined to ﴿greater﴾ (ashadd), so that we would say: they were greater than them, and they plowed the earth and cultivated it. Rather, it is conjoined to ﴿they were﴾.

﴿They plowed the earth﴾: he said, "they turned it over and tilled it for planting." What comes after it? 
* Students: "and planted."
* The Shaykh: "and planted." This is plowing the earth. When a person tills the land, there is no doubt that he plows the earth, is that not so? You know tilling with a hoe or with tractors, which turn the earth over, meaning they lift it. Likewise planting: a person turns the earth to dig for the tree so that he can plant it firmly. So those were stronger than them, and they also plowed the lands. The people of Makkah did not plow the land, because it was a valley without cultivation.

﴿And they plowed the earth and cultivated it more than they had cultivated it﴾: ﴿cultivated it﴾ means the earlier peoples cultivated the earth. What did that involve? Through trade, construction, factories, and other things.

Concerning Sulayman, peace be upon him, Allah said to him: ﴿They made for him whatever he willed of sanctuaries, statues, basins like reservoirs, and cooking pots fixed in place﴾ [Saba 13]. ﴿Jifan﴾ means the large dishes in which food is served. ﴿Kal-jawab﴾: what is al-Jabiya?
* A student: the pool.
* The Shaykh: a water pool. Are they large or small?
* The student: large.
* The Shaykh: large dishes, like a large water pool, that is immense. ﴿And cooking pots fixed in place﴾, which cannot be moved because of their size and the quantity of food in them. All of this, and what is like it, happened to those before the Quraysh.

(﴿And they cultivated it more than they had cultivated it, and their messengers came to them with the clear proofs﴾, with the manifest arguments.) The letter bāʾ (bi) is either for accompaniment or for transitivity; both are permissible. The meaning is that the messengers, peace be upon them, came to them with the clear proofs, their messengers from whom? From Allah, Glorified and Exalted.

﴿With the clear proofs﴾: with the clear arguments, or say: with the clear signs, which include arguments and rulings. When a ruling is just and beneficial for the servants, it is a clear sign indicating the truthfulness of the one who brought it. Did all the messengers come with clear proofs?
* A student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Yes, no messenger came without a proof: ﴿We sent Our messengers with clear proofs﴾, and then what? ﴿And We sent down with them the Book and the Balance﴾ [al-Hadid 25]. So with every prophet there is a Book; every prophet has a Book and has clear signs: ﴿Mankind was one community, and Allah sent the prophets as bearers of good tidings and warners, and sent down with them the Book in truth, to judge between people concerning that over which they differed﴾ [al-Baqarah 213]. The point is that there was no messenger except that he had a proof and had a Book with him.

And His saying: (﴿And their messengers came to them with the clear proofs, but Allah was not one to wrong them﴾, by destroying them without a crime, ﴿but they were wronging themselves﴾ by denying their messengers.)

﴿But Allah was not one to wrong them﴾: the lām in His saying ﴿li-yazlimahum﴾, what is its grammatical analysis?
* A student: it is the lām al-juhud.
* The Shaykh: the lām al-juhud, it is called lām al-juhud, meaning the lām of negation because of its association with them. We have previously studied, in al-Ajurrumiyya, that lām al-juhud is preceded by what? We read that lām al-juhud puts the present-tense verb in the subjunctive, and we said that lām al-juhud is preceded by what?
* A student: lam, or mā kāna.
* The Shaykh: lam yakun...
* The student: lam yakun, or mā kāna.
* The Shaykh: or mā kāna. Here it is preceded by mā kāna.

And His saying: ﴿Allah was not one to wrong them﴾. When it is said, "Allah was not one to do such and such," or something similar, know that it indicates an absolute impossibility, as in: ﴿and your Lord was never forgetful﴾ [Maryam 64], an utter impossibility; ﴿and your Lord was not one to destroy the cities until He sent a messenger to their mother-city﴾ [al-Qasas 59], an utter impossibility. Likewise, every expression of this form means that it is absolutely impossible.

And His saying: ﴿li-yazlimahum﴾. Wronging (ẓulm), in origin, is deficiency. In the linguistic origin, wronging is deficiency, and from it is His saying: ﴿Each of the two gardens brought forth its produce and did not fall short in anything﴾ [al-Kahf 33].

In the sharia it is likewise: a deficiency in what is obligatory. It includes neglecting an obligation and transgressing what is forbidden. Transgressing what is forbidden is a deficiency, because you have deprived yourself of its right by not avoiding what is forbidden. Likewise, neglecting an obligation is a deficiency. Whoever falls short in an obligation has wronged himself, and whoever transgresses a prohibition has wronged himself, because he has fallen short of what he should have treated himself with. So wronging is either abandoning an obligation or committing a prohibited act.

With regard to Allah the Mighty: ﴿But Allah was not one to wrong them.﴾ Is this attribute negative or affirmative?
* A student: negative.
* The Shaykh: negative. What does it include?
* A student: the perfection of justice.
* The Shaykh: the perfection of justice. He does not wrong them, not because He is incapable of it, nor because He is not susceptible to it, but because of the perfection of His justice, may He be glorified and exalted. It is not possible for Him to wrong.

The negation of wronging is for one of three reasons: either for perfection, or for incapacity, or for lack of susceptibility. For perfection, meaning the perfection of justice; or for incapacity; or for lack of susceptibility. Pay attention. If you say, "The wall does not wrong," then it is?
* Students: because of lack of susceptibility.
* The Shaykh: because of lack of susceptibility; wronging does not occur from it at all.
If you say, "So-and-so is weak and does not wrong his enemy"?
* The students: because of incapacity.
* The Shaykh: that is because of incapacity. The poet said:
A tribe that never breaks a covenant, and never wrongs people by so much as a mustard seed.
Why?
* A student: because of their incapacity.
* The Shaykh: because of their incapacity. And if you say: ﴿Allah does not wrong people in the least﴾ [Yunus 44]?
* A student: because of the perfection of His justice.
* The Shaykh: so it is because of the perfection of His justice. He, may He be glorified and exalted, is able to wrong, but it is impossible for Him because of the perfection of His attributes. Because of the perfection of His attributes He does not wrong. The Jabriyya said that He does not wrong because He is not susceptible to it (...). Allah, Glorified and Exalted, owns all creation, so His disposal of His own dominion is not wronging, nor is it conceivable. So wronging with respect to Allah is not because of the perfection of His justice, but because He is not susceptible to it. For this reason Ibn al-Qayyim said: "Wronging, according to them, is an impossibility in its very essence." So it is impossible in its essence according to them; wronging with respect to Allah is not conceivable. But if we adopt their view, would that be praise of Allah and an extolling of Him?
* A student: No.
* The Shaykh: No. The negation of wronging is not praise and perfection unless it is accompanied by the capacity for it and its possibility, but His perfect justice prevented Him from it. Do you understand?

And His saying: ﴿But they were wronging themselves﴾. ﴿Themselves﴾ is accusative because it is the predicate of kāna. How? kāna is a past-tense verb that raises the subject and puts the predicate in the accusative, and the wāw is its subject. And "themselves" is its predicate?
* A student: "themselves" is an emphatic for the pronoun.
* The Shaykh: if it were an emphatic for the pronoun, he would have said: kānū anfusuhum. But here it is: ﴿anfusahum﴾.
* A student: the clause "yazlimūna anfusahum" is the predicate, meaning it is circumstantial.
* The Shaykh: what is the grammatical analysis of ﴿anfusahum﴾?
* A student: it is the object.
* The Shaykh: the object of what?
* A student: the object of "yazlimūn".
* The Shaykh: the object of "yazlimūn", fronted: a fronted object of "yazlimūn". ﴿But they were wronging themselves﴾, meaning: but they were wronging themselves. By what did they wrong themselves? By disobedience to Allah, either by neglecting an obligation or committing a prohibited act. What this sentence indicates will come to us, Allah willing, in the benefits. The point is that Allah, Exalted, did not wrong these deniers whom He destroyed. He did not wrong them, but they were the ones who wronged themselves. So the offense was theirs against themselves, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, dealt with them with perfect justice (...).

* * *

﴿Have they not reflected within themselves? Allah did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except with truth and for a specified term. Indeed, many of the people are disbelievers in the meeting with their Lord﴾ [al-Rum 8].

What is derived from this noble verse:
First: a rebuke to whoever turns away from reflection, from His saying: ﴿Have they not reflected?﴾, for the interrogative here is for rebuke.
From this benefit follows another benefit, which is the encouragement to reflect, is it not so? And from it follows a second benefit, which is the benefit of reflection, because Allah does not urge toward something and rebuke for abandoning it unless there is benefit and good in it.

* From the benefits of the verse: the place of thinking is the intellect, from His saying: ﴿within themselves﴾. This is if we say that what is meant is that the self is the instrument of reflection and the path of remembrance. But if we say the place of remembrance, then a benefit is derived from it, which is the magnificence of Allah's creative craftsmanship in the human self and the wonders He placed within it.

If you want to know this, go to the people of the sciences and medicine, and you will find in your body wondrous and amazing things. This food you eat turns into blood and is distributed throughout the body according to its tissues. It gives the nerves an amount suited to them, gives the flesh an amount suited to it, and gives the bones an amount suited to them. Glory be to Allah the Great, thin tubes like hair distribute throughout this body as much as it needs.

In any case, we do not want to explain this now. Our point is that in Allah's creation of man there are such amazing wonders that they dazzle the intellects. Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned much of this in his book Miftah Dar al-Sa'ada, and that was before medicine advanced to where it has reached today.

* Also from the benefits of the verse: that the Creator is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. The creator of the heavens and the earth is Allah, from His saying: ﴿Allah did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except with truth﴾. No one else created them. For this reason He said in Surat al-Tur: ﴿Were they created out of nothing, or are they the creators? Or did they create the heavens and the earth? Rather, they are not certain﴾ [al-Tur 35–36].

* And from its benefits: the affirmation of the number of the heavens, which are seven. As for the earth, it is always mentioned in the singular in the Qur'an; it is never mentioned in the plural. But it has been indicated that there are seven [earths] in His saying: ﴿Allah is He who created seven heavens and of the earth the like of them﴾ [al-Talaq 12].

* And from its benefits: that between the heavens and the earth there are great created beings that deserve to be counted as a counterpart to the creation of the heavens and the earth. Is that so, or not?
* A student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Now check among yourselves: the heavens, the earth, and what is between them. We all know the greatness of the earth and the greatness of the sky. So the greatness of what is between them is commensurate with both.

* Also from the benefits of the verse: the perfection of Allah's wisdom, Glorified and Exalted, and His power.
By what do we infer the perfection of His power? By the greatness of what is brought into being. The perfection of power is derived from the greatness of what is made. This is a type of indication by implication, which we mentioned earlier. We said that when Allah opens to a servant the understanding of the implications of the texts, he benefits from that great benefits, to the point that he derives from a single text rulings that others do not derive, or only half of them, or less.

I say: From this verse is derived the greatness of Allah's power, Mighty and Majestic, and the extent of His wisdom. From where do we take the wisdom? From His saying: ﴿except with truth﴾. They were not created in vain: ﴿with truth﴾. As for the power, we take it from the greatness of the creature. The greatness of the creature indicates the greatness of the Creator.

* And from the benefits of the verse: a person should not waste his time in vain and aimlessly. From where do we take it? From His saying: ﴿except with truth﴾, because its opposite is falsehood. Falsehood is either harmful, or neither harmful nor beneficial. Every amusement a son of Adam engages in is falsehood, except such and such.

The point is that, since the heavens and the earth were all created with truth, with seriousness, sincerity, and steadfastness, it is fitting for you to be in accord with this wisdom for which the heavens and the earth were created.

* And from the benefits of the verse: that this creation, despite its greatness, has a limited term, from His saying: ﴿and for a specified term﴾, meaning determined. Everything in the heavens and the earth, whether whole or part, is limited to a specified term, and whether it is a substance or an attribute, it is limited to a specified term. For this reason one of the well-known maxims is: permanence of a state is impossible.

From this follows another benefit: that creation is imperfect, since it was not decreed eternal. It is imperfect. For this reason the afterlife comes perfect, because it is everlasting.

* And from the benefits of the verse: the perfection of wisdom, since everything has a predetermined, ordered term: ﴿And everything with Him is by measure﴾ [al-Ra'd 8]. Measure includes the measure of quantity, the measure of quality, the measure of time, and the measure of place. All four types are included in His saying: ﴿And everything with Him is by measure﴾, Glorified and Exalted.

Then He said: ﴿And indeed, many of the people are disbelievers in the meeting with their Lord.﴾ From this verse is derived: despite these great signs, the creation of the heavens, the earth, and what is between them, and the fixing of their terms by a specified term and their determination by a particular measure, despite all this, many people deny the meeting with Allah.

In reality, the intelligent person derives from this limitation of terms the obligation of meeting Allah. When he sees his companions and peers who were with him yesterday going away one by one, does that lead him to faith or not? Without doubt it leads him to faith, because he knows that if the world were to last for anyone, it would not have reached you. It did not reach you except after others had passed away.

So from these decreed terms you infer that there must be something beyond this. Is it wise for Allah to create this great creation with this marvelous order, and then the end be that a person dies like the carcass of a donkey, or not? Never, this is not wisdom. For this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, He who ordained the Qur'an for you will surely return you to a place of return﴾ [al-Qasas 85]. So these laws that were revealed must have something beyond them, and that is the resurrection, in which is the meeting with Allah, Mighty and Majestic. But despite this: ﴿And indeed, many of the people are disbelievers in the meeting with their Lord.﴾

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 30, verses 8–9 (part 3 of 3):

* Among the benefits of this verse is the affirmation of resurrection (al-ba'th), which is understood from His saying: ﴿with the meeting with their Lord﴾.
* And among them: that every person will meet Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. From where do we take this? From His saying: ﴿with the meeting with their Lord﴾. And the Exalted said in Surah al-Inshiqaq: ﴿O man, you are toiling toward your Lord with toil, and you will meet it﴾ [Al-Inshiqaq 6].
If someone says: "Does this meeting include both the believer and the disbeliever?" We say: Yes, but there is a difference between the two meetings. Just as a man meets Zayd and meets 'Amr, and there is a great difference between the two meetings: he meets this one with an angry face and that one with a pleased face, this one with a constricted expression and that one with an open expression, and so on.
* And among the benefits of the verse: does it affirm general lordship (rububiyyah 'ammah) or specific lordship (rububiyyah khassah)? General. This is because of His saying: ﴿with the meeting with their Lord﴾, even though it speaks of the disbelievers. So it is general lordship. Lordship is divided into two types: general and specific. Both are combined in the Exalted's saying: ﴿They said, "We believe in the Lord of the worlds (121), the Lord of Musa and Harun"﴾ [Al-A'raf 121–122]. So the first is general and the second is specific.
* And among the benefits of the verse: the censure of those who disbelieved in the meeting with Allah despite His great signs that indicate His existence and wisdom, because of His saying: ﴿And indeed, many of the people are, in the meeting with their Lord, disbelievers﴾. This sentence, without doubt, indicates censure.
* A student: Is it taken from it that the disbelievers are many, that they are the majority of people?
* The Shaykh: No. It means many of them, he did not say "most of them." In this verse it is not taken, but in other places it is taken.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: It does not act? This one whose faith does not act, its existence is like non-existence, because disbelief has two types: disbelief of denial (kufr jahd) and disbelief of arrogance (kufr istikbar).
* A student: Does the meeting (liqa') mean merely seeing?
* The Shaykh: The meaning of the meeting is confrontation (al-mawajahah), but it is after resurrection, and seeing is among its necessary consequences, which is resurrection.
* The student: And is seeing among its necessary consequences?
* The Shaykh: Allah knows best regarding the matter of seeing, because Allah mentioned regarding the disbelievers: ﴿Indeed, they will be, that Day, veiled from their Lord﴾ [Al-Mutaffifin 15].
* A student: The division of lordship into general and specific, what is the difference between them, given that lordship in principle...
* The Shaykh: The difference between them is that general lordship necessitates absolute disposal over the one who is lorded over, while specific lordship necessitates, along with absolute disposal, care for it, support for it, strengthening it, and so on. It resembles the general and specific companionship (ma'iyyah 'ammah and khassah), and it also resembles many matters of this kind.
He said: ﴿Have they not traveled through the land and seen how was the end of those before them? They were greater than them in strength and plowed the earth and populated it more than they have populated it, and their messengers came to them with clear proofs. And never would Allah have wronged them, but they were wronging themselves﴾ [Ar-Rum 9].
From this verse is derived: the rebuke of those who neglected traveling in the land, whether with their bodies or with their hearts, because the interrogative in His saying: ﴿Have they not traveled﴾ is for rebuke.
* A student: For rebuke.
* The Shaykh: For rebuke. And from this benefit there branches: the encouragement to travel in the land, and among that—travel in the land with the heart—is reviewing the books of history and the accounts of nations, because whoever reviews them, especially the histories that are careful about accuracy and are precisely recorded, a wondrous marvel becomes clear to him regarding the creation of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, His alternation of days among the people, and His changing of affairs. It increases a person in faith in Allah. But if these events are from the Prophetic biography (sirah nabawiyyah) and the biographies of the Rightly Guided Caliphs (al-Khulafa' ar-Rashidun), then along with faith in Allah his increase is that he becomes colored by their color and follows their example in conduct. And if they are from general, passing matters, then he uses them as evidence of the power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, the perfection of His authority, and His changing of affairs.
The important point is that traveling in the land, in the sense of reviewing events and histories, benefits a person and makes him take a lesson. But for whom does it benefit? ﴿Indeed, in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart or gives ear while he is a witness﴾ [Qaf 37].
* And it is also derived from this verse: that the end of the disbelievers is a grim end, because of His saying: ﴿and see how was the end of those before them﴾.
* And among its benefits: that a person, however strong he is, is weak in comparison to the strength of Allah. This is because of His saying: ﴿They were greater than them in strength and plowed the earth and populated it more than they have populated it﴾. And despite that, did they protect themselves by this from the punishment of Allah? The answer?
* A student: No.
* The Shaykh: No. Rather, Allah, by His wisdom, destroyed the most arrogant people of the earth with the most insignificant and subtle causes. The people of 'Ad were destroyed by a wind. And He destroyed the one who used to boast of the rivers flowing beneath him—with what did He destroy him?
* A student: Drowning.
* The Shaykh: With water, with the same water he used to boast of yesterday. This indicates the perfection of the authority of Allah, Glorified and Exalted, and His greatness, and that however strong a person is, he is weak in comparison to the strength of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
I think in the year four hundred or before it, an earthquake occurred in Iran that destroyed—in the blink of an eye—twenty-five thousand souls of the children of Adam, not to mention animals and livestock and so on, and destroyed two hundred and thirty villages and two large cities. And the quake is not a shaking like a swing; the quake is a glance of the eye. Just as a person described it who wrote to Shaykh 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Baz about the earthquake that struck Yemen—he portrayed it in a wondrous manner regarding its speed, the sounds that accompanied it, and the state of the people and the terror that befell them, to the point that every nursing woman forgets what she nursed and every pregnant woman casts her burden. So this great power—can anyone escape from it if Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, wills it?
* A student: No.
* The Shaykh: Never possible. ﴿Say, "He is Able to send upon you punishment from above you or from beneath your feet, or to confuse you into sects and make you taste the violence of one another"﴾ [Al-An'am 65].
* And among the benefits of the verse: that reflecting on the condition of the disbelievers for the sake of taking a lesson is required. Reflecting on the condition of the disbelievers for the sake of taking a lesson, by which a person learns, is a required matter. If a man came and wanted to study the history of a disbelieving nation, what befell them and what came upon them, do we forbid him from that? If he wants to benefit from this and know what was the end of the criminals, then he is commanded to do it. But if he wants to marvel at their strength and craftsmanship and so on, then he is forbidden from it. Just as we said about those who go to the dwellings of Thamud: if their purpose is sightseeing and recreation, this is forbidden; and whoever's purpose is taking a lesson, this is permissible under the condition mentioned by the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. What is it? That they do not enter them except while weeping.
* And among the benefits of the verse: that plowing the earth is one of the causes of worldly strength. That is, occupying oneself with agriculture is without doubt one of the causes of strength, because through it self-sufficiency from others is achieved. If our country, for example, produces fruits and crops, we become independent of others through that, and perhaps we will have a surplus that we export to others, so we gain. Thus plowing the earth is one of the causes of strength.
And likewise the populating of the earth. The populating of the earth by other than plowing—by building, trade, and similar things—is one of the causes of strength.
* And among the benefits of the verse: that Allah, the Exalted, has not left anyone without messengers, because of His saying: ﴿and their messengers came to them﴾.
* And among its benefits as well: that every messenger came with a proof (bayyinah) that supports him, because of His saying: ﴿and their messengers came to them with clear proofs﴾.
* And among its benefits—from the benefit of the messengers and their coming with clear proofs—two benefits are derived from it, other than what we have mentioned: they are the mercy of Allah and the wisdom of Allah. As for mercy: the intellects cannot be guided to what Allah wants from them except by revelation. Do you agree with me on this?
* A student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Yes. Is it possible for a person, by his intellect, to know how to perform ablution, how to pray, how to fast, how to perform Hajj, or is that not possible? It is not possible. Therefore there must be a messenger to whom revelation comes from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, to explain to us what Allah is pleased with and what He is not pleased with.
Second: that these messengers come with clear proofs is from mercy. If Allah had sent the messengers without proofs and obligated the servants to submit to them without there being a proof they could be reassured by, there would be in this such hardship and difficulty as only Allah knows. But from the mercy of Allah is that He placed with every prophet a proof. And note that the prophets whose prophethood and messengership were restricted to a time or a place—and they are all the prophets except Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him—you find their signs are mostly sensory signs that end with their ending, and after their death they become a report that is transmitted and related.
As for the sign of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, his signs encompassed both matters: sensory matters that were transmitted after him and related, and immaterial matters that remain after him, such as the Great Qur'an, and such as his informing of some unseen matters that occurred as he informed. This is because the message of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, is lasting, continuous, and established, so the signs that support the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, must remain so that the proof may be established by them upon whom? Upon the rest of mankind. Because the rest of mankind, if they did not witness the matter with their own eyes, and it was only reports that are transmitted, then, as came in the hadith: "The report is not like direct witnessing" [[Narrated by Ahmad (1841) and Ibn Hibban (Al-Ihsan, 6213) from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.]]. So from the sending of messengers and their being given clear proofs we derive two benefits: the mercy of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and His wisdom.
* And it is derived from this verse: the negation of injustice from Allah because of His perfect justice, because of His saying: ﴿And never would Allah have wronged them﴾. We say: the negation of injustice from Allah is because of His perfect justice.
If someone says: "We agree with you on the negation of injustice from Allah, because Allah negated it from Himself: ﴿And never would Allah have wronged them﴾. But from where do you have that it is due to His perfect justice?"
The answer: Because we say: negation indicates the non-existence of what is negated, and non-existence is equivalent to nothingness, and nothingness itself is not a thing. It is not a thing. Nothingness is nothingness by its name. So if it is not a thing, can it be an attribute of perfection by which Allah praises Himself when it is not a thing?
* A student: No.
* The Shaykh: The answer is no. Therefore it must include something, which is affirmation. This affirmation is either for incapacity, or for the non-receptivity of the attribute, or for perfect justice. Choose which of these possibilities befits Allah, the Mighty and Majestic—or see which possibility befits Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: perfect justice. And with this we know that the necessity of negating injustice for the sake of perfect justice is a rational implication with respect to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; it is not so with respect to everyone from whom injustice is negated. With respect to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, the obligation of that for the sake of perfect justice is an unavoidable rational implication. Then it is derived from it: the negation of injustice because of the perfect justice of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
* And among the benefits of the verse: that the self of a person holds a trust (amanah) that is to be taken: ﴿But they were wronging themselves﴾. So Allah affirmed that man wrongs his own self. And if it were not a trust, he would not be a wrongdoer, because he would be acting and disposing freely. But it is a trust in his keeping, which he must safeguard with its proper safeguarding. For this reason the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Indeed your self has a right over you" [[Narrated by al-Bukhari (1968) from Abu Juhayfah, may Allah be pleased with him, and its wording is: "Indeed your Lord has a right over you, and your self has a right over you."]]. And this includes, just as it includes giving the self its rest, giving the self its share of worship; do not neglect it.
* A student: His saying (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* The student: How is that meant?
* The Shaykh: It is contrasted with His saying: ﴿The soul at peace﴾ [Al-Fajr 27], because a human being has three souls: the commanding soul (nafs ammarah), the soul at peace (nafs mutma'innah), and the self-reproaching soul (nafs lawwamah).
As for the soul at peace: it is the one that commands him with the pleasure of Allah. As for the commanding soul: it is the one that commands him with disobedience to Allah. As for the self-reproaching soul: it is the one that blames him. And what does it blame him for? It is suitable for both directions: if it blames him for abandoning evil, then this is from the commanding soul—the one that said to him: "Would that you had gone with those people to drink wine, commit adultery, and gamble..." until the end, and it blames you: "Look, the girls went out (...) and enjoying themselves, and you did not go." This is self-reproaching, but which of the two souls is it?
* A student: The commanding soul.
* The Shaykh: The commanding soul to evil.
And there is a self-reproaching soul that blames him for doing evil and for abandoning good, and this is the soul at peace. So in a human being there are three souls, as Allah mentioned in the Qur'an.
* A student: The domain of the soul in him is three: there is a soul commanding to evil. How is it: ﴿they were wronging themselves﴾ while the soul is the person himself?
* The Shaykh: Yes, because he has another soul opposing it.
* The student: So every person has three souls?
* The Shaykh: Yes, every person must have these souls.
* A student: Are they attributes?
* The Shaykh: Yes, they are attributes. In reality they are attributes, or is the rational soul or the thinking one a single thing?
* A student: All of them exist?
* The Shaykh: Yes, all of them exist. All of them exist in a person. He senses from his soul at times what commands him to disobedience, and at times he senses what commands him to good, and at times he senses what blames him.
* A student: So they exist in him from the beginning (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, indeed; which of them is it that makes demands? Some people are made demands of by the commanding soul, and some people are commanded by the soul at peace; the soul at peace makes demands of him. They differ.
* A student: Did Allah create them from the beginning?
* The Shaykh: From the beginning Allah created these faculties in him. These psychological faculties are created in the human being.
He said: ﴿But they were wronging themselves﴾:
* Among the benefits of the verse: that a person, by his disobedience, harms only himself, or not?
* A student: Indeed.
* The Shaykh: Yes. And this is indicated by the saying of the Exalted in the sacred hadith: "O My servants, if the first of you and the last of you, your humans and your jinn, were upon the most wicked heart of one man among you, that would not decrease anything of My dominion" [[Narrated by Muslim (2577) from Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him.]]. That is, it does not harm Me; even if you turn away from My worship and devotion to Me, that does not harm Me. ﴿But they were wronging themselves﴾.
* A student: Is it derived from the verse the affirmation of voluntary actions for the servant?
* The Shaykh: For the servant? Yes, yes, indeed. It is derived from it that the servant's act is chosen, because of His saying: ﴿But they were wronging themselves﴾, so He affirmed the wrongdoing from them against themselves.
And from another aspect it is also derived from the same verse: ﴿And never would Allah have wronged them﴾, because if He were compelling them to that, their punishment would be injustice, or not? If a person believed that Allah compels a human to commit disobedience and then punishes him for it, would that be injustice?
* A student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Yes, injustice. So in it is evidence for voluntary actions from two aspects: from His saying: ﴿But they were wronging themselves﴾, and from His saying: ﴿And never would Allah have wronged them﴾.
Is it derived from that that injustice with respect to Allah, in itself, is possible—in terms of the capacity to do it, that is—is it possible or not?
* A student: It is possible.
* The Shaykh: Yes, it is possible. Therefore Allah praised Himself by the negation of injustice from Himself, or by negating His wronging of His servants—better: He praised Himself by negating His wronging of the servants. If this were among the impossible matters, there would be no place for disagreement. He, the Mighty and Majestic, is capable of wronging if He wills, but He does not will that because of His perfect justice. So injustice is impossible for Allah. Why?
* A student: Because of His perfect justice.
* The Shaykh: Because of His perfect justice, unlike the Jahmiyyah (the followers of Jahm ibn Safwan), who say: injustice is impossible because it is impossible in itself for Allah. They said: this is an impossible thing. Thus they made the object of praise an intellectually impossible matter.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 30, verses 8–9 (part 1 of 3):

Then Allah the Exalted said: (﴿Have they not reflected within themselves?﴾ [al-Rum 8]: so that they might turn back from their heedlessness).

His saying: ﴿Have they not reflected﴾. We have previously explained many times how such a construction is parsed (i'rab), and we said that the grammarians have two opinions regarding its parsing:

The first: that the hamza (interrogative particle) is placed before its original position, and that its original form is: (wa-alam yatafakkaru) [and did they not reflect], so that it is a clause conjoined to what precedes it.

The second view: that the hamza enters upon an omitted element which is to be estimated according to the context, and the conjunction that follows it is conjoining that omitted element.

In this verse, the estimate is: "Were they heedless and did they not reflect?" When He said: ﴿and they are heedless of the Hereafter﴾, He said: ﴿Have they not reflected?﴾ The interrogation is for reproach, because a person is commanded to reflect.

His saying: ﴿Have they not reflected within themselves?﴾ Is the phrase ﴿within themselves﴾ the place of reflection or the means of reflection? That is: is the intended meaning of the verse an exhortation to their reflecting upon themselves, as in His saying: ﴿And within yourselves; will you not see?﴾ [al-Dhariyat 21], or an exhortation to reflect upon the creation of the heavens and the earth within themselves?

* Student: Both matters.
* Shaykh: Both? Yes, both, but the closer one is the last; for this reason He said: ﴿what Allah created of the heavens﴾ [al-Rum 8].

So the meaning is: Have they not returned to themselves and reflected with genuine reflection upon this existence, so that they might thereby know the wisdom of Allah the Mighty and Majestic and what it entails of His great attributes?!

His saying: ﴿within themselves: what Allah created of the heavens and the earth and what is between them except with truth﴾ (ma): what is its parsing?
* Student: A relative pronoun.
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: A negation particle.
* Shaykh: A negation particle; the proof is His saying: ﴿except with truth﴾.

﴿What Allah created of the heavens and the earth﴾: (khalaqa) means to bring into existence and to originate, and it is not, for the most part, except with measure and arrangement; for the origin of creation is measuring within the self, as the poet said:
"And indeed you measure what you create, while some people create but do not measure."
That is: what you measured. So creation is origination with measure and arrangement.

His saying: ﴿the heavens﴾ has been discussed before, and that what is meant by them is the layers, and they are seven.

His saying: ﴿and the earth﴾ is singular, and what is meant is the genus, so it includes all the earths. It is conjoined to ﴿the heavens﴾ and is in the accusative; for this reason it is marked with a fatha, unlike ﴿the heavens﴾ [al-samawat], since that is a sound feminine plural.

His saying: ﴿and what is between them﴾ (ma): a relative pronoun conjoined to "the earth" or to "the heavens"?
* Student: To the heavens.
* Shaykh: To the heavens, yes.
