* Shaykh: A noun meaning "like." That is, like this bringing out you will be brought out. It may also be a preposition here, meaning "and like this bringing out you will be brought out," and it is not an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq, an object of the verb's own noun for emphasis).

According to the first view: "like that bringing out you will be brought out," and it is an absolute object.

According to the second view: the kaf is a preposition, and dhaa is a demonstrative noun built on sukun in a genitive position. That is: and like this bringing out you will be brought out.

As for his saying (﴿you will be brought out﴾ from the graves): the apparent meaning of the noble verse is that the people's coming out of the graves resembles the plants' coming out of the earth, and the plants' coming out of the earth happens by rain falling upon it. So this verse contains an allusion to what is reported in the hadith: "God sends down upon the graves a heavy rain like the semen of men for forty days, by which bodies grow in the graves. Then after that they come out when the Trumpet is blown." [Al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman (347), from Abu Hurayrah, may God be pleased with him.] Hadiths on this subject have been transmitted with weaknesses in their chains, but taken together they indicate that they are good hadiths, and the apparent meaning of the Quran also points to them.

As for his saying (﴿you will be brought out﴾ is read with the active and the passive voice): the active voice is like what? "takhrujun" (you go out).

* Student: ﴿You go out.﴾

* Shaykh: ﴿You go out﴾, and the passive: ﴿you will be brought out﴾. There are two readings. Are they both among the seven canonical readings, or is one of them irregular?

* Student: Both are among the seven.

* Shaykh: Both are among the seven, because it is the author's habit, may God have mercy on him, that when he mentions an irregular reading he says: "and it was read."

* Student: The one in the Mushaf?

* Shaykh: The one in the Mushaf is: ﴿you will be brought out﴾.

* Student: And the one not in the Mushaf?

* Shaykh: The tafsir?

* Student: Yes.

* Shaykh: I have here ﴿you will be brought out﴾. What is in the original (is "with the active and the passive voice").

* Student: No, here he said: ﴿You go out﴾ and not ﴿you will be brought out﴾.

* Shaykh: He did not mention a reading?

* Student: No, he did not mention a reading.

* Shaykh: Strange, because it is present in mine. Is it present in yours in the tafsir?

* Student: It is present.

* Shaykh: Is it not present in yours (with the active and passive voice)?

* Student: Apparently it is, it seems to be there.

* Shaykh: He said: (﴿And among His signs﴾: of God, exalted is He, which indicate His power). ﴿Among His signs﴾: the word "min" is a preposition meaning partitive, that is, some of His signs. The word "ayat" is the plural of "ayah," which linguistically means a clear, evident sign. ﴿His signs﴾: the author says: (which indicate His power).

﴿That He created you from dust﴾: "anna" and what follows it is in the sense of a verbal noun functioning as a delayed subject. That is: His creating. ﴿That He created you from dust﴾: "min" here indicates the starting point. The meaning: the starting of creation was from dust (meaning your origin, Adam). This is correct. As for the lineage of Adam, it was created from a drop.

(﴿Then, when you are humans﴾: of flesh and blood ﴿who disperse﴾ throughout the earth.) You were dust, and dust does not move from its place or spread out, and there is no movement in it. Then after that you became humans: ﴿Then, when you are humans, dispersing﴾.

As for His saying ﴿then when﴾: someone might say that there is an apparent contradiction here, because "idha" (when) indicates a sudden event, and "thumma" (then) indicates a delay, and suddenness and delay are contradictory, since suddenness indicates immediacy.

The answer is that the suddenness comes after the delay, because the dust did not become a human at once. It developed over a period until it reached humanity. This is if we say that "human" refers specifically to Adam.

But if we say that it refers to his descendants, the delay is clear, because this includes his descendants until when? Until the Hour is established. So the delay is clear, but the suddenness in His saying ﴿then when you are humans﴾ may suggest that the intended meaning is Adam, since Adam was a human and his descendants spread throughout the earth.

As for His saying ﴿then when you are humans﴾: this sentence is a subject and predicate. And ﴿dispersing﴾?

* Student: A circumstantial clause (hal).

* Shaykh: A circumstantial clause of what?

* Student: Of ﴿you﴾.

* Shaykh: Should we not make it an attribute of "humans"?

* Student: An attribute of "humans."

* Shaykh: An attribute of "humans." If we make it an attribute of "humans," there is a problem, because "bashar" (human) is singular and ﴿dispersing﴾ is plural. But a singular noun intended as a category can be plural. ﴿Then when you are humans, dispersing﴾: dispersing in what place? He says: (﴿dispersing﴾ throughout the earth), because of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when the prayer is concluded, disperse throughout the earth﴾ [al-Jumu'ah 10].

So dispersal is throughout the earth and its expansion. Now look: humanity is spread throughout all the regions of the world. Glory be to God, the Mighty. When a person reflects on what came before, he says, for example: What brought the people of America to America, and what brought them to other lands across these great oceans? Because Adam was undoubtedly on one of the continents, so what brought his descendants to the other continents? Do you have anything from the science of geology, as they say? We say: God knows best. Perhaps God facilitated for them, at that time, means that we still do not know. Until they reached these lands (...).

* Student: The blood comes from fruit, and fruit comes from the earth.

* Shaykh: Blood comes from fruit?!

* Student: I mean the blood (...) fruits and vegetables, I mean, being food, the food originally comes from the earth.

* Shaykh: That is permissible, because this blood is correct, but this is a drop, and the drop becomes a clot.

* Student: ﴿And We created man from an extract of clay﴾, meaning the essence of clay, which is fruit, then it mixed into blood.

* Shaykh: (...) fruit?

﴿And We created man from an extract of clay﴾ [al-Mu'minun 12].

* Student: ﴿Then He made his offspring from an extract of a liquid fluid﴾ [as-Sajdah 8].

* Shaykh: Now the verse: ﴿from an extract of clay﴾. The root meaning of "sulalah" is the essence of something, according to what is made clear. ﴿From an extract of clay﴾ refers to Adam. ﴿And We created man from an extract of clay (12). Then We made him a drop﴾ [al-Mu'minun 12–13]: these are the descendants of Adam, ﴿in a secure lodging﴾.

* Student: Where does the pronoun shift here in ﴿Then We made him﴾?

* Shaykh: Yes, to the species. Considering the species, ﴿We made him﴾ means the human considered as a species.

* Student: (...) the semen contains (...) from dust.

* Shaykh: Contains what?

* Student: Dust.

* Shaykh: We cannot assert either its negation or its affirmation, because it is possible that the human body itself contains earthy material. Now they say that the human contains lead, and lime, and this and that. The body itself is composed of these, so it is not far-fetched that this extract that comes out of it may contain these materials. In reality it is not far-fetched. We have no deep, certain knowledge on this matter. But God is capable of all things. What is known now is that the human contains all the minerals of the earth: it contains lead, copper, lime, dust, and everything, the body itself.

* Student: And iron.

* Shaykh: And iron.

* Student: And electricity.

* Shaykh: Yes, indeed, but we are not like an electric battery. God knows best.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: No, sometimes (...) the thing, with some movement (...), you feel something in your belly.

* Student: Some people say that Adam, when he first left Paradise and descended to earth (...), is that correct?

* Shaykh: God knows; we do not know. There are no authentic hadiths from the Prophet (ﷺ) on this; they are all Isra'iliyyat (narratives of Israelite origin).

He said: ﴿Then when you are humans dispersing﴾ (﴿And among His signs is that He created for you spouses from among yourselves﴾: Eve was formed from Adam's rib, and so she was created).

* Student: She was formed.

* Shaykh: I do not have "she was formed." Well, the meaning the author intends is ﴿that He created for you from your own selves spouses﴾. ﴿Yourselves﴾ means your essences, according to the author's view. So the meaning of "self" here is essence.

As for His saying ﴿that He created for you﴾: the lam indicates special relationship, not ownership, because a person does not own his wife. It may also be causal, meaning: He created for your sake. But the meaning is more eloquent in terms of blessing, since every person's wife belongs exclusively to him. For this reason, a woman may not marry more than one man at the same time.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Qur'an al-Karim) on Surah 30, verses 10–23 (part 5 of 6):**

﴿He created for you, from yourselves,﴾ The author (al-Mu'allif) takes the view that *nafs* (self) means the essence (*dhat*), and that *min* (from) is partitive (*li-l-tab'id*), meaning that the spouse's self is a part of the human's self. For this reason he said, may God have mercy on him, in his explanation: "by the creation of Hawwa' (Eve) from Adam's rib, and the rest of women from the drops of semen of men and women." This is what the author established: that the meaning of *nafs* is the essence.

It is possible that *nafs* means the kind (*jins*), as God Most High says: ﴿There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves﴾ [al-Tawbah 128], meaning from your own kind. This meaning is supported by His saying: ﴿that you may find tranquility in them﴾, for a person finds tranquility only with members of his own kind and not with others. If a woman were of a different kind from a man and not of his kind, that would be a problem, and he could not find tranquility with her. Therefore God, glory be to Him, made her of his kind so that he could find tranquility with her: ﴿that you may find tranquility in them﴾.

The *lam* in His saying ﴿li-taskunu﴾ (that you may find tranquility) is the *lam* of causation (*li-l-ta'lil*), meaning: for the sake of your finding tranquility. It gives the reason for His saying ﴿from yourselves﴾.

As for his saying "(wa-talfufuha)" (and you may become attached to them), is it like this, or "(i.e., that you may become attached to them)"?
* Student: "wa-talfufuha."
* Shaykh: "(wa-talfufuha)." *Al-sakan* (tranquility) means settling, as in *al-iskan* in a town, meaning settling in it. So the meaning is: you settle, feel at peace with them, and become attached to them, as the author said: "(﴿And He placed between you﴾ all together ﴿affection and mercy. Indeed in that﴾ mentioned ﴿are signs for a people who give thought﴾ to the handiwork of God)."

"(﴿And He placed between you﴾ all together)": does this mean between the husband and his wife, or between all people?
* Student: "Between the husband and his wife."
* Shaykh: That is the apparent meaning. But the author's words "(﴿And He placed between you﴾ all together)" imply generality. The context, however, is specifically about the woman and her husband. When this woman, a stranger whom you do not know and who does not know you beforehand, is joined to you by the marriage contract, God Most High places affection and mercy in your hearts.

It has been said that affection is in the woman's heart and mercy in the man's heart, because he is the one who holds authority over her and she is the one who inclines toward him. Thus affection comes from her and mercy from him, and the two qualities are distributed between the husband and the wife.

It has also been said that both qualities belong to each of the spouses: affection exists between the husband and his wife, and likewise mercy exists between them. This is the closer view, and reality supports it too. When a woman loves her husband, there is mercy in her. Were it not that the mother is the most merciful of women, we would say that her mercy is like a mother's mercy. For this reason you find her attentive to him when he is ill, sad when he is sad, and pleased when he is pleased. When the relationship between them is good, she may sell everything she owns for the sake of his comfort and happiness. This is undoubtedly mercy.

As for affection, it is evident. Were it not for the strength of affection between the spouses, the bond between them that God, the Mighty and Majestic, intended would not have formed, so that this creation might be completed and grow. For this reason God Most High placed affection and mercy.

Ibn al-Jawzi mentioned in *Sayd al-Khatir*: "Were it not that God, in His wisdom, decreed that this creation should continue, the union between husband and wife would be among the ugliest of matters, since each of them uncovers his nakedness to the other, and then this act, which some people may find repugnant, occurs. But God, glory be to Him, placed this affection between them so that affairs would be set right and creation would grow." This is correct and true. Were it not for God's placing this affection, union between the spouses would not occur. For this reason, whenever a husband or wife is averse to the other, the union between them diminishes.

﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who give thought﴾: ﴿Indeed in that﴾ refers to what has been mentioned, ﴿are signs﴾. The *lam* here is for emphasis (*li-l-tawkid*), and *ayat* is the plural of *ayah*.

Consider His saying: ﴿And of His signs is that He created for you from yourselves mates﴾, and then He said: ﴿Indeed in that are signs﴾. You may ask: what is this apparent contradiction, since He said at the beginning ﴿And of His signs﴾? We say to you: there is no contradiction in reality. Firstly, His saying ﴿And of His signs﴾ is partitive, and some signs may be a single sign while others may be more than one. Furthermore, ﴿He created for you from yourselves mates that you may find tranquility in them, and placed between you affection and mercy﴾ comprises four signs. So in the original creation there is one sign, but in the attributes of this creation, which develops, there are signs.
* Student: It is said that affection is at the beginning of married life, in the first years, and mercy comes after the children.
* Shaykh: This is contrary to the apparent meaning, because the apparent meaning is that they go together. Affection and mercy are linked.
* Student: Do affection and mercy exist after the contract, or after the union, or after the dealings between them?
* Shaykh: That relates to what takes place between the spouses. As for affection, the apparent meaning is that it exists from before. It has been said that it arises when the two are alone and become close. This courtship and agreement only occur out of affection, but it grows and increases in proportion to the union (...).

* * *

﴿He brings the living out of the dead and brings the dead out of the living﴾ [al-Rum 19]. What is meant here by the living and the dead?
* Student: Much. The dead is without a soul, and the living is that which has a soul.
* Shaykh: Give an example.
* Student: An example, according to the author's view, is the drop of semen, which is dead, from which something comes out...
* Shaykh: From which something comes out?
* Student: From it comes out the living.
* Shaykh: Does this include both moral and physical life?
* Student: Yes, it includes both physical and moral life.
* Shaykh: What is moral life?
* Student: A disbeliever brings forth a believer, or vice versa.
* Shaykh: A disbeliever brings forth a believer, or vice versa. Which of these is closer to the apparent meaning of the verse or its context?
* Student: Its apparent meaning is the physical.
* Shaykh: Yes, physical.

His Most High saying: ﴿And thus you will be brought forth﴾. What is its grammatical analysis (*i'rab*)?
* Student: The *kaf* can mean "like," and it is indeclinable in the accusative, functioning as an absolute object (*maf'ul mutlaq*). Or it may be (...).
* Shaykh: It is like the bringing forth of plants from the earth.

His Most High saying: ﴿And among His signs is that He created you from dust; then suddenly you are human beings dispersing﴾. How was man created from dust?
* Student: Originally, Adam was begun from dust, and Adam's offspring from semen.
* Shaykh: Yes. What is the meaning of His saying ﴿then suddenly you﴾? What is the meaning of *idha* (then suddenly), and what is its grammatical function?
* Student: It is *fuja'iyyah* (of sudden occurrence).
* Shaykh: *Idha* is *fuja'iyyah*.

His Most High saying: ﴿And among His signs is that He created for you from yourselves mates﴾. What is the meaning of ﴿from yourselves﴾?
* Student: It means from the human's essence.
* Shaykh: It means from your essences. Like what?
* Student: Like sight (...).
* Shaykh: A spouse is sight?! ﴿From yourselves mates﴾.

﴿And to Him belongs praise in the heavens and the earth, and at dusk and when you reach midday﴾ [al-Rum 18].

From this verse the following is derived:
* The mercy of God Most High toward His servants, in that He taught them what is in their interest.
* Among its benefits: that prayer is glorification and declaration of God's transcendence, because God applied the name of glorification (*tasbih*) to it.
* Among its benefits: the obligation of glorification within it, in the prayer, because we have already noted a principle: when a part of an act of worship is applied to the whole, this indicates that this part is one of its obligatory elements, and that it is indispensable within it.
* Among the benefits of the verse: a detailed indication of the five prayer times, from His saying ﴿when you reach the evening and when you reach the morning﴾.
* Among its benefits: that *masa'* (evening) is applied to the early part of the night. His saying ﴿when you reach the evening﴾ includes the sunset (*maghrib*) and the night (*'isha'*) prayers.

From this may be derived the permissibility of throwing the pebbles at night, the stoning of the pillars (*ramy al-jamarat*), because a man said: "O Messenger of God, I threw after I had reached the evening." He said: "There is no blame"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (83) and Muslim (1306/327), from 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr, may Allah be pleased with them both.]]. Since *masa'* applies to the early part of the night, and the Prophet (ﷺ) negated blame, it is known to be permissible.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the wisdom of God, the Mighty and Majestic, in distributing the prayers over these times. The wisdom has two aspects:

The first aspect: if they were all gathered into one time, the remaining times would be empty of connection with God, the Mighty and Majestic. Is this not so? That is, if a person prayed all five prayers at dawn, then the day and the night would have no obligatory prayers.

The second aspect: if they were made into a single time, there would be a kind of hardship. That is, it would be obligatory for a person to pray seventeen units (*raka'at*) at one moment. This involves hardship, hardship for the strong and the healthy, so how much more for the weak and the sick?!
* Among the benefits of the verses: the perfection of God, the Mighty and Majestic, as shown in His saying ﴿And to Him belongs praise in the heavens and the earth﴾.
* Among them: that He alone deserves to be praised absolutely. From where do we take this? From the placing of the predicate first: ﴿And to Him belongs praise﴾.
* Among its benefits: that whatever occurs in the heavens and the earth, whether good or evil, God Most High deserves praise for it. From where is this derived? From the unrestricted wording: ﴿And to Him belongs praise﴾, without specifying "for the good" or "for what is beneficial." Rather it is unrestricted.
* From it is derived: that God Most High is praised in every state.

Then He, Most High, said: ﴿He brings the living out of the dead and brings the dead out of the living, and gives life to the earth after its death; and thus you will be brought forth﴾ [al-Rum 19].
* In this verse: a demonstration of the power of God, the Mighty and Majestic, in that He brings the living out of the dead and the reverse. This is part of the completeness of power: that a thing be brought out of its opposite.
* Among its benefits also: His power to give life to the earth after its death, as shown in His saying ﴿and gives life to the earth after its death﴾.
* Among its benefits: the affirmation that voluntary acts (*al-af'al al-ikhtiyariyyah*) subsist in God, the Mighty and Majestic. Voluntary acts are those which He does by His will: if He wills, He does them, and if He wills, He does not. From where is this derived? From ﴿He brings the living out of the dead﴾ and His saying ﴿and gives life to the earth after its death﴾. The word ﴿after﴾ indicates that this thing comes into being.

The subsistence of voluntary acts in God, the Mighty and Majestic, is the position of the People of the Sunnah and the Community (*Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jama'ah*) entirely. None of them denies this. They affirm that the Istiwa' (settling) upon the Throne is an act of God, the descent to the lowest heaven is an act of God, the coming to judge between the servants is an act of God, wonder is an act of God, laughter is an act of God, and creation is an act of God.

They say: God does whatever He wills, however He wills, whenever He wills. But the people of innovation, such as the Mu'tazilah, the Ash'ariyyah and others, deny that voluntary acts subsist in Him. They say: if events subsisted in Him, He would be something that comes into being, whereas God, glory be to Him, has always been and always will be. We say: this is a false statement:
Firstly: because it is analogy (*qiyas*) against an explicit text, for the texts are abundant in affirming the voluntary acts of God, the Mighty and Majestic, which are connected to His will.
Secondly: your statement that events do not subsist except in something that comes into being is not correct. Events subsist only in a perfect being who is capable of what He wills. As for the claim that they subsist only in something that comes into being, what intellect requires this?

* Among the benefits of the verse: the analogy of the unseen to the seen, as shown in His saying ﴿and thus you will be brought forth﴾, for analogizing the unseen to the seen in order to bring about belief in it is an established method.
* Among its benefits: the affirmation of analogical reasoning (*qiyas*), from His saying ﴿and thus you will be brought forth﴾. The affirmation of analogy has many proofs in the Qur'an. Among them, in general terms and as an encouragement:
Every parable (*mathal*) God Most High struck in the Qur'an indicates the validity of analogy, such as ﴿The likeness of the life of this world is only﴾ [Yunus 24] and so on, and ﴿Their likeness is like that of one who kindled a fire﴾ [al-Baqarah 17], and what is similar to that. Parables consist of comparing one situation with another or one individual with another, so they indicate the validity of analogy.

Likewise, the stories of which God Most High said: ﴿There was certainly in their stories a lesson for those of understanding﴾ [Yusuf 111]. In the Sunnah too there is much of this, such as: "Do you have camels?" He said: "Yes." He said: "What colour are they?" He said: "Red"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5305) and Muslim (1500/18), from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]]. The hadith continues. And: "Do you see, if your mother had a debt, would you pay it off?"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6699) and Muslim (1148/155), from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.]]

Likewise, reason requires the validity of analogy, for sound and clear intellect cannot ever distinguish between two alike. Always, even a child: if you forbid him something and permit him its counterpart, he says: "How? Is this not like that?"

In short, this is something that intellects, natural dispositions and texts all testify to. As for false analogy, which some people expand so that they nullify the indication of the Book and the Sunnah, this is undoubtedly false. But sound analogy is beyond doubt.

Those who deny analogy are in reality confused. At times they resort to analogy without realizing it, and they cannot avoid analogizing. For if we wanted to confine the indication of the Book and the Sunnah regarding rulings to general principles, rules and standards alone, these would be complete, but individual cases and particulars have no end and no limit, and they will inevitably be compelled to establish these by analogy.
* Student: It must first come from generality, not analogy.
* Shaykh: Yes indeed. It falls under generality in terms of verbal inclusiveness if it is included in the wording. Sometimes it is not included in the wording, but it is covered by semantic generality, which is analogy, since semantic generality is analogy.

Then He, Most High, said: ﴿And among His signs is that He created you from dust; then suddenly you are human beings dispersing﴾ [al-Rum 20].
* From the benefits of the verse: the affirmation of signs (*ayat*) belonging to God, the Mighty and Majestic, meaning the indications that point to His attributes. Every act indicates some kind of sign, but in general terms all acts indicate power and wisdom. Yet each kind has its own specific sign: wisdom, power, might, and so on.
* Among the benefits of the verse: that the origin of the children of Adam is dust, from His saying ﴿that He created you from dust﴾.
* Among its benefits: the refutation of the atheistic theory, the theory of evolution (*nazariyyat al-nushu' wa al-tatawwur*), which was advanced by, or whose leader was..."
* Student: Darwin.
* Shaykh: Darwin.
* Student: Darwin.
* Shaykh: Or Darwin, yes. This is an erroneous and false theory without doubt. The way this is shown from the verse is that God says ﴿that He created you﴾, addressing humankind as human beings. Thus he has been a human since he was produced from dust until today.

As for those people, they say that the origin of man is not a human; it is an ape. They say the origin of man is an ape, which then evolved into a human. I do not know what they say about the origin of donkeys, mules, horses, and chickens, and what is their origin?! They evolved into...

Then we do not know what the other evolution is. Will we become angels?! In any case, this theory, praise be to God, has even been nullified by Western philosophers now, and it has become clear to them that it is a false and erroneous theory. Furthermore, we know with certainty that it is false and that believing in it is disbelief, because it is a denial of the Qur'an, the Sunnah and the consensus of the Muslims.
* Student: Explicit (...).
* Another student: He says: the separation from the sun, the mechanical structure of the universe, a self-formation. Man separated from the sun in the form of (...), then evolved into an amoeba, then into an ape, then into (...), then into a human.
* Shaykh: All of this is undoubtedly a lie. All of it is a lie with no basis. Man was created from dust, as God, the Mighty and Majestic, said: dust which God made into clay, then pottery, until it became sounding clay, which rings when struck ﴿like pottery﴾ [al-Rahman 14], as God, the Mighty and Majestic, said. Then he became a human being, and God is capable of all things.
* Student: Is this denial (...) by what is explicit, or by clear evidence?
* Shaykh: No, by what is explicit, by the explicit text of the Qur'an.
* Student: This is, I mean...
* Shaykh: This, and others besides it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 30, verses 10–23 (part 6 of 6):

* Among the benefits of the verse: this human race, which was created from one origin, spread out and filled the earth. This is shown by His saying: ﴿then, behold, you are human beings spreading out [across the earth]﴾. This is one of Allah's signs. How did one origin, one man, produce this creation that spread through all the regions of the earth?
* Another benefit of the verse: man is naturally in motion. He must move, spread out, go and come. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The most truthful of names are Harith (cultivator) and Hammam (one who is concerned)."[[Abu Dawud (4950) narrated with his chain from Abu Wahb al-Jushami, who had companionship with the Prophet, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Name yourselves with the names of the prophets. The names most beloved to Allah are 'Abd Allah and 'Abd al-Rahman, and the most truthful of them are Harith and Hammam, and the most repugnant of them are Harb (war) and Murrah (bitterness)."]] This is because a person is always concerned, tills the land, and seeks his livelihood.

Then the Exalted said: ﴿And of His signs is that He created for you﴾ [al-Rum 21].

Know that I have consulted many of the tafsirs I have, and I have not found the wisdom in why He, glorified and exalted is He, says: ﴿And of His signs is that He created you from dust﴾ [al-Rum 20], ﴿And of His signs is the creation of the heavens﴾ [al-Rum 22], ﴿And of His signs is your sleep﴾ [al-Rum 23], and ﴿And of His signs is that He created for you﴾ [al-Rum 21].

That is, I have not seen anyone explain the wisdom behind His sometimes using the verbal noun (al-masdar) and sometimes using ﴿an﴾ (أَنْ) followed by a verb, which is interpreted as a verbal noun. But do we say that this is a case of variation in expression that takes the wording into account, or is it a case of variation in expression that takes the meaning into account?

If we say it is a variation that takes the wording into account, the matter is simple: we say that Allah varied the expressions so that the listener would not grow bored when speech follows one pattern, since variation in expression renews a person's energy and vitality.

As for saying that there is a meaningful reason, I have not known it until now, and neither al-Zamakhshari nor Abu al-Su'ud nor those who speak on such matters have mentioned it.

As for His saying: ﴿And of His signs is that He created for you from yourselves mates that you may find tranquility in them﴾ [al-Rum 21], let us return to the benefits of the verse.

* Among the benefits of the verse: the mercy of Allah, blessed and exalted is He, toward us, in that He made our spouses from ourselves, that is, from our own kind.
* Among its benefits: one of the most important purposes and aims of marriage is tranquility with the wife, feeling secure with her, and living with her a happy life. A person who sees that there is no tranquility and that circumstances do not come together should part ways. For this reason the scholars said that divorce is recommended when the woman is harmed by remaining with the husband, because she is harmed and does not feel at ease with him. A husband should not force her to remain with him. Some people, may Allah protect us, force their wives to stay, or they withhold them so that they will ransom themselves and pay money in order to be divorced. All of this is forbidden.

When you see that your wife cannot live with you a happy life, you should divorce her. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever relieves a believer of one of the distresses of this world, Allah will relieve him of one of the distresses of the Day of Resurrection."[[Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (2442) and Muslim (2580/58), from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both.]] And the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Allah is in the aid of the servant as long as the servant is in the aid of his brother."[[Narrated by Muslim (2699) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]]

In the Qur'an: ﴿And if they separate, Allah will enrich each of them from His abundance﴾ [al-Nisa 130]. So if you intend good by providing generously for this woman who did not live with you and whom you separated from, perhaps Allah will make the matter easy for you by bringing you a wife with whom you are compatible and who is compatible with you. The point is that among the most important purposes of marriage is what? Tranquility, peace with the wife, and a happy life.

* Among the benefits of the verse: affirmation of the wisdom, power, and mercy of Allah, since He placed between the spouses affection and mercy.
* Among its benefits also: praise of reflection, based on His saying: ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who give thought﴾ [al-Rum 21]. It is clear that this is a place of praise for them.
* Among its benefits: reflection opens many doors through which a person comes to know, from the rulings and wisdoms of Allah, what he would not know if he did not reflect, because He specified the signs for whom?
* Student: For a people who give thought.
* Shaykh: For the people who give thought. This indicates that through reflection one gains knowledge of the rulings and wisdoms of Allah that one would not gain through heedlessness.

Reflection is directed at the signs of Allah, that is, His creation and His legislation, because the signs, as was previously mentioned, are either cosmic (kawniyyah) or legislative (shar'iyyah). From what aspect does reflection on the attributes of Allah take place: from the aspect of meaning, or from the aspect of modality (kayfiyyah)?
* Student: From the aspect of meaning.
* Shaykh: From the aspect of meaning. As for the aspect of modality, reflection is not permitted. It is not permitted to reflect on the attributes from the standpoint of their modality, because that is an attempt at what cannot be attained. For this reason Imam Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "Asking about it is an innovation (bid'ah)." So it is not permitted for us to reflect on the modality of any attribute of Allah. We reflect on the meaning without the modality.

Reflection on the essence (dhat) of Allah, glorified is He, is likewise not permitted, because it is an attempt at what cannot be reached. Moreover, such reflection leads to calamities and ruin. What harmed those who harmed themselves, among the people of ta'til (denial of attributes) and also among the people of tashbih (likening Allah to creation), was attempting to reach the modality. This led them to either ta'til or tamthil (comparison). The point is that reflection takes place on the creation of Allah, on His legislation, and on the meanings of His names and attributes. As for His essence and the modality of His attributes, there is no reflection on them, because however far a person goes, thought will return to him humbled and exhausted. Turning away from this is obligatory, as Imam Malik said.

* Student: How do we know that ﴿So glory be to Allah when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning﴾ [al-Rum 17] refers to the times of the prayers? What is the evidence?
* Shaykh: The evidence is that Allah specified general glorification (tasbih) at two times: ﴿And exalt with the praise of your Lord before the rising of the sun and before its setting﴾ [Qaf 39]. And when He made it five times, it became known from the contextual indication of the division of time that the intended meaning is the five prayers.
* Student: (...) His saying, glorified and exalted is He: (...) ﴿that you may find tranquility in them﴾.
* Shaykh: Yes, that is correct. The lam is for causation (ta'lil), so it affirms wisdom, in refutation of the Jahmiyyah. Likewise the Ash'ariyyah, who deny the wisdom of Allah, glorified is He, and the Mu'tazilah. Or not?
No, the Mu'tazilah go to excess in affirming wisdom. For this reason they hold that it is obligatory upon Allah to do what is best (al-aslah) or what is good (al-salah).
* Student: Shaykh, regarding (...) in rejecting the attributes.
* Shaykh: In what?
* Student: In rejecting the attributes. Is it (...) based on rational premises agreed upon among them, or does each one rationalize according to his own intellect?
* Shaykh: No, each one rationalizes. That is, they differ in the rationale for this rejection. They differ. Sometimes they say that it entails corporeality (jismiyyah), but most of what they rely upon is comparison (tamthil), that it entails comparison. But they differ in the methods that lead to it.
* Student: The matter of resurrection in His saying: ﴿And thus you will be brought forth﴾ [al-Rum 19].
* Shaykh: Did we not discuss it?
* Student: No, we mentioned analogy (qiyas).
* Shaykh: Correct. The affirmation of resurrection in His saying ﴿And thus you will be brought forth﴾ is something we did not mention in the first verse.

* * *

He says: ﴿And of His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Rum 22].

﴿Of His signs﴾ is the predicate placed first (khabar muqaddam), and ﴿the creation﴾ (khalq) is the postponed subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar). ﴿The creation of the heavens﴾ means their bringing into existence, bringing them into existence with precise measure and wondrous order. This includes the creation of these heavens considered as enormous celestial bodies, and considered as a benefit to the servants. This is one of the signs of Allah.

He says: ﴿And the difference of your languages﴾ [al-Rum 22]. The difference of languages is also one of the signs of Allah. The reason is that these tongues are of one kind or one genus. We are all human beings, and we all come from one father, yet languages differ enormously, is that not so?

Likewise, it is also one of the signs of Allah, because every person is recognized by his race through his language. For example, I can recognize that this one is Indian, this one is Turkish, this one is English, perhaps, this one is German, this one is Russian, by his language. This too is one of the signs of Allah, that He made it an indication of the human species.

His saying ﴿And the difference of your languages﴾ includes the basic language, includes dialects, includes soundness from defects, includes defects as well, and includes eloquence and its opposite. That is, do not think that our difference is merely the difference of language types. Rather, it includes all of this. The varieties of languages are among the signs of Allah, the Exalted. That this person pronounces the letters completely is one of the signs of Allah. The other, on the contrary, pronounces them with a lisp or a stammer, or something similar.

Likewise, we may say that among the differences of tongue is the voice, the differences of voices. This one's voice is good, this one's is pleasant, and the other is the opposite.

Likewise, among the differences of tongue is eloquence, is it not? Eloquence and its absence. Some people Allah grants eloquence in speech and good delivery, to the point that he conveys the meaning to you in clear expression that you understand the first time. Other people are the opposite. Everything that can occur in the difference of tongues falls within its being one of the signs of Allah, the Exalted.

As for colors, speak without restraint, for they are among the signs of Allah. You can hardly find two people identical in color ever. Even if they were twins, there must be some difference. Some of it is apparent and some of it is not. The white European man and the black man who lives on the equator, I believe, have between them a difference, a vast difference, and between these there are varying degrees. But you can hardly find two of the same color. This is part of wisdom, because if this were not so, people would be confused about one another. Perhaps someone would be seized and say: "Come, give me my right, you, so-and-so son of so-and-so," and he would say: "No, I am not." But he has become exactly like him. And what would make him know?

It is said that Allah made for every person forty look-alikes, but I do not think this is sound. Rather, it is said that the fingerprints on the fingertips differ, that each person has fingerprints of a shape that does not match another's. This is the apparent truth. For this reason, fingerprints are now relied upon in investigations, which indicates that they definitely differ. This is one of the things that shows the power of Allah, glorified and exalted is He. This tremendous difference, among millions upon millions of people, yet each person cannot be identical to another in every respect. There must be a distinguishing mark (...).

[[The author's speech has been abridged due to its great length.]]

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 30, verse 10–23 (part 1 of 6):

He said: ﴿Then the end of those who did evil was the worst, because they denied the signs of Allah and used to mock them﴾ [al-Rum 10]. First: His saying, ﴿Then the end of﴾, al-'Aqibah (the outcome, end) is a verbal noun meaning al-'Uqba, and there are two canonical readings for it: the accusative, ﴿'Aqibata﴾, and the nominative, ﴿'Aqibatu﴾.

On the nominative reading it is the subject (ism) of (kana), and on the accusative reading it is the predicate (khabar) of (kana) placed before its subject. The question then arises: where is the subject of (kana) on the accusative reading, or its predicate on the nominative reading? The author will mention it.

He said: ﴿Then the end of those who did evil﴾, meaning those who performed evil deeds from among the disbelievers who denied the messengers, as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has related. Their opposite, aḥsanū (they did good), is used of those of whom Allah said: ﴿For those who did good is the best (reward) and more﴾ [Yunus 26]. As for those who did evil, their end was what Allah mentions here.

And his saying: (﴿al-Su'a﴾ is the feminine of al-Asw'a, the worst).

﴿al-Su'a﴾ is therefore an elative (ism tafdil) in the feminine. Just as we say al-Fudhla is an elative, and al-'Uzhma is also an elative. What is the masculine of al-Fudhla? Al-Afḍal. And the masculine of al-'Uzhma is al-A'zam, the masculine of al-Ula is al-Awwal, and the masculine of al-Su'a is al-Asw'a.

So ﴿al-Su'a﴾ here is a feminine elative, the feminine of al-Asw'a.

The author says: the meaning of (al-Asw'a: the most ugly). That is, their evil deed resulted in something worse, and this is worse in comparison with the bliss they enjoyed in this world; after that they met the Hellfire.

Do not think that this verse indicates that an evil deed is recompensed with something worse than it, because Allah says: ﴿Whoever comes with an evil deed will be recompensed only with its like, and they will not be wronged﴾ [al-An'am 160]. Rather, "the worst" is relative to their state, not to the recompense for their evil. They had been blessed in this world, and for the disbeliever the world was a paradise. When they died upon disbelief they passed to something far worse, and it is not compared to their state in this world.

The author said in the grammatical analysis (i'rab): (The predicate of kana is in the nominative case of 'aqibah, and the subject of kana is in the accusative case of 'aqibah). The author has informed us that in ﴿'Aqibah﴾ there are two readings: the accusative and the nominative.

On the nominative reading, how do we parse it?
* A student: The predicate of (kana).
* The Shaykh: No, the subject of (kana). It is the subject of (kana), and ﴿al-Su'a﴾ is its predicate, in the accusative with a implied fatha on the alif, the utterance of which is prevented by the difficulty of pronunciation (ta'adhdhur).

On the accusative reading we parse ﴿'Aqibata﴾ as the predicate of (kana) placed first, and ﴿al-Su'a﴾ as its delayed subject. This is one of the grammatical possibilities.

It has also been said that ﴿al-Su'a﴾ is an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq), meaning: they committed the worst evil, so it is an absolute object. And the subject or predicate would be the interpreted verbal phrase from his saying ﴿that they denied﴾, meaning: their end, when they did evil, became that they denied, because evil deeds—may Allah protect us—lead to further evil, just as good deeds lead to further good deeds.

However, what the author favoured is better: that we make ﴿al-Su'a﴾ either the predicate of kana on the nominative reading, or its subject on the accusative reading.

He says: (What is meant by it is Hell, and their evil deed, ﴿that﴾, meaning in that ﴿they denied the signs of Allah﴾: the Qur'an, ﴿and they used to mock them﴾).

The author has made clear to us that the end was that they were punished with the Fire, and that the verbal phrase in ﴿that they denied﴾ is the reason (illah) for their end being the worst, meaning: because they denied Our signs. But he used the preposition bi (with), and bi indicates causation, while li (for) indicates purpose, and the meaning is the same: their end was ﴿al-Su'a﴾ because they denied the signs of Allah.

This applies to the reports of the signs, that they denied them and said they were not true. As for the action: ﴿and they used to mock them﴾, so they combined mocking the rulings with denying the reports.

This too is one of the possibilities he takes for the parsing of ﴿that they denied﴾, since there is another view that says ﴿that they denied﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿al-Su'a﴾, or an explanatory apposition (bayan) to it, and the meaning would be: they committed the worst evil, which is their denial; so their end would be denial and mockery.

In any case, whether we say it is a substitute or explanatory apposition for ﴿al-Su'a﴾, or we say it is a causal clause explaining the establishment of the worst for them, it indicates that these people were deniers and mockers: denying the report and mocking the ruling, taking Allah's signs in jest regarding the rulings and denying them regarding the reports. You find them, for example, in their prayer at the House praying with whistling and clapping, and mocking those who believed, and so on, taking them in jest.

The author's statement, may Allah have mercy on him: (﴿that they denied the signs of Allah﴾: the Qur'an) has clear difficulty, because the verse is general, so it includes whoever denied the signs of Allah by the Qur'an after the mission of the Messenger (ﷺ), and whoever denied the Torah in the time of Musa and the Gospel in the time of 'Isa. So the correct view regarding the verse is generality.

Indeed, even if it were said that those who denied the Qur'an are not included in it, there would be a basis for that; that is, if it were said that the matter is the reverse of what the author said. Allah said: ﴿Have they not travelled in the land and seen how was the end of those before them? They were greater than them in strength, and they tilled the earth and populated it more than these have populated it, and their messengers came to them with clear proofs. Allah would not have wronged them, but they used to wrong themselves (9). Then the end of those who did evil was the worst﴾. The context concerns peoples who came before, not present people.

Therefore the author's taking the signs here to mean the Qur'an is very far-fetched. We must either make it general or make it refer to the earlier nations; but to restrict it to the Qur'an has clear difficulty.

As for his saying: ﴿that they denied the signs of Allah and used to mock them﴾, the signs here mean the legislative signs (ayat shar'iyyah), since they are the object of denial, though denial may also be of the cosmic signs (ayat kawniyyah).

As for his saying: ﴿and they used to mock them﴾, is mockery verbal or practical?
* A student: No, verbal.
* The Shaykh: Mockery includes both verbal and practical mockery. Verbal mockery is to ridicule them, as was reported of the hypocrites who said: "We have never seen anyone like these reciters of ours, more gluttonous in their bellies, more lying in their tongues, and more cowardly in battle"[[Reported by al-Tabari in his Tafsir (16912) from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both.]]

Or someone who prays mocking the prayer, or performs Hajj mockingly, or does any act of worship in a manner of scorn, ridicule and belittlement: ﴿and they used to mock them﴾ [al-Rum 10].

Allah the Exalted said: (﴿Allah originates creation﴾: that is, He brings the creation of people into existence; ﴿then repeats it﴾: that is, their creation after their death; ﴿then to Him you will be returned﴾, with the yā' and with the tā' readings) [al-Rum 11].

This is to confirm faith in the Last Day. Allah, glorified and exalted, reminded His servants of a matter they acknowledge, namely that He originated creation, and no one denies that. No one claims that he created himself; everyone knows that he was made from nothing. It is evident that if someone claimed he was created without a creator, every person would refute him. And if he admits that there must be a creator, we say to him: who? Name Him for us. He then cannot name Him, and we say: the One who created you is Allah.

﴿Allah originates creation﴾: that is, He brings it into being the first time, as He said: ﴿Say: He will give them life who produced them the first time﴾ [Ya-Sin 79]. The development of creation and its being made in stages is a known matter, because this is what wisdom requires: the wisdom of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is that things develop gradually until they reach the limit of perfection.

And His saying: ﴿then repeats it﴾. Is (thumma) for ordering with an interval, or for ordering in immediate succession? For ordering with an interval, because the repetition only occurs at the establishment of the Hour, and the establishment of the Hour is far removed from the origination of creation.

And His saying: ﴿then repeats it﴾: that is, He returns it a second time, and He does not begin a new creation; rather He repeats what came before—pay attention—so it is not the creation of a new creature but the restoration of what preceded. There is a difference between the two matters: if we said it is the beginning of a new creation, it would mean that someone who did not act would be punished, and someone who did not act would be granted bliss. Moreover, the deniers of resurrection would not accept that it is a new creation, since they acknowledge the origination; they only deny what?
* Students: The repetition.
* The Shaykh: The repetition: ﴿Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?﴾ [Ya-Sin 78]. On this basis, resurrection is a repetition and a gathering of what was scattered, not the beginning of a new creation.

If it is said: this scattered thing became dust and vanished, or a person was eaten by beasts or fish or the like, we say: whatever the case, Allah, Exalted, is able to gather it and then repeat it. Therefore He said: ﴿then repeats it, then to Him you will be returned﴾: then to Him, not to anyone else.

﴿you will be returned﴾ has two readings: ﴿yurja'un﴾ and ﴿turja'un﴾. On the reading with tā', the sentence is addressed to the second person; on the reading with yā', it is in the third person. On the yā' reading the difficulty is that He said ﴿yurja'un﴾ although the subject ﴿creation﴾ ﴿originates creation﴾ is singular. The context would suggest: then to Him it is returned. But He said ﴿yurja'un﴾.

The answer to this is that "creation" (al-khalq) is a verbal noun used in the sense of the passive participle, so the meaning of ﴿originates creation﴾ is: originates the created beings. But since it is a verbal noun, a verbal noun is not made dual or plural. Ibn Malik said in the Alfiyyah:

"They used the verbal noun as an adjective often, so they adopted the singular and the masculine."

On this basis we say: creation here means the created beings, that is: then to Allah these created beings are returned after the repetition, and this return to Allah is for the sake of recompense and reckoning, then their final destination is either the abode of bliss or the abode of Hellfire: ﴿then to Him you will be returned﴾.

(﴿And on the day the Hour is established, the criminals will be dumbfounded﴾: the polytheists will fall silent because their argument is cut off.)

His saying: ﴿And on the day﴾: (day) here is an adverbial of time governing ﴿will be dumbfounded﴾, and it is annexed to the clause after it. Where is the clause after it?
* A student: ﴿the Hour is established﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿the Hour is established﴾, so the clause is in the genitive position by annexation.

His saying: ﴿And on the day the Hour is established﴾ means: it comes, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿It will not come to you except suddenly﴾ [al-A'raf 187].

The Hour meant here is the Hour of resurrection, so the definite article (al) in it is for a known reference. Which kind of reference?
* A student: The mental (dhihni) reference.
* The Shaykh: The mental reference, meaning the known, great Hour in which the creatures rise from their graves to Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

﴿will be dumbfounded﴾ he says: (will fall silent), ﴿the criminals﴾. So al-iblas means silence. It has also been said that al-iblas means despair, because of Allah's saying: ﴿And indeed they were, before it was sent down to them, utterly despairing﴾ [al-Rum 49], meaning: despairing. From it comes Iblis, because he despaired of Allah's mercy.

On this basis ﴿yublisu﴾ means "they despair", and it is not far-fetched that the verse combines both meanings: they despair and therefore fall silent, since when a person despairs he falls silent and says nothing, as speech will not benefit him. On this basis, what is the meaning of ﴿yublisu﴾?
* A student: They despair.
* The Shaykh: They despair, together with silence.

His saying: ﴿the criminals﴾ is the active participle of (ajrama), meaning he committed a crime (jurm), which is a grave sin. Therefore the author explained it as (the polytheists), and that it refers to the polytheists is shown by Allah's saying: ﴿And there will not be for them any intercessors from among their partners﴾ [al-Rum 13]. On the Day of Resurrection they will despair and fall silent, and they will not find any argument: ﴿And there will not be for them any intercessors from among their partners﴾.

﴿And there will not be﴾: the author said: (that is, there will not be). Note this: why did he explain lam (not) as la (not)? Because lam is used for the past tense, as in ﴿And there was not for them among their partners﴾, which suggests that this matter has already occurred. Has it occurred or not?
* A student: It has not happened.
* The Shaykh: It has not happened, because it is the Day of Resurrection. So the past form here has the sense of the future: they will despair and there will not be for them at that time. In my view there is no need for this interpretation, that is, no need to make lam mean la; because the saying ﴿yublisu﴾ and ﴿wa lam yakun﴾ is restricted by the word ﴿yublisu﴾, meaning: and there will not be for them in the state of despair, and the state of despair will be on the Day of Resurrection. But the author's view is to take the verse as unrestricted, without being limited by ﴿yublisu﴾, and on this basis we must say that lam means la.

He said: (﴿And there will not be for them among their partners﴾: that is, among those they associated with Allah—the idols—to intercede for them ﴿intercessors﴾), and so on to the end.

﴿There will not be for them among their partners intercessors﴾: what is the parsing of ﴿intercessors﴾?
* A student: Subject.
* The Shaykh: No.
* A student: The subject of ﴿yakun﴾.
* The Shaykh: The subject of ﴿yakun﴾. ﴿among their partners﴾ is its predicate, placed first.

His saying: ﴿their partners﴾ is the plural of (shareek), which has the sense of the passive participle, like qatil meaning maqtul: mashruk bihi, that is, those associated with Allah. The meaning is: those whom they made partners with Him, as the author said: (that is, those they associated with Allah). So the genitive construction here is an annexation of a thing to its object, not to its subject: those whom they made partners to them.

His saying: ﴿intercessors﴾ is the plural of (shafi'), in the sense of shafi'. The intercessor is one who mediates for you, either to bring a benefit or to ward off a harm. Intercessor: one who intercedes for you, either to bring a benefit or ward off a harm. He is called shafi' because through him you became a pair (shaf'); before him you were alone, and with him you became a pair. Therefore the intercessor is called shafi' for this reason.

We said that the intercessor is one who intercedes for you and mediates, either to bring a benefit or to ward off a harm. An example of bringing a benefit?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, like what?
* The student: A poor person who mediates for someone with the king so that he gives him from charity.
* The Shaykh: Correct, this is bringing a benefit.

And warding off harm? An example of warding off harm?
* A student: He takes him out of prison; he mediates for him.
* The Shaykh: He takes him out of prison?
* The student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Is that correct?
* Students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Yes. Its example in the Sharia also: the intercession of the Prophet (ﷺ) for the people of the Fire that they not enter it, yes?
* A student: Warding off harm.
* The Shaykh: Warding off harm.
And his intercession for the people of Paradise that they enter it.
* A student: Bringing a benefit.
* The Shaykh: This is bringing a benefit.

These ones: ﴿there will not be for them among their partners intercessors﴾.

(﴿And they will be﴾: that is, they will be—as he said regarding ﴿lam yakun﴾: "that is, will not be"—that is, they will be ﴿disbelievers in their partners﴾: that is, disavowing them.) Yes. On the Day of Resurrection, these partners whom they used to hope would benefit them—on the Day of Resurrection?
* A student: They will disbelieve.
* The Shaykh: They will disbelieve in them and disown them: ﴿When those who were followed disown those who followed﴾ [al-Baqarah 166]. ﴿And those who followed will say: If only we had another return, we would disown them as they have disowned us﴾ [al-Baqarah 167]. On the Day of Resurrection they will disbelieve in them: neither these nor those. The worshipped disbelieve and the worshippers also disbelieve; each of them disbelieves in some of the others, may Allah protect us. Whereas in the world they hoped for their intercession and benefit: ﴿We worship them only that they may bring us nearer to Allah in position﴾ [al-Zumar 3]. But on the Day of Resurrection—may Allah protect us—some of them disown others: ﴿And they will be disbelievers in their partners (13). And on the day the Hour is established, that day they will be separated﴾ [al-Rum 13–14].

﴿And on the day the Hour is established﴾: we say about it what we said before: that by the Hour is meant the known, well-understood Hour of resurrection.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 30, verses 10–23 (part 2 of 6):

And His saying: (﴿﴿يَوْمَئِذٍ﴾ ﴾ is emphasis, ﴿﴿يَتَفَرَّقُونَ﴾ ﴾ means the believers and the disbelievers).

His saying: ﴿يَتَفَرَّقُونَ﴾ is related to ﴿يَوْمَ تَقُومُ السَّاعَةُ﴾, meaning that ﴿يَوْمَ تَقُومُ السَّاعَةُ﴾ is connected to ﴿يَتَفَرَّقُونَ﴾. And the second ﴿يَوْمَئِذٍ﴾?

* Student: It is emphasis.
* Shaykh: It is emphasis for the first. The proof that it is emphasis is that if it were removed and it were said, "And on the day the Hour is established they will separate," would the sentence be sound or not?
* Student: It would be sound.
* Shaykh: It would be sound, but the emphasis that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, intended would be lost. That is: "on that day, on that day," for emphasis.

And His saying: ﴿يَوْمَئِذٍ﴾. The tanwin in ﴿يَوْمَئِذٍ﴾, in all its occurrences, they say it is a substitute ('iwad). For what?

* Student: For a clause.
* Shaykh: For a clause. That is: "the day when the Hour is established." The same is said of ḥīnaʾidh, and it is also said of waqtaʾidh: the tanwin here is a substitute for a clause, meaning "the day when, and the time when, such-and-such occurs, and the moment when such-and-such occurs."

And His saying: ﴿يَتَفَرَّقُونَ﴾. Does the pronoun refer to creation, so that it includes the believer and the disbeliever, even if they were relatives? If the father were Muslim and his son a disbeliever, or the reverse, they would separate, because it is the abode of recompense and each one will be recompensed for his deeds.

﴿يَوْمَئِذٍ يَتَفَرَّقُونَ﴾. How is the separation? He said: (﴿﴿فَأَمَّا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَعَمِلُوا الصَّالِحَاتِ فَهُمْ فِي رَوْضَةٍ﴾ ﴾: a garden ﴿﴿يُحْبَرُونَ﴾ ﴾: they will be made joyful) [Ar-Rum: 15].

(أمّا, ammā) They say it is a conditional and differentiating particle; therefore it is always used in places of differentiation: ﴿فَأَمَّا مَنْ أَعْطَى وَاتَّقَى﴾ [Al-Layl: 5], then he mentioned its opposite?

* Student: ﴿وَأَمَّا مَنْ بَخِلَ وَاسْتَغْنَى﴾ [Al-Layl: 8].
* Shaykh: ﴿وَأَمَّا مَنْ بَخِلَ وَاسْتَغْنَى﴾. It is also a conditional particle, and therefore it requires an answer: ﴿فَأَمَّا مَنْ أَعْطَى وَاتَّقَى (٥) وَصَدَّقَ بِالْحُسْنَى (٦) فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُ﴾ [Al-Layl: 5–7]. And here: ﴿فَأَمَّا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَعَمِلُوا الصَّالِحَاتِ فَهُمْ فِي رَوْضَةٍ﴾ [Ar-Rum: 15]. So it is a conditional and differentiating particle, and it also includes the meaning of emphasis, for it reinforces. Your saying, "As for whoever does such-and-such, he has such-and-such," is stronger than your saying, "Whoever does such-and-such, he has such-and-such." So it conveys, on this basis, the conditional, the differentiation, and the emphasis, and it strengthens the speech.

﴿فَأَمَّا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾: ﴿الَّذِينَ﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and the predicate is ﴿فَهُمْ فِي رَوْضَةٍ﴾.

His saying: ﴿آمَنُوا وَعَمِلُوا الصَّالِحَاتِ﴾ means they combined faith and action. Know that when faith (īmān) is mentioned alone, it includes action, just as when righteous deeds are mentioned alone, they include faith. That is, when each is mentioned singly, the intended meaning is its general sense. When one is joined with the other, faith refers to the inner deeds and deeds refer to the outward deeds performed by the limbs.

Faith includes belief in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and divine decree, both its good and its evil. This is how the Prophet (ﷺ) explained it to Jibril when he asked him: "What is faith?" He said: "That you believe in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, and the Last Day, and that you believe in the decree, its good and its evil."[[Narrated by Muslim (8/1) from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both.]]

As for righteous deeds: the word "deed" ('amal) includes both the act and the utterance. Righteous deeds include the speech of the tongue and the actions of the limbs. We have often been told that a righteous deed is that which combines two matters: sincerity to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and following His Messenger (ﷺ).

And His saying: ﴿الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَعَمِلُوا الصَّالِحَاتِ﴾: both of these matters are necessary: faith and action. Does faith alone benefit?

* Student: No.
* Shaykh: It does not benefit without action, and action without faith also does not benefit. Both faith and action are necessary. From this we understand that some unrestricted texts that promise Paradise to one who has in his heart an atom's weight of faith, and the like, mean faith that necessarily includes action, either actually or by implication.

* Student: What are "actually" and "by implication"?
* Shaykh: "Actually" means that he is in fact acting. "By implication" means that he was unable to act, but faith was with him, as with al-Usayram of Banu 'Abd al-Ashhal at Uhud, whose story is well known.

And His saying: ﴿فَهُمْ فِي رَوْضَةٍ يُحْبَرُونَ﴾. The sentence here is a nominal sentence, to indicate permanence and continuity. ﴿فِي رَوْضَةٍ﴾: the author says, "a garden" (jannah), and it is so. The rawḍah is an expression for gardens containing flowers, trees, pleasant fragrances, and delightful scenery. Therefore he said: (﴿﴿يُحْبَرُونَ﴾ ﴾: they will be made joyful). It has also been said: ﴿يُحْبَرُونَ﴾ means they will be given bounty, and the two are interrelated, since bounty brings about joy. Those who believed and did righteous deeds are in a garden, made joyful.

The second division: ﴿وَأَمَّا الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا وَكَذَّبُوا بِآيَاتِنَا وَلِقَاءِ الْآخِرَةِ فَأُولَئِكَ فِي الْعَذَابِ مُحْضَرُونَ﴾ [Ar-Rum: 16]. ﴿الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾ by abandoning righteous deeds; ﴿وَكَذَّبُوا بِآيَاتِنَا﴾ by not believing.

The author's saying: (﴿﴿بِآيَاتِنَا﴾ ﴾: the Qur'an) is it correct?

* Student: It is preceding.
* Shaykh: The Qur'an alone, no. It is not from what precedes it. "Our signs" includes the Qur'an and other than the Qur'an, definitely, because those who believed and did righteous deeds, and those who disbelieved and denied the signs of Allah and His meeting, will exist in this Ummah and in other than it.

And His saying: (﴿﴿وَلِقَاءِ الْآخِرَةِ﴾ ﴾: the resurrection and other matters). What is the resurrection? It is the bringing forth from the graves. (And other matters): such as the reckoning, recompense, Paradise, and Hellfire. They deny these and say: "There is no Paradise, no Hellfire, no reckoning, and no punishment."

And it is astonishing that this false and corrupt view has been adopted by those who call themselves "the wise," who are the philosophers. They say there is no Paradise, no Hellfire, and no resurrection, but that the messengers said this in order to keep people on the path they had devised for them. They claim, may Allah protect us, that the messengers were geniuses with intelligence, good conduct, and organization, but that if they had said to people, "Do this or do not do that," without encouragement or warning, people would not have obeyed them. So they told people: "You have a mighty Lord, a powerful God, and you have a return in which there is Paradise or Hellfire."

And they, while the matter is not so in their view, mentioned that only to keep people upon the path they had established for them. This implies disbelief in the resurrection, in prophethood, and even in themselves, for whoever does not believe in Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has first disbelieved in himself, since he has denied that he has a Creator.

And His saying: (﴿﴿وَلِقَاءِ الْآخِرَةِ﴾ ﴾: the resurrection and other matters ﴿﴿فَأُولَئِكَ فِي الْعَذَابِ مُحْضَرُونَ﴾ ﴾). I seek refuge in Allah. ﴿أُولَئِكَ فِي الْعَذَابِ﴾: by punishment is meant retribution here, and punishment is made a container for them, because it surrounds them from every side, as Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿يَوْمَ يَغْشَاهُمُ الْعَذَابُ مِنْ فَوْقِهِمْ وَمِنْ تَحْتِ أَرْجُلِهِمْ﴾ [Al-'Ankabut: 55].

﴿فَأُولَئِكَ فِي الْعَذَابِ مُحْضَرُونَ﴾: what is the meaning of ﴿مُحْضَرُونَ﴾? It is from ihḍār (causing to be present). "I brought him" means I made him present that thing. So these are brought forth in the punishment against their will. If the matter were left to themselves, they would not be present, but they are brought into it unwillingly: ﴿فَأُولَئِكَ فِي الْعَذَابِ مُحْضَرُونَ﴾.

Allah, Exalted, said: (﴿﴿فَأُولَئِكَ فِي الْعَذَابِ مُحْضَرُونَ (١٦) فَسُبْحَانَ اللَّهِ﴾ ﴾: that is, glorify Allah) [Ar-Rum: 16–17].

The i'rab (grammatical analysis) of ﴿سُبْحَانَ اللَّهِ﴾.

* Student: It is in the accusative because it is a verbal noun (maṣdar), and it is obligatorily so.
* Shaykh: And its governing verb?
* Student: Its governing verb is "glorify Allah."
* Shaykh: Yes. The author says: (that is, glorify Allah). He made the absolute object (maf'ul muṭlaq) here carry the sense of an imperative verb, not that its governing verb is omitted, but he made it a substitute for its verb (that is, glorify Allah). The glorification of Allah, Exalted, means declaring Him free from what does not befit Him, and this includes two things: first, freeing Allah from every deficiency in His attributes of perfection; second, freeing Allah from resemblance to created beings.

﴿سُبْحَانَ اللَّهِ﴾. I say: tanzih (declaring Allah free of imperfection) includes two matters:

First: freeing Allah from deficiency in His attributes of perfection.

Second: freeing Allah from resemblance to created beings.

As for the first, we often see that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is described as not becoming tired, not wronging, not being heedless, and the like. Why? Because of the perfection of His attributes.

As for resemblance to created beings, Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿لَيْسَ كَمِثْلِهِ شَيْءٌ وَهُوَ السَّمِيعُ الْبَصِيرُ﴾ [Ash-Shura: 11]. Freeing Allah from resemblance to created beings is in reality freeing Him from deficiency, because the created being is deficient, and likening the Perfect to the deficient makes Him deficient. Indeed, comparing Him with them diminishes His rank, as it was said:

Do you not see that the sword loses its worth when it is said that the sword is sharper than the staff?

﴿فَسُبْحَانَ اللَّهِ﴾. The author says: (that is, glorify Allah, meaning pray). The author has informed us that what is meant by glorifying Allah here is a specific glorification, namely prayer. From where did he derive this restriction? Someone might say: "Glorification is general, including prayer and other things." The author derived it from its being tied to these times, for tying it to these times indicates that prayer is meant.

Glorification was applied to prayer because glorification is one of its obligatory parts, as Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿فَسَبِّحْ بِاسْمِ رَبِّكَ الْعَظِيمِ﴾ [Al-Waqi'ah: 74]. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Put it in your bowing,"[and for ﴿سَبِّحِ اسْمَ رَبِّكَ الْأَعْلَى﴾ [Al-A'la: 1] he said: "Put it in your prostration."[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (869) from 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir, may Allah be pleased with him.]] Accordingly, prayer is what is meant by glorification. What indicates the restriction, or the specification? Its being tied to the times of prayer (...).

* * *

﴿ثُمَّ كَانَ عَاقِبَةَ الَّذِينَ أَسَاءُوا السُّوأَى أَنْ كَذَّبُوا بِآيَاتِ اللَّهِ وَكَانُوا بِهَا يَسْتَهْزِئُونَ﴾ [Ar-Rum: 10].

* From this verse is derived: the evil end of wrongdoers, for what is the end of those who did evil? ﴿السُّوأَى﴾.
* Student: (...) or is it doubt?
* Shaykh: Let us see. [It is] because of His saying ﴿السُّوأَى﴾, and this is clear according to the author's view, for he made ﴿السُّوأَى﴾ the predicate of (kāna) or its subject, depending on the reading of ﴿عَاقِبَةَ﴾.
* From this benefit it follows that the end of the doer of good is the good end, for the ruling revolves with its cause. If the end of the wrongdoers is evil, then the end of the good-doers is good, and His saying, Exalted, supports this: ﴿لِلَّذِينَ أَحْسَنُوا الْحُسْنَى وَزِيَادَةٌ﴾ [Yunus: 26].
* From the benefits of the verse: wrongdoing here is denying the signs of Allah and mocking them, according to the author's interpretation, for he said: (that is, that they denied). According to the second view, His saying ﴿أَنْ كَذَّبُوا﴾ is the end.
* From it is derived: that the end of sins is disbelief, namely denial of the signs of Allah and mockery of them, if we say that His saying ﴿أَسَاءُوا السُّوأَى﴾ means they committed evil deeds, then their end was denial and mockery. This means that sins are a cause of disbelief, and it is so. Scholars have said: sins are the courier of disbelief.
* From the benefits of the verse: the revelation that Allah sent down to the messengers is among His signs, as His saying shows: ﴿أَنْ كَذَّبُوا بِآيَاتِ اللَّهِ﴾. It is among His signs because of what it contains: truthfulness in reports, benefit in narratives, justice in rulings, and reform. So all revealed books contain these matters: truth in reports, benefit in narratives, justice in rulings, and welfare for the servants. Therefore these books are among the signs of Allah, because it is not possible for humans to produce the like of them.
* From the benefits of the verse: the difference between denial and mockery. Denial is rejecting a report; mockery is ridiculing outward or inward deeds. Which is more severe?
* Student: Mockery.
* Shaykh: Mockery is more severe, because it combines denial and ridicule.
* From the benefits of the verse: a warning against evil deeds, since this is their end, whether we say that "the evil" is the end, or that the end is denial, for it includes a warning against evil deeds.

Then Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿اللَّهُ يَبْدَأُ الْخَلْقَ ثُمَّ يُعِيدُهُ ثُمَّ إِلَيْهِ تُرْجَعُونَ﴾ [Ar-Rum: 11].

* From this noble verse is derived: the power of Allah, Glorified and Exalted, in that He originated creation.
* The second benefit: the proof that the world has a beginning, and that it is not eternal without a beginning, as the philosophers claim, because Allah originated it. Origination means that it was previously nonexistent?
* Student: Non-existence.
* Shaykh: Non-existence.
* From the benefits of the verse: the proof of resurrection, by His saying: ﴿ثُمَّ يُعِيدُهُ﴾.
* From its benefits: resurrection is not the origination of a new creation but a restoration, contrary to those who say that resurrection is an origination of creation. From where do we take this?
* Student: ﴿يُعِيدُهُ﴾.
* Shaykh: From His saying ﴿ثُمَّ يُعِيدُهُ﴾, and the pronoun refers to the creation that was originated. We have previously mentioned, in our discussion of this verse, that if resurrection were the origination of a new creation, then whoever did not work would be punished and whoever did not work would be given bounty. But resurrection is a restoration of what preceded.
* Student: Shaykh, is it a restoration of the same bodies, or does He cause a new growth?
* Shaykh: These very substances that were crumbled and went away will be restored, which Allah will bring back. The same dust, when it has turned to dust, will be restored, and so on.
* Student: It is not that He creates a body (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, but this created body is the very first one; Allah gathers what was scattered from it and then revives it.
* From the benefits of the verse: arguing from the beginning to the return. From where is this taken? From His saying ﴿يَبْدَأُ﴾ and ﴿ثُمَّ يُعِيدُهُ﴾, because this is an argument from the beginning to the return. Reasoning from the beginning to the return is true, logical, and rational reasoning. Which is harder and more difficult?
* Students: The first.
* Shaykh: The first. So the One able to originate is able to restore. Therefore Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿وَهُوَ الَّذِي يَبْدَأُ الْخَلْقَ ثُمَّ يُعِيدُهُ وَهُوَ أَهْوَنُ عَلَيْهِ وَلَهُ الْمَثَلُ الْأَعْلَى فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ﴾ [Ar-Rum: 27]. Everything is easy for Him, but this is easier, because it is a restoration.
* From the benefits of the verse: the return of all creatures is to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in the Hereafter, or even in this world? In this world and in the Hereafter. In the Hereafter they return to Allah so that He may judge between them with recompense, and in this world they return to Allah so that He may judge between them by their deeds: ﴿وَمَا اخْتَلَفْتُمْ فِيهِ مِنْ شَيْءٍ فَحُكْمُهُ إِلَى اللَّهِ﴾ [Ash-Shura: 10], which is a statement, and ﴿فَإِنْ تَنَازَعْتُمْ فِي شَيْءٍ فَرُدُّوهُ إِلَى اللَّهِ وَالرَّسُولِ﴾ [An-Nisa: 59]. The main point is that the return is to Allah in both this life and the next. We return to Allah in the affairs of our worldly life and in the affairs of our religion, and likewise in the matter of the Hereafter we return to Allah, and He will repay us according to what we deserve.
* Student: In the verse (...) the Hereafter.
* Shaykh: No, it is the Hereafter by priority only, because of this context. But there is no objection to its being general, especially since He mentioned: ﴿وَهُوَ الَّذِي يَبْدَأُ الْخَلْقَ﴾ [Ar-Rum: 27].
* From its benefits: it is not permissible to seek judgment from other than Allah. From where is this taken?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, it is taken from this sentence, but what is its basis? Restriction, by His saying ﴿إِلَيْهِ﴾, meaning: not to other than Him.

Then Allah, Glorified and Exalted, said: ﴿وَيَوْمَ تَقُومُ السَّاعَةُ يُبْلِسُ الْمُجْرِمُونَ وَلَمْ يَكُنْ لَهُمْ مِنْ شُرَكَائِهِمْ شُفَعَاءُ وَكَانُوا بِشُرَكَائِهِمْ كَافِرِينَ﴾ [Ar-Rum: 12–13].

* From this verse is derived: first, the establishment of the Hour, and that it is certain to occur, by His saying: ﴿وَيَوْمَ تَقُومُ السَّاعَةُ﴾.

Among its benefits: when the Hour comes, the people of shirk will fall silent and despair of mercy, as His saying shows: ﴿The criminals will be struck dumb﴾. This is unlike their state in this world, where they stubbornly resist and exalt themselves through their idols, as Abu Sufyan said: "Exalt Hubal!" [[As in the hadith of al-Bukhari (3039) from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, may Allah be pleased with him.]]. But in the Hereafter they have no movement and no voice: ﴿The criminals will be struck dumb﴾.

Among its benefits: these objects of worship do not benefit their worshippers at the time they most need them, do they? The indication in the verse is: ﴿And they will have no intercessors from among their partners﴾. That day is the time of intercession, yet they gain nothing from these idols. Moreover, a second benefit: they will disavow them: ﴿And they will disbelieve in their partners﴾, just as the idols will disavow them as well: ﴿And who is more astray than one who calls upon other than Allah those who will not respond to him until the Day of Resurrection, and who are unaware of their supplication? And when the people are gathered, they will be enemies to them and will deny their worship﴾ [al-Ahqaf 5–6]. Each will disown the other, although that is the place of distress and the place of relief.

Among the benefits of the verse: it points out that these polytheists only committed shirk seeking that these associated beings would be intercessors, and Allah stated this explicitly in His saying: ﴿We worship them only that they may bring us nearer to Allah in position﴾ [az-Zumar 3].

So when those who worship graves say: "We do not worship them because we hope for direct benefit from them, but we worship them so that they may intercede for us with Allah," we say: this is the shirk of the earlier people, and this is what Allah related of the polytheists: that they did not seek direct benefit, but wanted these to be their intercessors before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And on the day the Hour is established, that Day they will be separated. As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, they will be in a meadow, made happy﴾ [ar-Rum 14–15], and so on to the end.

From His saying ﴿And on the day the Hour is established﴾ is derived: the affirmation of the Resurrection.

Among its benefits: on that day people will separate into two groups: a group in Paradise and a group in the Blaze.

Among its benefits: fathers with their children, and mothers with their children, if one of them is a disbeliever and the other a believer, will be separated, and no one can rescue anyone on that day, due to the generality of His saying: ﴿They will be separated. As for those who believed﴾ [ar-Rum 14–15]; He did not exempt children with their parents or the reverse. On that day there is no gathering except for those who are upon the truth.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: No, it does not include (...), because the believers go in one direction; for this reason He said: ﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, they will be in a meadow﴾ and ﴿And as for those who disbelieved﴾, so He made them two divisions.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: In their dwellings in Paradise, it is known that each is in his station; but in the plains of Resurrection the group of believers as a whole and the group of disbelievers as a whole will be together. But in their dwellings in Paradise they differ; each is in his own station.
