[Reported by al-Bukhari (4974) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.] So it explains the verse: the originating of creation is not easier for Me than its restoration. It makes clear that all of this is easy for Him. But there is no doubt that restoration is easier in terms of what is understood by the addressees, so what the author, may Allah have mercy on him, adopted here is sound.

﴿وَهُوَ أَهْوَنُ عَلَيْهِ وَلَهُ الْمَثَلُ الْأَعْلَى فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ﴾ [al-Rum 27]: that is, the highest attribute, which is that there is no god but Allah.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿وَلَهُ الْمَثَلُ﴾. ﴿لَهُ﴾ is a fronted predicate, and ﴿الْمَثَلُ﴾ is a delayed subject. The word "mathal" is applied to several meanings. It is applied to resemblance, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿مَثَلُهُمْ كَمَثَلِ الَّذِي اسْتَوْقَدَ نَارًا﴾ [al-Baqarah 17], meaning: their likeness is like the likeness of one who kindled a fire. "Mathal" is also applied to attribute, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿مَثَلُ الْجَنَّةِ الَّتِي وُعِدَ الْمُتَّقُونَ فِيهَا أَنْهَارٌ مِنْ مَاءٍ غَيْرِ آسِنٍ﴾ [Muhammad 15]. And "mathal" is applied to essence. They said: among it is the words of the Exalted: ﴿لَيْسَ كَمِثْلِهِ شَيْءٌ﴾ [al-Shura 11], meaning: there is nothing like His essence. You also see that "mathal" and "mithl" are the same, their meaning is one. And they said: among it is the saying of the poet:

"There is none like the youth Zuhayr" ∗∗∗ ..........................

What is meant by "mathal" here, in "and to Him belongs the highest example"? Which of the meanings? The attribute: to Him belongs the highest attribute in the heavens and the earth. Every perfect attribute belongs to Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, in its most complete form, and every attribute of deficiency He is free of. Why is He exempted from the attribute of deficiency? Because once the highest, perfect attribute is established for Him, the absence of deficiency is necessarily implied by reason; for if He were characterized by any deficiency, He would not deserve to have the highest example. Is that not so?

Student: Yes.

Shaykh: So this noble verse indicates the attributes of perfection of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, absolute perfection, because He said: ﴿الْمَثَلُ الْأَعْلَى﴾, and it indicates the absence of deficiency in every respect, since if He were characterized by any deficiency, He would not deserve to have the highest example.

From this we derive that everything with which Allah described Himself is an attribute of perfection, with no deficiency in it. Is that not so?

Students: Yes.

Shaykh: Everything with which Allah described Himself is an attribute of perfection, and every perfection is one that Allah the Exalted is entitled to. These are two things. First: that we know with certainty that everything with which Allah described Himself is an attribute of perfection. Second: that we know that every attribute of perfection is one that Allah the Exalted is entitled to, He being worthy of it, as the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The One worthy of praise and glory" [Reported by Muslim (477/205) from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri]. What will come, Allah willing, in the benefits (fawa'id) is what can be used as evidence to refute those who deny the attributes of Allah on the pretext that they imply deficiency, which is anthropomorphism (tashbih).

As for His words: ﴿الْمَثَلُ الْأَعْلَى فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ﴾, what is the meaning of "the highest example in the heavens and the earth"? Yes: it means among the people of the heavens, the angels, and among the people of the earth. Every sound natural disposition (fitrah) acknowledges that the highest example and the highest attribute belong to Allah alone. As for the author's words, "that there is no god but Allah," this is one instance of the highest example, not the whole of it, for "there is no god but Allah" indicates His singularity in divinity, and this is part of the highest example. But the highest example is more general than that. For instance, He has complete power, complete knowledge, complete life, complete hearing, complete sight, and perfect wisdom, and so on. So it is more general than His singularity in divinity.

(﴿وَهُوَ الْعَزِيزُ﴾ [al-Rum 27] in His dominion, ﴿الْحَكِيمُ﴾ [al-Rum 27] in His creation.) This explanation of his has a shortcoming. "Al-'Aziz" means the possessor of might (izzah), which is domination, subjugation and power. So He has the might of subjugation and of power, the Mighty and Majestic. Thus "izzah" has three meanings: the might of subjugation, meaning He is the Subduer of everything, so no one overcomes Him. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿وَلِلَّهِ الْعِزَّةُ وَلِرَسُولِهِ وَلِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ وَلَكِنَّ الْمُنَافِقِينَ لَا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ [al-Munafiqun 8].

Second: the might of standing (qadr). What is meant by the might of standing? It means that He, glorified, has no equal and no likeness, because of the perfection of His standing and His greatness. Among its usage is when one says: this thing is 'aziz, meaning rare in existence with no equal.

The third meaning of 'izzah: the might of inaccessibility (imtina'), meaning that deficiency is impossible for Him because of the completeness of His strength. From this is the saying: "This land is 'azaz," meaning hard and strong, so nothing can penetrate it. A soft land is the opposite; everything affects it, even a man's foot leaves its mark when he walks on it, does it not? Unlike the hard land, which is called 'azaz.

So now the might of standing and the might of subjugation are established, and the third is the might of inaccessibility.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿وَمَا ذَلِكَ عَلَى اللَّهِ بِعَزِيزٍ﴾ [Ibrahim 20]: from which meaning?

Students: Inaccessibility.

Shaykh: Yes, inaccessibility. ﴿بِعَزِيزٍ﴾ means "not inaccessible" (bi-mimtani'), so it is of the might of inaccessibility.

As for His words ﴿الْحَكِيمُ﴾, the author says: "the Wise in His creation," and sometimes he says "in His making," and the two have one meaning. But this is also deficient, because "hakim" is derived from ḥukm (judgment) and ḥikmah (wisdom). So if we say it is derived from ḥukm, then hakim means ḥakim (judge), like raḥim meaning rāḥim (merciful). And if we say it is from ḥikmah, then hakim means mutqin (perfecter), so it is from aḥkama, yuḥkimu (to make firm and perfect).

Does the pattern fa'il come with the meaning of mufʻil in the Arabic language? The answer: yes. Among it is the words of the Exalted: ﴿عَذَابٌ أَلِيمٌ﴾ [al-Baqarah 10], meaning: painful (mu'lim). And among it is the saying of the poet:

"Does the caller Rayhanah, the listener (al-sami'), keep me awake while my companions sleep?"

"The caller ... al-sami'" means al-musmi' (the one who makes to hear), because the caller makes another hear, and he is not himself "sami'". So we say: if hakim is from wisdom, it is from what? From aḥkama, meaning perfected. Pay attention to its explanation: hakim, we say, is derived from ḥukm and ḥikmah. On the basis that it is derived from ḥukm, it means ḥakim (judge), like raḥim meaning rāḥim, sami' meaning sāmi'.

If we say it is from ḥikmah, it is from aḥkama, so it is hakim meaning muḥkim (the one who makes firm), i.e., an active participle of the quadriliteral form.

The ḥukm of Allah the Mighty and Majestic is divided into two kinds: cosmic (kawni) and legislative (shar'i). The cosmic judgment takes effect over all creation, whether they will or not; the legislative takes effect on whom? On whoever obeys Allah the Mighty and Majestic. As for whoever does not obey Him, His judgment does not take effect.

Are there examples in the Qur'an that show this division, that judgment is cosmic and legislative? We say: yes, it exists. One of the brothers of Yusuf said: ﴿فَلَنْ أَبْرَحَ الْأَرْضَ حَتَّى يَأْذَنَ لِي أَبِي أَوْ يَحْكُمَ اللَّهُ لِي وَهُوَ خَيْرُ الْحَاكِمِينَ﴾ [Yusuf 80]. The judgment meant here is the cosmic, decreed judgment, meaning: or Allah decrees that. As for the legislative judgment, when Allah mentioned what is obligatory regarding the emigrant women in Surah al-Mumtahanah, what did He say? He said: ﴿ذَلِكُمْ حُكْمُ اللَّهِ يَحْكُمُ بَيْنَكُمْ﴾ [al-Mumtahanah 10]. The judgment meant here is the legislative, because all the matters mentioned are legislative matters.

What do you say about His words: ﴿وَلَهُ الْحُكْمُ وَإِلَيْهِ تُرْجَعُونَ﴾ [al-Qasas 70]? Which of the two judgments? It is comprehensive. Likewise His words: ﴿وَمَنْ أَحْسَنُ مِنَ اللَّهِ حُكْمًا لِقَوْمٍ يُوقِنُونَ﴾ [al-Ma'idah 50]. The apparent meaning is that it is comprehensive, though in this verse it is more evident in the legislative sense, because Allah said: ﴿أَفَحُكْمَ الْجَاهِلِيَّةِ يَبْغُونَ وَمَنْ أَحْسَنُ مِنَ اللَّهِ حُكْمًا لِقَوْمٍ يُوقِنُونَ﴾ [al-Ma'idah 50].

So the Hakim, derived from ḥukm, is divided into two: legislative judgment and cosmic judgment. The cosmic judgment is His decree and His destiny, and everyone is subject to it. The legislative judgment is what He has judged by law, and is everyone subject to it? No, not everyone is subject to it.

As for if we say it is from aḥkama, hakim from wisdom meaning muḥkim, the scholars say wisdom is divided into two kinds: purposive wisdom (ḥikmah ghā'iyyah) and formal wisdom (ḥikmah ṣūriyyah), meaning the form of a thing is such and such. The fact that a thing is in a particular form: we find that everything Allah created in its attributes is in a form that accords with wisdom. Reflect on the creatures and you will find that the creatures, in their essences, movements, shapes and attributes, are all in accordance with wisdom.

Purposive wisdom is the praiseworthy ends in His acts and His legislative rulings. Everything Allah the Mighty and Majestic created is for a praiseworthy end; not in vain or aimless. ﴿وَمَا خَلَقْنَا السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضَ وَمَا بَيْنَهُمَا لَاعِبِينَ (38) مَا خَلَقْنَاهُمَا إِلَّا بِالْحَقِّ﴾ [al-Dukhan 38-39]. ﴿وَمَا خَلَقْنَا السَّمَاءَ وَالْأَرْضَ وَمَا بَيْنَهُمَا بَاطِلًا ذَلِكَ ظَنُّ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا فَوَيْلٌ لِلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا مِنَ النَّارِ﴾ [Sad 27]. Even what Allah decrees of painful matters is wisdom. The defeat of the believers on the day of Uhud was wisdom, was it not? Yes, undoubtedly wisdom. ﴿وَمَا أَصَابَكُمْ يَوْمَ الْتَقَى الْجَمْعَانِ فَبِإِذْنِ اللَّهِ وَلِيَعْلَمَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ (166) وَلِيَعْلَمَ الَّذِينَ نَافَقُوا﴾ [Al 'Imran 166-167]. And He said: ﴿وَلِيُمَحِّصَ اللَّهُ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَيَمْحَقَ الْكَافِرِينَ﴾ [Al 'Imran 141].

So all of Allah's acts, the Exalted, are wisdom and have a praiseworthy end. Likewise His legislative rulings are like His cosmic judgments: they are placed in a particular form that accords with wisdom, and their praiseworthy ends, by which the hearts, lands and servants are reformed, are also wisdom. So wisdom, O our brothers, is of two kinds: wisdom in a thing's particular form, and wisdom in its praiseworthy end. This wisdom appears both in the Shari'ah and in the destiny, in the cosmos. When we know that Allah the Exalted is Wise, we become completely reassured about what He has decreed and destined, and what He has legislated and judged, we are reassured, and that it accords with wisdom. At that point we cannot object, nor should there be an objection to (...) "why was this legislated, from where was that legislated," except as a seeking of guidance. The person who asks about the wisdom seeking guidance is fine; but the one who asks about wisdom in objection is deficient and has not measured Allah with His due measure.

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿ضَرَبَ لَكُمْ مَثَلًا مِنْ أَنْفُسِكُمْ﴾ [al-Rum 28]. Take care regarding the word ﴿الْحَكِيمُ﴾, and by this explanation we have given, it becomes clear that the author, may Allah have mercy on him, fell short in explaining it.

(﴿ضَرَبَ لَكُمْ مَثَلًا﴾: "daraba" means "ja'ala" (made); ﴿لَكُمْ﴾ O polytheists; ﴿مَثَلًا﴾ being, ﴿مِنْ أَنْفُسِكُمْ﴾, and it is..)

﴿ضَرَبَ لَكُمْ مَثَلًا﴾: "mathal" means resemblance and equal. That is: He presented to you a matter equal to what you have done regarding the side of Allah the Mighty and Majestic. What is this example? ﴿هَلْ لَكُمْ مِنْ مَا مَلَكَتْ أَيْمَانُكُمْ مِنْ شُرَكَاءَ فِي مَا رَزَقْنَاكُمْ﴾ [al-Rum 28]. He says: (and it is ﴿هَلْ لَكُمْ مِنْ مَا مَلَكَتْ﴾; ﴿مِنْ مَا﴾ means "from that which"; ﴿مَلَكَتْ أَيْمَانُكُمْ﴾ means "from your slaves"; ﴿مِنْ شُرَكَاءَ﴾ "partners" for you.)

The phrase ﴿مِنْ شُرَكَاءَ﴾ grammatically is a subject into which the particle "min" entered for generality. But it may be problematic for us, since "min" is only added after a negation. What does Ibn Malik say on this question?

"And it is added after negation and its like, so it governs an indefinite noun, as for a rebel there is no escape."

What we have now, ﴿مِنْ شُرَكَاءَ﴾: we said that this "min" is grammatically superfluous, but in meaning it has a meaning, which is to make explicit the generality. Ibn Malik mentioned that it is only added after a negation and its like. What we have now is like a negation, yes, because it is an interrogative in the sense of negation: meaning, "you have no partners from what your right hands possess in what We have provided you."

As for His words ﴿مِنْ شُرَكَاءَ﴾, meaning: partners with you (﴿فِي مَا رَزَقْنَاكُمْ﴾ from wealth and other things, ﴿فَأَنْتُمْ﴾ and they ﴿فِيهِ سَوَاءٌ﴾), this ﴿فَأَنْتُمْ فِيهِ سَوَاءٌ﴾ does not refer back to the negation, but refers back to the negated matter: meaning, "are you equal in what We have provided, fearing them as you fear yourselves?" That is, like your free peers. The interrogative has the sense of negation; the meaning is: your slaves are not partners with you, and so on, with you. So how do you make some of Allah's slaves partners with Him?!

As for His words ﴿تَخَافُونَهُمْ كَخِيفَتِكُمْ أَنْفُسَكُمْ﴾ [al-Rum 28], the author, may Allah have mercy on him, says: (i.e., your equals among the free), so he took "anfusakum" here in the sense of kind, since "nafs" as mentioned earlier comes in the sense of kind. He means: are these slaves partners with you in your provision of wealth and children, equal to you, and you fear them as you fear yourselves? What is the answer? No. If that is so, why do you make these idols partners with Allah, when they are created by Him, owned by Him, and nurtured by Him?

So the example is very clear: these polytheists distinguish between two equals, is that not so?

Student: Yes.

Shaykh: Just as you now acknowledge that your servants do not equal you in rank and do not share your provision, likewise what Allah the Mighty and Majestic possesses of these idols and others does not equal Allah the Exalted in rank and does not share in His rights. This is a very clear example.

An example from ourselves also: a man disciplines his son when he errs. Some people say to him: why do you discipline your son, why do you beat him, why do you scold him? What does he say to them? He says: Don't you do the same to your son? What is the answer? The answer: Yes. So how do you blame me for something you yourself do?

What is said to those whom Allah mentions: how do you make a partner with Allah in what belongs to Him alone, when you do not make for yourselves a partner from your servants in what you specially possess of provision? And strangely, this verse has been cited by those who hold socialism. When socialism first appeared in the Arab world, they began bringing ambiguous texts and said: this verse is explicit about socialism.

How so? He says: ﴿فَأَنْتُمْ فِيهِ سَوَاءٌ﴾. See how they deceive! This is not as they intended; this falls within the negation, meaning: you are not equal in it, is that not so?

Students: Yes.

Shaykh: This is the meaning of the verse. But always the people of falsehood dress up their falsehood with ambiguous texts, and this is among the wisdoms of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, that there are ambiguous things in the texts, so that whoever goes astray goes astray through them. And Allah knows best. And I found this (...)

﴿مِنَ السَّمَاءِ مَاءً﴾ and so on.

Among the benefits of this noble verse:

First: that lightning is among the signs of Allah, Glorified and Exalted, as He says: ﴿And among His signs is that He shows you lightning﴾.

Another benefit of the verse: that lightning contains both fear and hope, as He says: ﴿as a fear and a hope﴾.

It has already been noted that the correct view is that these are not distributed (between the two) as the author held; rather, it is a single comprehensive attribute.

Another benefit of the noble verse: the greatness of Allah's power in sending down water from the sky.

Among them: His mercy towards creation, in that this rain is sent down from the sky (this is one), and in that it descends little by little; for if it descended all at once, it would destroy people.

Among the benefits of the verse: the demonstration of Allah's power, in that He gives life to the earth after its death. You see the earth dry, with not a green twig in it; then after the rain falls, it becomes green and stirs with life.

Among them: His mercy towards creation as well, for the reviving of the earth is beneficial to humans and animals.

Another benefit of the noble verse: that only people of understanding benefit from the signs. Shall we take this? —

A student: ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who reason﴾.

The Shaykh: Yes.

Another benefit of the noble verse: the use of reason in analogy, in comparing similar things and applying the like to its like.

Another benefit: that analogy (qiyas) is among the rational proofs, even though it is established by the Sharia; but its method is reason, because the intellect is guided by this to that and moves from this to that.

Allah's words: ﴿And among His signs is that the heaven and the earth stand by His command﴾ and so on to the end.

Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the standing of the heavens and the earth by Allah's command is not connected in any way to created beings. It is Allah, Exalted, who holds them up, who sustains the heavens and the earth, whether in the sensory or the figurative sense.

Among them: the affirmation of speech for Allah. From where? —

A student: His words: ﴿when He calls you with a call﴾.

The Shaykh: No, before that.

A student: ﴿by His command﴾.

The Shaykh: ﴿by His command﴾. The author said "by His will," and this has been pointed out before: what is meant by ﴿by His command﴾ is speech.

Another benefit of the noble verse: the perfection of Allah's power in raising the dead with a single word: ﴿Then, when He calls you with one call from the earth, behold, you will come forth﴾. Notice, brothers, that the matter is not the creation of one person, or two, or three, or ten, but of what none can count except Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. A single call by which all creation comes forth — this is without doubt among the most eloquent demonstrations of power, and that Allah, Glorified and Exalted, is over all things capable.

It is also deduced from the verse that the abode of the children of Adam is the earth, as His words show: ﴿when He calls you with one call from the earth, behold, you will come forth﴾. This is supported by His words: ﴿From it We created you, into it We return you, and from it We bring you forth once more﴾ [Ta-Ha 55]. In this verse the complement is placed first: ﴿in it﴾ and ﴿from it﴾, and the fronting of the complement indicates restriction (exclusivity). And from this matter (...).

So life on the planets is impossible for the children of Adam; this is the apparent meaning of the verses, since the children of Adam were created from the earth, return to the earth, and will be called from the earth on the Day of Resurrection.

Among them: the affirmation of speech for Allah in His words: ﴿Then, when He calls you with one call from the earth﴾.

As for His words: ﴿And to Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾: it is deduced from it that Allah's dominion is general. From where is generality taken? From the words ﴿whoever is in the heavens﴾, since (man) is a relative pronoun, and all relative pronouns indicate generality.

It is also deduced from the verse that Allah, the Mighty, alone possesses dominion and is specially characterized by it. From where is this taken? From the fronting of the predicate: ﴿And to Him belongs whoever…﴾, meaning: not to anyone else. Or not?

Here an objection arises regarding His words ﴿And to Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾: we find that the children of Adam possess some things of this, or not?

Students: Yes.

The Shaykh: What is the answer to that?

We say: the answer is that the dominion of the children of Adam is a dominion restricted by the grant of the One who holds dominion. Therefore you cannot dispose of your property as you wish. Can you burn your property? You cannot burn it, nor destroy it. True, you own it in relation to other human beings, who cannot prevent you; but in relation to the Creator, who holds the dominion, He prevents you from this. So our possession of what we own is not complete ownership.

Its proof, or its basis, is that we cannot and do not have the power to dispose freely of what is in our hands as we wish.

It is also deduced from the noble verse: the submission of all creatures to their Lord, Glorified and Exalted. From where? ﴿All are devoutly obedient to Him﴾, and that all creatures are subject to Allah.

And it is deduced from this: that qunut (devout obedience) is not restricted to the legal qunut. Most people think qunut is restricted to the legal qunut: ﴿Guard strictly the prayers, and the middle prayer, and stand before Allah devoutly obedient﴾ [al-Baqara 238]. That is certainly a legal qunut; but this verse and similar ones indicate that qunut is submission to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, whether that submission is legal or cosmic (kawni).

Then He says: ﴿And He it is who originates creation, then repeats it, and that is easier for Him﴾.

It is deduced from this noble verse: that creation is originated after it was not, or not? Creation is originated after it was not. From where is this taken? ﴿And He it is who originates creation﴾. So the verse contains a refutation of the statements of the philosophers who hold that the world is eternal. The correct view is that the world is originated after it was not, by His words: ﴿He it is who originates creation﴾.

Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of the re-creation of creation, by His words: ﴿then repeats it﴾.

Also among its benefits: the use of qiyas al-awla (analogy a fortiori). I suppose you know qiyas al-awla in the principles of jurisprudence. Inferring the like from the like is qiyas al-musawat (analogy of equality); inferring a matter that is more fitting than the analogized case is called qiyas al-awla. Here the verse uses qiyas al-awla. From where is this taken?

A student: ﴿and that is easier for Him﴾.

The Shaykh: His words ﴿and that is easier for Him﴾ refer to His repeating it. For if He is capable of the beginning, then the repetition is a fortiori.

A student: On one of the two views, Shaykh?

The Shaykh: Yes, according to what the author adopted.

Among the benefits of the verse: the affirmation of the perfection of Allah's attributes, by His words: ﴿And His is the highest description in the heavens and the earth﴾.

Among its benefits: a refutation of the people of ta'til (denial of attributes) who deny Allah's attributes. Those who deny His attributes have not ascribed to Him the highest description; rather they have ascribed to Him deficiencies, may Allah protect us. Whether this denial is total or partial: if it is total, as the Jahmiyya did, stripping Him of all attributes, and likewise the Mu'tazila who said He has names without attributes, note that they stripped Allah of perfection. If it is partial, as the Ash'ariyya and Maturidiyya and their like did, this too involves stripping Allah of perfection in what He described Himself with. Is that not so?

A student: Yes.

The Shaykh: ﴿The Most Merciful, established over the Throne﴾ [al-A'raf 54]. Istiwa' is an attribute of perfection, and they say ﴿istawa﴾ means "istawla" (seized dominion), so they do not single out the Throne for istiwa' over it, since Allah is dominant over everything.

Likewise, when they say that the verses' intended meaning is contrary to the apparent meaning, they describe Allah, Mighty and Majestic, with deficiency. How so? Because a speaker intending something contrary to the apparent meaning of his speech, without clarification, is considered deception and concealment. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sent down the Qur'an only for clarification: ﴿Allah desires to make clear to you and to guide you to the ways of those before you﴾ [an-Nisa' 26]; ﴿Allah makes clear to you, lest you go astray﴾ [an-Nisa' 176]; ﴿And We sent down to you the Reminder, that you may make clear to the people﴾ [an-Nahl 44]. The verses on this are many. So if we say that Allah intended by this something contrary to the apparent meaning, this is an ascription to Him of obscurity, Glorified and Exalted, and that He does not desire clarification. This is without doubt a deficiency. Hence we say that all who deny Allah's attributes, whether totally or partially, have ascribed deficiency to Allah, Glorified and Exalted. Is it clear?

Among the benefits of this noble verse: every attribute by which Allah described Himself is an attribute of perfection. Is that not so?

A student: Yes.

The Shaykh: From where is this taken?

A student: ﴿And His is the highest description﴾.

The Shaykh: ﴿And His is the highest description.﴾ So when He affirms an attribute for Himself, we know it is an attribute of perfection. Mercy: Allah affirmed it for Himself. Is it an attribute of perfection or of deficiency?

A student: Perfection.

The Shaykh: Perfection. But to the people of ta'til and tahrif it is an attribute of deficiency. They say mercy indicates softness and weakness, so Allah's mercy is not meant as mercy but as kindness, or synonymous with kindness; they interpret it either as the created reward or as His will. And on this, measure the rest.

Can it be deduced from this noble verse the use of qiyas al-awla regarding Allah: that we say every attribute of perfection in a created being, the Creator is more deserving of it?

Students: Yes.

The Shaykh: Yes indeed. Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, affirms this: that the use of qiyas al-awla concerning Allah is permissible, whereas qiyas al-tamthil (analogy of likeness) and qiyas al-shumul (analogy of inclusion) are impermissible, since that is tashbih (likening). So if we say: every attribute of perfection in a created being, the Creator is more deserving of it, this is correct.

But we must know that the perfect attributes of the created being, which complete its deficiency, are perfect in relation to it; yet for the sake of completing its deficiency, Allah is not described by them. That is, they are perfect with respect to the created being, but since they complete its deficiency, the Creator is not described by them, because although they are perfect, in reality they are deficiency. Such as eating, sleeping, and marriage, and the like. These attributes, with respect to the created being, are what? Attributes of perfection; for one who does not eat is sick, one who does not sleep is sick, one who does not marry is sick. So the lack of these attributes is a deficiency in the created being; but since they complete its deficiency, the Creator is not described by them. Because the human has need of eating, he eats; and whoever has no appetite dies in the end.

Likewise, since the human becomes tired and needs an attribute that cuts off this tiredness: ﴿And We made your sleep a rest﴾ [an-Naba' 9]; sleep became a perfection for him. Likewise, since the human needs the continuation of offspring and kind, marriage became a perfection for him. In reality it is the completion of a deficiency, but Allah is not described by it, Mighty and Majestic, because Allah is perfect in all attributes.

A student: Shaykh, we have already said that attributes are tawqifi (determined by revelation only). If we open this door, as Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, said, perhaps a person will analogize by his intellect and err, because he may think something is a perfection when it is not an attribute of perfection. That is, it is tawqifi.

The Shaykh: This objection does arise, but we say: every attribute of perfection in general and as a genus. As for saying that every attribute affirmed for a created being we affirm for the Creator, that is not possible or correct. But as a genus, every attribute of perfection in the created being, Allah is more deserving of it.

A student: But what has not been transmitted (...).

The Shaykh: It is corroborated: ﴿And His is the highest description.﴾

Student: (...).

The Shaykh: As we said: the intended meaning is the genus. As for every attribute, for example, it is not possible, especially...

Student: The highest description, regarding the attributes that have been reported, those established by the text...

The Shaykh: No, absolutely. Even for example things that may not be in the text but are attributes of Allah; I mean they are of perfection, and Allah, Exalted, is characterized by them.

Student: And are they (...)?

The Shaykh: It is possible. As for the attributes of informing (khabariyya), we may say that the khabari attributes cannot be analogized to creation by qiyas al-awla, such as the eye and the hand and the like. In a created being, the ear is a perfection, but it is not affirmed for the Creator, because the Sharia has not reported it.

Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of might (al-'Aziz) by His words ﴿the Mighty﴾, the affirmation of wisdom ﴿the Wise﴾, and the affirmation of judgment also from His words ﴿the Wise﴾.

It is deduced from this noble verse: the cutting off of objection to creation and to the Sharia, meaning that you do not object to Allah's creation or His law, but submit. How so? Because when you believe in wisdom, that Allah is Wise, then objection ends completely; you do not say "why" or "from where," except as a seeking of guidance.

Among the benefits of the noble verse: the complete tranquility of a person in what Allah has decreed and legislated, since it proceeds from wisdom.

* * *

We now begin the new verses. He says: ﴿He has set forth for you a parable from yourselves: Do you have among those whom your right hands possess any partners in what We have provided you?﴾

His words ﴿from what your right hands possess﴾ mean: from among what. ﴿Possess﴾ is the relative clause, and the returning pronoun is omitted; the estimate is: "that which your right hands possess."

His words ﴿your right hands possess﴾: "the right hands" is the plural of yamin (right hand), which is the hand. The possession is attributed to the hand because most of a person's dealings are done by his hand, and it is attributed to the right because it is more honorable than the left.

His words ﴿from what your right hands possess﴾ mean: what the right hands possess of human beings. Therefore the author said: "i.e., your slaves," that is, from among your slaves.

His words ﴿partners﴾: this is the subject, and the predicate—where is the predicate?

A student: ﴿for you﴾.

The Shaykh: ﴿for you﴾, the fronted predicate. But the subject has been preceded by "min" (from) to indicate generality, or to make generality explicit, since the supplementary "min," as has been explained to us, indicates explicit generality.

His words ﴿Do you have﴾ ﴿any partners﴾: if someone asks, how did the supplementary "min" come when it is not preceded by negation?

A student: It was preceded by something similar to negation.

The Shaykh: Yes, preceded by something similar to it.

Do you have partners (﴿in what We have provided you﴾ of wealth and other things, ﴿so that you are equal in it﴾)? The author says: "﴿any partners in what We have provided you﴾ of wealth and other things." The answer is no, or yes? The answer is no: among what your right hands possess, we have no partners in what we have been provided; the slave does not share your property, nor does he share your child, nor does he share anything you own.

His words "(﴿so that you are equal in it﴾)": the author used the word "they" (wahum) because equality exists only between two things; so he wrote "and they," though in truth it is not needed; the speech is complete without it, for it is possible to say that the pronoun ﴿you﴾ refers to the owner and the owned: you, the owners and the owned, are equal in it, and then there is no need to estimate "they."

His words ﴿so you are equal in it﴾: this is what the negation governs, meaning: you are not equal in it.

(﴿You fear them as you fear one another﴾ i.e., your like among the free.) ﴿You fear them﴾: the pronoun refers to whom? To "what" (ma), ﴿from what﴾. Is that by the wording or by the meaning? By the meaning, because if the pronoun returned to "ma" by its wording it would return singular; since it returned plural, it is by the meaning.

His words ﴿as you fear one another﴾: the author, may Allah have mercy on him, took "anfus" to mean the kind, i.e., as you fear your own kind; therefore he said "i.e., your like among the free." It may also be said that it refers to the essence of the person: "you fear them as you fear yourselves," meaning: just as you have authority over your wealth, you fear that they will exercise authority over this wealth as your own selves exercise it.

And His saying: ﴿as you fear your own selves﴾. This is a verbal noun (maṣdar) construed with its agent, and *anfusakum* ("your selves") is the object.

The author, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "The interrogation carries the sense of negation, meaning: your slaves are not partners with you in what you possess, and so on. So how do you make some of Allah's slaves partners with Him?"

This is a clear example. If you own something, your slave does not share with you in your property, nor in what is specific to you. So how do you assign to Allah, exalted is He, a partner in what is specific to Him? The argument is very clear in obligating these people to abandon shirk. For this reason Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿Thus do We detail the signs﴾. The author said: "We make them clear in the same manner of this detailing, ﴿for a people who reason﴾, meaning, who reflect."

﴿Thus﴾: the *kaf* is a noun meaning "like," and so it is an absolute object (*maf'ul mutlaq*). What is its governing verb? It is ﴿We detail﴾. That is, in the same manner of this detailing and clarification, We detail the signs. But who benefits from them? ﴿For a people who reason.﴾

If someone says: Allah detailed the signs for both those who reason and those who do not, so why did He specify them for those who reason?

The answer: because they are the ones who benefit from this detailing. Just as Allah described the Qur'an as ﴿guidance for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Baqarah 2], and in another verse as ﴿guidance for mankind﴾ [al-Baqarah 185], in general. So, considered as absolute guidance, it is general; considered in terms of benefit, it is specific. And Allah knows best.

﴿Rather, those who did wrong followed their desires without knowledge. So who can guide one whom Allah has sent astray? They will have no helpers﴾ [al-Rum 29]. His saying ﴿Rather﴾ (*bal*) is for *iḍrāb* (transition, a shift to a new topic), and this transition is a shift, not a cancellation. The reason is that when Allah, glorified and exalted, clarified these signs that point to His power and that He is one God without partner, through the last parable, the parable that no one disputes except an obstinate person, what is the last parable? It is: how can you make a partner for Allah in what He owns? Allah owns it. Do you have partners in your wealth from among your slaves? The answer is no. Therefore this shows that Allah has no partner. After this, mighty and majestic, He made clear that those who departed from this, who denied resurrection and denied the oneness of God, are not upon the truth, but are wrongdoers. For this reason He said: ﴿Rather, those who did wrong followed their desires.﴾

His saying: ﴿those who did wrong﴾. The author said: "(by associating partners)." This is a specification that is not in its proper place. It appears to me that the author restricted it out of regard for the parable before it, since the parable before it is clearly aimed at refuting shirk. But if it is said that it includes this and other kinds of wrongdoing, such as denial of resurrection for example, denial of resurrection is undoubtedly wrongdoing, because it entails denying Allah, mighty and majestic, as is established in the sacred hadith that the denial of Allah is "that Allah will not restore him as He originated him" [al-Bukhari (4974) with his chain from Abu Hurairah, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet ﷺ who said: "Allah says: The son of Adam has denied Me, and he had no right to do so, and he has reviled Me, and he had no right to do so. As for his denial of Me, it is his saying: He will not restore me as He originated me, and the first creation is not easier for Me than its restoration. As for his reviling Me, it is his saying: Allah has taken a son, while I am the One, the Eternal Refuge. I neither beget nor was I begotten, and none is equal to Me."], which has already been mentioned. So the meaning of wrongdoing here is shirk and other things in which they wronged themselves.

His saying: ﴿their desires﴾. *Ahwā'* is the plural of *hawā*, and *hawā* in origin means inclination. It is generally not used except for blameworthy desire. One says: he followed his desire rather than his guidance. It may also come for praiseworthy desire, as in the hadith, though it is weak: "None of you truly believes until his desire is subject to what I have brought" [narrated by Ibn Abi 'Asim in al-Sunnah (15) from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr, may Allah be pleased with them both]. So here the desire that follows what the Messenger, may the prayers and peace of Allah be upon him, brought is undoubtedly praiseworthy desire.

His saying: ﴿their desires without knowledge﴾ means: this following is not based on knowledge, but on ignorance and misguidance for those who were ignorant, and on arrogance and obstinacy for those who were obstinate. So those who followed their desires followed them without knowledge. If they were ignorant, the matter is obvious: they have no knowledge in following their desires. But if they were obstinate, do we say they are without knowledge?

The answer: Yes, we say they are without knowledge, because whoever is arrogant and obstinate toward the truth is like one ignorant of what the Lord, mighty and majestic, deserves. In reality he is not a knower. Indeed the ignorant person is better than him.

If someone says: how is it valid to negate knowledge when it exists? We say: just as it is valid to negate hearing when it exists, and sight when it exists, for one who does not benefit from them. Does not Allah say: ﴿Do not be like those who said, "We hear," while they do not hear﴾ [al-Anfal 21], and He said: ﴿Deaf, dumb, blind, so they will not return﴾ [al-Baqarah 18], or ﴿they do not reason﴾ [al-Baqarah 171]? The point is that negating knowledge for one who does not benefit from it is valid, just as negating hearing for one who does not benefit from it is valid.

The conclusion is that those who follow their desires are of two kinds. One kind is truly ignorant, whose desire is built upon error, and we can give as an example of these: the Christians, for the Christians are misguided. The other kind is arrogant and obstinate. For this kind, in reality, there is no knowledge, and even if they possess knowledge, it does not benefit them but harms them, like the Jews.

Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿So who can guide one whom Allah has sent astray?﴾ ﴿Who can guide﴾: *man* is an interrogative particle, and the interrogation here is meant as negation. We have already stated a rule: when the interrogative comes in the sense of negation, it carries an element of challenge. For when you say "who would do such a thing," it is more emphatic than saying "no one does it," as though you are saying: this is an impossible matter; if you are truthful, then show me who does it. So when the interrogative carries the sense of negation, it is more eloquent than bare negation, because the interrogative in the sense of negation is imbued with the meaning of challenge.

His saying: ﴿one whom Allah has sent astray﴾: ﴿Allah﴾ is the agent. Where is the object? The object is omitted, and the sense is: whom Allah has sent astray. This object is the returning pronoun of the relative clause, and the returning pronoun is that to which the relative refers.

﴿So who can guide one whom Allah has sent astray?﴾ The author said: "(that is, he has no guide)." He interpreted the interrogative as negation, meaning: he has no guide. This is true, but, as I said, it is more emphatic than bare negation.

Then he said: "(﴿And they will have no helpers﴾, preventing them from the punishment of Allah)." Apparently the *wāw* here is for resumption (*isti'nāf*, beginning a new sentence), because this sentence is declarative, while the preceding one is performative. ﴿man﴾ is performative. Is that correct or not?

* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: Why?
* Student: It is an interrogative.
* Shaykh: An interrogative. The interrogative belongs to the category of performative speech, as we studied in rhetoric. Or is what is studied at night not given in the daytime?!

﴿And they will have no helpers﴾ means: those who followed their desires without knowledge deserve punishment, and they will not find anyone to help them against it, that is, against the punishment, that is, to prevent them.

His saying: ﴿And they will have no helpers﴾: the negation here is emphasized by the superfluous *min* attached to ﴿helpers﴾. The original form of the sentence without this would be: "and they will have no helpers." Now I ask: is *mā* here Ḥijāzī or ʿAmmī (Tamīmī)?

* Student: ʿAmmī (Tamīmī).
* Shaykh: Tamīmī? Do you know what Ḥijāzī means, the usage specific to the people of the Ḥijāz, and what Tamīmī means, the usage of the Ḥijāzīs and the Tamīmīs?
* Students: Tamīmī.
* Shaykh: Tamīmī? Yes. Why? Because of the difference of construction: its predicate is fronted. It is not Ḥijāzī unless the subject precedes the predicate. ﴿And they will have no helpers﴾.

Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So set your face toward the religion as a ḥanīf﴾ [al-Rum 30], after He threatened these polytheists with what He threatened them with, and made clear that no one can guide them when Allah, mighty and majestic, sends them astray...

[The author then says:] inclining toward it and away from everything else, is it not so? For this reason the complement of the noun was omitted, so that it would include inclining toward the religion and turning away from it.

The root *ḥanf* originally means the inclination of the foot. A foot that is inclined is called *ḥanfā'*. So *ḥanīf* means "inclining away from, and toward": away from shirk toward monotheism, and away from disobedience toward obedience.

His saying: "(that is: make your religion sincerely for Allah, you and whoever follows you)." "Make your religion sincerely for Allah" is a semantic interpretation of His saying ﴿set your face﴾. If it were made more general than that, it would be preferable, because setting one's face toward a thing entails following it and not opposing it. So it includes sincerity of intention and following, which are the foundation of action. Every act not built upon sincerity and following is void, because if it lacks sincerity it becomes shirk, and if it lacks following it becomes innovation. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Actions are only by intentions" [agreed upon: al-Bukhari (1) and Muslim (1907/155), from the hadith of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him]. This is for sincerity. And he said: "Whoever does an action that is not in accordance with our matter, it is rejected" [narrated by Muslim (1718/18) from the hadith of 'Aishah, may Allah be pleased with her]. This is for following.

His saying: "(you and whoever follows you)." The author added "whoever follows you" because there will come a description in the plural, which is His saying ﴿turning penitently to Him and fearing Him﴾ and so on, and a plural state cannot apply to a singular addressee, because a state is a description, and just as one does not report about a single person with a plural form, a state is not made plural for a singular.

What the author said is correct for two reasons: first, regard for the wording that follows, and second, that the address to the Messenger ﷺ is an address to him and to his community. For the leader of a people is addressed in a manner that applies to all of them. For example, a soldier says to the commander: "Go to such-and-such front." Who is meant? The commander and those with him, not him alone. So an address to the leader of a people is an address to all of them.

Allah, mighty and majestic, addresses His speech to the Messenger ﷺ, while meaning him and his community. The proof of this is His saying: ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women, divorce them for their waiting period﴾ [al-Talaq 1]. The address is singular, ﴿O Prophet﴾, and then ﴿when you divorce﴾ is not just for him alone, but for the whole community. It is also indicated by His saying: ﴿Indeed in the Messenger of Allah you have an excellent example for whoever hopes in Allah and the Last Day﴾ [al-Ahzab 21]. So we have in him an example, and we are followers of him.

So the reason the address is to the person of the Messenger ﷺ while it applies to the community has two aspects. The first: the address to the leader is an address to him and to those who follow him, as shown by ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women﴾ [al-Talaq 1]. The second: we are commanded to follow the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, so every address to him that commands or forbids us, we follow him in it.

The difference between the two aspects is clear. In the first, the address reaches us originally together with the Messenger ﷺ. In the second, the address reaches us through following.

He said: "(﴿The nature of Allah﴾: *khilqah*, His creation. ﴿in which He created mankind﴾: and it is His religion.)"

"(﴿The nature of Allah in which He created mankind﴾: and it is His religion, that is: hold fast to it.)"

His saying: ﴿fiṭrat﴾. The discussion of it has two aspects. The first concerns the orthography. The writing does not follow the known rules, neither in the ʿUthmānic script nor in the modern script. What is the reason for that? What is the reason?

* Student: (...) the *tā' marbūṭa*.
* Shaykh: That the *tā'* is open (*fiṭrah*) while it is written as a *tā' marbūṭa*, because it is singular, and in the singular the *tā'* is written as *marbūṭa*. And in the Qur'an there is no *fiṭrah* written as *marbūṭa* except this one. Is it *maftūḥa* or *muṭlaqa*?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Strange, *maftūḥa*? As if "open" were the opposite of "closed." We call it *marbūṭa* and *muṭlaqa*.
* Student: Open is the opposite of closed.
* Shaykh: Fine. What do you call it?
* Student: *Marbūṭa*.
* Shaykh: What is the opposite of *rabṭ* (binding)?
* Student: *Iṭlāq* (release).
* Shaykh: *Iṭlāq*. In any case, this is because the Qur'anic script follows the ʿUthmānic orthography. And at length in the research: the scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, differed over whether a person may write the Muṣḥaf in a script other than the ʿUthmānic script or not.

Some said it is permissible, because the ʿUthmānic script is only a form and an appearance. If the ʿUthmānic script at that time had been of a different description, the Qur'an would have been written in that way, is that not so? Thus its conformity to the ʿUthmānic script at that time was not because it was revealed in that form, but because the script at that time was in this form. Do you understand?

There is no doubt that if the script were in its present form, it would certainly be written in that form, is that not so? For example, *al-ṣalāh* in the present form has *alif* after the *ṣād*, meaning the present rule is *lām-alif*, but in the ʿUthmānic script it is *lām-wāw*.

* Student: *al-ṣalāh*.
* Shaykh: No, *al-ṣalāh* (...), *al-zakāh* is similar, *al-ribā* is with a *wāw* although in the present script it is with an *alif*. So the summary is that we say: some scholars say it is permissible to write the Qur'an according to the known rules now in use. Their reasoning is that this script is a form that happened to be in this way at that time, so they wrote it that way, and the Qur'an was not revealed written in this way. If it had been revealed written in this way, we would say perhaps it is not permissible. But this is a convention, and if it is a convention, then whatever fulfills the purpose is permissible.

Others say it is absolutely impermissible to deviate from the ʿUthmānic script, and that the script must remain, even if you write it for children on a board, it must be in the ʿUthmānic script out of respect for the Qur'an.

Others made a distinction and said: for the beginner it is permissible to write it according to the rules known to him, but not for others. They said: because the beginner needs to be taught. If you wrote for a beginner in the ʿUthmānic script and said: ﴿Allah destroys usury﴾ [al-Baqarah 276], how would he read it? He would read "yamḥaqu Allāhu al-ribū", is that not so? *al-zakāh* he says *al-zakūt*, *al-ṣalāh* he says *al-ṣalawt*, and similar. Unlike the knowledgeable person, who writes it in the ʿUthmānic script.

Whichever of these opinions is correct, what some people do today, making the Qur'an in the form of decorative designs and putting it in frames, competing over who has the finest calligraphy, is prohibited according to all opinions. Because when we do this, it becomes as if we have made the Qur'an an ornament and embroidery, and its value is lost. Worse than that is making it in the shape of a human being. I saw in a calendar (...) a picture of a person with a verse of the Qur'an, with a head and two feet placed as if he were sitting cross-legged, (I seek refuge in Allah) a clear contradiction and opposition to Allah and His Messenger. Pictures are forbidden, so how can the Qur'an be written with them? Likewise, writing the Qur'an in this way.

The conclusion is that people, we ask Allah to grant guidance to us and to them, have begun to exaggerate in matters that harm them and do not benefit them with regard to the noble Qur'an.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, that is correct. But those who say it is permissible say: we want to write it in one reading, and the readings are now fixed (...).
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No, I did not hear. No, the disagreement on this is well known, there is no (...).

The second discussion concerns His saying ﴿fiṭrat Allāh﴾: what is its governing element? The verb that governs ﴿fiṭrat Allāh﴾ is an omitted verb, which the author estimated with his words: "Hold fast to the nature of Allah." Similarly they say it is in the accusative of incitement (*ighrā'*), meaning a warning to hold fast to it. This omission is more eloquent than mentioning the verb "hold fast." Because when the governing verb is present, the sentence is restricted by it, but when the verb is omitted, the sentence is suitable for it and for other verbs that may govern the object: hold to it, take care of it, cling to it, and so on. For this reason they say it is in the accusative of incitement, which is an intensification of exhortation.

**Third:** ﴿فِطْرَتَ﴾ (*fitrah*, the innate nature). From what is the word *fitrah* derived? It derives from *fatara al-shay'* (فطر الشيء), which means to originate something without a prior model, as in the Almighty's saying: ﴿Praise be to Allah, Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾ [Fatir 1]; that is, the One who originated them without a prior model.

This *fitrah* was originated by Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in the human being, or in people, as the wording of the verse indicates, without a prior model. Therefore He said: (﴿﴿The fitrah of Allah﴾﴾ its creation, ﴿﴿upon which He created people﴾﴾ and it is His religion).

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No. *al-bid'* (innovation) and *al-fatr* (origination) have the same meaning. He said: "and it is His religion," or "adhere to it."

﴿upon which He created people﴾. This verse is evidence for the authentic hadith: "Every child is born upon the *fitrah*, then his parents make him a Jew, or a Christian, or a Magian."[[Agreed upon (Muttafaq 'alayh): al-Bukhari, whose wording this is (1385), and Muslim (2658/25), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]] If the created being were left to his *fitrah*, he would worship none but Allah. Therefore, do the dumb animals, which have nothing to entice them (...), could they worship al-Lat, al-'Uzza, the sun, or the moon?

The answer: No, or yes? No, because Allah says: ﴿The seven heavens and the earth and whoever is in them glorify Him. And there is nothing except that it exalts His praise, but you do not understand their glorification﴾ [al-Isra' 44]. So the essence of creation is innately disposed to glorify the Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, the Creator. But those who were given intellect are the ones who may deviate, because they have wills and inclinations, unlike one who has nothing but practical intellect, who does not depart from this *fitrah*. Therefore, as I said, dumb animals recognize their Creator and Originator and glorify none but Allah.

And His saying: ﴿upon which He created people﴾. He said: (﴿﴿There is no altering of the creation of Allah﴾﴾ for His religion; that is, do not alter it by associating partners with Him).

* Student: What is the definition of *fitrah*, what does it mean?
* Shaykh: It is what we mentioned a little earlier. *Fitrah* means the existence of a thing, or the bringing of a thing into being without a prior model. And what is meant by *fitrah* here is the monotheism of Allah and the religion of Allah.
* Student: Shall we say: an inclination within the soul (...) the Creator (...)?
* Shaykh: No, there is no need. "The religion of Allah" is clearer, as the author, may Allah have mercy on him, said.

And His saying: ﴿There is no altering of the creation of Allah﴾. ﴿There is no altering﴾: everyone knows it is a negation, because *lā* is a negative particle of genus. Does it remain a negation both in wording and in meaning, or is it a negation in wording that conveys a prohibition in meaning?

The author followed the latter view, that it is a negation carrying the meaning of a prohibition; that is, do not alter this *fitrah* by associating partners. A negation often carries the meaning of a prohibition, like...?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, there is much of it.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, this is a prohibition. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Alif. Lam. Mim. This is the Book about which there is no doubt﴾ [al-Baqarah 1–2]. There are two interpretations of it, as previously mentioned: one is that it means a prohibition, i.e., there is no doubt or suspicion in it; the second is that it means a prohibition, i.e., do not doubt it. And like His saying: ﴿and that the Hour is coming, there is no doubt about it﴾ [al-Hajj 7]. So ﴿There is no altering of the creation of Allah﴾ means: do not alter the creation of Allah by associating partners. Rather, ﴿set your face toward the religion, inclining to truth﴾. It is also permissible that it be a negation in its apparent sense, meaning that no one can alter the creation of Allah, as in His saying: ﴿There is no changer of His words, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾ [al-An'am 115]. The meaning would then be that the matter is in the hand of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Whoever He wills to guide, he remains upon his *fitrah*, and whoever He wills to misguide, He misguides him. No one can alter the creation of Allah; the matter is in the hand of Allah alone. Accordingly, the verse has two aspects:

The first aspect: it is a statement carrying the meaning of a prohibition.
The second: it is a statement in its own sense. In the first, the meaning is clear: you should not alter it, so it would be (...) the meaning of associating partners. In the second, its aspect is that this *fitrah* upon which Allah created creation cannot be altered by anyone; rather, it is Allah who alters it. Whoever Allah wills to guide, no one can misguide, and whoever Allah wills to misguide, no one can guide, especially since He said before this: ﴿So who can guide one whom Allah has sent astray?﴾ [al-Rum 29].

Now, among the reports of alteration is what the Messenger (ﷺ) mentioned in his saying: "then his parents make him a Jew, or a Christian, or a Magian." The mention of the two parents is not restrictive; rather, it is by way of comparison and example. That is, whoever associates with this person makes him a Jew or a Christian. How many a person has become Christian not through his parents, but through companions and friends? For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) warned against a bad companion and encouraged a good companion, and said: "The likeness of a good companion is like a carrier of musk: either he will give you some, or you will buy from him, or you will find a pleasant fragrance from him. And the likeness of a bad companion is like a bellows-blower: either he will burn your clothes, or you will find an offensive smell from him."[[Al-Bukhari (5534) and Muslim (2628/146), from the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The likeness of the good companion and the bad companion is like the carrier of musk and the bellows-blower. The carrier of musk will either give you some, or you will buy from him, or you will find a pleasant fragrance from him. The bellows-blower will either burn your clothes, or you will find a foul smell from him."]]

* Student: The bellows-blower (...).
* Shaykh: No, its meaning is "it is not for a believer." This indicates that it is absolutely impossible. In the Qur'an, *mā kāna* (it was not) and *mā yanbaghī* (it is not fitting) and what resembles them come to mean something that is utterly impossible.
* Student: (...).

﴿And Allah would never misguide a people after He had guided them﴾ [al-Tawbah 115].

* Student: (...) the last one (...) it is said: Jabriyyah (fatalism).
* Shaykh: No. The Messenger (ﷺ) says in his sermon. What does he say? "Whomever Allah guides, there is none to misguide him, and whomever He misguides, there is none to guide him."[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (2118), from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him.]]

* Student: (...) no one can ever, that is: if Allah wills, He guides him (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, there is no doubt. No one can ever guide a person or cause a person to deviate except by the permission of Allah. This Prophet (ﷺ) was extremely eager and exerted as much effort as he could to guide his uncle Abu Talib, but he could not: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you like, but Allah guides whom He wills﴾ [al-Qasas 56]. And that does not mean that if we say the matter is in the hand of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and that He is the One who misguides and guides, we should therefore abandon the means. Just as the matter is in the hand of Allah in bringing things into existence, in providing sustenance, in providing offspring, and in repelling harm, do we take the means or remain bewildered? We take the means.

We say: guidance is in the hand of Allah and misguidance is in the hand of Allah, but each of them has a cause.

* Student: And is this preferable to what the author followed?
* Shaykh: What the author said has a valid basis, because this usage occurs in the Arabic language. The second aspect is the original one, because what I hold is the negation, and whoever diverts it from its apparent meaning needs evidence.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 30, verse 24–33 (part 1 of 5):

His saying: ﴿He sends down water from the sky and thereby gives life to the earth after its death﴾ [al-Rum 24]. ﴿Yuhyi﴾ (gives life) is Allah, Mighty and Majestic. The ﴿bihi﴾ (thereby) — the ba' here indicates causation (sababiyyah), and it conveys — as will come, Allah willing — the affirmation of causes (ʿilal) in the acts of Allah, or not? The affirmation of causes in the acts of Allah has been mentioned to us many times and repeatedly: that the acts of Allah and His legislation are all accompanied by wisdom and reasoning (taʿlil).

From this is what has already passed, but I forgot to draw your attention to it: His saying: ﴿so that you may find tranquility in them﴾ [al-Rum 21]. The lam here indicates causation (taʿlil), so it conveys wisdom, the establishment of wisdom in the acts of Allah. It has passed with us in 'Aqidah that among the people of innovation (ahl al-bid'ah) are those who deny wisdom. Who are they? Principally the Jabriyyah, who are the Jahmiyyah; they deny wisdom. The Mu'tazilah are the opposite: the Mu'tazilah make wisdom obligatory, and for this reason they said that it is obligatory upon Allah to do what is best (al-aslah), as has passed with us in 'Aqidah.

His saying: ﴿gives life to the earth thereby after its death﴾. The word ﴿al-ardh﴾ (the earth) — is the intended meaning the very substance of the earth that is alive, or is the intended meaning the vegetation that is in the earth that comes to life?
* Student: The vegetation.
* Shaykh: The intended meaning is the vegetation that is in the earth.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: What is its type?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: (...).

The intended meaning of "the earth" is the vegetation of the earth. At this point an objector may object to us and say: You say there is no majaz (figurative usage) in the Qur'an, and here, if you take "the earth" to mean its vegetation, you have spoken of majaz. So what is the answer to this?

The answer is that we have repeatedly stated that a word in itself is not understood in meaning except by its context. So His saying: ﴿And of His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Rum 22] undoubtedly intends the very substance of the earth. But ﴿He gives life thereby to the earth after its death﴾ addresses people who know what lives and what dies; they know that it lives by rain and dies by the loss of rain. Does anyone addressed by this verse say that this clay, this sand, and this stone die by the loss of rain and live by its presence? No one says this, and the context determines the meaning of the word.

By this we are safe from the claim of majaz, because the most prominent sign of majaz is that its negation is valid, and there is nothing in the Qur'an whose negation is valid; for if the negation of something in the Qur'an were valid, its meaning would be denial (takdhib).

An example of this: ﴿wanting to collapse﴾ [al-Kahf 77]. Someone says: The wall does not want — what is the meaning of this? Its meaning is the negation of what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has affirmed. And this is what led some scholars to deny majaz in the Qur'an while affirming it in other Arabic language, saying: Because there is nothing in the Qur'an whose negation is valid, and the most prominent sign of majaz is that its negation is valid.

But the correct view is that chosen by Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him: there is no majaz neither in the Qur'an nor in the Arabic language; because we say that what determines the meaning is the context, and accordingly, when the meaning of a word is determined, it is its literal meaning (haqiqah) in every context. (...)

(﴿Indeed in that﴾ mentioned) — so what is referred to is everything that preceded: ﴿He shows you the lightning as fear and hope, and sends down water from the sky and thereby gives life to the earth after its death﴾ [al-Rum 24]. These are three things. Regarding this, the verse says ﴿there are signs for a people who reason﴾ — he says: (who reflect). Here he said: ﴿there are signs for a people who reason﴾ [al-Rum 24], meaning: for people of intellect. Intellect has been mentioned to be of two kinds: the intellect of perception (ʿaql idrak) and the intellect of right guidance (ʿaql rushd). The intellect of perception is the basis of moral responsibility (taklif), about which the scholars say: it is a condition for the obligation of prayer that one be of sound intellect; so they call it the intellect of perception, because by it a person perceives matters, distinguishing between the beneficial and the harmful and other things.

The second intellect: the intellect of right guidance, which is the basis of praise and commendation, and which is found frequently in the Qur'an: the intellect of right guidance.

For example, Allah, Glorified and Exalted, denied intellect from the disbelievers although they are clever; they have the intellect of perception, but they do not have the intellect of right guidance by which they conduct themselves as sensible people. And intellect is called ʿaql because it restrains (yaʿqil) its possessor from what harms him, and this is what made it called ʿaql, and it is also called ḥijr (restraint): ﴿Is there in that an oath for one of understanding?﴾ [al-Fajr 5]; because it restrains its possessor and holds him back from what does not benefit him.

His saying: ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who reason﴾ [al-Rum 24] — he brought in "intellect" here because it refers to what will be mentioned afterward; for the signs, as you observe, are all in establishing the return of the dead, and the transition of the intellect from these perceptible things to unseen, existing things occurs only through the intellect. For this reason he said here: ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who reason﴾.

Then He, Mighty and Majestic, said: (﴿And of His signs is that the heaven and earth stand by His command﴾ [al-Rum 25] by His will, without pillars).
﴿And of His signs that they stand﴾ — we say in its grammatical analysis what we said before: i.e., among His signs is the standing of the heavens and the earth by His command.

His saying: (﴿by His command﴾: by His will, without pillars). The author, may Allah have mercy on him, informed us that the intended meaning of "command" here is the cosmic command (al-amr al-kawni), because he said: by His will. Although in interpreting "command" as "will" there is some doubt, since I fear that he interpreted "command" as "will" to flee from speech, or from affirming speech to Allah, Mighty and Majestic; because command, even if cosmic, occurs by speech: ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [Ya-Sin 82]. So I fear that the author — may Allah forgive him — intended by interpreting command as will to flee from affirming speech. And it is well known that the Ash'arites do not affirm speech with letters and sound; rather they affirm speech as the meaning subsisting in the self, and they say that the written letter and the heard sound are an expression of Allah's speech, not Allah's speech itself.

His saying: ﴿that they stand﴾ — also he explained it by his saying "without pillars," and this indicates that he went to the view that the standing here is physical standing, meaning that they remain not falling upon the earth, rather they are held by the command of Allah, Glorified and Exalted, without pillars. This is a deficient explanation. The correct view is that the standing of the heavens and the earth is more general than being merely physical standing; it encompasses both physical standing and moral (maʿnawi) standing. The heavens stand by the command of Allah in physical standing through the order that is in them by what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, created of spheres containing the sun, the moon, the stars, and other things; and likewise the earth stands in physical standing by what Allah, Exalted, has deposited in it of benefits for creation: trees, plants, rivers, seas, and other things. This is physical standing.

There is also moral standing, which is their standing by obedience to Allah, for disobedience is corruption on the earth, as Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿And do not cause corruption on the earth after its reformation﴾ [al-A'raf 56]. So the heavens and the earth also stand by the legislative command of Allah just as they stand by His cosmic command, and there is no standing for the earth nor for the heavens except by adherence to the legislative command of Allah. Then the standing is explained as physical standing and moral standing. Have you understood?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: What is physical standing? Physical standing is the standing of these bodies with what is in them of spheres and stars, and what is on the earth of trees, seas, and other things; this is physical standing.

Moral standing — what is meant by it? That they stand by obedience to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and are set right and endure by obedience to Allah. So the verse encompasses both meanings, and accordingly the intended meaning of "command" is both the cosmic command and the legislative command.

He said: ﴿Then when He calls you with a call from the earth, behold, you will come out﴾ [al-Rum 25]. He brought "then" (thumma) after mentioning the standing of the heavens and the earth, because the resurrection is delayed; it occurs only after the Hour is established. He says: ﴿Then when He calls you﴾ — the doer is who? Allah, Mighty and Majestic. ﴿a call﴾ — i.e., one call. ﴿from the earth, behold, you will come out﴾ — (﴿from the earth﴾ by Israfil blowing into the Trumpet so that those in the graves are raised; ﴿behold, you will come out﴾ from them alive; your coming out from it by His call is among His signs, Exalted).

﴿When He calls you with a call from the earth﴾ — the phrase ﴿from the earth﴾: is it connected to ﴿you will come out﴾, meaning: when He calls you, you will come out from the earth, or is it connected to "called"? We say: it is connected to "called": when He calls you with a call from the earth, and not connected to ﴿you will come out﴾, because what precedes the sudden "idha" (إذا الفجائية) is not connected to what follows it.

﴿When He calls you﴾ — ﴿idha﴾ is conditional, and ﴿idha antum﴾ — the ﴿idha﴾ is sudden (fujaʾiyyah), so it stands in place of the fa' that occurs in the response of the condition.

His exalted saying: ﴿When He calls you with a call from the earth﴾ — meaning: He calls you from it. Is the call of Allah from the earth, or when He calls you from the earth, meaning that you are in the earth? The intended meaning is this: when He calls you from the earth, just as you say: "I called him from his house," not "I am in the house," but he is in the house, so I called him from it to come.

﴿When He calls you with a call from the earth, behold, you will come out﴾, and this verse is like His saying: ﴿It will be but one shout, and behold, they will be on the surface of the earth﴾ [al-Nazi'at 13–14]: meaning, on the face of the earth. ﴿Behold, you will come out﴾ — this is also among the signs of Allah.

Then He said: (﴿And to Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Rum 26] in dominion, creation, and servitude). ﴿And to Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ — the pronoun in ﴿lahu﴾ (to Him) refers to Allah, and it is a fronted predicate (khabar muqaddam) while the subject is indefinite (munkar) in a negative context; and fronting the predicate, as is well known in the science of rhetoric (balaghah), conveys restriction (hasr), meaning: Allah alone has whoever is in the heavens and the earth.

His saying: ﴿whoever is in the heavens﴾ — ﴿fi al-samawat﴾ is a prepositional phrase (jar and majrur) connected to an omitted element; what is its estimated form?
* Student: Sometimes.
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: Settled (mustaqirr).
* Shaykh: Not "settled."
* Student: Settled (istaqarra).
* Shaykh: Istaqarra; because a prepositional phrase that occurs as a relative clause (silah) of a relative pronoun is estimated as a verb, unlike one that occurs as the predicate of a subject, which is estimated as a noun. (...) that this is to distinguish between them: when the prepositional phrase or adverb occurs as a relative clause of a relative pronoun, estimate its complement as a verb, because the basic form of a relative clause is a sentence. But when a prepositional phrase or adverb occurs as the predicate of a subject, estimate it as a noun, because the basic form of the predicate is a single word, not a sentence. You say: Zayd fi al-bayt — you estimate it: "ka'in fi al-bayt" (being in the house), so that Zayd is the subject and "ka'in" the predicate. But if you say: Zayd fi al-bayt, meaning: Zayd settled in the house, the predicate becomes a sentence, and the basic form of the predicate is that it be singular. Is that so?

But when you say: "yu'jibuni alladhi fi al-masjid" (the one in the mosque pleases me), you do not say "alladhi ka'in fi al-masjid," because if you estimate "alladhi kai'n fi al-masjid," it would require that you estimate a subject as well, i.e., "alladhi huwa kai'n fi al-masjid," isn't it? Why must you estimate a subject? Because the relative clause must be a sentence, unlike the predicate of a subject, which is singular. Is it understood, everyone?

So when we estimate the complement of a prepositional phrase that occurs as a relative clause, what do we estimate it as? A verb, so that it becomes a sentence; and when we estimate the complement of a prepositional phrase or adverb that is the predicate of a subject, we estimate it as a noun.

﴿And to Him belongs whoever is in the heavens﴾ — i.e., whoever settled in the heavens and the earth. ﴿Whoever is in the heavens﴾ — among the angels, this we know; and the earth has humans and animals. Here He said ﴿man﴾ (whoever), giving precedence to the rational, though the earth contains both rational and non-rational beings. ﴿Whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ — he said: (in dominion, creation, and servitude). It would have been better to mention creation first, then dominion, then servitude. Whoever is in the heavens belongs to Him; He is the one who owns them, Glorified and Exalted; He created them, He is their Lord and they are His servants. To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and no one opposes Him in that: everyone in the heavens and the earth, as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant﴾ [Maryam 93].

(﴿All are devoutly obedient to Him﴾ [al-Rum 26]: obedient.) ﴿All﴾ is the subject, and ﴿qanitun﴾ is its predicate, and the prepositional phrase ﴿lahu﴾ is connected to ﴿qanitun﴾, but it was fronted before it for restriction and exclusivity.

His saying: ﴿kull﴾ — the tanwin here is a substitute for a singular noun; whenever ﴿kull﴾ or ﴿ba'd﴾ comes with tanwin, it is a substitute for a singular noun; the meaning, i.e., the estimate, is: every one who is in the heavens and the earth.

His saying: ﴿lahu qanitun﴾ — he says: (obedient), and the obedience here is obedience and submission to the cosmic command, and this includes believer and non-believer, isn't it?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: The second is obedience and devout submission to the legislative command, and this is specific to the believer. So is the intended meaning of qunut here legislative or cosmic? Cosmic, because he said: ﴿All to Him﴾, and this is conceivable only in the cosmic sense; everything is subject to the command of Allah, devoutly obedient in regard to His cosmic command: when He wills a thing for whoever is in the heavens and the earth, He says to it: "Be," and it is.

Then Allah, Exalted, said: (﴿And it is He who originates creation﴾ [al-Rum 27] for people, ﴿then repeats it﴾ [al-Rum 27] after its perishing, ﴿and it is easier for Him﴾ [al-Rum 27] than the beginning).
﴿And it is He who originates creation﴾ — i.e., He initiates it. He used the word ﴿yabda'u﴾ (originates), because creation is continuous; every day there is an initiation of creation, isn't it? Embryos in the wombs of mothers come into being every day; how many embryos are formed in the world in a single day? Very many. For this reason He used the present tense verb indicating continuity, and did not say "bada'a" (he originated).

His saying: ﴿then repeats it﴾ — i.e., then He, that is Allah, Mighty and Majestic, repeats it; the meaning of repetition (i'adah) is returning it to what it was at first, as in His saying: ﴿As We originated the first creation, We will repeat it﴾ [al-Anbiya' 104]. And the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, informed that people will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection barefoot, naked, uncircumcised, "as they were first created"[[Reported by al-Bukhari — and the wording is his — (3349) and Muslim (2860) from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, from the Prophet ﷺ who said: "Indeed you will be gathered barefoot, naked, uncircumcised." Then he recited: ﴿As We originated the first creation, We will repeat it — a promise upon Us; indeed We are ever doing it﴾ [al-Anbiya' 104].]].

He said: ﴿then repeats it, and it is He﴾ — the pronoun refers to the repetition, isn't it? That which is understood from ﴿yu'idu﴾, so the referent of the pronoun is the verbal noun understood from the verb; and it has been mentioned to us several times that the referent of a pronoun may not be mentioned by its word, but what indicates it is mentioned. Look at His saying: ﴿Be just; that is nearer to piety﴾ [al-Ma'idah 8]: where is the referent of ﴿huwa﴾ (that)? The justice understood from the word ﴿i'dilu﴾ (be just).

So in ﴿then repeats it﴾, we say: ﴿wa huwa﴾ (and it) — i.e., the repetition; and repetition is a verbal noun, so it is correct for the pronoun to refer to it in the masculine.

He said: ﴿ahwanu 'alayhi﴾ (easier for Him) — ﴿awhan﴾ is the elative form (ism al-tafdil) from hana, yahun; and the elative form indicates that the ease in His regard has degrees: hayyin (easy) and ahwan (easier); and the degrees of ease may suggest that there is difficulty, for were there no difficulty in some of them, one would not be easier than another. For this reason the commentators differed about the elative form here, ahwan. It was said that it means hayyin: ﴿and it is easier for Him﴾ — i.e., it is easy for Him.

Some exegetes said what the author went to: that it is easier for Him than the beginning, in view of what the addressees hold — that repeating a thing is easier than originating it. Otherwise, both are equal in ease with Allah, Exalted.

The Shaykh's commentary, part 2 of 5 on surah 30, verses 24–33:

So now, is the word (ahwan, "easier") to be taken in its literal sense or not? The author proceeded on the basis that it is taken in its literal sense, but relative to the addressees, because the addressee knows that restoring a thing is easier than originating it. The reason for this is that its restoration does not require fresh thought, since thought about it has already occurred. Second, the materials of formation already exist. Suppose, for example, that I have made a car. When I want to make it, I need thought first and materials. But if I want to make it again, for instance if this car has been dismantled and I want to rebuild it, the rebuilding is easier, because the thinking has already been completed and the materials are present and abundant. So the rebuilding is easier relative to the addressee.
