As for His saying ﴿they despair﴾ [al-Rum 36]: ﴿idha﴾ (then suddenly) is a sudden particle (idha fajā'iyyah) occurring in the answer of the conditional, which is His saying ﴿But if an evil afflicts them﴾.

As for His saying ﴿idha hum yaqnatun﴾: He used a nominal sentence to indicate that they are characterized by this on a continuous basis; so they are always in despair as long as the evil is in them. The author says "they despair," but this is an explanation with some deficiency, because qunut is not mere yaʾs (despair) but its extreme; for yaʾs, when it contains some hope, is not called qunut; and though it may be called yaʾs, when despair reaches its utmost limit it is called qunut. Allah the Exalted said about Ibrahim: ﴿And who despairs of the mercy of his Lord except the misguided?﴾ [al-Hijr 56], i.e., the ignorant of the wisdom of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in what befalls His servants of hardship and ease.

The author says: (It is the nature of the believer to give thanks in ease and to hope in his Lord in hardship). Accordingly, to whom does the verse refer? To the disbelievers.

(﴿Have they not seen﴾ means: have they not known; ﴿that Allah extends provision﴾ means: expands it; ﴿for whom He wills﴾ means: as a test; ﴿and restricts it﴾ means: narrows it for whom He wills as a trial.)

﴿Have they not seen﴾: the author said: (Have they not known?). Accordingly, the seeing is knowing, and the author's explanation is supported by the fact that it appears in other verses as "know," namely in Surah al-Zumar: ﴿Do they not know that Allah extends provision for whom He wills and restricts it?﴾ [al-Zumar 52]. ﴿Do they not know?﴾ So the best way to explain the Qur'an is by the Qur'an, and it is the highest type of tafsir. It may also be said that each verse has its own meaning: we explain "seeing" here as sight of the eye, not sight of insight which is knowledge, and we explain it there as knowledge, as is the wording of that verse; and the expansion and restriction would be known by the heart and seen by the eye, for a person also sees with his eye just as he knows with his heart. Which is more general: "know" or "see"?

If we do not interpret "see" as "know": knowledge is more general, because knowledge may be through sight and may be through hearing.

I may not see that Allah has expanded provision for His servants and restricted it, but I hear that in such-and-such lands there is poverty and in such-and-such lands there is wealth, and so on; so knowledge is more general, because the means of knowledge are many, unlike sight, whose route is the eye. Knowledge comes through all five senses that you know: touch, smell, taste, sight and hearing all convey knowledge. So it is more general, because whatever is seen is known, but knowledge is more general because its means are more numerous.

As for His saying ﴿that Allah extends provision﴾: expansion (basṭ) means widening, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿He spreads it in the sky however He wills﴾ [al-Rum 48], i.e., He widens it.

As for His saying ﴿for whom He wills﴾: we have previously said that whatever Allah restricts by will is linked with wisdom; the will of Allah is not bare will, because we know that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is Wise, and does nothing and legislates nothing except for a wisdom. So whenever something restricted by will passes before you, know that it is restricted by wisdom.

﴿for whom He wills﴾: the author said: (as a test; ﴿and restricts it﴾ means: narrows it for whom He wills as a trial). The author distinguished between narrowing provision and expanding it, making expansion a test and narrowing a trial. The correct view is that both are the same, as Allah said: ﴿And We test you with evil and good as a trial﴾ [al-Anbiya' 35]; both are trial. And Sulayman, upon him be prayer and peace, said: ﴿This is of the bounty of my Lord, to test me whether I will be grateful or ungrateful﴾ [al-Naml 40].

So the correct view is that both are trial, and that testing is close in meaning to trial; but the attendant duty of expanded provision is gratitude, and with narrowed provision is patience. This is the difference between them; and the believer fulfils both duties: if ease befalls him, he gives thanks, and that is good for him; if hardship befalls him, he is patient, and that is good for him. And this belongs to the believer alone.

As for His saying ﴿Have they not seen﴾: the interrogative here is intended as affirmation (taqrir); meaning, they see that matters are in the hand of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and that He expands provision for whom He wills and restricts it. How then do they despair when evil befalls them? And how do they rejoice and boast when mercy befalls them? Rather, it is obligatory upon them to know that this is by the wisdom of Allah, glorified and exalted be He.

Ibn 'Uthaymin's commentary on Surah al-Rum, verses 34–40 (part 2 of 5):

And His saying: ﴿Have they not seen?﴾ The waw here is a conjunctive particle (waw al-'atf), and the interrogative particle (hamza) has precedence, since interrogative particles must come first. So the waw is not preceded by anything it could be conjoined to. What, then, is the answer? We mentioned earlier that the grammarians have two opinions regarding this kind of construction. The first opinion is that the waw conjoins with something implied after the hamza. The second is that the waw conjoins with what came before, and on this view the hamza is placed before the conjunction. We mentioned that this second opinion is preferable, because although the first is sound from the standpoint of the principles, it is sometimes difficult for a person to supply something that seems appropriate to the context. Accordingly, saying that the hamza is the interrogative particle and that the waw is implied before it, meaning "and have they not seen," is easier.

﴿He extends provision for whom He wills and restricts it.﴾ [al-Rum 37] There is no doubt that the extension and restriction of provision is a trial from Allah, the Exalted, because a servant is sometimes suited to having provision extended to him, and sometimes the reverse, according to what wisdom requires. What is good for this person is not good for that one.

And Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe.﴾ [al-Rum 37] ﴿In that﴾ means in the extension and restriction of provision. ﴿Signs for a people who believe﴾: ﴿signs﴾ is the noun governed by ﴿inna﴾, so it is its noun, postponed, and ﴿in that﴾ is its predicate, preposed.

His saying: ﴿signs﴾ means indicators of Allah's absolute disposal over His servants. I think we sometimes see some people striving as much as they can in the means of provision, yet it does not come to them. You find him selling, buying, and traveling through the land seeking of Allah's bounty, yet he does not become wealthy, and his provision is restricted. And you find some people striving only modestly, yet Allah blesses their effort until they have abundant provision. This shows that matters are not attained by earning alone. Earning is a cause, but above that is the will of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

His saying: ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe﴾ — because they are the ones who benefit from this sight and this reflection. As for the non-believer, he does not benefit from this. Therefore you find that those who do not believe, when such matters occur, attribute them to nature: when rain increases they say, "This is due to such-and-such," and when it decreases they say, "This is due to such-and-such." We do not deny that matters have causes, but we deny that the causes are the actual agents. The Agent is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and the causes are only means by which the wisdom of Allah, the Exalted, is inferred, and that He is All-Wise, in that He linked effects to their causes. ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe.﴾ [al-Rum 37]

﴿So give to the near of kin his right, and to the needy and the wayfarer.﴾ [al-Rum 38] And so on to the end. ﴿Give﴾ (āti) means "give" (a'ti), because it is from the quadriliteral form; had it been from the triliteral, it would mean "come" (ji'). But it is from the quadriliteral form which means "to give" (a'ta).

His saying: ﴿Give﴾ is singular in address. Is it directed to the Messenger ﷺ personally, or to everyone to whom the address is directed? We have said that the scholars hold two opinions on this. However, where evidence indicates that it is specific to the Messenger ﷺ, then it is specific to him, such as: ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ [al-Sharh 1] This is specific to the Messenger ﷺ, and ﴿And He found you poor?﴾ [al-Duha 8], ﴿O Messenger, convey what has been revealed to you from your Lord﴾ [al-Ma'idah 67], and similar verses.

* The student: "Poor" (ā'ilan)?
* The Shaykh: "He found you [needy], but He made you rich through you."
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: His saying: ﴿So give to the near of kin﴾ — ﴿the near of kin﴾ means the one who has kinship, and for this the author said "kinship" (al-qarabah), so "al-qurba" here means "kinship." ﴿His right﴾ is from righteousness (al-birr) and maintaining ties (al-silah). The people most deserving of this are the mother and father, however far up they go, and their maintenance is called birr, because it must be higher than that owed to others. Birr is the abundance of good, while for others it is called silah, because the aim is simply to connect. So ﴿his right﴾ here is general, but it is specified by other texts from the Qur'an and the Sunnah: the right of the two parents is birr, and the right of others is silah. It is possible that the author's words "from righteousness and maintaining ties" are meant distributively: righteousness toward the two parents and maintaining ties toward others, namely relatives. He said: ﴿Give the near of kin his right.﴾

His saying: ﴿the near of kin﴾ includes every relative, even if he is a disbeliever, because the cause is kinship, not Islam. If he had said, "Give the believer his right," we would say the cause is faith, and the ruling would be specific to him.

﴿Give the near of kin his right, and the needy and the wayfarer.﴾ The miskin is the faqir (the poor). Here "miskin" is used in its general sense, meaning the faqir and the miskin in the verse on zakat. We have already noted that when "miskin" is used alone it includes the faqir, and when "faqir" is used alone it includes the miskin, but when both are mentioned together they are distinguished.

The miskin has a right. What is his right? His right is that his need be met, because he is poor. The scholars said: feeding the hungry and clothing the naked is a collective obligation (fard kifayah); if someone sufficient performs it, it is dropped from the rest.

﴿And the wayfarer﴾ is the traveler. He is called "son of the road" (ibn al-sabil) because of his constant association with it, and "sabil" means the road. Everyone who keeps company with something is called its son. They say, as one says "son of the water" for a water bird, and it is said of a man who travels much at night, "son of the nights," and similar expressions. So "ibn" applies to anyone who is constantly associated with a thing. He said: from the charity. This is an explanation of the right of the miskin and the wayfarer. It was also said that the wayfarer here refers to the guest, because he is one who passes along the road; but the correct view is that he is the traveler, and this includes the guest. Does it include the guest or not? It includes the guest, because a guest is a traveler.

He said: (And the Ummah of the Prophet ﷺ follow him in this.) The author conveyed in this sentence that the address in His saying ﴿So give﴾ is directed to the Messenger ﷺ personally, and the Ummah follows him. We have previously explained the reason for this: the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, is the leader of his Ummah, so the address was directed to him, even if it is inclusive, or it is specific to him, and his Ummah follows him by way of emulating him.

He said: ﴿That is better for those who desire the Face of Allah.﴾ [al-Rum 38]

﴿That﴾ refers to giving, or giving the near of kin his right. ﴿And the needy and the wayfarer﴾ ... ﴿Better﴾: is the word ﴿khayr﴾ here intended as a comparative, or is it a noun not in the comparative sense? We said earlier that khayr and sharr are used both as comparative forms and as nouns without comparison, as in His saying: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it. And whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it.﴾ [al-Zalzalah 7–8] This does not mean comparison. Likewise here, He said: ﴿That is better for those who desire the Face of Allah.﴾ Apparently it is not intended as a comparative, but rather that this is good, the opposite of evil, yet it is restricted by His saying ﴿for those who desire the Face of Allah﴾, and this is evidence of sincerity: it is good for the sincere who desire the Face of Allah. As for one who is not sincere, it is not good for him. But is it good for the believer?

(...) He, the Exalted, said: ﴿There is no good in much of their secret talk, except for one who enjoins charity, or what is right, or reconciliation between people.﴾ [al-Nisa' 114] Allah made that good absolutely, then said: ﴿And whoever does that seeking the pleasure of Allah, We will give him a great reward.﴾ He made this thing good absolutely because of the benefit it extends to others, but it is not good for the doer except with the intention of sincerity. I think this is clear. If you gave charity to a person in money or a garment he wears, he benefits, does he not?

* Students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Good. Do you benefit? You may benefit, you may be harmed, or you may neither benefit nor be harmed. If you do it for show, you are harmed; if you do it sincerely, you benefit; if you do it merely from habit and disposition, you do not benefit. Therefore He said here: ﴿for those who desire the Face of Allah﴾. The author said: (i.e., its reward for what they do); (i.e., its reward). This interpretation does not fit the correct understanding; it follows the method of the interpreters (ahl al-ta'wil) who do not affirm the descriptive attributes that Allah reported about Himself, such as the Face, the Hands, the Foot, and the like. So interpreting "Face" as "reward" is an error, and it is not the way of Ahl al-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah, but the way of the innovators who call themselves interpreters, while in reality they are distorters. The correct view is that "the Face of Allah" means His Face, which is one of His attributes, and that the verses point to the fact that whoever does such deeds for Allah will see Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and meet Him, as established in the Book, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the early scholars, that the believers will see their Lord as they see the moon on the night of the full moon.

* The student: Shaykh, we said that one benefits from what is given. So should it say: "That is good for those who desire the Face of Allah," meaning the matter (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, it is benefited from. How would it not be benefited from?!
* The student: I say it is benefited from, but what does the verse intend?
* The Shaykh: Yes. We say: it is not good except for those who desire the Face of Allah. This is with respect to the giver. As for the recipient, it is good for him, even if the giver is a disbeliever: if a disbeliever gives a person money, he benefits from it, and it becomes good.
* The student: But the meaning of the verse is that it is a benefit to the giver.
* The Shaykh: Yes, it is not good for the giver except through intention. For the giver it is only good with intention; as for the recipient, it is good in every case. Allah did not mention here the good for the giver except with this intention. As for the recipient, there is no doubt that he has good in every case, as the verse in al-Nisa' explains.
* The student: (...) the reward of Allah, does that not include seeing Allah (...)? Should we give him an excuse?
* The Shaykh: No, the path is well known.
* The student: Surah al-Insan, which indicates that in His saying (...).
* The Shaykh: ﴿Looking toward its Lord﴾ [al-Qiyamah 23]. The first is "nadirah" with a dad, meaning good and radiant; the second with a za, because it comes from looking with the eye.

He said: ﴿And those are the successful.﴾ [al-Rum 38] "Ula'ika" is the subject, ﴿hum﴾ is a separating pronoun (damir al-fasl), and ﴿al-muflihun﴾ is its predicate. The successful (al-muflih) is one who attains the sought and is saved from what is feared, from "aflaha" meaning to succeed. The root meaning of falah is remaining, as the poet said:

.......................... ∗∗∗ and evening and morning have no falah with them

That is, no remaining. But it became general for everything by which the sought is attained and one is saved from what is desired.

His saying: ﴿They are the successful﴾ is a nominal sentence, indicating that success is necessary for them. Is the separating pronoun a noun or a particle? No: the correct view is that it is a particle with no grammatical place (la mahall lahu min al-i'rab), and it is not parsed. Why? What is the benefit of the separating pronoun? Its benefit is restriction (al-hasr) only, and it has three benefits: first, restriction; second, emphasis; third, distinguishing a description from a predicate. For example, if you say: Zayd al-'aqil ("Zayd the intelligent"), Zayd is the subject and al-'aqil is the predicate. But it could be that al-'aqil is an adjective of Zayd, and the predicate is something after it, such as "praiseworthy." So if you say: Zayd huwa al-'aqil, it becomes determined that al-'aqil is the predicate. That is why it is called a separating pronoun, because it separates and distinguishes between the follower, which is the adjective, and the predicate. As for its emphatic function, it is clear, since your saying "Zayd huwa al-'aqil" is stronger in indicating restriction than "Zayd al-'aqil." As for it having no grammatical place, observe in the Qur'an: ﴿Perhaps we will follow the sorcerers if they are the victors.﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 40]

Had it had a grammatical place, it would say: "in kanu al-ghalibun" ("if they are the victorious"), with hum as the subject and al-ghalibun as the predicate, and the whole clause as the predicate of kana. This shows that it has no grammatical place, and according to the well-known view of the grammarians it is a particle, that is, it was brought in for separation.

* The student: May Allah keep you safe. When the term "pronoun" (damir) is applied to it, and all pronouns are nouns, then if it is a particle (...).
* The Shaykh: It has the form of a pronoun, but its meaning is not the meaning of a pronoun that is a noun (...).

Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And when We let people taste mercy, they rejoice in it; but if an evil befalls them because of what their hands have sent forth, behold, they despair.﴾ [al-Rum 36]

* From this noble verse is derived: (...) ﴿with what We have given them, so enjoy, for you will soon know.﴾ [al-Nahl 55]
* From this verse is derived: that Allah, the Exalted, may make blessings a cause of disbelief, so disbelief becomes their meaning, by His saying ﴿that they may disbelieve in what We have given them﴾ [al-Rum 34], since we mentioned that the lam here indicates consequence (lam al-'aqibah).
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: establishing causes, if we take the ba in His saying ﴿with what We have given them﴾ as causal. If we take it as specifying, then there is no proof in it.
* Among its benefits: that whatever blessing reaches us is from Allah, by His saying ﴿with what We have given them﴾.
* Among them: a warning to the disbelievers, and that their delight in Allah's blessings is a harm to them, by His saying ﴿so enjoy, for you will soon know.﴾
* Among them: the eloquence of the Qur'an, through the shift from the third person to the second person, which in the terminology of the rhetoricians is called (...), since we have already mentioned the benefits of such a shift.
* The student: And the reverse, Shaykh?
* The Shaykh: Except... how?
* Among them: establishing the recompense. From where do we take it? From His saying ﴿so you will soon know.﴾

Then He, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Or have We sent down to them an authority, so that it speaks of what they used to associate with Him?﴾ [al-Rum 35]

* Among the benefits of this verse: those polytheists have no proof for their polytheism, by His saying ﴿Or have We sent down to them an authority?﴾
* Among its benefits: whoever acts on the basis of evidence is not blameworthy. From where is this taken? From His saying ﴿Or have We sent down to them an authority?﴾, meaning that if they had an authority, We would not blame them or punish them.
* Among them: that the mujtahid who interprets bears no sin, why? Because he relies in his ijtihad on evidence, since he based himself on a proof. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ did not hold Usamah ibn Zayd liable for the blood of the man he killed after he had said "There is no god but Allah," the reason being that he was interpreting. He did not oblige 'Ammar ibn Yasir to make up the prayer when he performed tayammum from major impurity by rolling on the ground and rubbing himself in it, why? Because he was interpreting. He did not oblige the istihadah woman to make up the prayers she left during the time of her istihadah, because she was interpreting. Accordingly, every interpreter who thinks he is correct bears no sin. But does this include the fundamentals (usul) and the branches (furu'), or is it specific to the branches of religion?

Shaykh al-Islam said that it includes both fundamentals and branches. Shaykh al-Islam and his student Ibn al-Qayyim rejected the division of religion into fundamentals and branches, and said that this division has no basis either in the Book or in the Sunnah. Consider: according to those who make this division, is prayer among the fundamentals or the branches? It is among the branches, even though it is the very foundation of the foundations, the second pillar of Islam. Yet, in their view, it belongs to the category of branches. And there are matters on which they differ, and which they place in the category of fundamentals, and they consider disagreement about them permissible, such as the disagreement over whether the Prophet ﷺ saw his Lord, and the disagreement over the bliss and punishment of the grave in some cases, and similar matters of creed, and yet they hold that disagreement on them is acceptable.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 30, verse 34–40 (part 3 of 5):

The point is that the whole matter rests on one principle of the Shariah, namely the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ [al-Baqarah 286]. Whoever strives to seek the truth and sincerely pursues it, but is not granted it, despite good intention and sound method, do we say that he is sinful? That is not possible. For example, there are among the scholars eminent figures whom we testify to be religious, righteous, lovers of Islam and defenders of Islam, yet they oppose the early generations (al-Salaf) in matters of creed. We love them and do not hold them sinful, such as Ibn Hajar, Ibn al-Jawzi, and likewise al-Nawawi, and groups of scholars known for righteousness, reform and love of good. We know that they are mujtahids (scholars who exercise independent reasoning), whereas a person for whom the truth has become clear but who persists in obstinacy and insistence is treated according to what his obstinacy and insistence require.

Now, the verse in which Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿Or have We sent down to them an authority?﴾ concerns a fundamental matter, namely shirk. Had they had a proof on which to rely, they would not deserve punishment or blame, but they have no proof.

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Or have We sent down to them an authority, so that it speaks of what they used to associate with Him?﴾ [al-Rum 35].

* It is also derived from it that the authority or proof on which they rely must be clear, as shown by His words ﴿so that it speaks﴾. The expression "speaks" is the clearest form of manifestation.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the manifestation of the justice of Allah, the Exalted. Otherwise He would punish them without establishing proof against them. But to manifest His justice, He requires proof from them, even though they have no proof. Of this kind are the scales on the Day of Resurrection and the books on the Day of Resurrection. All of this is to manifest the justice of Allah. Otherwise, Allah has the judgment and to Him is the final return, and He is able to punish without scales and without a book. But with His perfect justice, He gives the person his book and says to him: ﴿Read your book; sufficient is yourself against you this day as a reckoner﴾ [al-Isra 14].

Some of the early generations said: "Whoever made you your own reckoner has been just to you." This is correct. If you think of an account between you and someone with whom you have dealings, with incoming and outgoing sums, and you say: "Take the ledger and reckon it yourself," is this justice or not? It is justice. This is unlike a case where you do not itemize the account and say: "You owe such-and-such, and I owe such-and-such." That may be open to doubt. But when you give him the ledger and say: "You reckon it yourself," this is the utmost fairness.

There is another point: ﴿And when We let people taste mercy, they rejoice in it; but if an evil befalls them for what their hands have put forth, behold, they despair﴾ [al-Rum 36].

* It is derived from the noble verse that mercy comes from Allah as an act of grace and bounty. How is that? That it is from Him is shown by His words ﴿When We let them taste﴾. As for it being an act of grace, that is because He did not mention a cause for it, so it is grace and bounty.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the censure of joy when it is out of insolence and exultation. You may say: from where do we take this from the verse?

* A student: From His words ﴿they rejoice﴾, O Shaykh.

* The Shaykh: Yes, but the restriction of joy to insolence and exultation can be taken from His words ﴿but if an evil befalls them for what their hands have put forth, behold, they despair﴾. It may be understood that the blameworthy joy is that described by what follows it.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: an evil is not attributed to Allah, because He said ﴿if an evil befalls them﴾ and did not say "and We did not afflict them."

If someone says: What do you say about the words of Allah in Surat al-Nisa: ﴿And if an evil befalls them, they say, "This is from you." Say, "All is from Allah"﴾ [al-Nisa 78]? So what is the reconciliation?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Good. Here we have said that an evil is not attributed to Allah. That is, is its bringing about an evil or not? Its bringing about is not an evil. It is evil in itself, but its existence is not evil; rather, it is for a wisdom. So a thing in itself may be evil, but in relation to the act of the doer, the doer's act is not evil. For example, a man's son was stung and needed cauterization, so he heated an iron in the fire and cauterized him. The son cried out: was it from joy or from pain? From pain. So is this an evil or not? But is the father's cauterizing of him an evil or a good? A good.

So we must know the difference between the act and the object of the act. Evil and harm pertain only to the object of Allah's act, which are attributes separate from Allah. As for the act itself, which is His own act, it can never be evil at all; rather it is good. And one may say that good is of two kinds: good in itself, and good for something else. What is evil in itself but which Allah has decreed is good for something else. What is good in itself is good. Is this clear? Can we say it this way? So for this there are two answers.

The first answer: it may be said that evil is not in Allah's act, but in what is acted upon. As for His bringing it into existence, it is good because of the profound wisdom it contains. This is one answer, and its parallel is a person's cauterizing his son to cure him of an illness. In itself, the cautery is evil, but in relation to the father's act it is good. That is one aspect.

Or it may be said: good is of two kinds, good in itself and good for something else. What is pure good is good in itself, like rain, plants, security, and the like. What is evil in itself is good for something else. When evil is good for something else, it thereby becomes good. Drought, famine, fear and the like are therefore good, because they lead to good, as Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Corruption has appeared on land and sea because of what the hands of people have earned, that He may let them taste part of what they have done that they may return﴾ [al-Rum 41].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: we now understand that evil is not attributed to Allah, but is attributed to what He acts upon.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: evil only reaches people because of their deeds, as shown by His words ﴿for what their hands have put forth﴾. Now, is this question about evil in religious matters and worldly matters, or only worldly matters? It applies to both. Drought and famine are due to evil deeds and sins. Likewise, deviation of the heart is due to sins: ﴿So when they deviated, Allah let their hearts deviate﴾ [al-Saff 5].

So religious and worldly calamities are all due to our own deeds. If we are upright, our affairs become upright for us. ﴿O you who have believed, if you fear Allah, He will grant you a criterion and will remove from you your misdeeds and forgive you﴾ [al-Anfal 29]. Note "a criterion" (furqan). So piety is a cause of knowledge, because the criterion is only by means of knowledge by which a person distinguishes between the beneficial and the harmful, and between truth and falsehood. So we say that this includes matters of religion and matters of this world.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the prohibition of despair of Allah's mercy. From where is this taken? Because Allah stated it in a blameworthy manner: ﴿behold, they despair﴾. This is evidence of its prohibition. There is also evidence for its prohibition by reflection: despair entails not returning to Allah. That is, if a person despairs of Allah's mercy, how can he hope for Allah's mercy? He then becomes weary and hopeless, and Allah forbid, and does not expose himself to what contains hope and expectation.

* A student: O Shaykh, the trial...

* The Shaykh: A trial that causes pain is an evil, while a trial that brings joy is a test, not an evil.

* A student: Is the believer tested according to the measure of his faith?

* The Shaykh: He is tested according to the measure of his faith, because sometimes afflictions are not for punishment but for making an example, that is, for clarification. This has passed us: ﴿And We will surely test you until We make evident those of you who strive and are patient﴾ [Muhammad 31], and ﴿Or do you think you will enter Paradise without there having come to you the like of those who passed on before you? Hardship and adversity touched them﴾ [al-Baqarah 214].

We have said that a trial when a person's state is upright is not meant to expiate a sin that occurred, but is meant to raise ranks, because patience is only exercised in affliction, and patience is a high station that is attained only with hardship.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of free choice in the servant, as shown by His words ﴿for what their hands have put forth﴾ [al-Rum 36]. This is a refutation of whom? The Jabriyyah (determinists), who say that man has no choice in his actions.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a person may be punished for deeds of the heart, or be blamed for deeds of the heart, because despair is a deed of the heart, since it is the utmost hopelessness and its seat is the heart.

[Shift to the third person:] ...to the third person (al-ghaybah). There is elevation of the matter in it, like the expression in His words: ﴿And your Lord said, "Call upon Me"﴾ [Ghafir 60], not "and I said to you" or "I say to you," glorifying His standing, the Exalted. And what is the meaning of this? The glorification of those who sought the face of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, by their obtaining a doubling of reward and recompense, unlike the earlier ones.

Then Allah, the Exalted, said: (﴿Allah is He who created you, then provided for you, then causes you to die, then gives you life. Is there any of your partners﴾ — of those you associate with Allah — ﴿who does anything of that?﴾). The author says: (No). ﴿Glorified is He and exalted above what they associate with Him﴾.

﴿Allah is He who created you﴾ means He brought you into existence from nothing. But creation is not merely bringing into existence; it is bringing into existence with measure. Some have even said that creation in origin means measuring, and they cited the words of a poet:

"And indeed you measure what you have not created, / while some people create and do not measure."

What is the meaning of "you have not created"? It means "you have not measured." But the correct view is that it applies to bringing into existence preceded by measuring. So the meaning of ﴿created you﴾ is brought you into existence preceded by measuring, precision and perfection. Is this agreed upon or not?

* Students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Even among the polytheists? Even among them, ﴿And if you asked them who created them, they would surely say, "Allah"﴾ [al-Zukhruf 87]. No one can claim that he created himself, except a madman, never. Nor can anyone claim that he was created without a creator: ﴿Or were they created from nothing, or are they the creators?﴾ [al-Tur 35]? No. Your father did not create you, nor did your mother create you, nor did any human create you, nor any non-human other than Allah, the Exalted. This is an accepted matter.

Second: ﴿then provided for you﴾...

* A student: The Communists say: stones created them (...).

* The Shaykh: They say it is nature. They acknowledge these creatures, but they are stubborn, and their words carry no weight.

* A student: The people of nature. What do they say about the creation?

* The Shaykh: They say: this is a thing that has existed from eternity with these attributes and continues to interact and reproduce, and the like.

* The student: But they do not affirm that Allah is the Creator.

* The Shaykh: But they affirm an originator. They do not say that this thing, for example... that this human or this animal came into being by chance. They affirm an originator, which is nature. So we say to them: who brought this nature into existence?

His words ﴿then provided for you﴾ [al-Rum 40]...

* A student: (...) the reality of the matter (...).

* The Shaykh: ﴿provided for you﴾ means gave you. In the language, provision (rizq) means giving. From it is His words: ﴿And when relatives, orphans and the needy are present at the division, provide them from it﴾ [al-Nisa 8], that is, give them.

Does anyone claim that there is a provider other than Allah? Someone may claim it. He may say: ﴿provide them from it﴾; Allah said ﴿provide them﴾, so I provided this person, I gave him. It is said to him: but who created what you gave? The one who provided you with this is Allah. Whatever work the children of Adam do is only transformation, not origination. All the work of the children of Adam, including crafts, construction and other things, is merely transformation, that is, change from one thing into another. Otherwise, the origin is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. He is the Creator and the Originator. This provision you gave, for example, you gave this man a bag of food. It is true that you provided him, but who brought this bag into existence? Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. So the origin of provision is from Allah, even if it occurs by the hands of some people, as shown by His words: ﴿provide them from it﴾, and the words of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him: "And for them is their provision and their clothing according to what is customary" [recorded by Muslim (1218/147) from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah].

But it may be said: who created this provision? Who brought it to you? Who decreed that you give him this? The answer to all of this is Allah.

His words ﴿then causes you to die﴾ mean: after this creation and provision. Creation is preparation, and provision is sustenance. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, brought you into existence, prepared you and equipped you, then sustained you with what sustains you. After that He causes you to die. ﴿Causes you to die﴾ means: after the life of this world there is death, which is the complete separation of the soul from the body. Sleep involves a separation in which the soul leaves the body, but not a complete separation. As for death, which is death, it is a complete separation. However, the soul is returned to the body in the grave, returned in a barzakh (intermediate) manner, not like its return in this world.

﴿then causes you to die, then gives you life﴾: the life of the Hereafter, after which there is no extinction.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Is there any of your partners﴾. Is "your partners" here in an object relation or a subject relation?

* A student: A subject relation.

* The Shaykh: ﴿of your partners﴾ means those whom you made partners, so it is in an object relation, i.e., are there any among those whom you made partners with Allah? That is why the author said: "of those you associate with Allah."

* A student: You associate this (...).

* The Shaykh: No, you associate, but you make them partners. Originally, it means of those whom you made partners.

* A student: That a person associates.

* The Shaykh: Yes. If one associates, then the one associated with is the object. So the meaning of ﴿your partners﴾ is not that they are the ones who associated you, but that you are the ones who made them partners with Allah. So it is an annexation to its object.

He said: ﴿Is there any of your partners who does anything of that?﴾ What is the grammatical analysis of ﴿who does﴾ (man yafʿal)? What is its position in the grammar?

* A student: The conditional verb.

* The Shaykh: Which condition?

* A student: (Hal).

* The Shaykh: No. In ﴿Is there of your partners man yafʿal﴾, what is the grammatical status of (man)?

* A student: The object of the verbal noun.

* The Shaykh: No. It may be an indefinite qualified noun, and the implied meaning is: is there among your partners anyone who does that? It may also be a relative pronoun, as a subject delayed, i.e., "the one who is among your partners, does the one who does that come from your partners?" The first is better: that it is an indefinite qualified noun, meaning: is there among your partners anyone who does any of that?

His words ﴿of anything﴾: (min) is additional. Its addition is valid because the interrogative here carries the meaning of negation, and (min) may be added in negation, as Ibn Malik said:

"And it is added in negation and the like, and it makes the indefinite noun genitive, like: 'there is no escape for the rebel from escape.'"

His words ﴿Is there any of your partners who does any of that?﴾: what does the referent (that) refer to? It refers to creation, provision, giving life and causing death. On this basis, the answer regarding the singular masculine demonstrative despite the earlier mention of four things is that it is a plural: it is interpreted as referring to what was mentioned. ﴿Who does any of that﴾ means from that which was mentioned. So it is correct for the demonstrative to come in the singular masculine, because it refers back to what was mentioned.

His words ﴿of anything﴾ mean: these cannot do any of these matters at all, neither creation, nor provision, nor giving life, nor causing death. This is by way of challenge. If these deities that are associated with Allah do none of this, can they be gods? No. Their worship is false, as shown by His words: ﴿That is because Allah is the Truth, and what they invoke other than Him is falsehood﴾ [al-Hajj 62].

There remains the case where a claimant claims that he gives life and causes death, like the one who argued with Ibrahim about his Lord. Ibrahim, peace be upon him, said to him: ﴿My Lord is He who gives life and causes death.﴾ He said: ﴿I give life and cause death﴾ [al-Baqarah 258]. What is the answer if someone says: among the worshipped ones there is one who can give life and cause death?

We say: this claim is false, because the giving of life and causing of death by a human being are not true giving of life and causing of death, but rather the action of a means through which something occurs (...).

﴿So give to the near of kin his right, and to the needy and the wayfarer﴾ [al-Rum 38], to the end of the verse.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: these three categories have a right: the near of kin, the needy, and the wayfarer.

* Among its benefits: it is obligatory to give these people their right. From where is this taken? From the imperative "(ātِ) give," and the basic meaning of an imperative is obligation.

* Among its benefits: the nearest are more entitled than the next nearest. From where is this taken? From His saying, ﴿the near of kin﴾. But how is it derived? It is derived from a principle we have previously established: when a ruling is attached to a descriptive attribute, then whatever possesses that attribute more strongly is more entitled to it. When a ruling is attached to an attribute, the more firmly that attribute is found in something, the more entitled that thing is.

For example, if you say, "Discipline the disobedient," the discipline is attached to what? To disobedience. What does that require? Whoever is more disobedient deserves more discipline, or not? And if we say, "Honor the believer," the meaning is that whoever is stronger in faith is more deserving of honor.

﴿The near of kin﴾: the right is attached to what? To kinship. So whoever is nearer is more entitled to the giving.

This principle is useful for the student of knowledge: when a ruling is attached to a strong attribute, that ruling is strengthened by the strength of that attribute, because attaching the ruling to the attribute indicates that the attribute is its cause ('illa). This is also the second principle: attaching a ruling to an attribute indicates that the attribute is the cause.

For example, you say, "Honor the believer," why? Because of his faith. "Discipline the wicked," why? Because of his wickedness. ﴿And Allah does not love the corrupters﴾ [al-Ma'idah 64], ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love the corrupters﴾ [al-Qasas 77]. The meaning is: because of their corruption. Thus we say: attaching a ruling to an attribute indicates that this attribute is its cause and the reason for the ruling. Based on this principle, the first principle also follows.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: whoever is more entitled to kindness is more deserving of it, because the needy is more entitled to kindness than the rich, and the wayfarer whose journey has cut him off is more entitled than others.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: beneficial action that extends to others is good in itself. Is it good for the doer? It is good for him on condition [of intention]. It is good in itself even if the doer does not benefit from it.

On that basis, it follows that the benefits that disbelievers provide to Muslims are good for the Muslims. We do not say, "This came from a disbeliever, so it is not good; there is no good in it." No. If one of the disbelievers improved a road from among these disbelieving companies, would this improvement be good? Yes, good without doubt. But it is not good for them; it is good for others.

* Among the benefits of the verse: a warning about the importance of sincerity, from His saying, ﴿That is better for those who seek the Face of Allah﴾.

* Among its benefits: whenever the action is more sincere to Allah, it is better for the doer. From where do we take this ruling?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No. We have taken that there is good for whoever intends sincerity. But whenever it is more sincere, it is greater good for the doer, from the principle that passed us: this ruling was attached to the cause ﴿for those who seek﴾, because the relative pronoun with its complement is exactly like the active participle. So it is good for "those who seek." Therefore, whenever a person is more sincere in seeking the Face of Allah, it is better, greater good for him.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of the Face for Allah, from His saying, ﴿the Face of Allah﴾.

The scholars said that the Face of Allah, glory be to Him, is among the attributes of information (ṣifāt khabariyya), because they hold that the attributes are purely attributes of information, and they describe them by this term so that they do not fall into what is forbidden. They do not say that they are partial or divisible, for asserting partition or division of the Essence of Allah, glory be to Him, is forbidden. So the Face, the Hand, the Eye, the Shin, and the Foot are all described as attributes of information. But hearing, knowledge, power, and life—what are they called? Attributes of meaning (ṣifāt ma'nawiyya), attributes of meanings.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: an allusion to seeing Allah, glory be to Him. How? From His saying, ﴿they seek the Face of Allah﴾.

There is no doubt that it is established: the seeing of Allah, glory be to Him, is established by the Qur'an, the Sunnah, and the consensus (ijmā') of the early generations (salaf). In the Qur'an, Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Faces that Day will be radiant, looking toward their Lord﴾ [al-Qiyamah 22-23]. What is the meaning of the first "radiant" (nāḍira)? It is from radiance (naḍāra), which is beauty. ﴿Looking toward their Lord (nāẓira)﴾, with the ḍād or the ẓā'? With the ẓā', from looking (naẓar), which is seeing with the eye. This verse is among the clearest in the Qur'an. There are other verses: ﴿Upon couches, they look﴾ [al-Mutaffifin 23]. And there is a third verse: ﴿For those who did good is the best reward and an increase﴾ [Yunus 26]. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, explained it as seeing the Face of Allah [narrated by Muslim (181/297) from the hadith of Suhayb]. There is a fourth verse: ﴿They will have therein whatever they wish, and with Us is more﴾ [Qaf 35]. There is a fifth verse, which is His saying in al-An'am: ﴿No vision can grasp Him, but He grasps all vision﴾ [al-An'am 103]. This verse indicates seeing, because Allah said, ﴿No vision can grasp Him﴾, and negating "grasping" indicates the establishment of the more general basis. If He could not be seen at all, He would have said, "Vision does not see Him." Negating the more specific implies the existence of the more general. For this reason, this verse, which the people of ta'til (denial of attributes) use as evidence for denying the seeing of Allah, becomes evidence against them, not evidence for them.

Now, the difference between the attributes of meaning and the attributes of information is that the attributes of meaning indicate meanings, such as hearing, sight, knowledge, power, and what is similar to them. As for the attributes of information, they indicate attributes that are parts (ab'ād) of us; relative to us they are parts. So a person's hand, face, shin, foot, and eye, for example, are parts of him. But we do not call them parts in relation to Allah. Rather, the scholars named them the attributes of information.

* A student: In the hadith: "On the Day of Resurrection, Allah, glory be to Him, will say: Whoever used to worship the tawaghit, let him follow the tawaghit, and whoever used to worship the sun, let him follow the sun. Then Allah, glory be to Him, will come to them in a form other than the form they know, and He will say: I am your Lord. They will say: We seek refuge in Allah from You; this is our place until our Lord comes to us. He will say: Then He will come to them in the form they know, and He will say: I am your Lord. They will say: You are our Lord. Then He will proceed, and they will follow Him" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6573), Muslim (182/299), from Abu Hurayrah].

* The Shaykh: No, it is not "then He will proceed, and they will follow Him."

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: "He will proceed."

* A student: "And they will follow Him."

* The Shaykh: Allah?

* A student: "He will uncover His shin."

* The Shaykh: "The shin will be uncovered, and everyone who used to prostrate to Allah in the world will prostrate to Him." In any case, what is the problem with it?

* A student: The question is, how does He proceed and they follow Him?

* The Shaykh: No, I do not know that; I do not know it. Verify it. We are not researching it now until it is confirmed. This did not pass me, but what passed us is that the nations follow what they used to worship until they are thrown into the Fire.

* A student: Every person follows his gods?

* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. Good.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: salvation comes through two matters: sincerity and doing what is commanded. From where do we take this? From His saying, ﴿and those are the successful﴾ [al-Rum 38]. Those referred to here acted, and the second, sincerity.

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And what you give in usury﴾ [al-Rum 39]...

* A student: What is the benefit?

* The Shaykh: The benefit is that salvation comes through doing what is commanded together with sincerity.

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And what you give in usury for increase within the wealth of people will not increase with Allah. But what you give in zakah, seeking the Face of Allah, those are the ones who will receive multiplication﴾ [al-Rum 39].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: whoever spends his wealth in order to obtain worldly matters has no reward for it. From where is this taken? From His saying, ﴿it will not increase with Allah﴾. This is the opposite of the first group mentioned in the previous verse. Those who gave in the previous verse, what did they seek? They sought the Face of Allah. These, on the contrary, seek an increase through what they gave.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse also: a warning about the importance of sincerity, from His saying, ﴿but what you give in zakah, seeking the Face of Allah﴾.

* A student: (...)?

* The Shaykh: With sincerity along with the action, righteous action together with sincerity.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: a warning about sincerity. From where is it taken? ﴿Seeking the Face of Allah﴾.

* Among its benefits also: multiplication of deeds is according to sincerity, from His saying, ﴿those are the ones who will receive multiplication.﴾ Allah, the Exalted, linked multiplication to seeking the Face of Allah. According to the principle we established just now, whoever is more sincere to Allah, his deed receives greater multiplication. This is a matter with no doubt, for the multiplication of deeds occurs through many causes: among them the nobility of time, the nobility of place, the nobility of the doer, the nobility of the deed, sincerity, and following the Sunnah. These six causes are all causes of multiplication.

Multiplication due to the nobility of time is like Ramadan and the first ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah. This is due to the nobility of time.

And place, like the two Harams and al-Aqsa; the deed done in them is more noble than elsewhere. Prayer in the three mosques is more excellent than elsewhere.

Among them is the doer, like the Companions, about whom the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "If one of you spent gold equal to Uhud, it would not reach the mudd of one of them, nor half of it" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3673), Muslim (2541/222), from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri].

Joined to this are those who act in the last times, in the days of patience, who hold fast to the Sunnah of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, while people turn away from it. Their reward is multiplied, even though they do not attain the rank of the Companions. Their reward is multiplied because of the strangeness they find and the opposition of people to them. No one doubts that acting in an environment where people act as he acts is easy; rather, opposition from people is what is difficult. But acting in an environment where people do not act this way is what is hard and burdensome, especially since the opposition will be fierce, because this person holds to obedience to Allah, while those who oppose him are the opposite. And the fiercest struggle between opposing parties is that between those who hold to the religion of Allah and those who cast it off. These are three. What remains?

* A student: The deed remains.

* The Shaykh: Multiplication also depends on the deed...

* A student: Its quantity.

* The Shaykh: According to the deed. Quantity is not what is intended, but the kind of deed. So prayer is better than other deeds, and the obligatory part of every deed is better and more noble than its supererogatory part (nafl). Jihad in the way of Allah is the peak of the hump of Islam. And so on, as we have explained to you many times. These are four. And the fifth?

* A student: Sincerity.

* The Shaykh: According to sincerity, as in this verse. Whenever a person is more sincere, even if the deed is the same, his deed is nobler than another's. For this reason, you find two men who rode one car, set out and entered together for Hajj or Umrah, returned together in the same car, and their actions are identical and their words identical, yet the difference between them is greater than the distance between East and West, according to their sincerity to Allah.

The sixth is according to following (ittibā'). For this reason, "the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, informed that the best deed after faith in Allah is prayer on its time" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7534), Muslim (85/137), from Ibn Mas'ud], because it was performed in accordance with the Messenger, ﷺ.

All these causes of nobility are things that oblige the servant to care for his deeds and to realize, as far as he can, these causes.

* A student: His saying (...), "in the days of patience he has the reward of fifty of you," what does it...?

* The Shaykh: The meaning is that he has the reward of fifty of you in this quality for which he endured and was tired. The basic deed, for example charity, is multiplied tenfold; ten times its like exists among the Companions and also in this later time. But this is multiplied further, so the reward of this person is like the reward of fifty of the Companions, because of the hardship he finds. But the quantity that the Companions obtained, that if one of us spent a gold equal to Uhud, it would not reach the mudd of one of them nor half of it, this is specific to them. So we have a reward for the basic deed and a multiplied reward according to the doer. The basic deed, such as charity for example, is for these later people equal to the reward of fifty of the Companions' deeds with regard to its basic nature, not with regard to it having occurred from the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them.

* A student: Does their statement not refute this, when they said: "Are we or they?" and he said: "Rather, from you"?

* The Shaykh: Yes. It does not refute this, because we consider the basic deed, not the multiplication according to being a Companion. The basic deed of a Companion, were it not for companionship, would have only the reward of the basic deed; by companionship it increases. So the meaning of the Messenger's, peace and blessings be upon him, statement, "the reward of fifty of you," means in terms of the basic deed. And it is necessary to return to this, because it is not possible to reconcile it with the other hadith except in this way.

* A student: Why did the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, not say "fifty workers," rather than "fifty Companions"?

* The Shaykh: We cannot say "why did he not say." Because the matter now is one of reconciliation, and if the matter were clear we would not need to ask what the reconciliation is. Since the matter is one of reconciliation, we need to look for the narrowest scope in which the two texts can be combined.

* A student: To whom was the Messenger speaking?

* The Shaykh: The Messenger was speaking to the Companions.

* The student: And do the Companions differ in merit?

* The Shaykh: Yes, it is well known that the Companions differ in merit. He addressed Khalid ibn al-Walid in response to his insulting 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf. 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf was without doubt among the earliest foremost, while Khalid ibn al-Walid embraced Islam later. There was a dispute between them, and he said to him: "Be calm, O Khalid. Do not revile my Companions. By Him in whose hand is my soul, if one of you spent gold equal to Uhud, it would not reach the mudd of one of them, nor half of it" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3673), Muslim (2541/222), from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri].

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: As for those below them, they undoubtedly attain it. But as for those above them, the people of hadith hold that one cannot attain it. For this reason Allah, glory be to Him, said: ﴿Not equal among you are those who spent and fought before the conquest. Those are greater in rank than those who spent afterward and fought. But to each Allah has promised the best﴾ [al-Hadid 10]. Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Allah is the One who created you and then provided for you, then causes you to die and then gives you life. Is there, among your partners, any who does [any of] that?﴾ [al-Rum 40], to the end of the verse.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: argument from what is clearer and more evident. Allah argued against the falsehood of the idols of the polytheists by a matter they themselves acknowledge, and their gods do not do it: creation, provision, causing death, and giving life.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the perfection of the power of Allah, glory be to Him, through these four matters: creation, provision... to the end.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse also: the affirmation that what a person acquires is from Allah. These four include three that no one disputes: creation, causing death, and giving life. But provision may be disputed by a disputer. Qarun, what did he say? ﴿I was only given it on knowledge I have﴾ [al-Qasas 78]. Mujahid explained it, I think, as: "by knowledge from me of the ways of gain"; that is, "I am skilled in knowing gains, and I obtained this wealth." But we say: this acquisition which you obtained by your skill, from where did it come to you? From Allah, the Exalted, because what came to you occurred through a cause, and the Creator of causes is Allah.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: we should seek provision from our Lord alone, as He says: ﴿Then He provided for you﴾.

When this is the case, another benefit follows from it: that we should not seek His provision through disobeying Him. What is the reasoning? If you seek provision from Allah, is it rational to offer Him an act of disobedience in order to be provided for?

* Student: No.

* The Shaykh: Someone who seeks provision from others, what does he offer them? He offers obedience and submission to them. For this reason Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And whoever fears Allah, He will make for him a way out, and will provide for him from where he does not expect﴾ [al-Talaq 65:2–3]. So whoever seeks Allah's provision through His disobedience has opposed wisdom and what is right. Is that not so?

Those who seek provision through riba (usury), who seek provision through deception, who seek it through lying and other forbidden means, are in reality most like those who mock Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and ridicule Him, as if they were saying: "O our Lord, we disobey You so that You will provide for us." Nothing could be more grave than this. For this reason Allah made those who seek increase of wealth through riba, what did He make them? He made them warriors against Him: ﴿O you who believe, fear Allah and give up what remains of riba, if you are believers. And if you do not, then be informed of a war from Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:278–279].

And riba, as Shaykh al-Islam (Ibn Taymiyyah) said, is such that no sin other than shirk has had more stringent texts revealed about it than riba. Yet it has become among people today one of the easiest and most common things. They practise it openly, and they practise it through trickery. Practising it through trickery is lighter than practising it openly, just as practising disbelief through hypocrisy is lighter than practising outright disbelief. This is because the one who uses a trick is deceiving Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. He has combined, and we seek refuge with Allah, the corruption of riba with the corruption of deception and trickery. The Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, when He forbids something, is not like others; nothing is hidden from Him. He knows the treachery of the eyes and what the hearts conceal. His Prophet, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, made clear that actions are by what? By intentions.

So if you intend riba, but you resort to a trick by introducing a commodity that is not really intended, this is manipulation and mockery of the signs of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. One comes to a lender and says: "I want 100,000 from you on condition that it becomes 120,000 by a year." Fine, how is this achieved? By Allah, we are Muslims; I cannot give you 100,000 in cash and write 120,000 against you, because we fear Allah. But here is a way we can take refuge in from another angle, and place a barrier between us and Allah. By what? By any commodity that you agree upon. We go and look at what people have. They find with this one sugar, so he says: "We will buy sugar." They find with him cardamom, and they say: "We will buy cardamom." They find cars, and they say: "We will buy cars." They find bags whose content is unknown, perhaps it is sand, and they say: "We will buy these bags." Is this not the reality? This is the reality.

And so today they do not look at these bags to see what they are. They say: "They are bags of sugar." And the most that is done in "taking possession" (qabd) is that one passes one's hand over them, or counts them: one, two, three, four, five, six... and so on. And they say: "This is possession." Is this possession linguistically, customarily, or legally? Not at all. This is not considered possession, because possession means that the thing is in your grasp, whereas this thing is sitting in its place while several sales pass over it within an hour or two.

And this calamity with which people are afflicted now, we ask Allah to rescue them from it, is a grave calamity. What makes it uglier is that they believe it is permissible while the work of the banks is forbidden. To the extent that some of them come in fuming and complaining: "I seek refuge in Allah! Look at the forbidden! Riba is openly announced in the banks!" And he who deals in this transaction weeps for others and does not weep for himself, while he is more entitled to weep for himself.

The point is that we say, having digressed from the subject: if provision is from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, then it is obligatory upon you, both legally and rationally, to seek this provision through what? Through obeying Allah, not through disobeying Him.

* Student: But, O Shaykh, does tawarruq (the "commodity-purchase" method of obtaining cash) not fall under this?

* The Shaykh: Tawarruq, Shaykh al-Islam says, is included in this. And his student Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, says: "Our Shaykh was asked about this many times, and he insisted that it is forbidden and that it is riba." Tawarruq, other than the work that people are now engaged in... They say: "This is tawarruq." The scholars said about tawarruq (...): "Whoever needs cash and buys something worth 100 for 120, there is no harm in it, and this is the issue of tawarruq." This is the wording of al-Rawd al-Murbi' Sharh Zad al-Mustaqni' (a classical Hanbali manual).

Now look: first, they said "whoever needs," so we know it is only permitted out of necessity.

Secondly: "he buys something worth 100 for 120." The contract is concluded on the specific item sold; they did not say "ten, eleven, or twelve." And the word "buys" is to be understood as a lawful purchase that fulfils the conditions, among which is knowledge of the item sold, its type and its kind, and so on. Is this present in what people do now? Not at all.

Likewise, "he buys something worth 100 for 120 on credit" applies, because they say: "twelve, thirteen, eleven," according to agreement.

Then the same jurists who permitted that said: it is disliked to say, in a murabahah sale (a sale at cost plus a stated profit), the familiar formula: "ten for eleven." They reported from Imam Ahmad an explicit statement that it is forbidden to say "ten for eleven," even outside the issue of tawarruq. In a murabahah sale, which some of you know, it is forbidden, according to one of the two narrations from Ahmad, to say "ten for eleven" while one intends the commodity itself and not the cash. The school's position is that it is disliked, and the second narration from Ahmad is that it is forbidden.

That is to say, for example: I bought this book and you are selling the book. You sell the book itself, not its dirhams. You say to me: "I want to buy it from you on murabahah." I say: "There is no objection. I bought it for 100 and I sell it to you on the basis that I make one dirham profit on every ten dirhams." How much is the 100? It is 110. This is permissible.

But if you say: "I want to buy from you ten for eleven," they say: it is disliked according to the school, and forbidden according to the second narration, even though it falls under the issue of tawarruq.

So these people now combine two matters: "ten for eleven" or "ten for twelve," and tawarruq. As for our present business, it does not fit even according to the opinion of those who permit tawarruq.

Note that Imam Ahmad has a second narration; he has another narration that it is permissible, and a second narration that it is among the issues of 'inah (a sham sale used to disguise interest); tawarruq. Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah mentioned this from him, and Ibn al-Qayyim mentioned in Tahdhib al-Sunan that the issue of tawarruq is among the issues of 'inah, and 'inah is well known to be forbidden.

The conclusion is that, in truth, in our present age, when people care only about acquiring wealth, they have made wealth an end that is served, after it was a means that serves. The reality of wealth is that it is a means that serves, but we have now made it an end that is served. And this is from the foolishness of a human being: that his own wealth, which was created for him, should make him its servant. ﴿He it is who created for you all that is on the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:29].

* Student: But the reality (...).

* The Shaykh: No. The sound opinion is what we know nothing of.

* Student: Now, the "ru'yat al-'ayn" (seeing the item) (...).

* The Shaykh: This is used in disbelieving countries, and it is the proper method of deposit. Because our saying that the banks now hold my money as a deposit is not correct. It does not meet the legal meaning of a deposit. And what is the legal meaning of a deposit? That you give him money to keep it as it is, not that you give him your money to place in a box and benefit from it. The scholars even said: if the depositor permits the depositary to use the deposit, it becomes a loan established in his liability. And people now do what they call (...).

He takes a salam (advance sale). Salam is that I give a person dirhams in cash for a commodity to be delivered later, the reverse of a sale on credit. For example, I give you ten thousand riyals on the condition that you give me a hundred sacks of sugar, or a car of such and such description, after a year. This is fine, because the Companions used to do it during the time of the Messenger of Allah, ﷺ. They would make salam in fruit for a year or two years. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Whoever makes salam in something, let him make salam in a known measure, a known weight, and for a known term." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2240) and Muslim (1604/127), from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.] The reason that there is no problem is: does the profit become guaranteed for one of the two parties or not? For example, if I give you ten thousand riyals for a car on credit, we do not know which of us will profit, is that correct? Because at the end of the term I may find the car for six thousand riyals, or I may find it only for fifteen thousand riyals. Yes, indeed. And it is rare that prices do not change over a year.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: There is no problem. If he needs money, he comes to someone and says: "Come, give us money now against a deferred item," or he buys the goods he needs at a deferred price higher than the cash price.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No. That applies if he buys the commodity itself, wanting it specifically. He is not doing tawarruq, because tawarruq is when he does not want the commodity. That is why it is called tawarruq, derived from what? From "warq" (silver). That is, he wants nothing but silver, the one seeking silver (mutawarriq).

* Student: Regarding salam, does it include (...)?

* The Shaykh: That is why the jurists said: if he makes salam in the price of a specific orchard, it is not valid, because its object is now the orchard, and it has not become a liability on the debtor. But if it becomes a liability, there is no problem, provided all the conditions are fulfilled.

* Student: (...)?

* The Shaykh: No, it is not valid, nor is its price.

* Student: (...)?

* The Shaykh: It is not obligatory, because he is selling things to him without taking payment for them.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: This may mean that he brings it. And he, for example, refused. They agree with him that we have bought from you such and such: cars for such and such dirhams, and he did not hand over the dirhams.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Not at all. That is why sometimes the government's procrastination is greater than the people's procrastination.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: This is not valid unless the cars are with him and he says: "Bring them," for example, so that when they agree with him, the cars are brought, and then they conclude the contract on their specific items. In that case it is valid, because it is then a sale of a specific item for a debt.

* Student: They concluded the contract on its descriptions?

* The Shaykh: No, on its descriptions it is not valid, because a described item that is not specified has its place in the liability, not in a specific thing. Therefore the contract that took place between the man and the government is a contract on something in a liability for something in a liability, with no specific item at all.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: There is no objection. If he brings the goods and says: "These goods are now here, and I sell them to you for such and such," and the contract is concluded after the specifying, there is no objection. If it means insurance, in the sense that he brings them and after bringing them the contract is applied to them, this is not a problem, because it is a sale of a specific item for a debt, and that is permissible.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: When they make it a fixed arrangement, when do they make the contract with him?

* Student: When they fix it, they say to him, for example: "After ten days you will receive the surplus, and when the warehouse delivers, he goes and takes (...)."

* The Shaykh: What do they consider a contract? Do they consider the contract to be after its arrival, or before? If it is before, then it is not valid. When do they conclude the contract? Does it mean he says: "It is here, and when I have it, I will buy it from you for such and such"? When it arrives, we give you the price. Then the contract is before the bringing, and the scholars have stated explicitly that this is not permissible. This is a sale of debt for debt, so it does not make the prohibited lawful, because the contract was not concluded on a specific item. Everything is in liabilities now.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: (...) Do you know that if I sell you a sa' for two sa's, while the two sa's are worth the same as one sa', there is no prohibition in it? It is not forbidden. We restrict ourselves to what the text has stated. What the text stated is either that the commodity is deferred, or that the price is deferred, or that neither is present in both ways. This is not permissible, and this is explicitly stated by the jurists. Any student of knowledge who reads the beginning of al-Rawd al-Murbi' knows this. That is why they said among the forms of sale (...). What are its forms? Sale of debt for a specific item, on condition of presence and the taking of possession of one of the two counter-values.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: we have said that it is appropriate to use the evidence that is clearest and most manifest in argument.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the incapacity of these deities to do anything that is specific to lordship. This is by His saying: ﴿Is there any of your partners who does any of that?﴾ [al-Rum 30:40], because this interrogation, as we have explained, means negation.

* Among its benefits: the establishment of the inseparable connection between the two kinds of tawhid: tawhid al-rububiyyah (Oneness of Lordship) and tawhid al-uluhiyyah (Oneness of Worship). Whoever affirms tawhid al-rububiyyah is obliged to affirm tawhid al-uluhiyyah. This meaning was established by Allah, the Exalted, in several verses.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: the glorification of Allah, Glorified and Exalted, above every imperfection. From where is this derived? From His saying: ﴿Glory be to Him﴾.

* Among its benefits: that the polytheists against Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, have fallen into belittling Allah. This is by His saying: ﴿Glory be to Him and exalted above what they associate﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse also: that Allah, the Exalted, combines in what He describes and names Himself both negation and affirmation. The negation is in His saying: ﴿Glory be to Him﴾, and the affirmation is in His saying: ﴿and exalted above what they associate﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse also: the strength of persuasion in the style of the Qur'an. Such a challenge as: ﴿Is there any of your partners who does any of that?﴾ is as strong as persuasion can be. Each of them would answer: "No." Then why do you worship them alongside Allah?!

Can the three categories of tawhid be derived from this verse? Lordship is present, and Worship is present. How? Because affirming Lordship necessitates affirming Worship. Then His saying: ﴿Is there any of your partners?﴾ aims to nullify their divinity, and the Names and Attributes are present in His saying: ﴿Glory be to Him and exalted above what they associate.﴾ And Allah knows best.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 30, verse 34–40 (part 1 of 5):

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿That they may disbelieve in what We have given them. So enjoy yourselves, for you will soon know.﴾ [al-Rum 34] ﴿That they may disbelieve﴾: the lam here is the lam of consequence (lam al-'aqibah); meaning, by their associating others with Allah, their outcome became disbelief in what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has given them. "Given them" means: bestowed upon them.

As for His saying ﴿That they may disbelieve in what We have given them﴾, do we say that the ba' (in bi-) is causal (lil-sababiyyah), or that it is for emphasis (lil-tahqiq), meaning that they disbelieve in this very thing? The answer: it may be causal, meaning that because of what Allah the Exalted gave them of mercy and of deliverance from hardship, this became a cause of their insolence, their arrogance and their disbelief, as is the habit of man, except whoever Allah, Mighty and Majestic, protects.

Or it may be said: ﴿That they may disbelieve in what We have given them﴾, meaning: that they may disbelieve in this thing We have given them, in that they do not render its thanks, whereas it was obligatory upon them to render thanks to Allah, glorified and exalted be He.

As for His saying ﴿So enjoy yourselves﴾, this is called in rhetoric (iltifat) (a shift of grammatical person); for He did not say "and let them enjoy themselves" as He said in another verse, but rather commanded them directly to enjoy themselves. The imperative here is for threat, as the author (may Allah have mercy on him) said: "He said: i.e., We gave them, intended as emphasis; so enjoy yourselves; the imperative here is for threat, not permission." The proof of this is His saying ﴿for you will soon know﴾, a shift from the third person (absence) — where is the absence? ﴿That they may disbelieve﴾.

We have previously mentioned that iltifat has two benefits: a benefit inherent in every iltifat, which is alerting the listener, because when speech is in one consistent pattern a person continues following it, but when it changes he pauses: why did the context change? Why was the sentence in the third person and then became second person, or the reverse? So he stops, pays attention and reflects. The second benefit varies according to context. The second benefit here in this verse is that when they are confronted with the imperative ﴿So enjoy yourselves﴾, the threat becomes stronger and more forceful than if it had said "and let them enjoy themselves."

As for His saying ﴿for you will soon know﴾: it has been said that sawfa (soon/will) conveys certainty but also conveys delay, unlike the sin (s), which conveys certainty and immediacy; each thing according to its context. It is so here because the greatest punishment that will come to them will be on the Day of Resurrection, which is delayed. Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Or have We sent down to them an authority?﴾ [al-Rum 35]

* The student: What does sawfa convey?
* The shaykh: It conveys certainty and delay. He said: (﴿Or﴾ means the hamzah of denial; ﴿have We sent down to them an authority﴾ means proof and a book; ﴿so it speaks﴾ means it speaks by indication; ﴿of what they used to associate with Him﴾ means it commands them to associate? No.) Here the author says "or" (am) is in the sense of the hamzah of denial, which is one of the two opinions concerning it. The second opinion is that it means "bal" (rather) together with the hamzah, so it conveys a transitional turning away (idrab intiqali): "rather, have We sent down to them an authority?" When the interrogative is for denial, its meaning is negation: that is, did We send down to them an authority supporting their association, confirming it and saying that it is true? The answer: No, We did not send down such a thing. ﴿Or have We sent down to them an authority?﴾

The author says: (﴿authority﴾: proof and a book). Proof is called sultan because the one who argues with it has authority (sultah) over the one he argues against; therefore it is called sultan, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿You have no authority for this﴾ [Yunus 68], i.e., no proof.
