What links this verse and the one we are explaining is that it may be said: punishments in general are beneficial, but in particular they may not benefit; because Allah said: ﴿And among the people is he who worships Allah﴾ — "among the people." And His saying: ﴿but if trial strikes him﴾ may mean a trial in religion such that he has no resistance, and so falls into the abyss, Allah forbid. But the more apparent view is that it is general: ﴿And We test you with evil and with good as a trial﴾ [al-Anbiya' 35].

Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿Say, "Travel through the earth and observe how was the end of those before you; most of them were polytheists"﴾ [ar-Rum 42]:
* In this noble verse: the command to take heed from what happened to the earlier peoples: ﴿Say, "Travel through the earth"﴾.
* Among the benefits of the verse: a person should read the books of past history for taking lessons. But, as we all know, some history books are fabricated and not as they really were. The source of history of past nations is what Allah and His Messenger have informed us of. Allah, Exalted, said in Surah Ibrahim: ﴿Has there not reached you the report of those before you — the people of Nuh, 'Ad and Thamud, and those after them, none knows them except Allah﴾ [Ibrahim 9]. So He denied that anyone has knowledge of them except Allah. Then from where do we take their reports? Since none knows them but Allah, we take them from Allah, either from the Book or from the Sunnah.
* Among the benefits of the verse: the cause of the destruction of the earlier nations was the shirk of most of them, by His saying: ﴿most of them were polytheists﴾.
* And from it: when punishment descends, it may strike the righteous and others, because He said: ﴿most of them﴾, meaning some did not commit shirk.
* And from this His saying: ﴿And fear a trial which will not strike those who have wronged among you exclusively; and know that Allah is severe in punishment﴾ [al-Anfal 25]. Allah may save the believers just as He saved the messengers and those who believed with them; He saved them.

Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿So set your face toward the upright religion before there comes a Day for which there is no repelling from Allah﴾ and so on to the end [ar-Rum 43]:
* In this is the obligation to turn toward the religion: ﴿So set your face toward the religion﴾. It necessarily follows from the obligation to turn toward it that one must turn away from everything else, because the direction is one: either toward here or toward there. So when it is necessary to turn toward the religion, it is necessary to turn away from other than it.
* Among the benefits of the verse: the prohibition of ruling by other than what Allah has revealed, because it contradicts turning toward the upright religion. Ruling by other than what Allah revealed may be disbelief, may be sinfulness, and may be injustice, as Allah mentioned in Surah al-Ma'idah: ﴿And whoever does not rule by what Allah has revealed — those are the disbelievers﴾ [al-Ma'idah 44]; and in the second verse: ﴿...those are the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Ma'idah 45]; and in the third verse: ﴿...those are the defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Ma'idah 47]. These descriptions apply according to the condition of the ruler: he may be a disbeliever, a wrongdoer, or a sinner.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: this religion is upright (qayyim). What is the meaning of qayyim? Moderate, with no crookedness in it, neither on the side of worship nor on the side of dealings.
* Among its benefits: if you think that there is in the religion something that contradicts uprightness, know that you are deficient, either in your knowledge or in your understanding. The reason is that Allah described this religion as upright. Whatever you examine in the religion of Allah and it appears to you not to be upright, know that you are mistaken, due to deficiency in your knowledge or in your understanding. A person is attacked from these two directions: either his knowledge is deficient, he has no knowledge, or his understanding is deficient, he has knowledge but does not understand.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: whoever is commanded to do something should mention what will attract and encourage people to it. From where is this taken?
* A student: ﴿before there comes [a Day]﴾ [ar-Rum 43].
* The Shaykh: No. That is correct, but before that it is from His saying: ﴿the upright﴾. When a person knows that it is upright, he will undoubtedly turn toward it. So when you want to command something, mention the qualities that make people inclined to it, with its beloved attributes and praiseworthy fruits.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: combining encouragement and warning: encouragement is ﴿the upright﴾, and warning is ﴿before there comes a Day for which there is no repelling from Allah﴾ [ar-Rum 43].
* Among its benefits: affirmation of the Day of Resurrection, that it will certainly come: ﴿for which there is no repelling from Allah﴾.
* Among its benefits: the Day of Resurrection is a great Day. From where? From the indefiniteness of ﴿a Day﴾ in ﴿before there comes a Day﴾, and indefiniteness indicates magnification. What confirms the greatness of this Day is the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿Do they not think that they will be resurrected, for a great Day, the Day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds?﴾ [al-Mutaffifin 4-6].
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the judgment belongs to Allah, Glorified and Exalted, by His saying: ﴿for which there is no repelling from Allah﴾ [ar-Rum 43]. No one can prevent what Allah wills, nor bring what Allah has not willed, ever. "O Allah, there is none who can withhold what You give, and none who can give what You withhold, and the might of the mighty person will not benefit him against You."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (844) and Muslim (593/137), from al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah.]]

Among the benefits of this noble verse: on the Day of Resurrection, people will be divided and separated, as shown by His saying: ﴿On that Day they will be separated﴾. In the first verse we took up earlier, ﴿for what the hands of people have earned﴾, there is evidence against the doctrine of the Jabriyya (determinists). How so? The Jabriyya say that a person is compelled in his deeds: he does not act by his own choice, and the act is not truly ascribed to him, except figuratively. Thus it is said "he prayed," "he fasted," "he gave zakat," but only metaphorically, not literally. The noble verse refutes them in two ways:

The first way: His saying ﴿for what the hands of people have earned﴾, where He ascribes the earning to the hands of people.

The second way: God, exalted is He, punished them for this act. Had they been compelled to it, their punishment would be injustice toward them. How could they be punished for what is not within their choice? So the verse refutes them in two respects: a verbal one, namely the ascription of the earning to their hands, and a meaningful one, namely that if they were compelled, punishing them for it would necessarily mean that God is unjust to them, and God is not unjust to His servants.

Likewise, it is also derived from His saying ﴿some of what they did﴾, where He ascribes the deed to them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 30, verse 41–43 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Corruption has appeared on land and sea by [reason of] what the hands of people have earned﴾ [al-Rum: 41]. ﴿Zahara﴾ means became manifest and clear. His words ﴿al-fasad﴾ (corruption) are the opposite of righteousness (salah), and it applies to everything according to what suits it. So the corruption of crops is their drying up and destruction by violent winds, flooding rains and damaging hail; likewise the corruption of livestock is their death and sickness, the corruption of fruits is their diminishing, and similar things. The point is that corruption exists in everything according to its nature.

Does ﴿al-fasad﴾ here refer to physical corruption or does it include both physical and moral corruption? The correct view is that it includes both physical and moral corruption. The physical is what we have mentioned examples of before, and the moral is the abundance of sins and transgressions and their spread among people, and the lack of concern for them, until the evil becomes known as good and the good becomes known as evil. This is among the greatest corruption. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And do not cause corruption on the earth after its reformation﴾ [al-A'raf: 56]. The scholars said: Do not corrupt it by sins.

As for His words ﴿fi al-bar wa al-bahr﴾ (on land and sea), the author says: (﴿al-bar﴾ means the deserts), meaning the wastelands far from cities and inhabitants; this is al-bar. It has been said that what is meant by al-bar is that which is not sea, so it includes cities, towns, deserts and other places.

As for his words (by the drought of rain and scarcity of vegetation; ﴿wa al-bahr﴾ means the lands by the rivers, through the scarcity of their water), the author, may Allah have mercy on him, followed the view that what is meant by al-bar is what lies outside inhabited areas, and what is meant by al-bahr is the inhabited areas on the shores of seas. Many exegetes said this. However, the correct view is that what is meant by al-bar is what is other than the sea, and what is meant by al-bahr is water. This is because what we have mentioned here is more general than what the author and others mentioned, and it is also more apparent. When "al-bahr" is used in the Qur'an, what is meant by it? It means water. So the corruption of the land, as the author said, is by drought and scarcity of vegetation, and the corruption of vegetation also after it has come into existence. For this reason Allah sent upon the people of Pharaoh locusts, lice, frogs and blood: four plagues. The locusts corrupt the crops after they emerge and eat them. The lice (al-qummal) corrupt the food when it is harvested; it is the weevil that destroys it. And the frogs, by what? By water: their waters were filled with frogs, to the point that a person could not drink water without [getting] frogs in it, may Allah protect us. As for blood, the correct view is that it refers to bleeding (nazif). Although some scholars say that what is meant by blood is that the water among the people of Pharaoh became like blood, the correct view is that it is bleeding, because Allah mentioned the corruption of water by what? By frogs. So the food, from beginning to end and its final outcome, which is blood, since blood comes from food, became—may Allah protect us—of no benefit to them, neither before entering their bodies nor after entering.

* Student: Al-qummal, O Shaykh, is it al-qaml or something else?
* The Shaykh: No, al-qummal is the weevil that lives in food; we call it al-khish here. It is a worm found in grains that spoils and eats them. The point is that this is corruption on land.

What is the corruption at sea by? The scholars said: it is by the death and decay of fish, and likewise the change of the waters and their failure to flow as usual. This is corruption at sea.

As for His words ﴿bi-ma kasabat aydi al-nas﴾ [al-Rum: 41]: the ba' is causal, and ﴿ma﴾ may be a verbal (masdariyyah) particle or a relative pronoun. If it is relative, it needs an omitted returning pronoun, and the meaning would be: by what the hands of people have earned. If it is masdariyyah, it needs no returning pronoun, and the meaning is: by the earning of people's hands.

As for His words ﴿bi-ma kasabat aydi al-nas﴾, the author said: (from sins). ﴿Aydi al-nas﴾ is the plural of yad (hand), and what is meant is what they earned. This is one of the methods of the Arabic language, where the hand is used to refer to its owner. What is meant is not only what the hand earned, because sins are not committed by hands alone; they are committed by the hand, the foot, the eye, the tongue, the ear, all the senses. Every sense can be used by a person to commit sin. So what is meant by hands here is the souls (anfus), not the hand which is a limb of the body.

* Student: Could this be a metaphor (majaz), O Shaykh?
* The Shaykh: No, it is not a metaphor, because in its context it indicates that what is meant is what they earned, so it is not a metaphor. As for the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿The penalty for those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive upon earth [to cause] corruption is only that they be killed or crucified or have their hands and feet cut off﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 33], the meaning of ﴿aydihim﴾ here is the limbs, so the word in its context is literal in its meaning.

Therefore, if anyone wanted to turn His words ﴿aw tuqatta'a aydihim﴾ (or have their hands cut off) to mean "or have their bodies cut off as much as possible", he could not; likewise if he wanted to make ﴿bi-ma kasabat aydi al-nas﴾ mean only what the hand itself earned, excluding the other limbs, he could not.

This is the basis of the statement of Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him: there is no metaphor in the Qur'an or in the Arabic language, because when a word's meaning has been determined by its context, it becomes, by the requirement of that context, literal in that meaning, and then there is no need for interpretation.

As for His words ﴿al-nas﴾ (the people): we have mentioned many times that its origin is (unas), but the hamzah was dropped for ease, as in His words "sharr" and "khayr", whose origins are "asharr" and "akhyar", and as in the word "Allah", whose origin is "al-Ilah". This is what has been said about Allah, though there is something to be considered in this.

He said: (﴿li-yudhiqahum﴾ with the ya' and the nun, ﴿ba'da alladhi 'amilu﴾). ﴿Li-yudhiqahum﴾: the lam here expresses purpose (ta'lil). And what is the thing being explained? The thing explained is what this lam is connected to, and the lam is connected to what? To ﴿zahara﴾. This is the thing explained: it appeared for such-and-such, meaning in order that it might make them taste. There are two Sab'i readings: ﴿li-nudhiqahum﴾ with the verb attributed to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, or ﴿li-yudhiqahum﴾ with the verb attributed to a third-person pronoun; yet even so, this absent pronoun refers back to whom? It refers back to Allah, glorified and exalted.

His words ﴿li-yudhiqahum﴾: "tasting" is always used to express affliction, because tasting is the highest type of sensory perception. A person hears of a thing, then sees it, then tastes it. Let me say to you: I have an apple. Your perception of the apple now is by hearing; then if I take it out and show it to you, that is by sight; and which is stronger? Sight is stronger than hearing. Then if I give it to you and you eat it, what is that? It is by tasting, and this is the highest. Because if I say "I have an apple" and you have neither seen it, it is possible that my statement is a lie; and if I show it to you but you have not tasted it, it is possible that it is another plant resembling an apple, or it is artificial apple made of plastic that you see as if it were a real apple. But when you taste it, it becomes certainty of certainties (haqq al-yaqin). For this reason Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, always expresses affliction by tasting, because it is the highest type of perception.

His words (﴿ba'da alladhi 'amilu﴾ means: its punishment) because what they did was other than the apparent corruption on land and sea, but the corruption is its punishment.

But someone may say: why did He express the punishment by the verb? We say: He expressed the punishment by the verb "some of what they did" for two reasons:

The first reason: to show the cause of this punishment.

The second reason: that this punishment is exactly proportionate to the deed; for this reason He expressed it as the deed, indicating that it is proportionate to it and that there is no injustice in it. This is common in the Qur'an, where Allah the Exalted expresses punishment by the verb for these two reasons:

The first: to show that the cause of the punishment is this deed.

The second: that the punishment is proportionate to the deed.

His words ﴿ba'da alladhi 'amilu﴾ mean: not all of it. Yes indeed, not all; because Allah says: ﴿And if Allah were to seize mankind for what they have earned, He would not leave upon it [the earth] any creature﴾ [Fatir: 45], and He said: ﴿And whatever disaster strikes you is for what your hands have earned, and He pardons much﴾ [al-Shura: 30]. This is true: if Allah, the Exalted, were to take people according to their sins, He would not leave on it a single creature; everyone would die and none would remain. But He, glorified and exalted, afflicts them only with some of their sins.

The wisdom: He said: ﴿So that He may let them taste part of what they have done that they might return﴾ [al-Rum: 41] (they might repent). "La'alla" here expresses purpose, and whenever "la'alla" occurs in the speech of Allah it is either for purpose or for expectation of something when it is expected; that is, so that they might return to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

This is among the wisdoms of Allah: that Allah tests His servants with adversity so that they might return to Him. How many people have had their punishment by adversity become the cause of their return to their Lord; indeed, sometimes it is a direct cause. ﴿And when a wave covers them like shade, they invoke Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾ [Luqman: 32]. This is a return; but they, may Allah protect us, when they are saved, return to their disbelief. ﴿So that they might return﴾.

Allah the Exalted said: (﴿Say﴾ to the disbelievers of Makkah: ﴿Travel through the earth and observe how was the end of those before [you]. Most of them were polytheists﴾ [al-Rum: 42]). The address in His words ﴿Say﴾ is to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and it may also include him and everyone who calls to his law and calls people to take admonition and reflection.

His words ﴿Travel through the earth﴾: "sayr" means walking. ﴿Fi al-ard﴾: "fi" here means "ala" (upon), meaning on the earth, not inside it. It has been said that "fi" indicates location, and that the location differs according to what is located and according to the location itself. For example, if we say "the water is in the jug", it is inside the jug, a jug of water; or a cup, or a pot for instance. Here the water is inside it. If we say "the writing is on the paper", it differs; and if we say "the face is in the mirror", it differs. Some scholars hold that "fi" here indicates location, but the location of each thing is according to it.

The travel commanded here: no one imagines it means dig a trench in the earth and enter it; no one imagines this. So there are two views regarding the word "fi":

The first view: it is taken to mean "ala" (upon): travel upon the earth, that is, on its surface.

The second view: "fi" is taken to indicate location, and it is said that the location is according to each place. This is the explanation of "fi".

The explanation of ﴿Travel through the earth﴾: ﴿Travel﴾ — is what is meant walking on foot, or travel by the intellect, by reflection? All of them: it includes travel by the body, by a person going to the dwellings of the people to take admonition and lesson, or travel by the hearts, by reading their histories and events so that he takes lesson from them. How many travels of the heart have become greater than travel on foot. But travel on foot for the sake of sightseeing and recreation is forbidden, as some people do now: they go to the dwellings of Thamud for sightseeing, recreation and to view their former strength, although the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Do not enter upon these people except while weeping; if you are not weeping, then do not enter them." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (433), and Muslim (2980/38), from Ibn 'Umar.] Where are those who go to the dwellings of Thamud weeping? When the Messenger ﷺ passed by them on his way to Tabuk, he hastened and covered his head; he dismounted there, peace and blessings be upon him, and hurried. Accordingly, we say: if you travel through the land of these who were punished, travel as one who takes admonition and lesson, as the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, commanded.

﴿Say: Travel through the earth and observe how was the end of those before﴾: ﴿fa-unzuru﴾: is it looking with reflection and contemplation, or looking with the eye? According to what we said about travel: if it is travel on foot, it is looking with the eye; if it is travel by the heart, it is looking with the eye of insight, reflection and contemplation. We can also say that even if we interpret travel here as physical travel on foot, it must be accompanied by looking with the eye of insight and lesson, since looking with the bare eye alone benefits nothing.

﴿Fa-unzuru kayfa kana 'aqibatu alladhina min qablu﴾: what is the grammatical position of "kayfa"? Its position is accusative, as the predicate of "kana" placed before it, and "'aqibah" is its subject, and the clause is suspended from action (mu'allaqah 'an al-'amal), suspended by the word "unzuru". A suspended clause is in the position of a single noun, and the meaning is: look at their condition, how it was.

His words ﴿kayfa kana 'aqibatu alladhina min qablu﴾: "'aqibah" here is a verbal noun (masdar), therefore the verb is masculine, meaning in the sense of "'uqba", ﴿alladhina min qablu kana aktharuhum﴾: "min" is a preposition, and "qablu" is a noun raised by "min", its sign of nominative being a visible damma at its end.

* Student: It is indeclinable, built on damma because it is cut off from the genitive.

* The Shaykh: Yes, built on damma because it is cut off from the genitive.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: The genitive noun is omitted and its meaning is intended, so it is built on damma; because they say of "qablu" and "ba'du": if the genitive noun is present verbally, it is inflected and not nunated; if it is omitted both verbally and in meaning, it is inflected and nunated. These are two opposite states: when the genitive noun is present, it is inflected and not nunated; you say "ataytu min qabli Zaydin wa min ba'dihi"; and when the genitive is omitted both verbally and in meaning, it is inflected and nunated.

When the genitive noun is omitted and its wording is intended, it is inflected and not nunated, as when its wording is present. When the genitive noun is omitted and its meaning is intended, it is built on damma. Yes indeed, it has four states.

﴿Kana aktharuhum mushrikin﴾: one might expect: "let them look how was the end of those before them, who were destroyed, annihilated, and so on". But the explanation came contrary to what was expected. What do you expect when Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Have they not traveled through the earth and observed how was the end of those before them?﴾ [al-Rum: 9]?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No, (...). You expect: We destroyed them and annihilated them and so on; this is their end. But the matter came contrary to what was expected: ﴿Kana aktharuhum mushrikin﴾ came explaining the cause of this end, because this is the state in which these deniers were, which is polytheism. That is: you now are polytheists, and they were polytheists and were destroyed. So this means your end will be like theirs, its outcome being destruction and perdition. This is among the eloquence of the Qur'an: Allah the Exalted mentioned the cause of the destruction of those people, which they were upon.

Now these addressees are polytheists; they have been upon polytheism until now and have not yet encountered the end. But if they know that the cause of the end of those people was polytheism, then without doubt, if they have minds, they will desist from polytheism.

﴿Kana aktharuhum mushrikin﴾: he says: (So they were destroyed for their polytheism, and their dwellings and homes were empty). The words of Allah the Exalted ﴿Kana aktharuhum mushrikin﴾: well, and the other part? The apparent meaning of the noble verse is that the other part, which is the smaller part, was not polytheist. Here there is a difficulty: were the monotheists destroyed along with the polytheists, although Allah the Exalted mentioned in many verses regarding past nations ﴿So We saved him and those with him﴾ [al-A'raf: 64], ﴿And Allah will save those who feared Him with their salvation﴾ [al-Zumar: 61]? Its apparent meaning is that the believers were not destroyed. Or we say: ﴿Kana aktharuhum mushrikin﴾ [al-Rum: 42] is considered with respect to the leaders and chiefs who knew that they were upon polytheism; as for the common people who did not know, they were followers and content, even if they did not have polytheism themselves, but they thought this was the truth. So which of the two possibilities is more preferable? Or a third possibility: that it is said that Allah commanded us to look at how was the end of the earlier ones, and when we look we find that most of them were polytheists and were destroyed, and that the believer was saved; so in this there is a warning against polytheism and an encouragement to faith and monotheism?

Here there are three possibilities:

The first possibility: that all were destroyed, and this is contradicted by many verses stating that Allah saved the believers. This is the first.

The second aspect: what is meant by ﴿most of them were polytheists﴾ is those who know that they are upon shirk, not the common mob and the general populace who do not know what they are upon and are merely followers of every caller.

The third aspect: it may be said that the outcome (al-'aqibah) can be good or bad, and Allah says: ﴿See how was the end of those before them; most of them were polytheists﴾. We know that among the wisdom of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is that He recompenses the polytheist for his shirk and the believer for his faith. In that case the verse contains encouragement to faith and monotheism and warning against shirk and disbelief. Which of the possibilities is more preferable?

The apparent view is that the last is preferable; that is, they should look at how the end of the earlier peoples was: whoever among them was a polytheist was seized for his shirk, and whoever was a believer was saved by his faith. This is so that they themselves may believe, and so that the believers of this Ummah may remain firm in their faith.

The author said: (So they were destroyed for their shirk, and their dwellings and homes are empty). This is the reality. Take the people of Salih, for example: Salih and those with him were saved, were they not? They were saved. And his people were seized by the quake and the blast, so they became prostrate in their homes. ﴿So those are their houses, empty because of what they wronged﴾ [an-Naml 52]. You find them now empty, and, as far as we know, they have not been inhabited after them until now.

Then He, Exalted, said: (﴿So set your face toward the upright religion﴾ — the religion of Islam). "Set" (aqim): the address is to whom? To the Messenger ﷺ, or to everyone to whom the address is directed. The direction of the first view has already been explained. If we make the address to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, then either the intended one is the Messenger himself and his Ummah follows him, or the Messenger and the Ummah are intended but the address was made to the Messenger because he is their leader and imam.

And His saying: ﴿So set your face toward the upright religion﴾. What is meant by "face"? Is it direction, or the physical face on the head? The apparent meaning is direction, because "face" is used to mean direction, as Allah says: ﴿And to Allah belong the east and the west; so wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 115]. It has already been stated that there are two views among the exegetes: one, that it means the real Face of Allah; and the other, that it means direction. There is no doubt that "face" is used to mean direction.

And His saying: ﴿for the upright religion﴾...
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No. If we say the intended meaning of "face" is direction — its direction toward the religion — it includes the case where the physical face is required to turn toward the qiblah.

And His saying: ﴿for the upright religion﴾. What is meant by "religion" here? It is meant as action. We have already noted that "religion" in the Qur'an is used to mean action and recompense. So His saying: ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾ [al-Fatihah 4] and ﴿And what can make you know what is the Day of Judgment?﴾ [al-Infitar 17]: "religion" means recompense. But ﴿I have approved Islam as a religion for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah 3] and ﴿Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam﴾ [Ali 'Imran 19]: it means action, as in this verse.

And His saying: ﴿the upright (al-qayyim)﴾. What is its opposite? The crooked (al-mu'waj), as Allah says: ﴿And that this is My path, straight, so follow it﴾ [al-An'am 153].
* A student: ﴿Praise be to Allah, who revealed to His servant the Book and did not make therein any deviance, [but made it] straight﴾ [al-Kahf 1-2].
* The Shaykh: Yes, the Book is qayyim. But we want the religion: ﴿Say, "Indeed, my Lord has guided me to a straight path, a correct religion (diinan qiyaman)"﴾ [al-An'am 161]; that is, qayyim. So the religion of Islam is a straight religion with no crookedness in it, neither in relation to the dealing with Allah, Mighty and Majestic, which is worship, nor in relation to dealing with creation. For this you find that in transactions He forbade lying, cheating, deception and the like, and forbade oppression and injustice and the killing of children and the like, because all of this contradicts uprightness. And in acts of worship He forbade shirk and innovation, because of the deviation from the straight path that they involve.
* A student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: ﴿Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam﴾ [Ali 'Imran 19]. This includes creed and outward acts. As we said previously: when Islam is mentioned alongside faith, Islam becomes outward acts and faith becomes inward acts; and when one of them is mentioned alone, it includes the other.

(﴿Before there comes a Day for which there is no repelling from Allah﴾ [ar-Rum 43], which is the Day of Resurrection, ﴿On that Day they will be separated﴾.) His saying: ﴿before﴾ is connected to (aqim): that is, establish it before this Day. And His saying: ﴿before there comes a Day﴾ is indefinite for the sake of magnification, because this Day is as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, described it in His saying: ﴿for a great Day, the Day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Mutaffifin 5-6].

And His saying: ﴿for which there is no repelling (maradd)﴾. Is "mard" a mimi noun (noun of place/instance formed with mim)? Yes, it is a mimi verbal noun; that is, there is no turning back (radd) for it. It means this cannot be repelled, its answer being that Allah has decreed it.

And His saying: ﴿from Allah﴾ is connected to an adjective of ﴿a Day﴾. This is an adjective; it is connected to an adjective of ﴿a Day﴾; that is: before there comes a Day from Allah; that is, this Day is from Allah and not from anyone else.

It may be that it is connected to ﴿comes﴾: that a Day comes from Allah. The first is more eloquent: that it is an adjective of ﴿a Day﴾, because its being from Allah indicates its greatness and that it cannot be repelled.

And His saying: ﴿before there comes a Day﴾. If someone says: this verse was addressed to people in the time of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and it is known that the Resurrection did not occur in the time of the Messenger ﷺ, so how did He say: ﴿before there comes a Day for which there is no repelling from Allah﴾?

The answer to this is that we say: death occurs even in the time of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and whoever dies, his resurrection has come and his deeds have ended. There is no difference between one who dies at that time and one who dies being the last of people to die, in terms of the cessation of deeds; each of them has had his deeds cut off. So it is as if the one who dies in the time of the Messenger ﷺ has reached the Day of Resurrection. For this reason the scholars say: a person's death is a resurrection with respect to him, and it is a lesser resurrection with respect to people in general, because the deeds have ended. End.

And His saying: ﴿for which there is no repelling from Allah﴾ indicates that this is a matter that must certainly happen, and so it is; because the Day of Resurrection is that for which mankind was created, to worship Allah, and its recompense takes place on the Day of Resurrection.

He said: ﴿On that Day they will be separated﴾. He said: (In it the tā' of the original (yatafarraqūn / yatasaddaʿūn) is assimilated into the ṣād, and its meaning is: they will scatter after the reckoning, to Paradise and Hell). ﴿On that Day﴾: (idh) is nunated, and the tanwin here replaces a clause; that is: on a Day when it comes, they will be separated.

The author says: (In it the tā' of the original is assimilated into the ṣād). What is the meaning of "the tā' of the original is assimilated into the ṣād"? Its original is yatafaʿʿalūn (yataṣaddaʿūn). So his saying "assimilation of the tā' in the original" means: according to the original form, the ṣād into which it was assimilated was originally a tā', and it was assimilated into its counterpart after being changed to a ṣād. The meaning of ﴿yaṣṣaddaʿūn﴾ is they will scatter.
* A student: Its original is ṣadaʿa, yataṣaddaʿu.
* The Shaykh: Its original is yatasaddaʿūn. The meaning of tasaddaʿ is scattering, and from it: "the earth splits (tasaddaʿa al-arḍ)," because its parts scatter and it bursts open. So on the Day of Resurrection...

[The text here breaks off mid-argument: "that the corruption is caused by the deeds of the children of Adam; because of His saying: ﴿by what the hands of people have earned﴾ [ar-Rum 41]. What confirms this is also His saying: ﴿And if the people of the towns had believed and feared Allah, We would have opened upon them blessings from the heaven and the earth; but they denied, so We seized them for what they had been earning﴾ [al-A'raf 96]."]

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: affirmation of causes and means, and that the acts of Allah are caused and have a reason. From where is this taken? From His saying: ﴿by what [they] have earned﴾. There is no doubt that the acts and rulings of Allah are purposeful, because one of His names is al-Hakim (the All-Wise).
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: people are only punished for their own causes, by His saying: ﴿by what the hands of people have earned﴾. From this it follows that whoever wants punishment lifted from him should repent to Allah, for repentance is among the causes of lifting punishment and bringing reward. For this reason Hud said to his people: ﴿And O my people, seek forgiveness from your Lord and then repent to Him; He will send the sky upon you in abundant rain and increase you in strength upon your strength﴾ [Hud 52]. And Nuh said to his people: ﴿So I said, "Seek forgiveness of your Lord; indeed, He is ever Forgiving. He will send the sky upon you in abundant rain, and provide you with wealth and sons and make for you gardens and make for you rivers"﴾ [Nuh 10-12].
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: recompense is of the same kind as the deed and in proportion to it, by His saying: ﴿that He may let them taste part of what they did﴾ [ar-Rum 41].
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the demonstration of the vastness of Allah's mercy, and that His mercy precedes His wrath, by His saying: ﴿part of what they did﴾. Had the wrath been equal to the mercy, Allah would make us taste all that we did. And had mercy been dominant, would He make us taste more than we did, or not?
So there are three possibilities now: making us taste a part, or the equivalent, or more. The equivalent or more is impossible; Allah, Exalted, only makes us taste a part, because it is established in the sound hadith: "Indeed Allah, Exalted, wrote a book with Him above the Throne: Indeed My mercy precedes My wrath,"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7422) and Muslim (2751/15), from Abu Hurayrah.]] and were it not for this, Allah would take mankind to account for what they did.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: punishments may be a cause of returning to Allah. From where? ﴿so that they may return﴾ [ar-Rum 41]. Just as they may also be the opposite: they may be a cause of increased defiance and aversion, and Allah forbid. This is shown by His saying: ﴿And among the people is he who worships Allah on an edge; if good touches him, he is reassured by it, but if trial strikes him, he turns back on his face; he has lost this world and the Hereafter﴾ [al-Hajj 11]. What links this verse and the one we are explaining is that it may be said: punishments in general are beneficial, but in particular they may not benefit; because Allah said: ﴿And among the people is he who worships Allah﴾ — "among the people." And His saying: ﴿but if trial strikes him﴾ may mean a trial in religion such that he has no resistance, and so falls into the abyss, Allah forbid. But the more apparent view is that it is general: ﴿And We test you with evil and with good as a trial﴾ [al-Anbiya' 35].

Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿Say, "Travel through the earth and observe how was the end of those before you; most of them were polytheists"﴾ [ar-Rum 42]:
* In this noble verse: the command to take heed from what happened to the earlier peoples: ﴿Say, "Travel through the earth"﴾.
* Among the benefits of the verse: a person should read the books of past history for taking lessons. But, as we all know, some history books are fabricated and not as they really were. The source of history of past nations is what Allah and His Messenger have informed us of. Allah, Exalted, said in Surah Ibrahim: ﴿Has there not reached you the report of those before you — the people of Nuh, 'Ad and Thamud, and those after them, none knows them except Allah﴾ [Ibrahim 9]. So He denied that anyone has knowledge of them except Allah. Then from where do we take their reports? Since none knows them but Allah, we take them from Allah, either from the Book or from the Sunnah.
* Among the benefits of the verse: the cause of the destruction of the earlier nations was the shirk of most of them, by His saying: ﴿most of them were polytheists﴾.
* And from it: when punishment descends, it may strike the righteous and others, because He said: ﴿most of them﴾, meaning some did not commit shirk.
* And from this His saying: ﴿And fear a trial which will not strike those who have wronged among you exclusively; and know that Allah is severe in punishment﴾ [al-Anfal 25]. Allah may save the believers just as He saved the messengers and those who believed with them; He saved them.

Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿So set your face toward the upright religion before there comes a Day for which there is no repelling from Allah﴾ and so on to the end [ar-Rum 43]:
* In this is the obligation to turn toward the religion: ﴿So set your face toward the religion﴾. It necessarily follows from the obligation to turn toward it that one must turn away from everything else, because the direction is one: either toward here or toward there. So when it is necessary to turn toward the religion, it is necessary to turn away from other than it.
* Among the benefits of the verse: the prohibition of ruling by other than what Allah has revealed, because it contradicts turning toward the upright religion. Ruling by other than what Allah revealed may be disbelief, may be sinfulness, and may be injustice, as Allah mentioned in Surah al-Ma'idah: ﴿And whoever does not rule by what Allah has revealed — those are the disbelievers﴾ [al-Ma'idah 44]; and in the second verse: ﴿...those are the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Ma'idah 45]; and in the third verse: ﴿...those are the defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Ma'idah 47]. These descriptions apply according to the condition of the ruler: he may be a disbeliever, a wrongdoer, or a sinner.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: this religion is upright (qayyim). What is the meaning of qayyim? Moderate, with no crookedness in it, neither on the side of worship nor on the side of dealings.
* Among its benefits: if you think that there is in the religion something that contradicts uprightness, know that you are deficient, either in your knowledge or in your understanding. The reason is that Allah described this religion as upright. Whatever you examine in the religion of Allah and it appears to you not to be upright, know that you are mistaken, due to deficiency in your knowledge or in your understanding. A person is attacked from these two directions: either his knowledge is deficient, he has no knowledge, or his understanding is deficient, he has knowledge but does not understand.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: whoever is commanded to do something should mention what will attract and encourage people to it. From where is this taken?
* A student: ﴿before there comes [a Day]﴾ [ar-Rum 43].
* The Shaykh: No. That is correct, but before that it is from His saying: ﴿the upright﴾. When a person knows that it is upright, he will undoubtedly turn toward it. So when you want to command something, mention the qualities that make people inclined to it, with its beloved attributes and praiseworthy fruits.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: combining encouragement and warning: encouragement is ﴿the upright﴾, and warning is ﴿before there comes a Day for which there is no repelling from Allah﴾ [ar-Rum 43].
* Among its benefits: affirmation of the Day of Resurrection, that it will certainly come: ﴿for which there is no repelling from Allah﴾.
* Among its benefits: the Day of Resurrection is a great Day. From where? From the indefiniteness of ﴿a Day﴾ in ﴿before there comes a Day﴾, and indefiniteness indicates magnification. What confirms the greatness of this Day is the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿Do they not think that they will be resurrected, for a great Day, the Day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds?﴾ [al-Mutaffifin 4-6].
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the judgment belongs to Allah, Glorified and Exalted, by His saying: ﴿for which there is no repelling from Allah﴾ [ar-Rum 43]. No one can prevent what Allah wills, nor bring what Allah has not willed, ever. "O Allah, there is none who can withhold what You give, and none who can give what You withhold, and the might of the mighty person will not benefit him against You."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (844) and Muslim (593/137), from al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah.]]

Among the benefits of this noble verse: on the Day of Resurrection, people will be divided and separated, as shown by His saying: ﴿On that Day they will be separated﴾. In the first verse we took up earlier, ﴿for what the hands of people have earned﴾, there is evidence against the doctrine of the Jabriyya (determinists). How so? The Jabriyya say that a person is compelled in his deeds: he does not act by his own choice, and the act is not truly ascribed to him, except figuratively. Thus it is said "he prayed," "he fasted," "he gave zakat," but only metaphorically, not literally. The noble verse refutes them in two ways:

The first way: His saying ﴿for what the hands of people have earned﴾, where He ascribes the earning to the hands of people.

The second way: God, exalted is He, punished them for this act. Had they been compelled to it, their punishment would be injustice toward them. How could they be punished for what is not within their choice? So the verse refutes them in two respects: a verbal one, namely the ascription of the earning to their hands, and a meaningful one, namely that if they were compelled, punishing them for it would necessarily mean that God is unjust to them, and God is not unjust to His servants.

Likewise, it is also derived from His saying ﴿some of what they did﴾, where He ascribes the deed to them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 30, verse 41–43 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Corruption has appeared on land and sea by [reason of] what the hands of people have earned﴾ [al-Rum: 41]. ﴿Zahara﴾ means became manifest and clear. His words ﴿al-fasad﴾ (corruption) are the opposite of righteousness (salah), and it applies to everything according to what suits it. So the corruption of crops is their drying up and destruction by violent winds, flooding rains and damaging hail; likewise the corruption of livestock is their death and sickness, the corruption of fruits is their diminishing, and similar things. The point is that corruption exists in everything according to its nature.

Does ﴿al-fasad﴾ here refer to physical corruption or does it include both physical and moral corruption? The correct view is that it includes both physical and moral corruption. The physical is what we have mentioned examples of before, and the moral is the abundance of sins and transgressions and their spread among people, and the lack of concern for them, until the evil becomes known as good and the good becomes known as evil. This is among the greatest corruption. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And do not cause corruption on the earth after its reformation﴾ [al-A'raf: 56]. The scholars said: Do not corrupt it by sins.

As for His words ﴿fi al-bar wa al-bahr﴾ (on land and sea), the author says: (﴿al-bar﴾ means the deserts), meaning the wastelands far from cities and inhabitants; this is al-bar. It has been said that what is meant by al-bar is that which is not sea, so it includes cities, towns, deserts and other places.

As for his words (by the drought of rain and scarcity of vegetation; ﴿wa al-bahr﴾ means the lands by the rivers, through the scarcity of their water), the author, may Allah have mercy on him, followed the view that what is meant by al-bar is what lies outside inhabited areas, and what is meant by al-bahr is the inhabited areas on the shores of seas. Many exegetes said this. However, the correct view is that what is meant by al-bar is what is other than the sea, and what is meant by al-bahr is water. This is because what we have mentioned here is more general than what the author and others mentioned, and it is also more apparent. When "al-bahr" is used in the Qur'an, what is meant by it? It means water. So the corruption of the land, as the author said, is by drought and scarcity of vegetation, and the corruption of vegetation also after it has come into existence. For this reason Allah sent upon the people of Pharaoh locusts, lice, frogs and blood: four plagues. The locusts corrupt the crops after they emerge and eat them. The lice (al-qummal) corrupt the food when it is harvested; it is the weevil that destroys it. And the frogs, by what? By water: their waters were filled with frogs, to the point that a person could not drink water without [getting] frogs in it, may Allah protect us. As for blood, the correct view is that it refers to bleeding (nazif). Although some scholars say that what is meant by blood is that the water among the people of Pharaoh became like blood, the correct view is that it is bleeding, because Allah mentioned the corruption of water by what? By frogs. So the food, from beginning to end and its final outcome, which is blood, since blood comes from food, became—may Allah protect us—of no benefit to them, neither before entering their bodies nor after entering.

* Student: Al-qummal, O Shaykh, is it al-qaml or something else?
* The Shaykh: No, al-qummal is the weevil that lives in food; we call it al-khish here. It is a worm found in grains that spoils and eats them. The point is that this is corruption on land.

What is the corruption at sea by? The scholars said: it is by the death and decay of fish, and likewise the change of the waters and their failure to flow as usual. This is corruption at sea.

As for His words ﴿bi-ma kasabat aydi al-nas﴾ [al-Rum: 41]: the ba' is causal, and ﴿ma﴾ may be a verbal (masdariyyah) particle or a relative pronoun. If it is relative, it needs an omitted returning pronoun, and the meaning would be: by what the hands of people have earned. If it is masdariyyah, it needs no returning pronoun, and the meaning is: by the earning of people's hands.

As for His words ﴿bi-ma kasabat aydi al-nas﴾, the author said: (from sins). ﴿Aydi al-nas﴾ is the plural of yad (hand), and what is meant is what they earned. This is one of the methods of the Arabic language, where the hand is used to refer to its owner. What is meant is not only what the hand earned, because sins are not committed by hands alone; they are committed by the hand, the foot, the eye, the tongue, the ear, all the senses. Every sense can be used by a person to commit sin. So what is meant by hands here is the souls (anfus), not the hand which is a limb of the body.

* Student: Could this be a metaphor (majaz), O Shaykh?
* The Shaykh: No, it is not a metaphor, because in its context it indicates that what is meant is what they earned, so it is not a metaphor. As for the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿The penalty for those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive upon earth [to cause] corruption is only that they be killed or crucified or have their hands and feet cut off﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 33], the meaning of ﴿aydihim﴾ here is the limbs, so the word in its context is literal in its meaning.

Therefore, if anyone wanted to turn His words ﴿aw tuqatta'a aydihim﴾ (or have their hands cut off) to mean "or have their bodies cut off as much as possible", he could not; likewise if he wanted to make ﴿bi-ma kasabat aydi al-nas﴾ mean only what the hand itself earned, excluding the other limbs, he could not.

This is the basis of the statement of Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him: there is no metaphor in the Qur'an or in the Arabic language, because when a word's meaning has been determined by its context, it becomes, by the requirement of that context, literal in that meaning, and then there is no need for interpretation.

As for His words ﴿al-nas﴾ (the people): we have mentioned many times that its origin is (unas), but the hamzah was dropped for ease, as in His words "sharr" and "khayr", whose origins are "asharr" and "akhyar", and as in the word "Allah", whose origin is "al-Ilah". This is what has been said about Allah, though there is something to be considered in this.

He said: (﴿li-yudhiqahum﴾ with the ya' and the nun, ﴿ba'da alladhi 'amilu﴾). ﴿Li-yudhiqahum﴾: the lam here expresses purpose (ta'lil). And what is the thing being explained? The thing explained is what this lam is connected to, and the lam is connected to what? To ﴿zahara﴾. This is the thing explained: it appeared for such-and-such, meaning in order that it might make them taste. There are two Sab'i readings: ﴿li-nudhiqahum﴾ with the verb attributed to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, or ﴿li-yudhiqahum﴾ with the verb attributed to a third-person pronoun; yet even so, this absent pronoun refers back to whom? It refers back to Allah, glorified and exalted.

His words ﴿li-yudhiqahum﴾: "tasting" is always used to express affliction, because tasting is the highest type of sensory perception. A person hears of a thing, then sees it, then tastes it. Let me say to you: I have an apple. Your perception of the apple now is by hearing; then if I take it out and show it to you, that is by sight; and which is stronger? Sight is stronger than hearing. Then if I give it to you and you eat it, what is that? It is by tasting, and this is the highest. Because if I say "I have an apple" and you have neither seen it, it is possible that my statement is a lie; and if I show it to you but you have not tasted it, it is possible that it is another plant resembling an apple, or it is artificial apple made of plastic that you see as if it were a real apple. But when you taste it, it becomes certainty of certainties (haqq al-yaqin). For this reason Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, always expresses affliction by tasting, because it is the highest type of perception.

His words (﴿ba'da alladhi 'amilu﴾ means: its punishment) because what they did was other than the apparent corruption on land and sea, but the corruption is its punishment.

But someone may say: why did He express the punishment by the verb? We say: He expressed the punishment by the verb "some of what they did" for two reasons:

The first reason: to show the cause of this punishment.

The second reason: that this punishment is exactly proportionate to the deed; for this reason He expressed it as the deed, indicating that it is proportionate to it and that there is no injustice in it. This is common in the Qur'an, where Allah the Exalted expresses punishment by the verb for these two reasons:

The first: to show that the cause of the punishment is this deed.

The second: that the punishment is proportionate to the deed.

His words ﴿ba'da alladhi 'amilu﴾ mean: not all of it. Yes indeed, not all; because Allah says: ﴿And if Allah were to seize mankind for what they have earned, He would not leave upon it [the earth] any creature﴾ [Fatir: 45], and He said: ﴿And whatever disaster strikes you is for what your hands have earned, and He pardons much﴾ [al-Shura: 30]. This is true: if Allah, the Exalted, were to take people according to their sins, He would not leave on it a single creature; everyone would die and none would remain. But He, glorified and exalted, afflicts them only with some of their sins.

The wisdom: He said: ﴿So that He may let them taste part of what they have done that they might return﴾ [al-Rum: 41] (they might repent). "La'alla" here expresses purpose, and whenever "la'alla" occurs in the speech of Allah it is either for purpose or for expectation of something when it is expected; that is, so that they might return to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

This is among the wisdoms of Allah: that Allah tests His servants with adversity so that they might return to Him. How many people have had their punishment by adversity become the cause of their return to their Lord; indeed, sometimes it is a direct cause. ﴿And when a wave covers them like shade, they invoke Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾ [Luqman: 32]. This is a return; but they, may Allah protect us, when they are saved, return to their disbelief. ﴿So that they might return﴾.

Allah the Exalted said: (﴿Say﴾ to the disbelievers of Makkah: ﴿Travel through the earth and observe how was the end of those before [you]. Most of them were polytheists﴾ [al-Rum: 42]). The address in His words ﴿Say﴾ is to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and it may also include him and everyone who calls to his law and calls people to take admonition and reflection.

His words ﴿Travel through the earth﴾: "sayr" means walking. ﴿Fi al-ard﴾: "fi" here means "ala" (upon), meaning on the earth, not inside it. It has been said that "fi" indicates location, and that the location differs according to what is located and according to the location itself. For example, if we say "the water is in the jug", it is inside the jug, a jug of water; or a cup, or a pot for instance. Here the water is inside it. If we say "the writing is on the paper", it differs; and if we say "the face is in the mirror", it differs. Some scholars hold that "fi" here indicates location, but the location of each thing is according to it.

The travel commanded here: no one imagines it means dig a trench in the earth and enter it; no one imagines this. So there are two views regarding the word "fi":

The first view: it is taken to mean "ala" (upon): travel upon the earth, that is, on its surface.

The second view: "fi" is taken to indicate location, and it is said that the location is according to each place. This is the explanation of "fi".

The explanation of ﴿Travel through the earth﴾: ﴿Travel﴾ — is what is meant walking on foot, or travel by the intellect, by reflection? All of them: it includes travel by the body, by a person going to the dwellings of the people to take admonition and lesson, or travel by the hearts, by reading their histories and events so that he takes lesson from them. How many travels of the heart have become greater than travel on foot. But travel on foot for the sake of sightseeing and recreation is forbidden, as some people do now: they go to the dwellings of Thamud for sightseeing, recreation and to view their former strength, although the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Do not enter upon these people except while weeping; if you are not weeping, then do not enter them." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (433), and Muslim (2980/38), from Ibn 'Umar.] Where are those who go to the dwellings of Thamud weeping? When the Messenger ﷺ passed by them on his way to Tabuk, he hastened and covered his head; he dismounted there, peace and blessings be upon him, and hurried. Accordingly, we say: if you travel through the land of these who were punished, travel as one who takes admonition and lesson, as the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, commanded.

﴿Say: Travel through the earth and observe how was the end of those before﴾: ﴿fa-unzuru﴾: is it looking with reflection and contemplation, or looking with the eye? According to what we said about travel: if it is travel on foot, it is looking with the eye; if it is travel by the heart, it is looking with the eye of insight, reflection and contemplation. We can also say that even if we interpret travel here as physical travel on foot, it must be accompanied by looking with the eye of insight and lesson, since looking with the bare eye alone benefits nothing.

﴿Fa-unzuru kayfa kana 'aqibatu alladhina min qablu﴾: what is the grammatical position of "kayfa"? Its position is accusative, as the predicate of "kana" placed before it, and "'aqibah" is its subject, and the clause is suspended from action (mu'allaqah 'an al-'amal), suspended by the word "unzuru". A suspended clause is in the position of a single noun, and the meaning is: look at their condition, how it was.

His words ﴿kayfa kana 'aqibatu alladhina min qablu﴾: "'aqibah" here is a verbal noun (masdar), therefore the verb is masculine, meaning in the sense of "'uqba", ﴿alladhina min qablu kana aktharuhum﴾: "min" is a preposition, and "qablu" is a noun raised by "min", its sign of nominative being a visible damma at its end.

* Student: It is indeclinable, built on damma because it is cut off from the genitive.

* The Shaykh: Yes, built on damma because it is cut off from the genitive.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: The genitive noun is omitted and its meaning is intended, so it is built on damma; because they say of "qablu" and "ba'du": if the genitive noun is present verbally, it is inflected and not nunated; if it is omitted both verbally and in meaning, it is inflected and nunated. These are two opposite states: when the genitive noun is present, it is inflected and not nunated; you say "ataytu min qabli Zaydin wa min ba'dihi"; and when the genitive is omitted both verbally and in meaning, it is inflected and nunated.

When the genitive noun is omitted and its wording is intended, it is inflected and not nunated, as when its wording is present. When the genitive noun is omitted and its meaning is intended, it is built on damma. Yes indeed, it has four states.

﴿Kana aktharuhum mushrikin﴾: one might expect: "let them look how was the end of those before them, who were destroyed, annihilated, and so on". But the explanation came contrary to what was expected. What do you expect when Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Have they not traveled through the earth and observed how was the end of those before them?﴾ [al-Rum: 9]?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No, (...). You expect: We destroyed them and annihilated them and so on; this is their end. But the matter came contrary to what was expected: ﴿Kana aktharuhum mushrikin﴾ came explaining the cause of this end, because this is the state in which these deniers were, which is polytheism. That is: you now are polytheists, and they were polytheists and were destroyed. So this means your end will be like theirs, its outcome being destruction and perdition. This is among the eloquence of the Qur'an: Allah the Exalted mentioned the cause of the destruction of those people, which they were upon.

Now these addressees are polytheists; they have been upon polytheism until now and have not yet encountered the end. But if they know that the cause of the end of those people was polytheism, then without doubt, if they have minds, they will desist from polytheism.

﴿Kana aktharuhum mushrikin﴾: he says: (So they were destroyed for their polytheism, and their dwellings and homes were empty). The words of Allah the Exalted ﴿Kana aktharuhum mushrikin﴾: well, and the other part? The apparent meaning of the noble verse is that the other part, which is the smaller part, was not polytheist. Here there is a difficulty: were the monotheists destroyed along with the polytheists, although Allah the Exalted mentioned in many verses regarding past nations ﴿So We saved him and those with him﴾ [al-A'raf: 64], ﴿And Allah will save those who feared Him with their salvation﴾ [al-Zumar: 61]? Its apparent meaning is that the believers were not destroyed. Or we say: ﴿Kana aktharuhum mushrikin﴾ [al-Rum: 42] is considered with respect to the leaders and chiefs who knew that they were upon polytheism; as for the common people who did not know, they were followers and content, even if they did not have polytheism themselves, but they thought this was the truth. So which of the two possibilities is more preferable? Or a third possibility: that it is said that Allah commanded us to look at how was the end of the earlier ones, and when we look we find that most of them were polytheists and were destroyed, and that the believer was saved; so in this there is a warning against polytheism and an encouragement to faith and monotheism?

Here there are three possibilities:

The first possibility: that all were destroyed, and this is contradicted by many verses stating that Allah saved the believers. This is the first.

The second aspect: what is meant by ﴿most of them were polytheists﴾ is those who know that they are upon shirk, not the common mob and the general populace who do not know what they are upon and are merely followers of every caller.

The third aspect: it may be said that the outcome (al-'aqibah) can be good or bad, and Allah says: ﴿See how was the end of those before them; most of them were polytheists﴾. We know that among the wisdom of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is that He recompenses the polytheist for his shirk and the believer for his faith. In that case the verse contains encouragement to faith and monotheism and warning against shirk and disbelief. Which of the possibilities is more preferable?

The apparent view is that the last is preferable; that is, they should look at how the end of the earlier peoples was: whoever among them was a polytheist was seized for his shirk, and whoever was a believer was saved by his faith. This is so that they themselves may believe, and so that the believers of this Ummah may remain firm in their faith.

The author said: (So they were destroyed for their shirk, and their dwellings and homes are empty). This is the reality. Take the people of Salih, for example: Salih and those with him were saved, were they not? They were saved. And his people were seized by the quake and the blast, so they became prostrate in their homes. ﴿So those are their houses, empty because of what they wronged﴾ [an-Naml 52]. You find them now empty, and, as far as we know, they have not been inhabited after them until now.

Then He, Exalted, said: (﴿So set your face toward the upright religion﴾ — the religion of Islam). "Set" (aqim): the address is to whom? To the Messenger ﷺ, or to everyone to whom the address is directed. The direction of the first view has already been explained. If we make the address to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, then either the intended one is the Messenger himself and his Ummah follows him, or the Messenger and the Ummah are intended but the address was made to the Messenger because he is their leader and imam.

And His saying: ﴿So set your face toward the upright religion﴾. What is meant by "face"? Is it direction, or the physical face on the head? The apparent meaning is direction, because "face" is used to mean direction, as Allah says: ﴿And to Allah belong the east and the west; so wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 115]. It has already been stated that there are two views among the exegetes: one, that it means the real Face of Allah; and the other, that it means direction. There is no doubt that "face" is used to mean direction.

And His saying: ﴿for the upright religion﴾...
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No. If we say the intended meaning of "face" is direction — its direction toward the religion — it includes the case where the physical face is required to turn toward the qiblah.

And His saying: ﴿for the upright religion﴾. What is meant by "religion" here? It is meant as action. We have already noted that "religion" in the Qur'an is used to mean action and recompense. So His saying: ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾ [al-Fatihah 4] and ﴿And what can make you know what is the Day of Judgment?﴾ [al-Infitar 17]: "religion" means recompense. But ﴿I have approved Islam as a religion for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah 3] and ﴿Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam﴾ [Ali 'Imran 19]: it means action, as in this verse.

And His saying: ﴿the upright (al-qayyim)﴾. What is its opposite? The crooked (al-mu'waj), as Allah says: ﴿And that this is My path, straight, so follow it﴾ [al-An'am 153].
* A student: ﴿Praise be to Allah, who revealed to His servant the Book and did not make therein any deviance, [but made it] straight﴾ [al-Kahf 1-2].
* The Shaykh: Yes, the Book is qayyim. But we want the religion: ﴿Say, "Indeed, my Lord has guided me to a straight path, a correct religion (diinan qiyaman)"﴾ [al-An'am 161]; that is, qayyim. So the religion of Islam is a straight religion with no crookedness in it, neither in relation to the dealing with Allah, Mighty and Majestic, which is worship, nor in relation to dealing with creation. For this you find that in transactions He forbade lying, cheating, deception and the like, and forbade oppression and injustice and the killing of children and the like, because all of this contradicts uprightness. And in acts of worship He forbade shirk and innovation, because of the deviation from the straight path that they involve.
* A student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: ﴿Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam﴾ [Ali 'Imran 19]. This includes creed and outward acts. As we said previously: when Islam is mentioned alongside faith, Islam becomes outward acts and faith becomes inward acts; and when one of them is mentioned alone, it includes the other.

(﴿Before there comes a Day for which there is no repelling from Allah﴾ [ar-Rum 43], which is the Day of Resurrection, ﴿On that Day they will be separated﴾.) His saying: ﴿before﴾ is connected to (aqim): that is, establish it before this Day. And His saying: ﴿before there comes a Day﴾ is indefinite for the sake of magnification, because this Day is as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, described it in His saying: ﴿for a great Day, the Day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Mutaffifin 5-6].

And His saying: ﴿for which there is no repelling (maradd)﴾. Is "mard" a mimi noun (noun of place/instance formed with mim)? Yes, it is a mimi verbal noun; that is, there is no turning back (radd) for it. It means this cannot be repelled, its answer being that Allah has decreed it.

And His saying: ﴿from Allah﴾ is connected to an adjective of ﴿a Day﴾. This is an adjective; it is connected to an adjective of ﴿a Day﴾; that is: before there comes a Day from Allah; that is, this Day is from Allah and not from anyone else.

It may be that it is connected to ﴿comes﴾: that a Day comes from Allah. The first is more eloquent: that it is an adjective of ﴿a Day﴾, because its being from Allah indicates its greatness and that it cannot be repelled.

And His saying: ﴿before there comes a Day﴾. If someone says: this verse was addressed to people in the time of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and it is known that the Resurrection did not occur in the time of the Messenger ﷺ, so how did He say: ﴿before there comes a Day for which there is no repelling from Allah﴾?

The answer to this is that we say: death occurs even in the time of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and whoever dies, his resurrection has come and his deeds have ended. There is no difference between one who dies at that time and one who dies being the last of people to die, in terms of the cessation of deeds; each of them has had his deeds cut off. So it is as if the one who dies in the time of the Messenger ﷺ has reached the Day of Resurrection. For this reason the scholars say: a person's death is a resurrection with respect to him, and it is a lesser resurrection with respect to people in general, because the deeds have ended. End.

And His saying: ﴿for which there is no repelling from Allah﴾ indicates that this is a matter that must certainly happen, and so it is; because the Day of Resurrection is that for which mankind was created, to worship Allah, and its recompense takes place on the Day of Resurrection.

He said: ﴿On that Day they will be separated﴾. He said: (In it the tā' of the original (yatafarraqūn / yatasaddaʿūn) is assimilated into the ṣād, and its meaning is: they will scatter after the reckoning, to Paradise and Hell). ﴿On that Day﴾: (idh) is nunated, and the tanwin here replaces a clause; that is: on a Day when it comes, they will be separated.

The author says: (In it the tā' of the original is assimilated into the ṣād). What is the meaning of "the tā' of the original is assimilated into the ṣād"? Its original is yatafaʿʿalūn (yataṣaddaʿūn). So his saying "assimilation of the tā' in the original" means: according to the original form, the ṣād into which it was assimilated was originally a tā', and it was assimilated into its counterpart after being changed to a ṣād. The meaning of ﴿yaṣṣaddaʿūn﴾ is they will scatter.
* A student: Its original is ṣadaʿa, yataṣaddaʿu.
* The Shaykh: Its original is yatasaddaʿūn. The meaning of tasaddaʿ is scattering, and from it: "the earth splits (tasaddaʿa al-arḍ)," because its parts scatter and it bursts open. So on the Day of Resurrection...

[The text here breaks off mid-argument: "that the corruption is caused by the deeds of the children of Adam; because of His saying: ﴿by what the hands of people have earned﴾ [ar-Rum 41]. What confirms this is also His saying: ﴿And if the people of the towns had believed and feared Allah, We would have opened upon them blessings from the heaven and the earth; but they denied, so We seized them for what they had been earning﴾ [al-A'raf 96]."]

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: affirmation of causes and means, and that the acts of Allah are caused and have a reason. From where is this taken? From His saying: ﴿by what [they] have earned﴾. There is no doubt that the acts and rulings of Allah are purposeful, because one of His names is al-Hakim (the All-Wise).
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: people are only punished for their own causes, by His saying: ﴿by what the hands of people have earned﴾. From this it follows that whoever wants punishment lifted from him should repent to Allah, for repentance is among the causes of lifting punishment and bringing reward. For this reason Hud said to his people: ﴿And O my people, seek forgiveness from your Lord and then repent to Him; He will send the sky upon you in abundant rain and increase you in strength upon your strength﴾ [Hud 52]. And Nuh said to his people: ﴿So I said, "Seek forgiveness of your Lord; indeed, He is ever Forgiving. He will send the sky upon you in abundant rain, and provide you with wealth and sons and make for you gardens and make for you rivers"﴾ [Nuh 10-12].
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: recompense is of the same kind as the deed and in proportion to it, by His saying: ﴿that He may let them taste part of what they did﴾ [ar-Rum 41].
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the demonstration of the vastness of Allah's mercy, and that His mercy precedes His wrath, by His saying: ﴿part of what they did﴾. Had the wrath been equal to the mercy, Allah would make us taste all that we did. And had mercy been dominant, would He make us taste more than we did, or not?
So there are three possibilities now: making us taste a part, or the equivalent, or more. The equivalent or more is impossible; Allah, Exalted, only makes us taste a part, because it is established in the sound hadith: "Indeed Allah, Exalted, wrote a book with Him above the Throne: Indeed My mercy precedes My wrath,"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7422) and Muslim (2751/15), from Abu Hurayrah.]] and were it not for this, Allah would take mankind to account for what they did.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: punishments may be a cause of returning to Allah. From where? ﴿so that they may return﴾ [ar-Rum 41]. Just as they may also be the opposite: they may be a cause of increased defiance and aversion, and Allah forbid. This is shown by His saying: ﴿And among the people is he who worships Allah on an edge; if good touches him, he is reassured by it, but if trial strikes him, he turns back on his face; he has lost this world and the Hereafter﴾ [al-Hajj 11]. What links this verse and the one we are explaining is that it may be said: punishments in general are beneficial, but in particular they may not benefit; because Allah said: ﴿And among the people is he who worships Allah﴾ — "among the people." And His saying: ﴿but if trial strikes him﴾ may mean a trial in religion such that he has no resistance, and so falls into the abyss, Allah forbid. But the more apparent view is that it is general: ﴿And We test you with evil and with good as a trial﴾ [al-Anbiya' 35].

Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿Say, "Travel through the earth and observe how was the end of those before you; most of them were polytheists"﴾ [ar-Rum 42]:
* In this noble verse: the command to take heed from what happened to the earlier peoples: ﴿Say, "Travel through the earth"﴾.
* Among the benefits of the verse: a person should read the books of past history for taking lessons. But, as we all know, some history books are fabricated and not as they really were. The source of history of past nations is what Allah and His Messenger have informed us of. Allah, Exalted, said in Surah Ibrahim: ﴿Has there not reached you the report of those before you — the people of Nuh, 'Ad and Thamud, and those after them, none knows them except Allah﴾ [Ibrahim 9]. So He denied that anyone has knowledge of them except Allah. Then from where do we take their reports? Since none knows them but Allah, we take them from Allah, either from the Book or from the Sunnah.
* Among the benefits of the verse: the cause of the destruction of the earlier nations was the shirk of most of them, by His saying: ﴿most of them were polytheists﴾.
* And from it: when punishment descends, it may strike the righteous and others, because He said: ﴿most of them﴾, meaning some did not commit shirk.
* And from this His saying: ﴿And fear a trial which will not strike those who have wronged among you exclusively; and know that Allah is severe in punishment﴾ [al-Anfal 25]. Allah may save the believers just as He saved the messengers and those who believed with them; He saved them.

Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿So set your face toward the upright religion before there comes a Day for which there is no repelling from Allah﴾ and so on to the end [ar-Rum 43]:
* In this is the obligation to turn toward the religion: ﴿So set your face toward the religion﴾. It necessarily follows from the obligation to turn toward it that one must turn away from everything else, because the direction is one: either toward here or toward there. So when it is necessary to turn toward the religion, it is necessary to turn away from other than it.
* Among the benefits of the verse: the prohibition of ruling by other than what Allah has revealed, because it contradicts turning toward the upright religion. Ruling by other than what Allah revealed may be disbelief, may be sinfulness, and may be injustice, as Allah mentioned in Surah al-Ma'idah: ﴿And whoever does not rule by what Allah has revealed — those are the disbelievers﴾ [al-Ma'idah 44]; and in the second verse: ﴿...those are the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Ma'idah 45]; and in the third verse: ﴿...those are the defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Ma'idah 47]. These descriptions apply according to the condition of the ruler: he may be a disbeliever, a wrongdoer, or a sinner.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: this religion is upright (qayyim). What is the meaning of qayyim? Moderate, with no crookedness in it, neither on the side of worship nor on the side of dealings.
* Among its benefits: if you think that there is in the religion something that contradicts uprightness, know that you are deficient, either in your knowledge or in your understanding. The reason is that Allah described this religion as upright. Whatever you examine in the religion of Allah and it appears to you not to be upright, know that you are mistaken, due to deficiency in your knowledge or in your understanding. A person is attacked from these two directions: either his knowledge is deficient, he has no knowledge, or his understanding is deficient, he has knowledge but does not understand.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: whoever is commanded to do something should mention what will attract and encourage people to it. From where is this taken?
* A student: ﴿before there comes [a Day]﴾ [ar-Rum 43].
* The Shaykh: No. That is correct, but before that it is from His saying: ﴿the upright﴾. When a person knows that it is upright, he will undoubtedly turn toward it. So when you want to command something, mention the qualities that make people inclined to it, with its beloved attributes and praiseworthy fruits.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: combining encouragement and warning: encouragement is ﴿the upright﴾, and warning is ﴿before there comes a Day for which there is no repelling from Allah﴾ [ar-Rum 43].
* Among its benefits: affirmation of the Day of Resurrection, that it will certainly come: ﴿for which there is no repelling from Allah﴾.
* Among its benefits: the Day of Resurrection is a great Day. From where? From the indefiniteness of ﴿a Day﴾ in ﴿before there comes a Day﴾, and indefiniteness indicates magnification. What confirms the greatness of this Day is the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿Do they not think that they will be resurrected, for a great Day, the Day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds?﴾ [al-Mutaffifin 4-6].
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the judgment belongs to Allah, Glorified and Exalted, by His saying: ﴿for which there is no repelling from Allah﴾ [ar-Rum 43]. No one can prevent what Allah wills, nor bring what Allah has not willed, ever. "O Allah, there is none who can withhold what You give, and none who can give what You withhold, and the might of the mighty person will not benefit him against You."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (844) and Muslim (593/137), from al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah.]]

Among the benefits of this noble verse: on the Day of Resurrection, people will be divided and separated, as shown by His saying: ﴿On that Day they will be separated﴾.
