He says: (related to "yusaddaʿun"). You always see the scholars, when an adverbial phrase (ẓarf) or a prepositional phrase (jarr and majrur) occurs, they say: "related to such-and-such" (mutaʿallaq). What does "related to" mean? It means that this is the thing it operates upon, because the prepositional phrase and the adverbial phrase function like the direct object, and the direct object must have a governing element that acts upon it. So when he says "related to such-and-such," it means that this is what it operates on. Every prepositional or adverbial phrase must have something it relates to:
"There must be for the preposition a relation / to a verb or its meaning, like 'murtaqi' (climbing)."
So the meaning of his saying "(related to yusaddaʿun)" is that the governing element in the word (li-yajziya) is His saying ﴿yusaddaʿun﴾, and this is the opinion of the author.
It may also be related to His saying ﴿yaʾtiya﴾: ﴿before there comes a Day for which there is no repelling from Allah﴾, ﴿that He may reward those who believed and did righteous deeds﴾, because the scattering in reality is the very recompense, so how could a thing be the cause of itself? This does not weaken the author's words; but if it is said that this Day comes for the purpose of recompense, the meaning becomes sound and clear. If we say that this "li" (li-yajziya) — since "li" is a preposition — is related to "yaʾtiya," that is clearer than saying it is related to "yusaddaʿun," because the very scattering and separation that leads to the Fire is the very recompense.
Some scholars, some grammarians, said: it is a predicate of an elided subject, so it is related to an elided predicate, and the estimate is: "That is in order that He may reward," and the referent is what preceded. This is also very well founded: that it be related to an elided predicate of an elided subject.
We have said that the "li" in (li-yajziya) is a preposition, and it is known that prepositions enter only upon nouns. It has become clear to you that among the signs of a noun is being in the genitive case, and the entry of (...) upon it. The Ajurrumiyya says: the noun is known by the genitive (khafḍ), by tanwin, by the entry of the definite article (al-) and by prepositions.
So how is it correct to say that the "li" in His saying ﴿li-yajziya﴾ is a preposition, even though it enters upon a verb? We say: because this verb is in the position of a noun, since it is a verb with an implied (an) in it; the estimate is "li-an yajziya," and "an" is a verbal particle that turns the verb into a verbal noun (maṣdar), and the verbal noun is a noun, is it not? The verbal noun is a noun. Therefore the meaning is: "for His recompense, for the recompense of those who believed and did righteous deeds," and so on. Do you understand now? When the "li" of purpose (lām al-taʿlil) enters upon a verb, an implied "an" (that) is estimated between it and the verb: "li-an yajziya." And His saying ﴿li-yajziya alladhina amanu﴾: the subject of the recompense is Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, and it is a hidden pronoun referring to Him.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, on the basis that it is in the accusative after an implied "an" after the "li": li-yajziya, and the "li" governs what follows it, on the basis that the verb will be a verbal noun.
* A student: But it is itself a preposition.
* The Shaykh: Yes, it is itself a preposition.
* A student: It is the very "lām al-taʿlil" that puts the imperfect verb in the subjunctive.
* The Shaykh: It is the very "lām al-taʿlil" which, according to the opinion of the Basrans, puts the imperfect verb in the subjunctive by means of "an" after it.
* A student: (...) the "lām al-taʿlil."
* The Shaykh: No, the "lam" is one, and the "lām al-taʿlil," just as it enters upon a verb, enters upon nouns. So if you say "I came for your honouring (li-ikramika)," it is the "lām al-taʿlil"; and "I came that I might honour you (li-ukrimaka)," it is also the "lām al-taʿlil."
His saying ﴿li-yajziya alladhina amanu﴾: "jaza'" means recompense (mukafa'a), meaning that He may reward them. ﴿li-yajziya alladhina amanu wa-ʿamilu al-ṣāliḥāt min faḍlihi﴾ — (yuthībuhum, "He will reward them") is an explanation of "jaza'" in the sense of granting reward (ithaba). "Thawab" is recompense, and it is called thawab because it comes from "thaba yathūbu," meaning to return, because it returns to the person as the recompense of his deed. His saying ﴿li-yajziya alladhina amanu wa-ʿamilu al-ṣāliḥāt﴾: pay attention to these two conditions: faith and righteous deed. Faith alone is not sufficient, and righteous deed alone is not sufficient; this applies when faith is coupled with deed. But if it is said: righteous deed suffices, or faith includes deed, faith is in the heart, so whoever has no faith in his heart, however many righteous deeds he does, will not benefit him. The hypocrite remembers Allah, prays and spends; does he? And perhaps he goes out to jihad; does his deed benefit him? Why? Because there is no faith in his heart.
A person who has faith in Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, but has not done a righteous deed, has not done a righteous deed.
* A student: Possible.
* The Shaykh: Possible what? It is possible that he is rewarded except in one case only, which is the prayer: if he does not perform it, his faith does not benefit him, because the evidences indicate that this act, although it is a physical act, makes a person a disbeliever by abandoning it, a disbelief that takes one out of the religion. As for other acts, ʿAbdullah ibn Shaqiq said: «The companions of the Prophet ﷺ did not consider abandoning any act to be disbelief except the prayer»[[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (2622) from the hadith of ʿAbdullah ibn Shaqiq.]]. Meaning: if he does not pay zakat, he does not leave faith; if he does not fast, he does not leave faith; if he does not perform Hajj, he does not leave faith. This is the correct view. Yet there is a narration from Imam Ahmad that all the pillars of Islam, if a person abandons them out of negligence, he is a disbeliever: if he does not pay zakat he is a disbeliever, if he does not fast he is a disbeliever, if he does not perform Hajj he is a disbeliever, saying: because a pillar is what a thing rests upon, and if the pillar is absent the thing does not stand. This certainly has a basis, but the evidences prevent saying this; for the hadith of Abu Hurayrah in the Sahih concerning one who does not pay his zakat mentions the Prophet's ﷺ punishment for him and then says: «Then he sees his path, either to Paradise or to the Fire»[[Narrated by Muslim (987/26) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]. His saying «he sees his path, either to Paradise or to the Fire» indicates that he does not become a disbeliever by withholding zakat. What is the proof? If he had become a disbeliever by that, he would have no path to Paradise. If he does not become a disbeliever by abandoning zakat, then what is below it is even more so. There is no doubt that the pillars of Islam below zakat are less than it; fasting is less than zakat, and Hajj is less than zakat.
If someone says: What do you say about His saying: ﴿And due to Allah from the people is pilgrimage to the House — for whoever is able to find thereto a way. And whoever disbelieves — indeed, Allah is free from need of the worlds﴾ [Al ʿImran 97]? Its apparent meaning is: whoever disbelieves and does not perform Hajj, Allah is free from the worlds?
The answer: it is said that what is meant by disbelief here is other than major disbelief, that is, a lesser disbelief (kufr dun kufr). This is why He did not say: "whoever does not perform Hajj is the disbeliever," or "abandoning Hajj is disbelief," as He said regarding prayer. And "kafara" is a verb, and a verb indicates the unrestricted sense and does not indicate generality. This is the answer to this verse. Those who said that one becomes a disbeliever by abandoning Hajj argued with this verse.
* A student: ʿAli ibn Abi Talib says: «Whoever dies without performing Hajj, let him die, if he wishes, a Jew, and if he wishes, a Christian»[[Narrated by al-Darimi in his Sunan (1826) from the hadith of Abu Umamah al-Bahili.]].
* The Shaykh: This is ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, and this is said by way of warning, or it is his own opinion, as others among the people of knowledge also held it; and this too, if the hadith is authentic, for there is discussion about the hadith. But if it is authentic, it is understood as meaning that this is a warning, or that it is his opinion as others among the people of knowledge also held.
* A student: O Shaykh, the saying: «Whoever dies without having fought and without having resolved in his soul to fight, dies a death of jahiliyya».
* The Shaykh: What I understand from the hadith «he dies upon a branch of hypocrisy»[[Narrated by Muslim (1910/158) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] — dying a death of jahiliyya does not prevent a person from dying a death of jahiliyya, because he committed an act of the jahiliyya, in that he did not fulfil the duty of jihad.
* A student: Alright, O Shaykh, ʿIsa, peace be upon him, says on the Day of Resurrection: ﴿I did not say to them except what You commanded me: 'Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord'﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 117], then at the end he says: ﴿If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, indeed You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 118]. It seems that ʿIsa, peace be upon him, mentions forgiveness as a second possibility, mentioning both punishment and forgiveness, like the hadith you mentioned.
* The Shaykh: What is the difficulty?
* A student: The difficulty is: does he see his path either to the Fire or to Paradise?
* The Shaykh: No; because this is not a report of that kind. ʿIsa, peace be upon him, says: ﴿And I was a witness over them as long as I was among them; but when You caused me to die, You were the Watcher over them﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 117], then he explains ﴿If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants﴾, for they have deserved that, ﴿and if You forgive them, indeed You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 118].
* A student: And how about the polytheists?
* The Shaykh: No, that is, "if You forgive them" means: I do not know whether they committed shirk or committed other sins for which they deserve forgiveness.

* Student: (...) ﴿Did you say to the people, "Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah?"﴾ "To the people" is general. ﴿He said, "Glory be to You! It is not for me to say what I have no right to say. Had I said it, You would have known it. You know what is within myself, and I do not know what is within Yourself. Indeed, You are the Knower of the unseen. I said to them only what You commanded me: 'Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord. And I was a witness over them while I remained among them. But when You caused me to die, You were the Watcher over them, and You are Witness over all things.' If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, indeed You are the Mighty, the Wise"﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 116–118]. This command (is the one referred to). ﴿These people who are Your servants worship me and my mother, or take us as two gods besides Allah.﴾ Then he said: ﴿If You punish them, they are Your servants, and if You forgive them...﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 118] (...).

* Shaykh: (﴿And of His signs﴾ [Ar-Rum 46], Exalted is He.) The "min" here is for partitive (tab'id, indicating a part), and "āyātihi" (His signs) is governed by "min". The phrase ﴿an yursila al-riyāh﴾ ("that He sends the winds") is a verb converted into a verbal noun (masdar) and it is the subject (mubtada'), meaning: among His signs is the sending of the winds. ﴿Mubashshirāt﴾ ("bearing good news") is a circumstantial clause (hal) describing "the winds." Allah the Mighty and Majestic says in this verse: ﴿And of His signs﴾, meaning some of His signs, because "min" here is partitive. That is because the signs of Allah the Mighty cannot be counted or enumerated:

*"And in everything there is a sign / that points to His being the One."*

Everything: if a person wanted to count the signs of Allah the Mighty that are in his body alone, he could not do so, so how about the signs of Allah the Exalted that fill the universe? For this reason, "min" indicating partiality is used. His saying ﴿āyātihi﴾ means His signs, i.e. His indications.

Know that every sign indicates knowledge, indicates power, and indicates wisdom. This is necessary; it must be so in every sign, that it is a sign, an indication, of these three matters: knowledge, power and wisdom. Then some signs are specified by what is specific to them: for example, what follows may be mercy, or something that indicates authority and greatness. The point is that every sign has something specific and something general. The general element is these three: knowledge, power and wisdom. To these three is added mercy, because these winds herald rain. ﴿That He sends the winds﴾: "irsāl" means release, and from it is the poet's saying: *"So he let them loose in a melee."* That is, he released them. From it is also the jurists' (al-fara'iḍiyyūn, specialists in inheritance law) saying: "dayn mursal," meaning an unsecured debt, one without collateral.

﴿That He sends the winds﴾ means He releases them, glorified and exalted is He. "Riyāḥ" is the plural of "rīḥ," which means the air currents. Know that "rīḥ" is mentioned both in singular and plural. When it is mentioned in plural, it is generally for mercy; when it is mentioned in singular, it is generally for punishment: ﴿They were destroyed by a violent, roaring wind﴾ [Al-Haqqah 6]; ﴿When We sent upon them the barren wind﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat 41]; ﴿A wind in which is a painful punishment﴾ [Al-Ahqaf 24], and the like. However, "rīḥ" (wind) itself may appear in singular while being in the context of blessing, especially when it is described with something that indicates that, as in His saying: ﴿And they sailed with them by a good wind﴾ [Yunus 22]. Here, is the wind a punishment or a blessing? A blessing. It was a blessing because it is described as "good" (ṭayyibah). Also, regarding ships: is it better that the winds vary or that the wind be one? It is one, because when they vary, the ship's course varies. Previously, when ships were sail-powered... here the winds are in the context of blessing, and for this reason "riyāḥ" is plural. ﴿Mubashshirāt﴾ is a circumstantial clause describing the winds, meaning they bring good news of goodness. For this reason, when some winds blow, people rejoice, because Allah the Exalted has established the custom that a particular wind forms clouds and then rain; sometimes people rejoice at the wind when they see it gathering the clouds, gathering and thickening them, and they rejoice at it. His saying ﴿mubashshirāt﴾: "bishārah" (glad tidings) is the report of what generally gladdens, and it is called bishārah because it affects the skin (bashrah). When a person rejoices, his face brightens and shines, and you find on him the sign of good news. Good news may also be used for what is bad, as in His saying: ﴿So give them tidings of a painful punishment﴾ [Ali 'Imran 21].

﴿Mubashshirāt﴾: he (the author, may Allah have mercy on him) said: "meaning, to give you good news of rain." Notice that the author, may Allah have mercy on him, explained the active participle with a verb of purpose, saying "meaning, to give you good news," in order to make the conjunction smooth in His saying ﴿and that He may make you taste of His mercy﴾; because between "mubashshirāt" and "liyudhīqakum" a person finds a gap. The author wanted to bridge this gap by saying "meaning, to give you good news with them." But in my view the correct understanding is that "mubashshirāt" stays as it is, as a noun, but we supply a verb that suits what follows, so that the verb can be coordinated with it. What I see as the best is to supply: "that you may rejoice with them (as) bearers of good news, that you may rejoice with them, and that He may make you taste of His mercy." Or we make it: "to give you good news," as the author said, and we do not treat it as meaning "bearers of good news," but rather as an independent verb which we supply so that the conjunction in His saying ﴿and that He may make you taste of His mercy﴾ is correct.

His saying: (﴿and that He may make you taste﴾ by them ﴿of His mercy﴾: the rain and fertility). It has been mentioned before that Allah the Exalted expresses reaching something as "making one taste," because it is the highest and most complete form of reaching. ﴿And that He may make you taste by them of His mercy﴾: he says, "the rain and fertility." He explained "mercy" by its effect. On this basis, is the mercy in this verse created, or is it one of Allah's attributes? It is created. This interpretation is possible, because Allah the Exalted may apply "mercy" to a created thing which is one of the effects of His mercy, as is established in the authentic hadith that Allah said to Paradise: "You are My mercy; I show mercy through you to whom I will" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4850) and Muslim (2846/34), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah]. It is well known that He, glorified is He, did not mean that Paradise is His mercy which is His attribute, because Paradise is a created thing, separate from Him. Rather, He meant that it is one of the effects of His mercy, or a requirement of His mercy. So here it is valid to say ﴿and that He may make you taste of His mercy﴾, meaning of this rain and fertility, and the mercy here is a created thing among the created things. It is possible that the mercy (...).

If we take it as an attribute, then it is for the source (ibtida'), meaning: that He may make you taste a blessing issuing from this mercy. (﴿And that the ships may sail﴾ by it, ﴿by His command﴾, by His will, ﴿and that you may seek of His bounty﴾, seeking ﴿of His bounty﴾, the provision through trade at sea ﴿and perhaps you will be grateful﴾.)

His saying ﴿wa litajriya al-fulk﴾ ("and that the ships may sail"): he says, "the ships by it." "By it" refers back to the winds. So Allah sends the winds so that by them the water is driven through the atmosphere of the sky, which is the clouds, and He sends the winds so that by them the ships sail on the seas. Both the clouds and the ships carry many blessings. What do the ships carry? They carry provisions, people, animals and other things, while the clouds carry water, which is the substance of life: ﴿Have you considered the water which you drink? Did you bring it down from the rain-cloud, or are We the Bringer-down?﴾ [Al-Waqi'ah 68–69]. So in the winds there are two benefits: moving the clouds through the atmosphere of the sky, and moving ships through the expanses of the seas.

His saying ﴿al-fulk﴾: is it singular or plural? It may be used for both this and that. Al-fulk is suitable for both the plural and the singular, or not?

* Student: It occurs in the Qur'an.

* Shaykh: It occurs in the Qur'an. Give me an example of it used as singular?

* Student: ﴿And you see the ships therein, ploughing through it﴾ [An-Nahl 14]; this one is plural in origin, O Shaykh. ﴿And the ship which sails in the sea﴾ [Al-Baqarah 164]; this is singular.

* Another student: ﴿And construct the ship﴾ [Hud 37].

* Shaykh: No.

* Another student: In the story of Noah, peace be upon him: ﴿And he was constructing the ship, and whenever a group of his people passed by him﴾ [Hud 38].

* Shaykh: That is the answer.

* Another student: ﴿Have you not seen that the ship﴾ [Luqman 31].

* Shaykh: In any case, the example he gave is also correct: ﴿Until when you are in the ship and they sail with them by a good wind﴾ [Yunus 22]. Is this plural or singular? Plural: ﴿in the ship and they sail﴾; he did not say "in the ship and it sailed."

* Student: Singular, O Shaykh: ﴿in the laden ship﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 119].

* Shaykh: Yes. ﴿And you see the ship in it, ploughing through﴾ [Fatir 12] is also plural.

In any case, al-fulk is suitable for both the singular and the plural.

The jurists mentioned a point that I told you earlier. They said: the hunchback intends the bowing (ruku') with his heart. The hunchback is not standing straight so that he could bow; he intends it in his heart. Some jurists said: "He is like al-fulk in the Arabic language," meaning the bending of this hunchback resembles al-fulk in Arabic, since it is known only through intention. Al-fulk is suitable for the singular and the plural, and it is known only through intention or context. This poor hunchback in the state of bowing: what tells us whether he is bowing or not bowing? So his bowing and his standing are alike. This may serve as evidence for what is reported about al-Kisa'i, who said that when a person masters one branch of knowledge, he is able to understand other branches. They mention a story that he and Abu Yusuf were before al-Rashid, one of the caliphs of the Abbasid dynasty, and they debated a question. Abu Yusuf said to al-Kisa'i: "What do you think if a person forgets in the prostration of forgetfulness (sujud al-sahw)? Does your grammar teach you the ruling on this question?" He said: "Yes; if he forgets in the prostration of forgetfulness, he does not prostrate." He said: "Where is the rule in your grammar?" He said: "We have a rule in grammar that the diminutive (al-muṣaghghar) is not diminutized." He based this on the idea that the prostration of forgetfulness is a diminutive prayer, so if one forgets in it, there is no need for another... (...) Whether this actually happened or not, Allah knows best; they mentioned it.

He says: ﴿It is Allah who sends the winds﴾ [Ar-Rum 48]; ﴿and that the ships may sail by His command﴾. He said "by His will." The correct meaning is "by His command," meaning the command that is by speech, not will alone. Because the ship does not know what Allah the Mighty wills; rather, it complies only with His spoken command. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [Ya-Sin 82]. So every desire of Allah, if it is not accompanied by speech, does not come to pass. How could existing things come into being merely by a will that no one knows except Allah? There must be speech. So the correct view is that "by His command" means His spoken command, based on His saying: ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is.﴾ This does not prevent that this sailing by His command takes place through perceptible causes known to us, because the one who determined the causes is Allah the Mighty. He, glorified and exalted is He, creates and subjects, but through means: ﴿and that the ships may sail by His command, and that you may seek of His bounty﴾ [Ar-Rum 46]. All of this is among what Allah the Mighty created for these great wisdoms.

(﴿And that you may seek﴾: seek ﴿of His bounty﴾, the provision through trade at sea.) That is indeed so. How many people have trade at sea, moving provisions from one place to another by means of these ships? Were it not for these ships, it would be impossible for provisions to move from the land beyond the sea to another place. But Allah the Mighty made these ships so that they might carry these provisions and blessings.

(﴿And that you may seek of His bounty, and perhaps you will be grateful﴾ [Ar-Rum 46]: these blessings, O people of Makkah, so that you may affirm His oneness.) ﴿Perhaps you will be grateful﴾: "la'alla" here means causation (ta'lil). "Tashkurūn" (you will be grateful): gratitude (shukr) is the performance of obedience to the Benefactor. It is done with the tongue, the heart, and the limbs. Gratitude is with the heart, the tongue, and the limbs; it is the performance of obedience to the Benefactor. As for gratitude with the heart, it is that a person believes this blessing comes from Allah the Mighty; He is the one who supplied it, facilitated it for him, and brought it to him. This is gratitude with the heart.

Gratitude with the tongue is that one praises Allah for it, which is part of thanking for blessings, and that one speaks of it acknowledging Allah's grace, not boasting about it over others. As for gratitude with the limbs, it is that one performs bodily worship for Allah the Exalted, such as prayer, zakah, fasting, Hajj and others. For this reason the poet says:

*"Bounty from me has given you three things: / my hand, my tongue, and the veiled heart."*

The hand is the limbs, the tongue is speech, and the veiled heart is the heart. What is the connection or relation between praise (hamd) and gratitude (shukr)?

We say: praise is more general in terms of its cause, and gratitude is more general in terms of its object. Because praise is by the tongue, and it is for blessings and for the perfection of the attributes of the one praised; that is, one praises the praised for his blessings and his kindness to the praiser, and for the perfection of his attributes. As for its object, it is related to the tongue; especially praise is only by the tongue, though it may also be with the heart, by believing in the perfection of the one praised, but linguistically it is called praise only when it is by the tongue. As for gratitude, it is more specific than praise in terms of its cause, and more general in terms of its object. How is it more specific in terms of its cause? Because its cause is only a blessing: bestowing a favour on the one who is grateful is the cause. Otherwise, if the praised were the most perfect of people but had given you nothing, would you thank him? You would not thank him. Gratitude is for blessings, so it is more specific in terms of its cause, and it can be with the heart, the tongue, and the limbs, so in terms of its object it is more general. Therefore the relation between them is one of partial generality and partial specificity (al-'umum wa'l-khusus al-wajhi).

﴿And perhaps you will be grateful﴾: we said gratitude is the performance of obedience to the Benefactor. This is correct in the general sense. But the gratitude for a specific blessing is by performing its specific function of obedience. The gratitude for a specific blessing is by performing its specific function. For example, a person's gratitude to his Lord for knowledge is by what? By acting upon it and teaching it. This is specific gratitude for a specific blessing. A person's gratitude to his Lord for a dwelling, for example, is by obeying Him in this dwelling, by not being wasteful or extravagant, and the like. So gratitude has two meanings: the general meaning is performing what? The performance of obedience to the Benefactor. The specific meaning is performing obedience to Allah the Exalted regarding that specific blessing. Every blessing has a specific gratitude.

* * *

﴿And We certainly sent before you messengers to their peoples, and they brought them clear proofs; then We took vengeance upon those who committed crime﴾ [Ar-Rum 47], and so on. The lam in His saying ﴿wa-laqad﴾ ("and certainly") is a lam of oath (lam al-muwaṭṭi'ah), meaning it is the answer to an implied oath. The estimate: "By Allah, indeed." From this we know that the sentence here is emphasized by three things: the oath, the lam, and "qad": ﴿And We certainly sent before you messengers to their peoples﴾.

It is well known among the scholars that a messenger (rasul) is one to whom a law is revealed and who is commanded to convey it, because he is sent. This category of people is the highest type of human beings; they are the highest kind. After them come the prophets (anbiya'), then the truthful (siddiqun), then the martyrs (shuhada'), then the righteous (salihun). So the highest of human kinds are the messengers, peace be upon them, because they combine being specially chosen for the message and for worship. ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ [Al-An'am 124]. He gives the message only to one who is fit for it. So the people most deserving of the message, without doubt, are those eminent ones whom Allah the Mighty sent, and it is impossible that anyone among people could be more deserving of it than them.

From this we know the error, indeed the disbelief, of those who say that 'Ali ibn Abi Talib is more deserving of the message than Muhammad (ﷺ). For they have thereby attributed to Allah the Mighty what is not fitting for Him, because if He gave the message to Muhammad while 'Ali had a better claim to it, then He would be either ignorant of who deserves it, or unwilling to give the right to its people. Both of these are impossible and inconceivable for Allah. Anyone who describes Allah with this, or with what necessarily implies this, is undoubtedly a disbeliever.

Therefore the messengers, peace be upon them, are the noblest of creation, the noblest categories of creation, and they are without doubt the most deserving of people of prophethood, and none is more deserving than they. Yet there are, we seek refuge with Allah, some people among the philosophers who hold that the messengers are of the lowest ranks of creation, and they say: the walī (friend of Allah) is better than the prophet, and the prophet is better than the messenger, because the walī is the elite of the elite, a walī in his own name, while the prophet has a distinction in revelation, and the messenger is in the position of the servant in the house who is sent to buy the needs. Look, we seek refuge with Allah, at this misguidance, and among what they say:

The station of prophethood is in an intermediate realm, above the messenger by a little and below the walī.

Look, we seek refuge with Allah: the station of prophethood is in an intermediate realm "above the messenger" meaning a little above the messenger, and in relation to the walī it is "below the walī," meaning far lowered from the walī. Accordingly, the rank of walāyah (friendship with Allah) in their view is the highest of all things. This is undoubtedly disbelief. Rather, we say: the station of messengerhood is above everything, then prophethood, then walāyah; because the messenger combines messengerhood, prophethood and walāyah, does he not? And the prophet has prophethood and walāyah, while the walī has walāyah without prophethood and messengerhood. And it is known that whenever the attribute of perfection increases in a person, he becomes more perfect than others.

﴿And We certainly sent messengers before you to their peoples﴾. The "qawm" (people) are the group to which a person belongs, for by them is his standing; he stands by them, and they stand by him. And His saying ﴿to their peoples﴾ is because no messenger was sent, other than the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, except that his message was specific to his people, as established in the sound hadith of Jābir: "Every prophet was sent specifically to his people, and I have been sent to all mankind"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (335), and Muslim (521/3) from the hadith of Jābir ibn ʿAbdullāh.]].

﴿to their peoples, and they came to them﴾: the subject is the messengers and the object is the peoples (﴿and they came to them with clear proofs﴾), with clear evidences on the truthfulness of their messengership to them, but they denied them. Regarding His saying ﴿with the clear proofs﴾: is the intended meaning "the clear proofs" – it is known that they are the manifest ones – but is the intended meaning of "clear proofs" here what shows the truthfulness of their messengership, so that it refers to the miracles with which they were supported, or is the intended meaning the clear, manifest laws, which whoever examines them knows that they are from Allah, or are both meant?

Both are meant. The messengers came with clear signs that support them and indicate their truthfulness, and they also came with clear proofs, clear manifest laws known to be from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. The "bā'" in His saying ﴿with the clear proofs﴾ is then for accompaniment, meaning they were sent with a message accompanied by clear proofs, or for specificity according to the view that the clear proofs are the laws. This is from the wisdom and mercy of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: Allah did not send a messenger except that He supported him with a sign, out of His wisdom and mercy. For if a messenger came to people without a sign and said, "I am the messenger of Allah," without a sign, would they accept? It is in human nature not to accept until one knows. Likewise, if one of the people came and said, "Look, I am a scholar with knowledge of the Sharia, so ask me; whatever you ask, I will give you a ruling," would they obey him? Never; they will not obey him until they test him and question him. So how about one who claims that revelation comes to him? He will not be accepted unless he brings a sign. This is from the wisdom of Allah, and from His mercy too, so that He does not punish anyone for a sin without a proof. For if He had sent the messengers without signs, and the nations denied them, they would have been excused in denying for lack of a sign. Yet they might not be excused, since they must submit; but from His mercy He said: We have placed with them clear signs so that people may be reassured by them and believe in them through conviction.

And His saying ﴿And We certainly sent messengers before you to their peoples﴾ [al-Rūm 47]. ﴿messengers before you﴾: perhaps from the words "before you" one may infer that there is no messenger after him, as we will mention, God willing, in the benefits, and we will discuss this benefit. ﴿and they came to them with clear proofs, then We took vengeance on those who committed crime﴾. ﴿Then We took vengeance﴾: intiqām (vengeance) is the taking of punishment. This is an act of Allah, and it is not one of His names. In the hadith that contains the list of the Most Beautiful Names[[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (3507) from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah.]], which is an interpolated addition and not authentically from the Prophet ﷺ, it states that among His names is al-Muntaqim (the Avenger), but it is not one of His names; rather it is one of His attributes and acts. For this reason it is not stated absolutely; He said: ﴿Indeed, We will take vengeance upon the criminals﴾ [al-Sajdah 22]. So it is an act. As for His saying ﴿We took vengeance on those who committed crime﴾, what is ijrām (crime)? Ijrām is the doing of a crime (jurm), and jurm is anything that is a cause of sin, and what is meant by ijrām here is disbelief. From the noble verse ﴿We took vengeance on those who committed crime﴾ it is understood that whoever does not commit crime is not avenged upon. Therefore He said: ﴿And it was truly incumbent upon Us to help the believers﴾ [al-Rūm 47]. ﴿And it was truly incumbent upon Us, to help﴾ — nasr: what is its i'rab (grammatical analysis)? It is the ism of kāna (its subject); where is its khabar (predicate)? ḥaqqan (truly). ﴿And it was truly incumbent upon Us to help the believers﴾: this is the best and most preferable i'rab of the verse, and the easiest, though there are other possibilities.

His saying ﴿And it was truly incumbent upon Us﴾: al-ḥaqq means a thing that is established and binding. ﴿the help of the believers﴾, the believers in what must be believed in: belief in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and the divine decree, both its good and its evil. So Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, obligated Himself to help the believers; He made it obligatory, "it was incumbent upon Us," a commitment and guarantee from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. ﴿the help of the believers﴾: with what did He help the believers?

The help of the believers means protecting them from their enemies, by granting them sensory and spiritual support such that the final outcome is theirs. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We will surely help Our messengers and those who believed in the life of this world and on the day when the witnesses stand﴾ [Ghāfir 51].

If someone says: this truth which Allah committed Himself to may seem problematic to us, since Allah sometimes forsakes the believers, as at Uhud for example; for the victory at Uhud went to whom? To Quraysh and their followers. So what is the answer to this verse?

We say: the answer is that the victory of Quraysh over the Messenger ﷺ was not a lasting victory whose final outcome was theirs; rather, in reality it is part of the help of the believers against them. If you wish to see this clearly, read what Allah mentioned of this battle in Surah Āl ʿImrān among the wisdoms cited: ﴿and that He might destroy the disbelievers﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 141]. "To destroy the disbelievers" means it is a help by bringing them on, for if they were defeated in every encounter they would not have stood up or fought; but when they gain some victory it incites them to fight until the final outcome is for the believers and Allah annihilates them.

And among it also is the help of the believers against themselves, for what befell them at Uhud came only because of their disobedience, as Allah said: ﴿and you disobeyed after He had shown you what you love﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 152]. Here they recognize the gravity of disobedience and that by it there is lost of what is beloved (...). The summary is that this verse stands on its own: Allah, exalted is He, helps the believers, a truth incumbent upon Him which He Himself made obligatory on Himself, as in His saying: ﴿Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy﴾ [al-An'ām 54]. He said: ﴿Whoever disbelieves, upon him is his disbelief; and whoever does righteousness, for themselves they prepare﴾ [al-Rūm 44].

* Among the benefits of this verse: combining encouragement and warning: the warning in His saying ﴿whoever disbelieves, upon him is his disbelief﴾, and the encouragement in His saying ﴿and whoever does righteousness, for themselves they prepare﴾.
* Among its benefits: the evil of the disbeliever does not extend beyond him to others; this is from His saying ﴿whoever disbelieves, upon him is his disbelief﴾, and the placing of the predicate first indicates restriction.
* Among the benefits of the verse: reward is not complete except through righteous deeds based on two matters: sincerity to Allah, exalted is He, and following His Messenger ﷺ; from His saying ﴿and whoever does righteousness﴾.
* Among its benefits: wisdom and prudence in righteous deeds; from His saying ﴿for themselves they prepare﴾, because when they do so they will be at ease in the future, for they have prepared for themselves the best of abodes.

We have mentioned ﴿upon him is his disbelief﴾, meaning: combine it with the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever establishes an evil practice in Islam, upon him is its burden and the burden of whoever acts by it until the Day of Resurrection"[[Narrated by Muslim (1017/69) from the hadith of Jarir ibn ʿAbdullāh.]], and His saying exalted is He: ﴿And they will surely carry their burdens and additional burdens along with their burdens﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt 13], and His saying: ﴿that they may bear their burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection, and some of the burdens of those whom they mislead without knowledge﴾ [al-Naḥl 25]. What did we mention about combining them?

* Student: that these evil deeds are from their own actions.
* Shaykh: Yes, because they are the cause.
* Student: in misguiding these people.
* Shaykh: Yes. Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿that He may reward those who believed and did righteous deeds from His bounty. Indeed, He does not love the disbelievers﴾ [al-Rūm 45].

* From this verse is derived: the affirmation of causes in the acts of Allah; from His saying ﴿that He may reward those who believed﴾. People have divided on this into three categories. One group denied causes in the acts of Allah and in His legislation, and said: He, glorified and exalted, does what He wills and judges as He wills without any cause or wisdom, like the Jabriyyah.

Another group affirmed causes in Allah's acts and said: Allah, exalted is He, does nothing except for a wisdom, and legislates only for a wisdom; but they made those causes necessitating, and said: it is obligatory upon Him to do such-and-such for such-and-such. These are the Mu'tazilah.

A third group took a middle position and said: Allah's acts are for a wisdom, and His legislation is for a wisdom, but this wisdom is not necessitating; rather, it is Allah who made wisdom obligatory upon Himself, and wisdom follows from the requirement of His name al-Ḥakīm (the All-Wise), so it is necessary, not by the obligation of anyone, but by the requirement of His being All-Wise; He Himself made it obligatory on Himself. This is the correct view. If we hold it, we cannot object to any of Allah's rulings, whether cosmic or decreed; for we know that the One who made His acts and legislation accompanied by wisdom is Allah, not us. So we do not say that Allah is obliged to do what is best, nor that doing good is an independent obligation apart from His will. This is the truth. So from it we take that all of Allah's acts and rulings are motivated by wisdom, by the requirement of His name al-Ḥakīm.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: the reward is not obligatory upon Allah; from His saying ﴿that He may reward those who believed and did righteous deeds from His bounty﴾ [al-Rūm 45]; but He made it obligatory upon Himself, in His saying: ﴿Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy: that whoever of you does evil in ignorance and then repents after it and corrects himself, indeed He is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-An'ām 54]. He, glorified and exalted, made it obligatory upon Himself. For this reason the poet said:

Nothing is owed to His servants as an obligation upon Him, no, nor does any deed go to waste before Him.
If they are punished, it is by His justice; if they are blessed, it is by His bounty, and He is the Generous, the Vast.

Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, versified the meaning of these two verses but gave a reason, saying:

Nothing is owed to His servants as an obligation upon Him; He Himself made obligatory the great reward.
If they are punished, it is by His justice; if they are blessed, it is by His bounty, and bounty belongs to the Bestower.

So the absolute statement in the two preceding verses is restricted: that it was He who made that obligatory, by His own grace, exalted is He.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of love for Allah. From where is it derived? ﴿He does not love the disbelievers﴾. But this is a negation; how do we derive affirmation from it? Because if love is negated from the disbelievers, it necessarily follows that He loves the believers; for if not, there would be no difference between the believers and the disbelievers. If love were negated from both, there would be no distinction between them, would there not?

For this reason the scholars took as evidence for the affirmation of the vision of Allah, exalted is He, His saying: ﴿No! Indeed, they, that Day, will be veiled from their Lord﴾ [al-Muṭaffifīn 15]. They said: since these were veiled in the state of wrath, it indicates that those others are not veiled in the state of pleasure.

So from this verse we derive the affirmation of love, which, as has been discussed before, is an attribute established for Allah in its true sense; it is not the meaning of reward nor the will to reward. Rather, reward follows from it and is its consequence: when He loves a people, He rewards them, and He rewards them only by His will: ﴿His command, when He wills a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [Yā Sīn 82].

* From the benefits of the noble verse: encouragement to faith and righteous deeds. Allah did not say "believe and do righteous deeds," but the mention of the reward necessitates encouragement to the act. This is one of the ways by which it is shown that a thing is commanded. Do not think that what is commanded is only what comes in the imperative form "do"; rather, command is derived from several matters, so when encouragement to something is mentioned, it is commanded.

So from this, encouragement to faith and righteous deeds is derived.

* Also derived from the noble verse: the dispraise of disbelief. From where is this taken? From His saying: ﴿Indeed, He does not love the disbelievers﴾. When Allah negates love from them, it implies the dispraise of their deeds.

* Also: when a ruling is attached to a derived noun (mushtaqq), which is a point of usul (legal theory): when a ruling is attached to a derived noun, this is evidence that the derived attribute is the cause of the ruling. For example, He does not love the disbelievers: why? Because of their disbelief. So the ruling here is attached to an attribute, and one says: He does not love them because of their disbelief; thus disbelief is the cause of the absence of love. Likewise if He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who fight in His cause in a row﴾ [al-Ṣaff 4]: what is the cause of love? Fighting in His cause in a row. And so every ruling attached to a derived noun indicates the causality of that thing.

* Also derived from the verse is a benefit: the consideration of the necessary implication (lāzim), meaning that if such-and-such follows from a thing, then this implication is established following the establishment of what necessitates it. For example, observe regarding the believers: ﴿that He may reward those who believed and did righteous deeds﴾. He did not say "He loves" or "He does not love" the disbelievers; He said: ﴿that He may reward those who believed and did righteous deeds from His bounty﴾, and the counterpart: ﴿Indeed, He does not love the disbelievers﴾. What does it necessarily entail? That He does not reward them from His bounty; rather, He deals with them by what? By His justice. So the punishment of the disbelievers is derived from the necessary implication of the negation of love. This implication-based inference is very useful to the student of knowledge: that from such-and-such it follows such-and-such. But two conditions are necessary:

The first condition: the implication must be valid. If the implication is invalid, it is not an implication, even if a person claims it is.

The second condition: that this occurs in the speech of Allah and the speech of His Messenger ﷺ.

As for the first condition, that the implication be valid, we guard against cases where the implication is not valid. For example, the deniers of attributes, or some of them, what was their doubt in denying? They said: it necessarily leads to anthropomorphism (tamthīl). Is this implication valid? It is not valid; therefore we do not say that affirming the attributes necessarily leads to anthropomorphism, because it is not a necessary implication.

In the speech of Allah and of His Messenger, when the implication is sound, it is true, and the text indicates it. But in the speech of anyone else, the implication is not attributed to the speaker as his statement. For this reason the scholars have a section on this question: Is the implication of a statement itself a statement, or not? Some said that the logical implication (*lazim al-qawl*) of a statement is not a statement. Others said that it is. The correct view is that the implication of a statement in the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger ﷺ is a statement, on condition that the implication is sound. Why is it a statement? Because Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, knows what follows from His speech by way of implications, and if Allah does not negate them, this indicates that they are established. But do humans know what follows from their words? Sometimes a person says a statement he thinks is correct, and it implies corrupt matters. It truly and necessarily implies corrupt matters. If the speaker were alerted to them, what would he do? He would retract his statement. Therefore we say: the implication of a statement outside the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger is not a statement, although it may be used as evidence for the falsity of the statement. But one does not say that it is the statement of so-and-so.

The summary is that this question should be borne in mind. We say this because a human being is a human, who does not encompass all the implications, whether sound or false, that his speech entails. Now, we see that a person often orders his children to do something or forbids them from something, and then when they do it, he realises that it entails a corruption, so he retracts it. Did he know this implication beforehand? If he had known, he would not have ordered them. And often he forbids them from something, and then when they abandon it, he sees a corruption in that. It entailed a corruption he did not know about at the time of the prohibition, so you find him retracting.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No. The implication of a statement in the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger is a statement, but on condition that the implication is sound. As for anything else, it is not so; it is not a statement.

Then Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿And among His signs is that He sends the winds as bringers of good news, that He may let you taste of His mercy, and that the ships may run by His command, and that you may seek of His bounty, and perhaps you will be grateful.﴾ [al-Rum 46]

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: there are signs and indications of the existence of the Creator, and of His knowledge, power and wisdom. These signs by which Allah makes Himself known to His servants are among the blessings of Allah upon them, that Allah, the Exalted, shows them His signs so that they may thank Him and acknowledge His favour.
* Among the benefits of this verse, in addition to the three signs we mentioned: the establishment of mercy, as shown by His saying: ﴿that He sends the winds as bringers of good news﴾. If all of creation gathered to blow with every means of blowing, could they cover a single town with that blowing? They could not. Yet the Lord, glorified is His power, overwhelms whatever He wills with this wind, which may uproot trees and demolish dwellings. Is this not evidence of Allah's great power? Yes. And that they are bringers of good news indicates the establishment of mercy.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: Allah's blessing upon His servants through the ships that run by His command. Had Allah, glorified and exalted, not facilitated the means by which that occurs, people would not have known how to cross from one shore to another by way of the sea.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the manifestation of signs to a person is a cause for thanking Allah for His blessing upon him. From where do we derive this? From His saying: ﴿and perhaps you will be grateful﴾.
* Among its benefits: the establishment of causes and wisdoms in the acts of Allah, from His saying "perhaps" (*la'alla*), since it expresses causation.

Then He, the Exalted, says: ﴿And We had already sent messengers before you to their peoples, and they came to them with clear proofs﴾ [al-Rum 47], and so on to the end.

* From this noble verse is derived: consolation for the Messenger ﷺ and a warning to those who oppose him. He is consoled by the messengers who came before him, for they were denied and harmed. When he knows that someone else shared in such things, the matter becomes easier for him, because every person is consoled by what befalls another like himself, or by what befell another like himself. For this reason Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And it will not benefit you today, since you did wrong, that you will share in the punishment﴾ [al-Zukhruf 39].
.. the situation of those messengers who came before him.
* Among its benefits: a warning to those who oppose him, from His saying: ﴿So We took vengeance upon those who committed crime﴾ [al-Rum 47].
* Among the benefits of the verse also: Allah's mercy to His servants by sending messengers. Had it not been for this messengership, people would not have known how to worship Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and they would not have known the details of His names and attributes, as was mentioned in the lesson on *tawhid* (monotheism). The messengers are a great mercy to creation, as Allah said: ﴿And We did not send you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya 107].
* Among the benefits of the noble verse also: the vengeance upon the deniers was because of their deeds, from His saying: ﴿So We took vengeance upon those who committed crime﴾; that is, because of their crime. They were the cause.
* Among its benefits: that the earlier messengerships were specific.
* Student: ﴿to their peoples﴾.
* Shaykh: From His saying: ﴿to their peoples﴾. It is explained by the authentic hadith in the two Sahihs: "Every prophet used to be sent to his own people specifically, but I have been sent to all people generally."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (335), and Muslim (521/3), from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah.]]
* Among the benefits of the verse: Allah, the Exalted, sent the messengers only with clear proofs that testify to their truthfulness, and with clear laws that do not cause confusion for those who follow them. From where is this taken? ﴿and they came to them with clear proofs﴾ [al-Rum 47]; that is, with clear signs indicating their truthfulness, and with clear, evident laws that do not entail confusion for the follower.

The people of knowledge said: The signs of the prophets correspond to their eras. In the time of Musa, sorcery spread and became widespread, so Allah gave him signs that nullify sorcery and are not sorcery: He gave him the hand and He gave him the staff.

They said: In the time of 'Isa, medicine advanced, so Allah gave him signs that medicine cannot achieve, namely healing the blind-born (*al-akmah*) and the leper, and reviving the dead and bringing them out of their graves. Medicine can never do that; the dead cannot be revived by medicine. They also said: a leper cannot be cured by medicine.

Who is the *akmah*? They said: he who was created without an eye. In earlier eras that could not be remedied by placing an eye for him, but now, if the place of the eye is present, an eye can be placed by medicine. But if it is not present, for example, when Allah created him without creating a place for the eye, an eye cannot be placed.

In the time of the Messenger ﷺ, they said: eloquence had reached its peak, so among the greatest signs of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, was this Qur'an, which rendered the eloquent and the articulate incapable. Indeed, Allah challenged with it all the jinn and mankind: ﴿Say: If mankind and the jinn gathered to produce the like of this Qur'an, they would not produce its like﴾, neither individually nor by helping one another. For this reason He said: ﴿even if some of them were helpers to others﴾ [al-Isra 88].

* Student: Shaykh, those who speak of the scientific miraculousness of the Qur'an use this meaning (...).
* Shaykh: (...)?
* Student: That the miraculousness is of the type of what each people excelled in. They say: now eloquence has disappeared among people; they do not know (...) the aspects of eloquence (...), but now science has dominated (...) scientific indications so that it may be confirmed (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, perhaps. This is not far-fetched. I say: it is not far-fetched. Yes, it may be correct that the Qur'an is a miracle in every age in a manner suited to that age, because it was revealed for all creation until the Day of Resurrection. So this is not far-fetched; the Qur'an in all (...). But at that time the greatest of its features was eloquence.
* Also among its benefits: the establishment of the act of vengeance to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿So We took vengeance﴾.
* Also among its benefits: the establishment of greatness, from His saying ﴿So We took vengeance﴾ and ﴿We sent﴾. This is for exaltation, not plurality, by the consensus of the Muslims that it is for exaltation.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: Allah made it binding upon Himself to help the believers, from His saying: ﴿And it was a right upon Us to help the believers﴾ [al-Rum 47].
* Among it: that this help must occur, because it came in the form of exaltation: ﴿it was a right upon Us﴾, and He did not say "upon Me" but "upon Us", indicating that this right must come to pass, because Allah, the Exalted, is greater than everything.
* Also among it: evidence that those who are not believers are not helped, from His saying: ﴿a right upon Us to help the believers﴾.

So if someone raises against us the swift victories gained by the disbelievers, what is the answer?

* Student: It is a respite (*istidraj*) from Allah, the Exalted.
* Shaykh: That this is a respite from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, so that the victory may ultimately be completed for the believers.
* Student: It may be a discipline for the believers.
* Shaykh: Yes, and it may be in the believers' interest, because (...) a victory for themselves over themselves. Then this victory never lasts; the final outcome must be for the believers.

Some people of knowledge said: victory is of two kinds: victory by proof and demonstration, and victory by the sword and the spear.

As for victory by proof and demonstration, it is guaranteed and established, with no exception. Is that so? Yes, because proof and demonstration are with the believers in every state. Even if they are defeated militarily, proof and demonstration are with them; they prevail by their proof and demonstration. There is no exception in this.

The second is military victory, meaning by the sword and the spear. We say now: by aircraft and bombs and the like. Victory may occur for non-believers as a trial for the believers and a respite for the disbelievers.

Then He, the Mighty and Majestic, said..

* Student: Shaykh, yesterday you mentioned: can it be derived from it that the Messenger is the Seal of the Prophets?
* Shaykh: Yes. What do you say? Can it be derived from it that the Messenger ﷺ is the Seal of the Prophets, ﴿messengers before you﴾?
* Students: It does not necessarily follow.
* Shaykh: That is, it does not necessarily follow that no one comes after him?
* Student: Yes, from this verse.
* Shaykh: Yes, it is known, from this verse.
* Student: (...) ﴿to their peoples﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿to their peoples﴾. Yes, this indicates that their messengership was specific. But does it indicate that it has ended?
* Student: (...) comprehensive, to all people (...).
* Another student: The Qadianis use this verse (...), the verse of al-Nahl: ﴿He sends down the angels with the Spirit by His command upon whom He wills of His servants, [saying]: Warn that there is no god except Me, so fear Me﴾ [al-Nahl 2].
* Shaykh: For what? (...) the Qadianiyyah? (Qadianis, followers of Mirza Ghulam Ahmad of Qadian.)
* Student: The messengership continues, ﴿He sends down the angels﴾ (...) the present tense form...
* Shaykh: This is kufr (disbelief).
* Student: It indicates (...) among them, among the Qadianis.
* Shaykh: The discussion is about whether this verse indicates that messengership ended with the Messenger ﷺ, by His saying: ﴿And We had already sent messengers before you to their peoples﴾, or does it not indicate this? The aspect he mentioned says: it may indicate it, insofar as the Messenger is sent to people generally, and this generality includes generality in time, place and nations. This requires that there be no messenger after him. If a messenger came after him, the generality to all people would be negated. It would mean that the messenger after him would be a messenger to these people, but not to Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him.
* Student: But, Shaykh, there is no evidence in this that he was sent to all people (...).
* Shaykh: No, there is (...), because if he were not the last of them, then whoever comes after him would be sent to some people, namely those who came later. Well, in any case, deriving it from this involves some ambiguity, and the matter is clear in this regard. What is strange is that some people, by way of digression, denied the descent of 'Isa ibn Maryam ﷺ and said: If we said he would descend, that would be a denial of the Qur'an: ﴿But he is the Messenger of Allah and the Seal of the Prophets﴾ [al-Ahzab 40]. What do you say?
* Student: But there is a verse that says: ﴿And indeed it is a sign of the Hour﴾ [al-Zukhruf 61]. This indicates his descent. And the second thing, Shaykh, is that they deny the coming of the Mahdi.
* Shaykh: (...) Do not bring one matter into another. I say: is their use of the noble verse valid or not?
* Students: No.
* Shaykh: It is not valid, because 'Isa will not descend as a lawgiver. Rather, he will descend as a follower of the Messenger ﷺ, and will not originate anything, nor any part of the law. Even breaking the cross and killing the pig: the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, informed of this and affirmed it. That is, it is said that he will come and judge by that, and accept nothing but Islam. There will be no jizyah (poll tax) after the descent of 'Isa, no taking of jizyah and no covenant; there will be nothing but Islam.[[Al-Bukhari (2476) and Muslim (155/242), the wording of Muslim, from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, the son of Maryam will surely soon descend among you as a just judge. He will break the cross, kill the pig, abolish the jizyah, and wealth will overflow until no one accepts it."]] It is said: this is not a new law abrogating the law of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, but rather a law established by the Messenger ﷺ. The Messenger informed that he would do this, affirming it. So he did not descend as a messenger with a new law, but as a follower of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him. Perhaps this, and Allah knows best, is so that what Allah has informed of may actually come to pass: ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of the prophets: Whatever I have given you of Scripture and wisdom, then there comes to you a messenger confirming what is with you, you shall believe in him and you shall support him. He said: Do you affirm and accept My covenant on that condition? They said: We affirm it. He said: Then bear witness, and I am with you among the witnesses﴾ [Al 'Imran 81]. This is a report from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. But have we known that a prophet actually followed the Messenger? No. But the descent of 'Isa and his following of the message of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, will be the certainty of certainty (*haqq al-yaqin*), because the verse of Al 'Imran contains knowledge of certainty (*'ilm al-yaqin*). When that occurs in reality, it becomes haqq al-yaqin. This is part of the wisdom of his descent ﷺ at the end of time.

Also, we have clear, authentic, explicit hadiths, received with acceptance by the people of knowledge. How can one deny them? But, and Allah forbid, some people come with a principle that is among the most corrupt and invalid principles: that belief (*'aqidah*) is not established by single-transmitted reports (*akhbar al-ahad*), even if the report is authentic. In reality this is a slip on the part of the one who says it. For we say to him: you establish practical rulings on the basis of evidence that does not reach the level of authenticity; you establish a practical ruling on evidence that reaches the level of goodness (*husn*), and perhaps it reaches the level of goodness for you and for others, but not for others. Establishing a practical ruling necessarily entails belief, because implementing it is a requirement of faith, and because a person does not act upon it unless he believes that it is from the law of Allah. Otherwise he would not act upon it. So there is a prior belief that this is from the judgment of Allah and from the law of Allah, that it brings one closer to Allah, and that it is an act of worship to Allah, and then he acts upon it.

Then what is this?! If we adopt that view, we would have to deny many things related to scientific matters, because the Shari'ah, as you know, consists either of matters of belief ('ilmiyyah) or matters of practice ('amaliyyah). The correct position, without doubt, is that there is no difference between them, and that whatever has been authentically reported from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) must be affirmed, both in belief and in practice. If you want further clarification, read what Ibn al-Qayyim (may Allah have mercy on him) wrote at the end of al-Sawa'iq al-Mursalah, for he discussed this issue at sufficient length.
* A student: Shaykh, it is mutawatir.
* The Shaykh: By Allah, I do not know whether it reaches the level of tawatur or not.
* A student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: If it is mutawatir, then it gives certain knowledge, and no one (...).
* A student: Regarding the descent of 'Isa ibn Maryam (...), does Allah, glorified and exalted, inspire him with what is right in (...)?
* The Shaykh: Apparently, and Allah knows best, because the Qur'an and the Sunnah are preserved until that time. It is remarkable that some people have mentioned among the doubts about his descent the claim: "'Isa's language is Syriac, and the language of the Messenger (ﷺ) is Arabic. How can he descend and judge by the Shari'ah while he speaks Syriac?" Is this a doubt or not?
* A student: No.
* The Shaykh: What is the answer? We say: Yes, the answer is by acceptance (...). First: there are people now who speak the Arabic language and are Muslims committed to the rulings of Islam, upholding it in the most complete manner, while their language is not Arabic. Second: Allah is over all things capable. His language may become Arabic; when a person is practiced and in contact with a people, his tongue changes from Syriac to Arabic. How much more so by the power of Allah! But, glory be to Allah the Mighty, when a person desires something, he brings forth a semblance that deceives no one (...).
* * *
Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿And We had certainly sent messengers before you to their peoples, and they came to them with clear proofs. Then We took vengeance upon those who committed crime, and it was incumbent upon Us to aid the believers.﴾ [al-Rum 47]. Have we taken its benefits? What are they?
* A student: (...) warning those who oppose him (...).
That the previous messages were specific (...).
That Allah has obligated Himself to aid the believers, and it must come to pass, while those who are not believers are not aided.
(...) sometimes, and it (...).
* The Shaykh: There is also a benefit in it.
* Among the benefits of the verse also: that Allah has a right which He made incumbent upon Himself, due to His saying: ﴿وَكَانَ حَقًّا عَلَيْنَا﴾ (and it was a right upon Us). So if we say: Is anything obligatory upon Allah? We say: As for our intellects, nothing is obligatory upon Allah; but that He makes something obligatory upon Himself is a established reality.
* And among its benefits also: the virtue of faith and that it is a cause of victory; ﴿وَكَانَ حَقًّا عَلَيْنَا نَصْرُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 30, verse 44–47 (part 1 of 5):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Whoever disbelieves, upon him is his disbelief﴾ [Ar-Rum 44]. The author says: (The burden of his disbelief, which is the Fire). This is like an elaboration of His saying: ﴿they will be separated﴾, because "yusaddaʿun" means they will be scattered according to their deeds. As for His saying: ﴿Whoever disbelieves﴾, let us look at the grammar: ﴿man﴾ (whoever) is a conditional particle, the conditional verb is "kafara" (disbelieves), and its response is the clause "fa-ʿalayhi kufruhu" (upon him is his disbelief). His saying: ﴿fa-ʿalayhi kufruhu﴾ is a declarative clause made up of a subject and a predicate. The subject is ﴿kufruhu﴾ (his disbelief), and the predicate is ﴿ʿalayhi﴾ (upon him), which has been placed first. The benefit of placing it first is restriction (ḥaṣr).
﴿And whoever does righteousness – for themselves they prepare [the way]﴾ [Ar-Rum 44]. It is similarly conditional, and the response of the condition is His saying: ﴿fa-li-anfusihim yamhadun﴾ (for themselves they prepare [the way]). The object, which is (li-anfusihim yamhadun, "for themselves they prepare"), has been placed first for restriction, which is a semantic benefit, and for the sake of matching the rhyming endings (fawasil), which is a verbal benefit; for if he had said "yamhadun li-anfusihim" the sentence would have been sound, but he placed it first for these two benefits.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Whoever disbelieves, upon him is his disbelief﴾. Yes, meaning: any person who disbelieves, the burden of his disbelief falls upon him; it harms only himself. Does it fall upon others? No, it does not fall upon others unless that other person was the cause of it. If he was the cause of it, he bears a burden like its burden. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿That they may bear their burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection, and of the burdens of those whom they mislead without knowledge. Unquestionably, evil is that which they bear﴾ [An-Nahl 25], and He the Exalted says: ﴿And they will surely bear their burdens and additional burdens along with their own burdens﴾ [Al-ʿAnkabut 13]. And it is established from the Prophet ﷺ that: «Whoever establishes an evil practice in Islam, upon him is its burden and the burden of whoever acts upon it until the Day of Resurrection»[[Narrated by Muslim (1017/69) from the hadith of Jarir ibn ʿAbdullah.]].
If it is said: Does this contradict the verse ﴿Whoever disbelieves, upon him is his disbelief﴾ [Ar-Rum 44]?
The answer: It does not contradict it, because when he is the cause, that is from his own deed. But the reality of the matter is different: it is the deed of another and his own deed; in reality, the one who points to disbelief is a doer of that for which he bears the burden.
He says: ﴿And whoever does righteousness – for themselves they prepare [the way]﴾ [Ar-Rum 44] (they level their dwellings in Paradise). "Whoever does righteousness": disbelief (kufr) in the Arabic language means concealment, and from it comes "al-kafrā," which is the sheath of the date-palm spathe (ṭalʿ), and which in our colloquial language is called al-kafūr; it is the sheath of the palm spathe, which covers the spathe. So kufr in origin is this, and what is intended by it is departing from obedience to Allah, because one who departs from obedience to Allah has concealed what Allah has bestowed upon him of intellect, knowledge and the like.
As for His saying: ﴿And whoever does righteousness﴾, the people of knowledge said: righteous deed is that which combines two fundamental conditions: the first is sincerity (ikhlas), and the second is following the Messenger ﷺ. And what is the opposite of sincerity? Its opposite is shirk; and the opposite of following is innovation (ibtidaʿ). For example, if we find a man who prays the usual prayer but does it to show off to people, his deed is not righteous. What is lacking in it? Sincerity. And if we find a man who has introduced a type of worship for which the Sharia did not come, but he is sincere, seeking thereby the face of Allah, and you find him humble, weeping and moved by this worship, yet it is not in accordance with the Law of Allah, then his worship is invalid, because it lacks following the Messenger ﷺ. Among this is the case where one takes a legislated act of worship out of the form in which it was legislated; it is a legislated act in origin, but he has removed it from what it was upon, and his deed is not accepted. As if he prays the prayer after its time has passed, deliberately and without excuse; is this accepted from him?
* Students: No.
* The Shaykh: Why? Because there is no following in it. He is sincere, but he does not follow. Likewise, if he prays a prayer without tranquility (ṭumaʾnina), if he prays a prayer in which he does not settle; if he says "Allah hears the one who praises Him" and immediately prostrates, or when he rises from prostration and immediately prostrates a second time, his prayer is invalid. Even if he prays until the Day of Judgment, Allah would not accept it from him. Why? Because of the lack of following. For this reason, when a man prayed without settling in it, the Prophet ﷺ said to him: «Return and pray, for you have not prayed»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (757) and Muslim (397/45) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]], so he negated the act because its validity was absent; otherwise he is now a person who prays, but it is not a prayer.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. If you asked him: Why did you pray? He would say: I prayed only for Allah, but he opposed the command of Allah.
* A student: Does this not negate sincerity?
* The Shaykh: No, it does not negate sincerity. Sincerity is in the heart; he did not stand to pray for the sake of people, he did not care whether people say he prayed or did not pray. He prayed for Allah, but he opposed the command of Allah.
* A student: Is it necessary that the one praying understands what he recites?
* The Shaykh: No, it is not required, it is not obligatory; but it is better that he understands what he says if his heart is present, meaning humble and attentive in his prayer; that is better.
* A student: And is the one whose heart is humble now humbled by things outside the prayer?
* The Shaykh: What do you mean?
* A student: For example, while praying he reflects on... 
* The Shaykh: No, he should not be humbled by matters outside the prayer; that is, he should be mindful of what he says in his prayer and what he does in his prayer, not that he goes off remembering a sitting in which he was humble in the past.
* A student: No, for example, he remembers graves, Paradise and Hell.
* The Shaykh: Yes, that is not valid unless it passes through him, for example, during his recitation.
He says: ﴿And whoever does righteousness﴾. So what is righteous deed? It is that which combines two conditions: sincerity to Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, and following the Messenger ﷺ.
﴿fa-li-anfusihim yamhadun﴾: "mahd" and "tamhid" mean preparation (tawṭiʾa), and from it their saying: "This is a paved (mumahhad) road," meaning: prepared and smoothed so that feet may tread upon it. So the meaning of ﴿yamhadun﴾ is: they make things good so that they become prepared for them; this is because those who do righteousness reach Paradise through their righteous deeds, so the path that leads them to it is made easy for them.
His saying: ﴿fa-li-anfusihim yamhadun﴾: placing the object first indicates restriction. If someone says: Does this contradict the hadith in which «Whoever establishes a good practice in Islam, for him is its reward and the reward of whoever acts upon it until the Day of Resurrection»[[Narrated by Muslim (1017/69) from the hadith of Jarir ibn ʿAbdullah.]]? We say: It does not contradict it, because those who do good establish good practices. Did they act or not? They acted, so others followed them in it; the reward that comes to them from others' following them is in reality from their own deed. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿That He may reward those who believed and did righteous deeds from His bounty﴾ [Ar-Rum 45].
He says: (related to "yusaddaʿun"). You always see the scholars, when an adverbial phrase (ẓarf) or a prepositional phrase (jarr and majrur) occurs, they say: "related to such-and-such" (mutaʿallaq). What does "related to" mean? It means that this is the thing it operates upon, because the prepositional phrase and the adverbial phrase function like the direct object, and the direct object must have a governing element that acts upon it. So when he says "related to such-and-such," it means that this is what it operates on. Every prepositional or adverbial phrase must have something it relates to:
"There must be for the preposition a relation / to a verb or its meaning, like 'murtaqi' (climbing)."
So the meaning of his saying "(related to yusaddaʿun)" is that the governing element in the word (li-yajziya) is His saying ﴿yusaddaʿun﴾, and this is the opinion of the author.
It may also be related to His saying ﴿yaʾtiya﴾: ﴿before there comes a Day for which there is no repelling from Allah﴾, ﴿that He may reward those who believed and did righteous deeds﴾, because the scattering in reality is the very recompense, so how could a thing be the cause of itself? This does not weaken the author's words; but if it is said that this Day comes for the purpose of recompense, the meaning becomes sound and clear. If we say that this "li" (li-yajziya) — since "li" is a preposition — is related to "yaʾtiya," that is clearer than saying it is related to "yusaddaʿun," because the very scattering and separation that leads to the Fire is the very recompense.
Some scholars, some grammarians, said: it is a predicate of an elided subject, so it is related to an elided predicate, and the estimate is: "That is in order that He may reward," and the referent is what preceded. This is also very well founded: that it be related to an elided predicate of an elided subject.
We have said that the "li" in (li-yajziya) is a preposition, and it is known that prepositions enter only upon nouns. It has become clear to you that among the signs of a noun is being in the genitive case, and the entry of (...) upon it. The Ajurrumiyya says: the noun is known by the genitive (khafḍ), by tanwin, by the entry of the definite article (al-) and by prepositions.
So how is it correct to say that the "li" in His saying ﴿li-yajziya﴾ is a preposition, even though it enters upon a verb? We say: because this verb is in the position of a noun, since it is a verb with an implied (an) in it; the estimate is "li-an yajziya," and "an" is a verbal particle that turns the verb into a verbal noun (maṣdar), and the verbal noun is a noun, is it not? The verbal noun is a noun. Therefore the meaning is: "for His recompense, for the recompense of those who believed and did righteous deeds," and so on. Do you understand now? When the "li" of purpose (lām al-taʿlil) enters upon a verb, an implied "an" (that) is estimated between it and the verb: "li-an yajziya." And His saying ﴿li-yajziya alladhina amanu﴾: the subject of the recompense is Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, and it is a hidden pronoun referring to Him.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, on the basis that it is in the accusative after an implied "an" after the "li": li-yajziya, and the "li" governs what follows it, on the basis that the verb will be a verbal noun.
* A student: But it is itself a preposition.
* The Shaykh: Yes, it is itself a preposition.
* A student: It is the very "lām al-taʿlil" that puts the imperfect verb in the subjunctive.
* The Shaykh: It is the very "lām al-taʿlil" which, according to the opinion of the Basrans, puts the imperfect verb in the subjunctive by means of "an" after it.
* A student: (...) the "lām al-taʿlil."
* The Shaykh: No, the "lam" is one, and the "lām al-taʿlil," just as it enters upon a verb, enters upon nouns. So if you say "I came for your honouring (li-ikramika)," it is the "lām al-taʿlil"; and "I came that I might honour you (li-ukrimaka)," it is also the "lām al-taʿlil."
His saying ﴿li-yajziya alladhina amanu﴾: "jaza'" means recompense (mukafa'a), meaning that He may reward them. ﴿li-yajziya alladhina amanu wa-ʿamilu al-ṣāliḥāt min faḍlihi﴾ — (yuthībuhum, "He will reward them") is an explanation of "jaza'" in the sense of granting reward (ithaba). "Thawab" is recompense, and it is called thawab because it comes from "thaba yathūbu," meaning to return, because it returns to the person as the recompense of his deed. His saying ﴿li-yajziya alladhina amanu wa-ʿamilu al-ṣāliḥāt﴾: pay attention to these two conditions: faith and righteous deed. Faith alone is not sufficient, and righteous deed alone is not sufficient; this applies when faith is coupled with deed.
