But the difference between them in the specific sense is that *athar* includes the genus considered as one single thing, whereas *āthār* includes the genus considered as types.

How is it considered as types? Like the trace of rain, by which crops grow, by which trees grow, by which something small and something large grow, and something that has open branches, and something that has thin trees like reeds. Therefore these are considered traces with respect to their types.

Furthermore, the traces differ from land to land. This land grows such-and-such, and that land grows such-and-such. This land produces pasture, and that land does not produce... and so on. So they are traces with respect to their types. As for with respect to the genus, and that all of it came about through the rain, it is one thing. And this is the specific difference between *athar* and *āthār*.

(﴿the traces of Allah's mercy﴾, meaning: His blessing, the rain.) We have already mentioned that mercy in such a context may be a name for the created thing, and may also be one of Allah's attributes. If the intended meaning is the direct effect, then mercy means the rain, because this vegetation grew by what? By the rain. If the intended meaning is the indirect cause, then mercy means the attribute of Allah. That is, because Allah, may He be exalted, is Merciful, this is one of the traces of mercy: that He sends down rain, by which the earth grows and drought is removed. So the verse is applicable to both meanings.

He says: ﴿how He gives life to the earth after its death﴾ [Ar-Rum 50]. This is among what favours the view that the intended meaning of mercy is the attribute, the mercy of Allah. ﴿How He gives life﴾: He, that is, by His mercy, glorified and exalted is He. ﴿gives life to the earth﴾, makes it alive, ﴿after its death﴾. The author says: (that is, its dryness). The life of everything is according to its nature. So the dry land in which there is no greenery is called dead, there is nothing living in it. When the rain falls upon it and the vegetation comes to life, it is called alive.

﴿He gives life to the earth after its death﴾. This is evidence of the power of the Lord, mighty and majestic, and of His mercy. For who is able to split the seed and the grain within the earth until this growing plant emerges from it? Can anyone do this? No one can. Therefore it has come in the authentic sacred hadith: "Let them create a grain, or let them create a barley seed" [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7559) and Muslim (2111/101), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]. They cannot; no one can create this. ﴿Indeed, Allah is the splitter of the grain and the date-pit. He brings the living out of the dead and brings the dead out of the living. That is Allah; so how are you deluded?﴾ [Al-An'am 95].

﴿How He gives life to the earth after its death﴾. ﴿How﴾ means: look at the manner and the power. How this earth, which was dusty and as if burnt, has now become a green garden! (That is, its dryness, by its growing.)

Allah, mighty and majestic, says: ﴿Indeed, that is the one who gives life to the dead﴾ [Ar-Rum 50]. ﴿Indeed, that﴾: the one referred to (...).

* * *

(...) it would be pointless. A rational human would be created, who knows, understands, and acts, and some of them kill others, and some plunder others, and some make peace with others, and the outcome is that they become dust. This is absolutely impossible. That is to say, if a person considers it even slightly, he will find that reason decisively indicates that there must be a resurrection and (...), otherwise the whole world would be pointless. ﴿We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vain. That is the assumption of those who disbelieve, so woe to those who disbelieve from the Fire﴾ [Sad 27].

Do we not, for example, see those who oppose us in action, who oppose us in morals, who oppose us in belief, and are pained by that, or not? Yes. If it were not that Allah consoles the Messenger ﷺ: ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief that they do not believe﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara 3], and similar things by which He consoles him, his heart would break over them, peace and blessings be upon him. We now feel pain for those who oppose us in belief, for those who oppose us in morals, for those who oppose us in deeds. We undoubtedly feel pain. This pain affects us. But Allah, mighty and majestic, says: ﴿If you suffer, indeed they suffer as you suffer﴾, but there is a difference: ﴿but you hope from Allah for what they do not hope﴾ [An-Nisa' 104]. So the conclusion is that this great universe cannot be pointless in this way, living and then becoming dust. Allah, mighty and majestic, gives life to the dead, not only human beings, but human beings and others. ﴿There is no creature on the earth, nor bird that flies with its two wings, but they are communities like yourselves. We have not neglected anything in the Book. Then to their Lord they will be gathered﴾ [Al-An'am 38]. ﴿And when the wild beasts are gathered﴾ [At-Takwir 5]. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, informed that the animals will be judged for the hornless one against the horned one [[Narrated by Muslim (2582/60) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]. Even the animals will have judgment passed between them. Is it clear, brothers? Therefore we say: ﴿the dead﴾ is not restricted to humans only, but includes humans and non-humans. ﴿Indeed, that is the one who gives life to the dead﴾ [Ar-Rum 50].

Then He emphasised this, the giving of life to the dead, with another emphasis: the sentence after it, His saying: ﴿And He is Able over all things﴾ [Ar-Rum 50]. So the giving of life to the dead has been emphasised with two verbal emphases and two semantic emphases.

As for His saying ﴿And He is Able over all things﴾: Allah is able over everything, everything without exception, everything to which power relates and which can be within His power. Allah, may He be exalted, is capable, Able over all things, not only over what He wills, but over what He wills and what He does not will. The guidance of the disbeliever who died in his disbelief: is Allah able over it or not?

* Students: Yes, He is able.

* The Shaykh: And did He will it? He did not will it, yet He is able over it. So His power is not restricted to what He wills. From this we know that the expression of some people, that He is able over what He wills, is not appropriate. Rather, say as Allah said about Himself: ﴿Indeed, He is Able over all things﴾ [Fussilat 39].

As for the hadith of the man whom Allah will resurrect on the Day of Resurrection, He mentioned the story, and in it Allah said to him: "Indeed, I am Able over what I will" [[Narrated by Muslim (187/310) from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud.]]. This does not mean describing Allah with power absolutely. Rather it describes Allah with power over this particular thing which the addressee considered unlikely. Allah is saying: I have willed it, so I am able over it. Likewise His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He is Able to gather them when He wills﴾ [Ash-Shura 29]. The qualifier of will here does not refer to the power, but refers to the gathering. A particular thing may be qualified by power. But if you want to describe Allah with power, do not qualify it with will. There is a difference between linking power to a specific particular thing and mentioning it as a general description of Allah. If it is a general description, then no. Allah, exalted is He, never mentioned the qualifier of will: ﴿And your Lord is ever Competent﴾ [Al-Furqan 54], ﴿And Allah is ever Competent over all things﴾ [Al-Ahzab 27], ﴿And Allah is Competent over all things﴾ [Al-Baqarah 284], and similar.

Power is the opposite of incapacity. Look at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah would never be incapacitated by anything in the heavens or on the earth. Indeed, He is ever Knowing and Competent﴾ [Fatir 44]. Knowledge is mentioned here, because the incapable may be incapable due to lack of knowledge of the thing. For example, an engineer who has rheumatism and cannot move. He is a perfect engineer. We told him: make this car. Can he? He cannot. Why? He does not have the power; he is incapable, because he cannot move. And another man who is energetic and carries a stone bigger than himself, but does not know this craft. We told him: make the car. He said: I cannot. Why? Because of lack of knowledge. So the negation of power may be due to lack of knowledge, and it may be due to lack of ability. He has no knowledge, he has nothing, meaning he is incapable.

Now, (...) the explanation of this is in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is in them, and He is Able over all things﴾, at the end of Surat al-Ma'idah [Al-Ma'idah 120]. Someone stated a objectionable phrase; he did not intend evil by it, Allah knows best. He did not intend evil when he said: (Reason has restricted His essence, so He is not able over it). (Reason has restricted His essence): that is, reason requires restricting the essence of Allah, so Allah is not able over it. Is this correct?

* A student: This is not correct.

* The Shaykh: This is not correct. Rather, Allah is Able over all things. Therefore Allah, exalted is He, established Himself upon the Throne, by His action or not? By His action and His power. He descends to the lowest heaven, He comes to judge between His servants, He speaks whatever He wills. All of this relates to His essence, and He is able over it.

If someone says: Allah is able to cause so-and-so to die; is He able to cause Himself to die?

This is not possible, not because of a lack of power, but because this is a matter that is not fitting for Him, and it is worse than incapacity. So we say: its impossibility is because it is impossible for Allah, mighty and majestic. Therefore al-Saffarini, may Allah have mercy on him, in his creed, when he mentioned the attribute of power, said:

*By a power that relates to the possible* ***...*** 

As for the impossible, it is impossible; the impossible is essentially something that power does not relate to. It is said that when a scholar dies, Satan rejoices greatly, and when worshippers die, it does not concern him. His soldiers said to him: How do you rejoice so greatly at the death of this scholar, and not rejoice at the death of the worshipper who spends the whole day in his prayer niche? He said: Yes, because the scholar is more harmful to us than the worshipper. And if you wish, I will now give you an example. He went to the worshipper and said: Is Allah, mighty and majestic, able to place the heavens and the earth inside an egg? The worshipper said: No, He is not able. He said: Is Allah able to create its like? He said: ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [Ya-Sin 82]. He may be able to create its like. Is this correct?! This is not correct and not possible. Then he went to the scholar and said something similar. He said: As for creating a likeness, this is something impossible, and it is not possible for a created being to be like the Creator at all, no matter what. As for His placing the heavens and the earth inside an egg, He is Able over all things.

The poor worshipper disbelieved in two ways: he affirmed what is not possible, and he negated what is possible. And this is truly... that is, worshippers, just as Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah said: "Whoever among our worshippers becomes corrupt has some resemblance to the Christians, and whoever among our scholars becomes corrupt has some resemblance to the Jews" [[See al-Fatawa al-Kubra of Ibn Taymiyyah (2/142).]]. The Jews are undoubtedly more wicked than the Christians, because the corruption of the scholar, may Allah protect us, is from knowledge, and the corruption of the worshipper is from ignorance, and what comes from ignorance is less severe than what comes from knowledge.

* A student: Regarding the saying of the one who said: He is Able over what He wills. Can we not derive a rule that the essential attributes (...) the active attributes (...) will in general?

* The Shaykh: (...). Their rule is that the essential attributes are those necessarily belonging to the essence, and the active ones are those related to the will. This is their rule.

* A student: Regarding the sending down (*tanzil*) and the causing to descend (*inzal*) in the Qur'an, how is this answered?

* The Shaykh: Which verse?

* A student: In the Qur'an itself, it is stated that He sent it down, and He said: "a revelation (*tanzil*)." What is the difference?

* The Shaykh: When it is stated that He sent it down, like: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree﴾ [Al-Qadr 1], the intended meaning is the beginning of its sending down. That is, We sent down the whole of it at once, not all of it in parts. As for *tanzil*, it is considered with respect to its entirety, being sent down gradually, as in His saying: ﴿And a Qur'an We have separated so that you may recite it to the people over time, and We have sent it down in stages﴾ [Al-Isra' 106]. Although *tanzil* may also come for something that occurred all at once, like His saying: ﴿And it has already come down to you in the Book that when you hear the verses of Allah being denied and ridiculed, do not sit with them﴾ [An-Nisa' 140]. So based on this, the rule that the scholars mentioned on this matter is a general rule, not a necessary one.

* * *

﴿It is Allah who sends the winds, and they stir up clouds, and He spreads them across the sky however He wills﴾ [Ar-Rum 48], and so on to the end.

* The following benefits are derived from this noble verse:

* First: the perfection of Allah's power, glorified and exalted is He, by sending the winds, stirring the clouds, spreading them in the sky, making them into fragments, and the rain descending from them. Yes, how many aspects is this? The perfection of Allah's power is derived from several aspects: first, the sending of the winds, the stirring of the clouds, their spreading in the sky, their making into fragments, the rain descending from them; that is five aspects.

* Also among the benefits of this noble verse: the word "sky" is applied to everything that is high, because of His saying: ﴿and spreads them in the sky﴾. For they are not spread in the sky that is the protected ceiling, but they are spread in the high atmosphere.

* And among its benefits: the wisdom of Allah, mighty and majestic, in sending the rain down from above, because when it descends from above it reaches both the low and the high, whereas if it flowed along the ground, it would flood what is low before reaching what is high.

* And among the benefits of this noble verse: showing the extent of the creation's need for Allah's mercy, because of His saying: ﴿then when He causes it to strike whom He wills of His servants﴾.

* And among them: the affirmation of will, because of His saying: ﴿whom He wills﴾.

* And among them: the affirmation of general servitude, because of His saying: ﴿of His servants﴾.

* And among them, and let us see whether this benefit is appropriate or not: the permissibility of rejoicing in the rain, and that people may give each other the good news of it. Or is that not possible? The main question is whether it can be derived that rejoicing in the rain is permissible, or whether it is said that this is a report of an actual event, so no ruling can be derived from it. There is a possibility that permissibility of rejoicing in the rain can be derived from it, and there is a possibility that this is merely an explanation of the reality, so no ruling is derived from it. At most it can be said that it is permissible, because Allah, exalted is He, mentioned it and did not disapprove of it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 30, verse 48–50 (part 3 of 3):

* Among the benefits of the verse: it shows the mercy of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in that rain descends in drops and not all at once; this is from His saying: ﴿then you see the rain coming out from within it﴾. For if it descended like the mouths of waterskins, or like torrents that flow, what would happen? It would destroy the homes, destroy the trees, and harm the animals upon whom it falls. But Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, made it this fine drizzle.
Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And even though they were, before it was sent down upon them, before it, certainly in despair﴾ [ar-Rum 49].
* In this: an explanation of the state of the servant before the rain falls, and that the servant is weak; this is from His saying: ﴿in despair﴾, for he is weak. When he is afflicted with something, he despairs and considers relief far off. But Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, removes this condition from him. He said: ﴿And even though they were, before it was sent down upon them, before it, certainly in despair﴾. Fine, from where is this taken? From His saying: ﴿And even though they were, before it was sent down upon them, before it, certainly in despair﴾.
Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿So look at the effects of the mercy of Allah, how He gives life to the earth after its death﴾ [ar-Rum 50]. In this verse is the command to look, which may be with the eye that sees, and with the eye of insight as well; so the command here is to look in both respects together. A person looks with his seeing eye and with the eye of insight.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: just as looking is beneficial to a person, it is commanded by the Sharia; that is, the person is rewarded, or given reward, for looking at the signs of Allah, because it is commanded.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse also: all the effects that result from the rain are from the mercy of Allah; the giving of life to the earth with plants and the abundance of water in it, all of it is from the mercy of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: affirming the power of Allah, the Exalted, to give life to the dead; this is from His saying: ﴿Indeed, that is the one who gives life to the dead﴾.
* Among its benefits: reasoning from the perceptible seen to the perceptible awaited. How? The perceptible seen is what occurs of the life of the earth, and the perceptible awaited is what occurs of the resurrection of the dead.
* Among them: that the proof must be clearer and more manifest than what it proves; meaning, it is not possible for us to reason from the hidden to the more manifest and clearer; for the proof makes the thing proved known and explains it. How then can you reason from something hidden to something clear?! Is that not so?
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: * Among the benefits of the noble verse: the mercy of Allah, the Exalted, toward His servants, in that He sets forth examples for them and explains the proofs so that they may reach certainty regarding what must be believed. For it would suffice that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, say: Believe that I give life to the dead; that would suffice to establish the proof against them. But out of His mercy He explains to us and sets forth examples for us so that we reach the level of certainty regarding what He has informed us. From where do we take this? From His saying: ﴿So look at the effects of the mercy of Allah, how He gives life to the earth after its death; indeed, that is the one who gives life to the dead﴾.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the blessing of Allah upon the servants in giving life to the earth; this is from His saying: ﴿So look at the effects of the mercy of Allah, how He gives life to the earth after its death﴾.
* Among them: that inanimate matter is described as living and dead. In this is a refutation of the philosophers who say that inanimate matter cannot be described as living or dead because it is not capable of them. We say: Allah, the Exalted, described inanimate matter as living and dead, as in this verse, and as in His saying: ﴿And those they call upon besides Allah create nothing, and they are created. (20) They are dead, not alive﴾ [an-Nahl 20, 21], even though they are idols made of stones, trees, and the like.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the establishment of the attribute of power and its comprehensiveness; this is from His saying: ﴿And He is over all things Competent﴾; nothing overcomes Him in the heavens or on the earth.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 30, verse 48–50 (part 1 of 3):

Then He said: ﴿It is Allah Who sends the winds, so they stir up clouds﴾ [Ar-Rum 48]. The author said: (He drives them), because it is derived from: athāra al-ṣayd (he roused the game), if he startled it.
﴿It is Allah Who sends the winds﴾ means: He dispatches them however He wills, glorified and exalted is He.
﴿so they stir up clouds﴾. The author said: so (He drives it), like the stirring up of game, for stirring up game from its place means startling it until it rises.
And His saying: ﴿clouds﴾. Al-sahāb is the known thing; it is the cloud.
﴿then He spreads them across the sky however He wills﴾ (in few or in many). ﴿Then He spreads them﴾: al-basṭ means al-nashr (spreading out). ﴿however He wills﴾ refers to the manner of this spreading; it may be wide, it may be sparse, it may be dense, it may be thin. For this reason He said (﴿and He makes it fragments﴾, with the sīn vowelled and with it unvowelled: scattered pieces). With the sīn vowelled, it is ﴿kisafan﴾; with it unvowelled, it is ﴿kisfan﴾. Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿And if they should see a fragment of the sky falling, they would say, "Layered clouds."﴾ [At-Tur 44] ﴿kisfan﴾. Al-kisaf means the pieces. It seems that the author, may Allah have mercy on him, wants to make clear that the cloud may be wide, spread out and extended, and it may be few, in scattered pieces.
Some of the exegetes said: the meaning of its being ﴿kisafan﴾ is that they are pieces piled one upon another until it turns black and dark, and thunder and lightning occur within it. This is more correct, that what is meant by al-kisaf is the pieces piled upon one another until they become dark and black, and this is generally more abundant in rain.
He says: ﴿and He makes it fragments, then you see the rain coming out from within it﴾. ﴿then you see﴾: the address is to everyone who can be addressed, because this seeing is not specific to the Messenger ﷺ.
And His saying: ﴿al-wadq﴾ means (the rain); that is, the drops of rain are called wadq.
﴿coming out from within it﴾ (i.e., from its midst), and it was said: from between it; from between this cloud.
And His saying: ﴿then you see the rain﴾. If someone says: we do not see it with our naked eyes, we do not see the rain penetrating this cloud (...).
It is said: it is a true report, so what is the result? It is as if witnessed; since Allah the Exalted has informed of it, it is as though we are witnessing it with our own eyes. Moreover, in the present time there have been developed powerful instruments by which a person can see how this rain comes out, these droplets, from within the cloud.
And His saying: ﴿So when He causes it [the rain] to fall upon whom He wills of His servants, behold, they rejoice﴾. This is a conditional sentence: ﴿when He causes it to fall﴾ (idhā) indicates that those who are struck by the rain are in extreme longing for it, and for this reason, the moment it strikes them, joy occurs. Our saying "the moment" is not a result of the consequent of the condition following the condition itself, but a result of that plus another matter, namely the use of the sudden idhā which indicates suddenness and speed. So idhā conveys the condition, the verb of the condition is ﴿asāba﴾, and the consequent of the condition is the clause ﴿they rejoice﴾, introduced by the sudden idhā.
We said: this expression indicates that these people are at the utmost of longing for the descent of the rain; the proof of that is their rejoicing at the very moment of being struck, and it is not ordinary rejoicing as the consequence following the condition, but it is more emphatic because it uses the sudden idhā, which indicates the immediacy of the occurrence of that thing.
And His saying: ﴿they rejoice﴾. The author said: (they are glad about the rain), and istibshār is more intense than mere joy; rejoicing (istibshār) is more intense than mere joy, rather one rejoices in oneself and perhaps congratulates and gives glad tidings to others. For this reason, in the rainy season, during the season of rain, you find for example that when people meet one another, especially those who come from the deserts, one says: "I give you good news, rain has fallen, and it is abundant," or as is the case. So istibshār here is more emphatic than mere joy, but the author, may Allah have mercy on him, sometimes explains it approximately.
And His saying: ﴿So when He causes it to fall upon whom He wills of His servants﴾: ﴿whom He wills﴾, not whom people will. The one who sends down the rain is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; no one can send it down. As for what is mentioned, that they now spray chemical materials upon the clouds so that rain falls, we say: if this is true, then who created this rain? Allah, glorified and exalted is He, and the One who brought this cloud into being is Allah, glorified and exalted is He. Their arriving at means by which this cloud evaporates until it falls as rain does not negate that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is the One who sends down the rain. Moreover, the verse ﴿He sends down the rain (al-ghayth)﴾ [Ash-Shura 28] is more eloquent than "He sends down the rain (al-matar)", since rain may fall without being al-ghayth; as is established in Sahih Muslim[[(2904/44) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]: "Drought (al-sanah) is not that you are not given rain; rather, drought is that you are given rain but the earth does not produce vegetation." (Al-sanah): what does it mean? Dearth and famine; that is, it is not merely that rain does not come; true drought is that it comes but no vegetation results.
And His saying: ﴿So when He causes it to fall upon whom He wills of His servants﴾. Here the word ʿibād means the plural of ʿabd; is this the special servitude or the general servitude? The general, why? Because the rain falls upon believers and disbelievers alike. Yes, indeed, its falling upon disbelievers may be even more abundant, more copious and more persistent, as a trial for them, so that their good things are hastened to them in their worldly life, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And on the Day the disbelievers are exposed to the Fire: "You have used up your good things in your worldly life and enjoyed them"﴾, that is, these good things, ﴿so today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation﴾ [Al-Ahqaf 20], and so on to its end.
Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And indeed, they were﴾ [Ar-Rum 49]. The author said: (qad ﴿kānū﴾), (qad): he estimated ʾin as qad, and in this he followed al-Baghawi; the author (al-Jalalayn) derived from al-Baghawi, that is, as if it were an abridgement of it; for if you reflect upon his tafsir, may Allah have mercy on him, you will find that it is precisely the tafsir of al-Baghawi, but al-Baghawi is expanded and this is abridged.
He said: (﴿in﴾ is qad). None of the grammarians said this, except if he meant it only by way of interpretation. The correct view, about which there is no doubt, is that ﴿in﴾ here is the light (mukhaffafah) form of the heavy (thaqīlah) one, as in the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And indeed, they were before that in clear error﴾ [Al Imran 164]. On this basis we say: its origin was (inna), which was lightened, and where is its noun?
* Students: The pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-shaʾn).
* The Shaykh: The pronoun of the matter; its noun is an omitted pronoun of the matter, and the estimate is: "and indeed they". We have previously mentioned that the correct view among the grammarians' opinions is that the pronoun of the matter is not estimated as singular masculine, but is estimated according to the context: if the context requires feminine, it is feminine; if it requires masculine, it is masculine; if it requires plural, it is plural; if it requires dual, it is dual.[[The correct view is that the pronoun of the matter varies in masculine and feminine according to context, but it is not made dual or plural. See Hashiyat al-Sabban ʿala al-Ashmuni (1/370).]] So its origin is: "and indeed they were." But (inna) was lightened, so its noun was omitted as the pronoun of the matter.
﴿And indeed they were, before it was sent down upon them﴾ [Ar-Rum 49]: ﴿before it was sent down upon them﴾: what? The rain.
How do we know that it is the rain? Has the sending down of rain been mentioned before? The answer: yes, in His saying: ﴿you see the rain coming out from within it﴾; for when the rain comes out from within the cloud, where does it go? It descends to the earth.
And His saying: ﴿before it was sent down upon them﴾: Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, expresses the descent of rain as inzāl and tanzīl; this is because the rain sometimes comes all at once in abundance and heavy flow, so it is inzāl; and sometimes it comes gradually, weak and intermittent, so it is called tanzīl, because tanzīl means sending down a thing little by little. ﴿before it was sent down upon them, before it, they were despairing﴾.
* A student: Regarding (...) tanzīl and inzāl (...) considering the rain as a whole, we say "nazala", considering its individual parts...
* The Shaykh: No, it is anzala.
* Student: Considering its individual parts...
* The Shaykh: No, considering the abundance and the dispersion.
* Student: (...) this cloud at the time, and after days...
* The Shaykh: After days it comes; then it also comes sometimes in small amounts; for example, the rain may last two days, three, but it is little, and sometimes it comes, as you witness, great clouds as if they were the mouths of waterskins.
And His saying: ﴿before it, [before it was sent down upon them]﴾: the word ﴿min qablihi﴾ has been differed over by the scholars. Some of them said, as the author said, that it is (emphasis); like His saying: ﴿So do not think them to be in an escape from the punishment, and for them is a painful punishment﴾; ﴿Do not think that those who rejoice in what they have done and love to be praised for what they did not do — do not think them to be in an escape from the punishment﴾ [Al Imran 188]: He repeated the verb for emphasis. This is one view, and it is what the author followed, and it is the view of most exegetes, that His saying ﴿min qablihi﴾ means: before it was sent down upon them; so it is as if He said: "And indeed they were before it was sent down upon them, before it was sent down upon them, despairing," so its repetition is for emphasis.
Some of the exegetes said: it was repeated for establishing new meaning (taʾsīs), not for emphasis. It is known that when speech is between being emphatic (tawkīd) and being establishing (taʾsīs), the default is taʾsīs; that is, the default is no emphasis, because emphasis is repetition and the default is no repetition; so some exegetes hold that it is not for emphasis but for establishing. Take care of the difference (...) the scholars, may Allah have mercy on them: the difference between tawkīd and taʾsīs is that tawkīd means this is the first, and taʾsīs means this is other than the first, and it is an independent statement.
On the view that it is taʾsīs, what does it mean? Some said: ﴿min qablihi﴾ means: before the joy; "and indeed they were, before it was sent down upon them, before the joy, despairing," so Allah mentioned for them two states, before the joy and after it. Do you understand? This is what Abu al-Suʿud followed, and it is good and has no difficulty in terms of conception and meaning; (...) the meaning: and indeed they were, before the descent of the rain, before that joy, despairing, so Allah alerted them to their state before the joy, which is despair, and to their state after that.
Some said: ﴿min qablihi﴾ means: before the before, "before it was sent down upon them"; ﴿min qablihi﴾ means: "and indeed they were, before it was sent down upon them, before that before," so the pronoun in ﴿min qablihi﴾ does not refer to the rain nor to the joy, but they make it refer to the "before", so the meaning on this is: "And indeed they were, before it was sent down upon them, before that before, despairing," so its benefit is that despair was continuous with them since ancient times: a season comes in which no rain falls and they despair, then another season comes and they despair, then another season comes and they despair... and so on. It is known that when seasons repeat without rain, the despair is more intense, so the meaning is that this joy came after despair twice or more. This also was mentioned by Ibn Kathir, may Allah have mercy on him, in his tafsir. So we have in ﴿min qablihi﴾ how many views? Three views:
The first view: it is emphasis.
The second: the pronoun refers to the joy.
The third: the pronoun refers to the "before"; i.e., "and indeed they were, before it was sent down upon them, before that before as well, despairing."

As for His saying ﴿mublisīn﴾: it is in the accusative as the predicate of (kāna). Where is (kāna)? ﴿And indeed they were﴾. The lām was attached to it because of ﴿in﴾. Is the attachment here obligatory or permissible?
* Student: No, obligatory.
* Another student: No, permissible.
* The Shaykh: No, permissible, and not obligatory.
* Student: No, permissible.
* The Shaykh: You said "no, permissible", and this one says "no, obligatory." No, it is obligatory; no, it is permissible.
* Student: Obligatory.
* The Shaykh: Good, what is the reason for the obligation?
* Student: The lightened form of the heavy one must be accompanied by the lām.
* The Shaykh: It must be accompanied by the lām?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: And what is the basis for permissibility?
* Student: The basis for permissibility is that (in) resembles (...), it is obligatory for (inna) lightened to be accompanied when it resembles (mā).
* The Shaykh: From where do you know that from the words of Ibn Malik?
* Student: From his saying:
"And inna was lightened, so its action became rare, and the lām is obligatory when it is left unused. And sometimes it is dispensed with, if the speaker's intended meaning is clear from context."
* The Shaykh: And what do you say about this argument? Now, if we drop it, would (in) lightened not resemble (in) the negating (in)? That is, if it were: "and they were not, before it was sent down upon them, despairing"? It would resemble; that is, they rejoice though they had not despaired nor been in despair before. This may occur, that they rejoice even though they had no despair before. So the apparent view is obligation, not for the reason he mentioned; for he thought that attachment is obligatory absolutely, but it is obligatory because it may resemble the negating (in); but if it does not resemble, then attachment is not obligatory.
Is there evidence from the grammar for this? Yes, the saying of the poet:
"...................... And indeed Malik were noble of origins"
He boasts of being from the Banu Malik and then says: "And indeed Malik were noble of origins." Here (in) cannot be confused with (mā); why? Because he cannot boast of a people whose nobility of origin is denied. Or not? If you say: "I am, for example, from a tribe; this tribe was not noble of origin" — is that suitable? It does not fit.
The conclusion is that the lām here is for emphasis, and some scholars call it: the lām of distinction (lām al-farq), the distinguishing lām; this is more precise in expression, and though it is distinguishing, it conveys emphasis. They named it the distinguishing lām because it distinguishes the negating (in) from the lightened (in).
Good. If someone asks: can it be attached with the lām while (in) means negation?
The answer: no, and this is the secret of why it is distinguishing; the lām cannot be attached to it, because the lām conveys emphasis of affirmation, while negation is the opposite; negation conveys negation.
He said: ﴿mublisīn﴾; he says: (despairing of its descent). Iblās is like qunūt, the utmost despair; and from it Iblis was named, we seek refuge in Allah from him, because he is ublis, despairing of the mercy of Allah. ﴿And indeed they were, before it was sent down upon them, before it, despairing of its descent.﴾
﴿So look at the traces of the mercy of Allah﴾ [Ar-Rum 50]: ﴿look﴾, the address is to whom?
* Student: To the Messenger.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 30, verses 48–50 (part 2 of 3):

* The Shaykh: "For mankind," no. "Not for the Messenger." The address is to mankind, to whoever can be addressed, the Messenger ﷺ and others. This is because He said in the first verse: ﴿then you see the rain come out from within it﴾. Then He says here: ﴿So look﴾, meaning: look, O human being, ﴿at the traces of Allah's mercy﴾. And in another reading, the author says: ﴿at the traces of Allah's mercy﴾ (plural, *āthār*). Look at the 'Uthmanic script. One of the benefits of its consistency is that it does not change with the variant readings (qira'at). ﴿Āthār﴾ (plural): how would it be written according to the rules of modern orthography? With an alif between the thā' and the rā'. But according to the rules of the 'Uthmanic Mushaf, is an alif written in it? No. (*Athar*) is thā' and rā'. So the form *āthār* is valid, and the form *athar* is valid.

And His saying ﴿ilā āthār﴾ and ﴿ilā athar﴾ do not differ in general in meaning, because *āthār* is a construct (*muḍāf*) and so conveys generality, and *athar* is a construct and so conveys generality, since a singular noun when made a construct conveys generality. So *athar* and *āthār* are, in general, no different. This is because ﴿athar raḥmat Allāh﴾ means the same as *āthār*. But the difference between them in the specific sense is that *athar* includes the genus considered as one single thing, whereas *āthār* includes the genus considered as types.

How is it considered as types? Like the trace of rain, by which crops grow, by which trees grow, by which something small and something large grow, and something that has open branches, and something that has thin trees like reeds. Therefore these are considered traces with respect to their types.

Furthermore, the traces differ from land to land. This land grows such-and-such, and that land grows such-and-such. This land produces pasture, and that land does not produce... and so on. So they are traces with respect to their types. As for with respect to the genus, and that all of it came about through the rain, it is one thing. And this is the specific difference between *athar* and *āthār*.

(﴿the traces of Allah's mercy﴾, meaning: His blessing, the rain.) We have already mentioned that mercy in such a context may be a name for the created thing, and may also be one of Allah's attributes. If the intended meaning is the direct effect, then mercy means the rain, because this vegetation grew by what? By the rain. If the intended meaning is the indirect cause, then mercy means the attribute of Allah. That is, because Allah, may He be exalted, is Merciful, this is one of the traces of mercy: that He sends down rain, by which the earth grows and drought is removed. So the verse is applicable to both meanings.

He says: ﴿how He gives life to the earth after its death﴾ [Ar-Rum 50]. This is among what favours the view that the intended meaning of mercy is the attribute, the mercy of Allah. ﴿How He gives life﴾: He, that is, by His mercy, glorified and exalted is He. ﴿gives life to the earth﴾, makes it alive, ﴿after its death﴾. The author says: (that is, its dryness). The life of everything is according to its nature. So the dry land in which there is no greenery is called dead, there is nothing living in it. When the rain falls upon it and the vegetation comes to life, it is called alive.

﴿He gives life to the earth after its death﴾. This is evidence of the power of the Lord, mighty and majestic, and of His mercy. For who is able to split the seed and the grain within the earth until this growing plant emerges from it? Can anyone do this? No one can. Therefore it has come in the authentic sacred hadith: "Let them create a grain, or let them create a barley seed" [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7559) and Muslim (2111/101), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]. They cannot; no one can create this. ﴿Indeed, Allah is the splitter of the grain and the date-pit. He brings the living out of the dead and brings the dead out of the living. That is Allah; so how are you deluded?﴾ [Al-An'am 95].

﴿How He gives life to the earth after its death﴾. ﴿How﴾ means: look at the manner and the power. How this earth, which was dusty and as if burnt, has now become a green garden! (That is, its dryness, by its growing.)

Allah, mighty and majestic, says: ﴿Indeed, that is the one who gives life to the dead﴾ [Ar-Rum 50]. ﴿Indeed, that﴾: the one referred to (...).

* * *

(...) it would be pointless. A rational human would be created, who knows, understands, and acts, and some of them kill others, and some plunder others, and some make peace with others, and the outcome is that they become dust. This is absolutely impossible. That is to say, if a person considers it even slightly, he will find that reason decisively indicates that there must be a resurrection and (...), otherwise the whole world would be pointless. ﴿We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vain. That is the assumption of those who disbelieve, so woe to those who disbelieve from the Fire﴾ [Sad 27].

Do we not, for example, see those who oppose us in action, who oppose us in morals, who oppose us in belief, and are pained by that, or not? Yes. If it were not that Allah consoles the Messenger ﷺ: ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief that they do not believe﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara 3], and similar things by which He consoles him, his heart would break over them, peace and blessings be upon him. We now feel pain for those who oppose us in belief, for those who oppose us in morals, for those who oppose us in deeds. We undoubtedly feel pain. This pain affects us. But Allah, mighty and majestic, says: ﴿If you suffer, indeed they suffer as you suffer﴾, but there is a difference: ﴿but you hope from Allah for what they do not hope﴾ [An-Nisa' 104]. So the conclusion is that this great universe cannot be pointless in this way, living and then becoming dust. Allah, mighty and majestic, gives life to the dead, not only human beings, but human beings and others. ﴿There is no creature on the earth, nor bird that flies with its two wings, but they are communities like yourselves. We have not neglected anything in the Book. Then to their Lord they will be gathered﴾ [Al-An'am 38]. ﴿And when the wild beasts are gathered﴾ [At-Takwir 5]. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, informed that the animals will be judged for the hornless one against the horned one [[Narrated by Muslim (2582/60) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]. Even the animals will have judgment passed between them. Is it clear, brothers? Therefore we say: ﴿the dead﴾ is not restricted to humans only, but includes humans and non-humans. ﴿Indeed, that is the one who gives life to the dead﴾ [Ar-Rum 50].

Then He emphasised this, the giving of life to the dead, with another emphasis: the sentence after it, His saying: ﴿And He is Able over all things﴾ [Ar-Rum 50]. So the giving of life to the dead has been emphasised with two verbal emphases and two semantic emphases.

As for His saying ﴿And He is Able over all things﴾: Allah is able over everything, everything without exception, everything to which power relates and which can be within His power. Allah, may He be exalted, is capable, Able over all things, not only over what He wills, but over what He wills and what He does not will. The guidance of the disbeliever who died in his disbelief: is Allah able over it or not?

* Students: Yes, He is able.

* The Shaykh: And did He will it? He did not will it, yet He is able over it. So His power is not restricted to what He wills. From this we know that the expression of some people, that He is able over what He wills, is not appropriate. Rather, say as Allah said about Himself: ﴿Indeed, He is Able over all things﴾ [Fussilat 39].

As for the hadith of the man whom Allah will resurrect on the Day of Resurrection, He mentioned the story, and in it Allah said to him: "Indeed, I am Able over what I will" [[Narrated by Muslim (187/310) from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud.]]. This does not mean describing Allah with power absolutely. Rather it describes Allah with power over this particular thing which the addressee considered unlikely. Allah is saying: I have willed it, so I am able over it. Likewise His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He is Able to gather them when He wills﴾ [Ash-Shura 29]. The qualifier of will here does not refer to the power, but refers to the gathering. A particular thing may be qualified by power. But if you want to describe Allah with power, do not qualify it with will. There is a difference between linking power to a specific particular thing and mentioning it as a general description of Allah. If it is a general description, then no. Allah, exalted is He, never mentioned the qualifier of will: ﴿And your Lord is ever Competent﴾ [Al-Furqan 54], ﴿And Allah is ever Competent over all things﴾ [Al-Ahzab 27], ﴿And Allah is Competent over all things﴾ [Al-Baqarah 284], and similar.

Power is the opposite of incapacity. Look at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah would never be incapacitated by anything in the heavens or on the earth. Indeed, He is ever Knowing and Competent﴾ [Fatir 44]. Knowledge is mentioned here, because the incapable may be incapable due to lack of knowledge of the thing. For example, an engineer who has rheumatism and cannot move. He is a perfect engineer. We told him: make this car. Can he? He cannot. Why? He does not have the power; he is incapable, because he cannot move. And another man who is energetic and carries a stone bigger than himself, but does not know this craft. We told him: make the car. He said: I cannot. Why? Because of lack of knowledge. So the negation of power may be due to lack of knowledge, and it may be due to lack of ability. He has no knowledge, he has nothing, meaning he is incapable.

Now, (...) the explanation of this is in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is in them, and He is Able over all things﴾, at the end of Surat al-Ma'idah [Al-Ma'idah 120]. Someone stated a objectionable phrase; he did not intend evil by it, Allah knows best. He did not intend evil when he said: (Reason has restricted His essence, so He is not able over it). (Reason has restricted His essence): that is, reason requires restricting the essence of Allah, so Allah is not able over it. Is this correct?

* A student: This is not correct.

* The Shaykh: This is not correct. Rather, Allah is Able over all things. Therefore Allah, exalted is He, established Himself upon the Throne, by His action or not? By His action and His power. He descends to the lowest heaven, He comes to judge between His servants, He speaks whatever He wills. All of this relates to His essence, and He is able over it.

If someone says: Allah is able to cause so-and-so to die; is He able to cause Himself to die?

This is not possible, not because of a lack of power, but because this is a matter that is not fitting for Him, and it is worse than incapacity. So we say: its impossibility is because it is impossible for Allah, mighty and majestic. Therefore al-Saffarini, may Allah have mercy on him, in his creed, when he mentioned the attribute of power, said:

*By a power that relates to the possible* ***...*** 

As for the impossible, it is impossible; the impossible is essentially something that power does not relate to. It is said that when a scholar dies, Satan rejoices greatly, and when worshippers die, it does not concern him. His soldiers said to him: How do you rejoice so greatly at the death of this scholar, and not rejoice at the death of the worshipper who spends the whole day in his prayer niche? He said: Yes, because the scholar is more harmful to us than the worshipper. And if you wish, I will now give you an example. He went to the worshipper and said: Is Allah, mighty and majestic, able to place the heavens and the earth inside an egg? The worshipper said: No, He is not able. He said: Is Allah able to create its like? He said: ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [Ya-Sin 82]. He may be able to create its like. Is this correct?! This is not correct and not possible. Then he went to the scholar and said something similar. He said: As for creating a likeness, this is something impossible, and it is not possible for a created being to be like the Creator at all, no matter what. As for His placing the heavens and the earth inside an egg, He is Able over all things.

The poor worshipper disbelieved in two ways: he affirmed what is not possible, and he negated what is possible. And this is truly... that is, worshippers, just as Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah said: "Whoever among our worshippers becomes corrupt has some resemblance to the Christians, and whoever among our scholars becomes corrupt has some resemblance to the Jews" [[See al-Fatawa al-Kubra of Ibn Taymiyyah (2/142).]]. The Jews are undoubtedly more wicked than the Christians, because the corruption of the scholar, may Allah protect us, is from knowledge, and the corruption of the worshipper is from ignorance, and what comes from ignorance is less severe than what comes from knowledge.

* A student: Regarding the saying of the one who said: He is Able over what He wills. Can we not derive a rule that the essential attributes (...) the active attributes (...) will in general?

* The Shaykh: (...). Their rule is that the essential attributes are those necessarily belonging to the essence, and the active ones are those related to the will. This is their rule.

* A student: Regarding the sending down (*tanzil*) and the causing to descend (*inzal*) in the Qur'an, how is this answered?

* The Shaykh: Which verse?

* A student: In the Qur'an itself, it is stated that He sent it down, and He said: "a revelation (*tanzil*)." What is the difference?

* The Shaykh: When it is stated that He sent it down, like: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree﴾ [Al-Qadr 1], the intended meaning is the beginning of its sending down. That is, We sent down the whole of it at once, not all of it in parts. As for *tanzil*, it is considered with respect to its entirety, being sent down gradually, as in His saying: ﴿And a Qur'an We have separated so that you may recite it to the people over time, and We have sent it down in stages﴾ [Al-Isra' 106]. Although *tanzil* may also come for something that occurred all at once, like His saying: ﴿And it has already come down to you in the Book that when you hear the verses of Allah being denied and ridiculed, do not sit with them﴾ [An-Nisa' 140]. So based on this, the rule that the scholars mentioned on this matter is a general rule, not a necessary one.

* * *

﴿It is Allah who sends the winds, and they stir up clouds, and He spreads them across the sky however He wills﴾ [Ar-Rum 48], and so on to the end.

* The following benefits are derived from this noble verse:

* First: the perfection of Allah's power, glorified and exalted is He, by sending the winds, stirring the clouds, spreading them in the sky, making them into fragments, and the rain descending from them. Yes, how many aspects is this? The perfection of Allah's power is derived from several aspects: first, the sending of the winds, the stirring of the clouds, their spreading in the sky, their making into fragments, the rain descending from them; that is five aspects.

* Also among the benefits of this noble verse: the word "sky" is applied to everything that is high, because of His saying: ﴿and spreads them in the sky﴾. For they are not spread in the sky that is the protected ceiling, but they are spread in the high atmosphere.

* And among its benefits: the wisdom of Allah, mighty and majestic, in sending the rain down from above, because when it descends from above it reaches both the low and the high, whereas if it flowed along the ground, it would flood what is low before reaching what is high.

* And among the benefits of this noble verse: showing the extent of the creation's need for Allah's mercy, because of His saying: ﴿then when He causes it to strike whom He wills of His servants﴾.

* And among them: the affirmation of will, because of His saying: ﴿whom He wills﴾.

* And among them: the affirmation of general servitude, because of His saying: ﴿of His servants﴾.

* And among them, and let us see whether this benefit is appropriate or not: the permissibility of rejoicing in the rain, and that people may give each other the good news of it. Or is that not possible? The main question is whether it can be derived that rejoicing in the rain is permissible, or whether it is said that this is a report of an actual event, so no ruling can be derived from it. There is a possibility that permissibility of rejoicing in the rain can be derived from it, and there is a possibility that this is merely an explanation of the reality, so no ruling is derived from it. At most it can be said that it is permissible, because Allah, exalted is He, mentioned it and did not disapprove of it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 30, verse 48–50 (part 3 of 3):

* Among the benefits of the verse: it shows the mercy of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in that rain descends in drops and not all at once; this is from His saying: ﴿then you see the rain coming out from within it﴾. For if it descended like the mouths of waterskins, or like torrents that flow, what would happen? It would destroy the homes, destroy the trees, and harm the animals upon whom it falls. But Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, made it this fine drizzle.
Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And even though they were, before it was sent down upon them, before it, certainly in despair﴾ [ar-Rum 49].
* In this: an explanation of the state of the servant before the rain falls, and that the servant is weak; this is from His saying: ﴿in despair﴾, for he is weak. When he is afflicted with something, he despairs and considers relief far off. But Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, removes this condition from him. He said: ﴿And even though they were, before it was sent down upon them, before it, certainly in despair﴾. Fine, from where is this taken? From His saying: ﴿And even though they were, before it was sent down upon them, before it, certainly in despair﴾.
Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿So look at the effects of the mercy of Allah, how He gives life to the earth after its death﴾ [ar-Rum 50]. In this verse is the command to look, which may be with the eye that sees, and with the eye of insight as well; so the command here is to look in both respects together. A person looks with his seeing eye and with the eye of insight.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: just as looking is beneficial to a person, it is commanded by the Sharia; that is, the person is rewarded, or given reward, for looking at the signs of Allah, because it is commanded.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse also: all the effects that result from the rain are from the mercy of Allah; the giving of life to the earth with plants and the abundance of water in it, all of it is from the mercy of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: affirming the power of Allah, the Exalted, to give life to the dead; this is from His saying: ﴿Indeed, that is the one who gives life to the dead﴾.
* Among its benefits: reasoning from the perceptible seen to the perceptible awaited. How? The perceptible seen is what occurs of the life of the earth, and the perceptible awaited is what occurs of the resurrection of the dead.
* Among them: that the proof must be clearer and more manifest than what it proves; meaning, it is not possible for us to reason from the hidden to the more manifest and clearer; for the proof makes the thing proved known and explains it. How then can you reason from something hidden to something clear?! Is that not so?
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: * Among the benefits of the noble verse: the mercy of Allah, the Exalted, toward His servants, in that He sets forth examples for them and explains the proofs so that they may reach certainty regarding what must be believed. For it would suffice that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, say: Believe that I give life to the dead; that would suffice to establish the proof against them. But out of His mercy He explains to us and sets forth examples for us so that we reach the level of certainty regarding what He has informed us. From where do we take this? From His saying: ﴿So look at the effects of the mercy of Allah, how He gives life to the earth after its death; indeed, that is the one who gives life to the dead﴾.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the blessing of Allah upon the servants in giving life to the earth; this is from His saying: ﴿So look at the effects of the mercy of Allah, how He gives life to the earth after its death﴾.
* Among them: that inanimate matter is described as living and dead. In this is a refutation of the philosophers who say that inanimate matter cannot be described as living or dead because it is not capable of them. We say: Allah, the Exalted, described inanimate matter as living and dead, as in this verse, and as in His saying: ﴿And those they call upon besides Allah create nothing, and they are created. (20) They are dead, not alive﴾ [an-Nahl 20, 21], even though they are idols made of stones, trees, and the like.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the establishment of the attribute of power and its comprehensiveness; this is from His saying: ﴿And He is over all things Competent﴾; nothing overcomes Him in the heavens or on the earth.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 30, verse 48–50 (part 1 of 3):

Then He said: ﴿It is Allah Who sends the winds, so they stir up clouds﴾ [Ar-Rum 48]. The author said: (He drives them), because it is derived from: athāra al-ṣayd (he roused the game), if he startled it.
﴿It is Allah Who sends the winds﴾ means: He dispatches them however He wills, glorified and exalted is He.
﴿so they stir up clouds﴾. The author said: so (He drives it), like the stirring up of game, for stirring up game from its place means startling it until it rises.
And His saying: ﴿clouds﴾. Al-sahāb is the known thing; it is the cloud.
﴿then He spreads them across the sky however He wills﴾ (in few or in many). ﴿Then He spreads them﴾: al-basṭ means al-nashr (spreading out). ﴿however He wills﴾ refers to the manner of this spreading; it may be wide, it may be sparse, it may be dense, it may be thin. For this reason He said (﴿and He makes it fragments﴾, with the sīn vowelled and with it unvowelled: scattered pieces). With the sīn vowelled, it is ﴿kisafan﴾; with it unvowelled, it is ﴿kisfan﴾. Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿And if they should see a fragment of the sky falling, they would say, "Layered clouds."﴾ [At-Tur 44] ﴿kisfan﴾. Al-kisaf means the pieces. It seems that the author, may Allah have mercy on him, wants to make clear that the cloud may be wide, spread out and extended, and it may be few, in scattered pieces.
Some of the exegetes said: the meaning of its being ﴿kisafan﴾ is that they are pieces piled one upon another until it turns black and dark, and thunder and lightning occur within it. This is more correct, that what is meant by al-kisaf is the pieces piled upon one another until they become dark and black, and this is generally more abundant in rain.
He says: ﴿and He makes it fragments, then you see the rain coming out from within it﴾. ﴿then you see﴾: the address is to everyone who can be addressed, because this seeing is not specific to the Messenger ﷺ.
And His saying: ﴿al-wadq﴾ means (the rain); that is, the drops of rain are called wadq.
﴿coming out from within it﴾ (i.e., from its midst), and it was said: from between it; from between this cloud.
And His saying: ﴿then you see the rain﴾. If someone says: we do not see it with our naked eyes, we do not see the rain penetrating this cloud (...).
It is said: it is a true report, so what is the result? It is as if witnessed; since Allah the Exalted has informed of it, it is as though we are witnessing it with our own eyes. Moreover, in the present time there have been developed powerful instruments by which a person can see how this rain comes out, these droplets, from within the cloud.
And His saying: ﴿So when He causes it [the rain] to fall upon whom He wills of His servants, behold, they rejoice﴾. This is a conditional sentence: ﴿when He causes it to fall﴾ (idhā) indicates that those who are struck by the rain are in extreme longing for it, and for this reason, the moment it strikes them, joy occurs. Our saying "the moment" is not a result of the consequent of the condition following the condition itself, but a result of that plus another matter, namely the use of the sudden idhā which indicates suddenness and speed. So idhā conveys the condition, the verb of the condition is ﴿asāba﴾, and the consequent of the condition is the clause ﴿they rejoice﴾, introduced by the sudden idhā.
We said: this expression indicates that these people are at the utmost of longing for the descent of the rain; the proof of that is their rejoicing at the very moment of being struck, and it is not ordinary rejoicing as the consequence following the condition, but it is more emphatic because it uses the sudden idhā, which indicates the immediacy of the occurrence of that thing.
And His saying: ﴿they rejoice﴾. The author said: (they are glad about the rain), and istibshār is more intense than mere joy; rejoicing (istibshār) is more intense than mere joy, rather one rejoices in oneself and perhaps congratulates and gives glad tidings to others. For this reason, in the rainy season, during the season of rain, you find for example that when people meet one another, especially those who come from the deserts, one says: "I give you good news, rain has fallen, and it is abundant," or as is the case. So istibshār here is more emphatic than mere joy, but the author, may Allah have mercy on him, sometimes explains it approximately.
And His saying: ﴿So when He causes it to fall upon whom He wills of His servants﴾: ﴿whom He wills﴾, not whom people will. The one who sends down the rain is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; no one can send it down. As for what is mentioned, that they now spray chemical materials upon the clouds so that rain falls, we say: if this is true, then who created this rain? Allah, glorified and exalted is He, and the One who brought this cloud into being is Allah, glorified and exalted is He. Their arriving at means by which this cloud evaporates until it falls as rain does not negate that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is the One who sends down the rain. Moreover, the verse ﴿He sends down the rain (al-ghayth)﴾ [Ash-Shura 28] is more eloquent than "He sends down the rain (al-matar)", since rain may fall without being al-ghayth; as is established in Sahih Muslim[[(2904/44) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]: "Drought (al-sanah) is not that you are not given rain; rather, drought is that you are given rain but the earth does not produce vegetation." (Al-sanah): what does it mean? Dearth and famine; that is, it is not merely that rain does not come; true drought is that it comes but no vegetation results.
And His saying: ﴿So when He causes it to fall upon whom He wills of His servants﴾. Here the word ʿibād means the plural of ʿabd; is this the special servitude or the general servitude? The general, why? Because the rain falls upon believers and disbelievers alike. Yes, indeed, its falling upon disbelievers may be even more abundant, more copious and more persistent, as a trial for them, so that their good things are hastened to them in their worldly life, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And on the Day the disbelievers are exposed to the Fire: "You have used up your good things in your worldly life and enjoyed them"﴾, that is, these good things, ﴿so today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation﴾ [Al-Ahqaf 20], and so on to its end.
Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And indeed, they were﴾ [Ar-Rum 49]. The author said: (qad ﴿kānū﴾), (qad): he estimated ʾin as qad, and in this he followed al-Baghawi; the author (al-Jalalayn) derived from al-Baghawi, that is, as if it were an abridgement of it; for if you reflect upon his tafsir, may Allah have mercy on him, you will find that it is precisely the tafsir of al-Baghawi, but al-Baghawi is expanded and this is abridged.
He said: (﴿in﴾ is qad). None of the grammarians said this, except if he meant it only by way of interpretation. The correct view, about which there is no doubt, is that ﴿in﴾ here is the light (mukhaffafah) form of the heavy (thaqīlah) one, as in the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And indeed, they were before that in clear error﴾ [Al Imran 164]. On this basis we say: its origin was (inna), which was lightened, and where is its noun?
* Students: The pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-shaʾn).
* The Shaykh: The pronoun of the matter; its noun is an omitted pronoun of the matter, and the estimate is: "and indeed they". We have previously mentioned that the correct view among the grammarians' opinions is that the pronoun of the matter is not estimated as singular masculine, but is estimated according to the context: if the context requires feminine, it is feminine; if it requires masculine, it is masculine; if it requires plural, it is plural; if it requires dual, it is dual.[[The correct view is that the pronoun of the matter varies in masculine and feminine according to context, but it is not made dual or plural. See Hashiyat al-Sabban ʿala al-Ashmuni (1/370).]] So its origin is: "and indeed they were." But (inna) was lightened, so its noun was omitted as the pronoun of the matter.
﴿And indeed they were, before it was sent down upon them﴾ [Ar-Rum 49]: ﴿before it was sent down upon them﴾: what? The rain.
How do we know that it is the rain? Has the sending down of rain been mentioned before? The answer: yes, in His saying: ﴿you see the rain coming out from within it﴾; for when the rain comes out from within the cloud, where does it go? It descends to the earth.
And His saying: ﴿before it was sent down upon them﴾: Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, expresses the descent of rain as inzāl and tanzīl; this is because the rain sometimes comes all at once in abundance and heavy flow, so it is inzāl; and sometimes it comes gradually, weak and intermittent, so it is called tanzīl, because tanzīl means sending down a thing little by little. ﴿before it was sent down upon them, before it, they were despairing﴾.
* A student: Regarding (...) tanzīl and inzāl (...) considering the rain as a whole, we say "nazala", considering its individual parts...
* The Shaykh: No, it is anzala.
* Student: Considering its individual parts...
* The Shaykh: No, considering the abundance and the dispersion.
* Student: (...) this cloud at the time, and after days...
* The Shaykh: After days it comes; then it also comes sometimes in small amounts; for example, the rain may last two days, three, but it is little, and sometimes it comes, as you witness, great clouds as if they were the mouths of waterskins.
And His saying: ﴿before it, [before it was sent down upon them]﴾: the word ﴿min qablihi﴾ has been differed over by the scholars. Some of them said, as the author said, that it is (emphasis); like His saying: ﴿So do not think them to be in an escape from the punishment, and for them is a painful punishment﴾; ﴿Do not think that those who rejoice in what they have done and love to be praised for what they did not do — do not think them to be in an escape from the punishment﴾ [Al Imran 188]: He repeated the verb for emphasis. This is one view, and it is what the author followed, and it is the view of most exegetes, that His saying ﴿min qablihi﴾ means: before it was sent down upon them; so it is as if He said: "And indeed they were before it was sent down upon them, before it was sent down upon them, despairing," so its repetition is for emphasis.
Some of the exegetes said: it was repeated for establishing new meaning (taʾsīs), not for emphasis. It is known that when speech is between being emphatic (tawkīd) and being establishing (taʾsīs), the default is taʾsīs; that is, the default is no emphasis, because emphasis is repetition and the default is no repetition; so some exegetes hold that it is not for emphasis but for establishing. Take care of the difference (...) the scholars, may Allah have mercy on them: the difference between tawkīd and taʾsīs is that tawkīd means this is the first, and taʾsīs means this is other than the first, and it is an independent statement.
On the view that it is taʾsīs, what does it mean? Some said: ﴿min qablihi﴾ means: before the joy; "and indeed they were, before it was sent down upon them, before the joy, despairing," so Allah mentioned for them two states, before the joy and after it. Do you understand? This is what Abu al-Suʿud followed, and it is good and has no difficulty in terms of conception and meaning; (...) the meaning: and indeed they were, before the descent of the rain, before that joy, despairing, so Allah alerted them to their state before the joy, which is despair, and to their state after that.
Some said: ﴿min qablihi﴾ means: before the before, "before it was sent down upon them"; ﴿min qablihi﴾ means: "and indeed they were, before it was sent down upon them, before that before," so the pronoun in ﴿min qablihi﴾ does not refer to the rain nor to the joy, but they make it refer to the "before", so the meaning on this is: "And indeed they were, before it was sent down upon them, before that before, despairing," so its benefit is that despair was continuous with them since ancient times: a season comes in which no rain falls and they despair, then another season comes and they despair, then another season comes and they despair... and so on. It is known that when seasons repeat without rain, the despair is more intense, so the meaning is that this joy came after despair twice or more. This also was mentioned by Ibn Kathir, may Allah have mercy on him, in his tafsir. So we have in ﴿min qablihi﴾ how many views? Three views:
The first view: it is emphasis.
The second: the pronoun refers to the joy.
The third: the pronoun refers to the "before"; i.e., "and indeed they were, before it was sent down upon them, before that before as well, despairing."

As for His saying ﴿mublisīn﴾: it is in the accusative as the predicate of (kāna). Where is (kāna)? ﴿And indeed they were﴾. The lām was attached to it because of ﴿in﴾. Is the attachment here obligatory or permissible?
* Student: No, obligatory.
* Another student: No, permissible.
* The Shaykh: No, permissible, and not obligatory.
* Student: No, permissible.
* The Shaykh: You said "no, permissible", and this one says "no, obligatory." No, it is obligatory; no, it is permissible.
* Student: Obligatory.
* The Shaykh: Good, what is the reason for the obligation?
* Student: The lightened form of the heavy one must be accompanied by the lām.
* The Shaykh: It must be accompanied by the lām?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: And what is the basis for permissibility?
* Student: The basis for permissibility is that (in) resembles (...), it is obligatory for (inna) lightened to be accompanied when it resembles (mā).
* The Shaykh: From where do you know that from the words of Ibn Malik?
* Student: From his saying:
"And inna was lightened, so its action became rare, and the lām is obligatory when it is left unused. And sometimes it is dispensed with, if the speaker's intended meaning is clear from context."
* The Shaykh: And what do you say about this argument? Now, if we drop it, would (in) lightened not resemble (in) the negating (in)? That is, if it were: "and they were not, before it was sent down upon them, despairing"? It would resemble; that is, they rejoice though they had not despaired nor been in despair before. This may occur, that they rejoice even though they had no despair before. So the apparent view is obligation, not for the reason he mentioned; for he thought that attachment is obligatory absolutely, but it is obligatory because it may resemble the negating (in); but if it does not resemble, then attachment is not obligatory.
Is there evidence from the grammar for this? Yes, the saying of the poet:
"...................... And indeed Malik were noble of origins"
He boasts of being from the Banu Malik and then says: "And indeed Malik were noble of origins." Here (in) cannot be confused with (mā); why? Because he cannot boast of a people whose nobility of origin is denied. Or not? If you say: "I am, for example, from a tribe; this tribe was not noble of origin" — is that suitable? It does not fit.
The conclusion is that the lām here is for emphasis, and some scholars call it: the lām of distinction (lām al-farq), the distinguishing lām; this is more precise in expression, and though it is distinguishing, it conveys emphasis. They named it the distinguishing lām because it distinguishes the negating (in) from the lightened (in).
Good. If someone asks: can it be attached with the lām while (in) means negation?
The answer: no, and this is the secret of why it is distinguishing; the lām cannot be attached to it, because the lām conveys emphasis of affirmation, while negation is the opposite; negation conveys negation.
He said: ﴿mublisīn﴾; he says: (despairing of its descent). Iblās is like qunūt, the utmost despair; and from it Iblis was named, we seek refuge in Allah from him, because he is ublis, despairing of the mercy of Allah. ﴿And indeed they were, before it was sent down upon them, before it, despairing of its descent.﴾
﴿So look at the traces of the mercy of Allah﴾ [Ar-Rum 50]: ﴿look﴾, the address is to whom?
* Student: To the Messenger.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 30, verses 48–50 (part 2 of 3):

* The Shaykh: "For mankind," no. "Not for the Messenger." The address is to mankind, to whoever can be addressed, the Messenger ﷺ and others. This is because He said in the first verse: ﴿then you see the rain come out from within it﴾. Then He says here: ﴿So look﴾, meaning: look, O human being, ﴿at the traces of Allah's mercy﴾. And in another reading, the author says: ﴿at the traces of Allah's mercy﴾ (plural, *āthār*). Look at the 'Uthmanic script. One of the benefits of its consistency is that it does not change with the variant readings (qira'at). ﴿Āthār﴾ (plural): how would it be written according to the rules of modern orthography? With an alif between the thā' and the rā'. But according to the rules of the 'Uthmanic Mushaf, is an alif written in it? No. (*Athar*) is thā' and rā'. So the form *āthār* is valid, and the form *athar* is valid.

And His saying ﴿ilā āthār﴾ and ﴿ilā athar﴾ do not differ in general in meaning, because *āthār* is a construct (*muḍāf*) and so conveys generality, and *athar* is a construct and so conveys generality, since a singular noun when made a construct conveys generality. So *athar* and *āthār* are, in general, no different. This is because ﴿athar raḥmat Allāh﴾ means the same as *āthār*. But the difference between them in the specific sense is that *athar* includes the genus considered as one single thing, whereas *āthār* includes the genus considered as types.

How is it considered as types? Like the trace of rain, by which crops grow, by which trees grow, by which something small and something large grow, and something that has open branches, and something that has thin trees like reeds. Therefore these are considered traces with respect to their types.

Furthermore, the traces differ from land to land. This land grows such-and-such, and that land grows such-and-such. This land produces pasture, and that land does not produce... and so on. So they are traces with respect to their types. As for with respect to the genus, and that all of it came about through the rain, it is one thing. And this is the specific difference between *athar* and *āthār*.

(﴿the traces of Allah's mercy﴾, meaning: His blessing, the rain.) We have already mentioned that mercy in such a context may be a name for the created thing, and may also be one of Allah's attributes. If the intended meaning is the direct effect, then mercy means the rain, because this vegetation grew by what? By the rain. If the intended meaning is the indirect cause, then mercy means the attribute of Allah. That is, because Allah, may He be exalted, is Merciful, this is one of the traces of mercy: that He sends down rain, by which the earth grows and drought is removed. So the verse is applicable to both meanings.

He says: ﴿how He gives life to the earth after its death﴾ [Ar-Rum 50]. This is among what favours the view that the intended meaning of mercy is the attribute, the mercy of Allah. ﴿How He gives life﴾: He, that is, by His mercy, glorified and exalted is He. ﴿gives life to the earth﴾, makes it alive, ﴿after its death﴾. The author says: (that is, its dryness). The life of everything is according to its nature. So the dry land in which there is no greenery is called dead, there is nothing living in it. When the rain falls upon it and the vegetation comes to life, it is called alive.

﴿He gives life to the earth after its death﴾. This is evidence of the power of the Lord, mighty and majestic, and of His mercy. For who is able to split the seed and the grain within the earth until this growing plant emerges from it? Can anyone do this? No one can. Therefore it has come in the authentic sacred hadith: "Let them create a grain, or let them create a barley seed" [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7559) and Muslim (2111/101), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]. They cannot; no one can create this. ﴿Indeed, Allah is the splitter of the grain and the date-pit. He brings the living out of the dead and brings the dead out of the living. That is Allah; so how are you deluded?﴾ [Al-An'am 95].

﴿How He gives life to the earth after its death﴾. ﴿How﴾ means: look at the manner and the power. How this earth, which was dusty and as if burnt, has now become a green garden! (That is, its dryness, by its growing.)

Allah, mighty and majestic, says: ﴿Indeed, that is the one who gives life to the dead﴾ [Ar-Rum 50]. ﴿Indeed, that﴾: the one referred to (...).

* * *

(...) it would be pointless. A rational human would be created, who knows, understands, and acts, and some of them kill others, and some plunder others, and some make peace with others, and the outcome is that they become dust. This is absolutely impossible. That is to say, if a person considers it even slightly, he will find that reason decisively indicates that there must be a resurrection and (...), otherwise the whole world would be pointless. ﴿We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vain. That is the assumption of those who disbelieve, so woe to those who disbelieve from the Fire﴾ [Sad 27].

Do we not, for example, see those who oppose us in action, who oppose us in morals, who oppose us in belief, and are pained by that, or not? Yes.
