If it were not that Allah consoles the Messenger ﷺ: ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief that they do not believe﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara 3], and similar things by which He consoles him, his heart would break over them, peace and blessings be upon him. We now feel pain for those who oppose us in belief, for those who oppose us in morals, for those who oppose us in deeds. We undoubtedly feel pain. This pain affects us. But Allah, mighty and majestic, says: ﴿If you suffer, indeed they suffer as you suffer﴾, but there is a difference: ﴿but you hope from Allah for what they do not hope﴾ [An-Nisa' 104]. So the conclusion is that this great universe cannot be pointless in this way, living and then becoming dust. Allah, mighty and majestic, gives life to the dead, not only human beings, but human beings and others. ﴿There is no creature on the earth, nor bird that flies with its two wings, but they are communities like yourselves. We have not neglected anything in the Book. Then to their Lord they will be gathered﴾ [Al-An'am 38]. ﴿And when the wild beasts are gathered﴾ [At-Takwir 5]. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, informed that the animals will be judged for the hornless one against the horned one [[Narrated by Muslim (2582/60) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]. Even the animals will have judgment passed between them. Is it clear, brothers? Therefore we say: ﴿the dead﴾ is not restricted to humans only, but includes humans and non-humans. ﴿Indeed, that is the one who gives life to the dead﴾ [Ar-Rum 50].

Then He emphasised this, the giving of life to the dead, with another emphasis: the sentence after it, His saying: ﴿And He is Able over all things﴾ [Ar-Rum 50]. So the giving of life to the dead has been emphasised with two verbal emphases and two semantic emphases.

As for His saying ﴿And He is Able over all things﴾: Allah is able over everything, everything without exception, everything to which power relates and which can be within His power. Allah, may He be exalted, is capable, Able over all things, not only over what He wills, but over what He wills and what He does not will. The guidance of the disbeliever who died in his disbelief: is Allah able over it or not?

* Students: Yes, He is able.

* The Shaykh: And did He will it? He did not will it, yet He is able over it. So His power is not restricted to what He wills. From this we know that the expression of some people, that He is able over what He wills, is not appropriate. Rather, say as Allah said about Himself: ﴿Indeed, He is Able over all things﴾ [Fussilat 39].

As for the hadith of the man whom Allah will resurrect on the Day of Resurrection, He mentioned the story, and in it Allah said to him: "Indeed, I am Able over what I will" [[Narrated by Muslim (187/310) from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud.]]. This does not mean describing Allah with power absolutely. Rather it describes Allah with power over this particular thing which the addressee considered unlikely. Allah is saying: I have willed it, so I am able over it. Likewise His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He is Able to gather them when He wills﴾ [Ash-Shura 29]. The qualifier of will here does not refer to the power, but refers to the gathering. A particular thing may be qualified by power. But if you want to describe Allah with power, do not qualify it with will. There is a difference between linking power to a specific particular thing and mentioning it as a general description of Allah. If it is a general description, then no. Allah, exalted is He, never mentioned the qualifier of will: ﴿And your Lord is ever Competent﴾ [Al-Furqan 54], ﴿And Allah is ever Competent over all things﴾ [Al-Ahzab 27], ﴿And Allah is Competent over all things﴾ [Al-Baqarah 284], and similar.

Power is the opposite of incapacity. Look at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah would never be incapacitated by anything in the heavens or on the earth. Indeed, He is ever Knowing and Competent﴾ [Fatir 44]. Knowledge is mentioned here, because the incapable may be incapable due to lack of knowledge of the thing. For example, an engineer who has rheumatism and cannot move. He is a perfect engineer. We told him: make this car. Can he? He cannot. Why? He does not have the power; he is incapable, because he cannot move. And another man who is energetic and carries a stone bigger than himself, but does not know this craft. We told him: make the car. He said: I cannot. Why? Because of lack of knowledge. So the negation of power may be due to lack of knowledge, and it may be due to lack of ability. He has no knowledge, he has nothing, meaning he is incapable.

Now, (...) the explanation of this is in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is in them, and He is Able over all things﴾, at the end of Surat al-Ma'idah [Al-Ma'idah 120]. Someone stated a objectionable phrase; he did not intend evil by it, Allah knows best. He did not intend evil when he said: (Reason has restricted His essence, so He is not able over it). (Reason has restricted His essence): that is, reason requires restricting the essence of Allah, so Allah is not able over it. Is this correct?

* A student: This is not correct.

* The Shaykh: This is not correct. Rather, Allah is Able over all things. Therefore Allah, exalted is He, established Himself upon the Throne, by His action or not? By His action and His power. He descends to the lowest heaven, He comes to judge between His servants, He speaks whatever He wills. All of this relates to His essence, and He is able over it.

If someone says: Allah is able to cause so-and-so to die; is He able to cause Himself to die?

This is not possible, not because of a lack of power, but because this is a matter that is not fitting for Him, and it is worse than incapacity. So we say: its impossibility is because it is impossible for Allah, mighty and majestic. Therefore al-Saffarini, may Allah have mercy on him, in his creed, when he mentioned the attribute of power, said:

*By a power that relates to the possible* ***...*** 

As for the impossible, it is impossible; the impossible is essentially something that power does not relate to. It is said that when a scholar dies, Satan rejoices greatly, and when worshippers die, it does not concern him. His soldiers said to him: How do you rejoice so greatly at the death of this scholar, and not rejoice at the death of the worshipper who spends the whole day in his prayer niche? He said: Yes, because the scholar is more harmful to us than the worshipper. And if you wish, I will now give you an example. He went to the worshipper and said: Is Allah, mighty and majestic, able to place the heavens and the earth inside an egg? The worshipper said: No, He is not able. He said: Is Allah able to create its like? He said: ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [Ya-Sin 82]. He may be able to create its like. Is this correct?! This is not correct and not possible. Then he went to the scholar and said something similar. He said: As for creating a likeness, this is something impossible, and it is not possible for a created being to be like the Creator at all, no matter what. As for His placing the heavens and the earth inside an egg, He is Able over all things.

The poor worshipper disbelieved in two ways: he affirmed what is not possible, and he negated what is possible. And this is truly... that is, worshippers, just as Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah said: "Whoever among our worshippers becomes corrupt has some resemblance to the Christians, and whoever among our scholars becomes corrupt has some resemblance to the Jews" [[See al-Fatawa al-Kubra of Ibn Taymiyyah (2/142).]]. The Jews are undoubtedly more wicked than the Christians, because the corruption of the scholar, may Allah protect us, is from knowledge, and the corruption of the worshipper is from ignorance, and what comes from ignorance is less severe than what comes from knowledge.

* A student: Regarding the saying of the one who said: He is Able over what He wills. Can we not derive a rule that the essential attributes (...) the active attributes (...) will in general?

* The Shaykh: (...). Their rule is that the essential attributes are those necessarily belonging to the essence, and the active ones are those related to the will. This is their rule.

* A student: Regarding the sending down (*tanzil*) and the causing to descend (*inzal*) in the Qur'an, how is this answered?

* The Shaykh: Which verse?

* A student: In the Qur'an itself, it is stated that He sent it down, and He said: "a revelation (*tanzil*)." What is the difference?

* The Shaykh: When it is stated that He sent it down, like: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree﴾ [Al-Qadr 1], the intended meaning is the beginning of its sending down. That is, We sent down the whole of it at once, not all of it in parts. As for *tanzil*, it is considered with respect to its entirety, being sent down gradually, as in His saying: ﴿And a Qur'an We have separated so that you may recite it to the people over time, and We have sent it down in stages﴾ [Al-Isra' 106]. Although *tanzil* may also come for something that occurred all at once, like His saying: ﴿And it has already come down to you in the Book that when you hear the verses of Allah being denied and ridiculed, do not sit with them﴾ [An-Nisa' 140]. So based on this, the rule that the scholars mentioned on this matter is a general rule, not a necessary one.

* * *

﴿It is Allah who sends the winds, and they stir up clouds, and He spreads them across the sky however He wills﴾ [Ar-Rum 48], and so on to the end.

* The following benefits are derived from this noble verse:

* First: the perfection of Allah's power, glorified and exalted is He, by sending the winds, stirring the clouds, spreading them in the sky, making them into fragments, and the rain descending from them. Yes, how many aspects is this? The perfection of Allah's power is derived from several aspects: first, the sending of the winds, the stirring of the clouds, their spreading in the sky, their making into fragments, the rain descending from them; that is five aspects.

* Also among the benefits of this noble verse: the word "sky" is applied to everything that is high, because of His saying: ﴿and spreads them in the sky﴾. For they are not spread in the sky that is the protected ceiling, but they are spread in the high atmosphere.

* And among its benefits: the wisdom of Allah, mighty and majestic, in sending the rain down from above, because when it descends from above it reaches both the low and the high, whereas if it flowed along the ground, it would flood what is low before reaching what is high.

* And among the benefits of this noble verse: showing the extent of the creation's need for Allah's mercy, because of His saying: ﴿then when He causes it to strike whom He wills of His servants﴾.

* And among them: the affirmation of will, because of His saying: ﴿whom He wills﴾.

* And among them: the affirmation of general servitude, because of His saying: ﴿of His servants﴾.

* And among them, and let us see whether this benefit is appropriate or not: the permissibility of rejoicing in the rain, and that people may give each other the good news of it. Or is that not possible? The main question is whether it can be derived that rejoicing in the rain is permissible, or whether it is said that this is a report of an actual event, so no ruling can be derived from it. There is a possibility that permissibility of rejoicing in the rain can be derived from it, and there is a possibility that this is merely an explanation of the reality, so no ruling is derived from it. At most it can be said that it is permissible, because Allah, exalted is He, mentioned it and did not disapprove of it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 30, verse 48–50 (part 3 of 3):

* Among the benefits of the verse: it shows the mercy of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in that rain descends in drops and not all at once; this is from His saying: ﴿then you see the rain coming out from within it﴾. For if it descended like the mouths of waterskins, or like torrents that flow, what would happen? It would destroy the homes, destroy the trees, and harm the animals upon whom it falls. But Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, made it this fine drizzle.
Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And even though they were, before it was sent down upon them, before it, certainly in despair﴾ [ar-Rum 49].
* In this: an explanation of the state of the servant before the rain falls, and that the servant is weak; this is from His saying: ﴿in despair﴾, for he is weak. When he is afflicted with something, he despairs and considers relief far off. But Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, removes this condition from him. He said: ﴿And even though they were, before it was sent down upon them, before it, certainly in despair﴾. Fine, from where is this taken? From His saying: ﴿And even though they were, before it was sent down upon them, before it, certainly in despair﴾.
Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿So look at the effects of the mercy of Allah, how He gives life to the earth after its death﴾ [ar-Rum 50]. In this verse is the command to look, which may be with the eye that sees, and with the eye of insight as well; so the command here is to look in both respects together. A person looks with his seeing eye and with the eye of insight.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: just as looking is beneficial to a person, it is commanded by the Sharia; that is, the person is rewarded, or given reward, for looking at the signs of Allah, because it is commanded.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse also: all the effects that result from the rain are from the mercy of Allah; the giving of life to the earth with plants and the abundance of water in it, all of it is from the mercy of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: affirming the power of Allah, the Exalted, to give life to the dead; this is from His saying: ﴿Indeed, that is the one who gives life to the dead﴾.
* Among its benefits: reasoning from the perceptible seen to the perceptible awaited. How? The perceptible seen is what occurs of the life of the earth, and the perceptible awaited is what occurs of the resurrection of the dead.
* Among them: that the proof must be clearer and more manifest than what it proves; meaning, it is not possible for us to reason from the hidden to the more manifest and clearer; for the proof makes the thing proved known and explains it. How then can you reason from something hidden to something clear?! Is that not so?
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: * Among the benefits of the noble verse: the mercy of Allah, the Exalted, toward His servants, in that He sets forth examples for them and explains the proofs so that they may reach certainty regarding what must be believed. For it would suffice that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, say: Believe that I give life to the dead; that would suffice to establish the proof against them. But out of His mercy He explains to us and sets forth examples for us so that we reach the level of certainty regarding what He has informed us. From where do we take this? From His saying: ﴿So look at the effects of the mercy of Allah, how He gives life to the earth after its death; indeed, that is the one who gives life to the dead﴾.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the blessing of Allah upon the servants in giving life to the earth; this is from His saying: ﴿So look at the effects of the mercy of Allah, how He gives life to the earth after its death﴾.
* Among them: that inanimate matter is described as living and dead. In this is a refutation of the philosophers who say that inanimate matter cannot be described as living or dead because it is not capable of them. We say: Allah, the Exalted, described inanimate matter as living and dead, as in this verse, and as in His saying: ﴿And those they call upon besides Allah create nothing, and they are created. (20) They are dead, not alive﴾ [an-Nahl 20, 21], even though they are idols made of stones, trees, and the like.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the establishment of the attribute of power and its comprehensiveness; this is from His saying: ﴿And He is over all things Competent﴾; nothing overcomes Him in the heavens or on the earth.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 30, verses 51–54 (part 1 of 2):

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And if We were to send a wind and they saw it turn yellow, they would surely continue to disbelieve after it﴾ [al-Rum 51].

﴿And if﴾: the lam here is the lam of oath (lam al-qasam), which has entered upon the conditional particle (in), ﴿And if We send﴾. His saying ﴿they would surely [continue]﴾ is the response, but to which of the two is it a response: the condition or the oath? It is a response to the oath, because if it were the response to the condition it would not need the lam. The past-tense verb is answered directly without an intermediary. Furthermore, the rule among the scholars of Arabic grammar is that when a condition and an oath are combined, the response of whichever comes later is omitted. Ibn Malik said:

*"When a condition and an oath come together, omit the response of the one that comes later; it is then obligatory."*

(...) It is indicated by the lam that prepares for the oath, and in it is the conditional (in). The response now belongs to the oath: ﴿they would surely continue to disbelieve after it﴾, and the response of the condition is omitted, indicated by the response of the oath.

﴿And if We send a wind﴾: notice the difference. In the first verse Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿It is Allah who sends the winds﴾, whereas here He says ﴿a wind﴾ in the singular. We have mentioned previously that the plural is used for mercy and the singular for punishment; this is the general rule.

﴿And if We send a wind and they see it turn yellow﴾: the pronoun in ﴿they saw it﴾ does not refer to the wind, but refers to what was brought to life by the water that descended from the sky, because it was mentioned earlier: ﴿how He gives life to the earth after its death﴾. The meaning is: if We send a wind and they see this that was brought to life ﴿turn yellow﴾, that is, dry and crushed by these winds, ﴿they would surely continue to disbelieve after it﴾.

Let us read the author's words: (﴿And if﴾ the lam of oath, ﴿We send a wind﴾ harmful to vegetation, ﴿and they see it﴾: the pronoun refers to what? To the vegetation) ﴿turn yellow, they would [surely]﴾: "they became", the response of the oath; ﴿after it﴾: that is, after its yellowing; ﴿continue to disbelieve﴾: deny the blessing of the rain. The meaning is that when Allah, Mighty and Majestic, gives life to the earth after its death and sends upon it a wind so that the vegetation turns yellow, and after its yellowing it is destroyed, as a trial from Him, exalted is He, they would, after this rejoicing and after seeing the signs of mercy, become disbelievers.

﴿they would surely continue to disbelieve after it﴾: they say, "How can this be? The rain comes and descends, the earth is revived, and then this wind comes and destroys it?" So they disbelieve, may Allah protect us, and forget the blessing of Allah that came before. They forget it, and this is part of the trial, and it falls under the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿And among the people is he who worships Allah on an edge; if good befalls him, he is content with it, but if a trial befalls him, he turns back on his face. He loses this world and the Hereafter﴾ [al-Hajj 11]. When Allah sends this wind and the vegetation turns yellow, they should have met that with patience, not disbelief, patience with this affliction, because patience... the patient one is given his reward without reckoning, and perhaps this trial will turn into another blessing, since Allah, Exalted, says: ﴿But if you are patient, it is better for the patient﴾ [al-Nahl 126]; ﴿And if you believe and fear Allah, He will give you your rewards and will not ask you for your wealth﴾ [Muhammad 36]; ﴿And if you are patient and fear Allah, indeed that is of the matters requiring determination﴾ [Al 'Imran 186]. So the believer is patient at the time of affliction and thankful at the time of ease.

* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No, on (...).

He, Exalted, says: ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear﴾ [al-Rum 52]. ﴿You﴾ is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, and it is permissible that the address be general to everyone who can be addressed.

﴿You cannot make the dead hear﴾: that is, you cannot make them hear in a way that benefits them, or: you cannot make them hear at the time of invitation. The closer meaning is the first, because it is not reasonable that someone stands over the dead and says, "O people, worship Allah and fear Him." This is not reasonable. But if it were supposed that he invited them, would they hear in a way that benefits them? The answer is no, they do not hear in a way that benefits them.

If someone says: this is a restriction of the verse. The verse is unrestricted, ﴿You cannot make the dead hear﴾, so how is it permissible for you to restrict it by saying "in a way that benefits them"?

We say: this negation of hearing is applied to the negation of beneficial hearing, as in the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿And do not be like those who said, "We hear," while they do not hear﴾ [al-Anfal 21]. They hear with their ears, but they do not hear in a way that benefits them. And we do not take it in its absolute sense, because the hearing of the dead is reported in narrations. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ is established as having "stood over the companions of the well of Badr from among the polytheists and began calling them by their names and the names of their fathers: 'O so-and-so son of so-and-so, O so-and-so son of so-and-so, have you found what your Lord promised to be true? For we have found what our Lord promised us to be true.' Then 'Umar said, 'O Messenger of Allah, do you address people who have decayed?' (meaning: how do you address carcasses, the dead?) He said: 'You are not more hearing of what I say than they are.'"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3976), and Muslim (2875/78), from the hadith of Abu Talhah.]] That is, they hear more intensely than your hearing. So it is established that the dead do hear. Likewise Ibn 'Abd al-Barr declared sound a hadith related from the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, that "No one greets a dead person whom he knew in the world except that Allah returns his soul to him, and he returns the greeting."[[Related by Ibn 'Abd al-Barr in al-Istidhkar (1/185), from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.]] Ibn al-Qayyim mentioned this in his book al-Ruh, and he mentioned Ibn 'Abd al-Barr's authentication of it without objecting to it. Based on this, they do hear, but they do not benefit from this hearing.

Other reports have also come from the Companions on this matter, which Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned at this verse. It is also established in the Sahih that when a person is left by his companions after the burial, to the extent that he hears the sound of their sandals, two angels come to him.[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1338), and Muslim (2870/70), from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik.]] He hears the sound of their sandals on the ground, just as a person walks on the ceiling and we hear his walking on the ceiling. This one also hears the sound of the sandals (...) the sound of the sandals, but Allah, Exalted, makes them hear that.

So the conclusion is that we say: all of this supports that the meaning of ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear﴾ is: hearing in a way that benefits them. It is well known that the Messenger ﷺ did not invite the dead; he did not go to the graves to call them. But those who call on the dead from among the living, the dead do not respond and do not benefit from the call.

He, Exalted, says: ﴿Nor can you make the deaf hear the call﴾. ﴿The deaf﴾ is the first object, and ﴿the call﴾ is the second object. As for ﴿you cannot make the dead hear﴾ in the first instance, the second object has been omitted, because it is a supplementary element (fadlah), and it has already been mentioned to us that it is permissible to omit a supplementary element even without evidence.

And He said: ﴿Nor can you make the deaf hear the call﴾. ﴿The deaf﴾ is the plural of aṣamm, the one who does not hear, the one who does not hear; you cannot make him hear, especially when turning away is joined to it: ﴿when they turn back and flee﴾. This is the strongest form of the absence of hearing from the deaf. The deaf person does not hear even if he is facing you. How much more so when he turns away! (...) For this reason, if the deaf person is in front of you and you call him with some voice, perhaps he will hear. But if he turns away, however much you call him, he will not hear unless you reach him and take hold of him. So the deaf, when they turn back and flee, do not hear. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, restricted the deaf to this state only because it is the state in which they absolutely do not hear, unlike when they are in front of you, for they may hear and infer what you say from the movements of your lips.

﴿Nor can you make the deaf hear the call﴾: the author said: (with the two hamzas realized, and the second softened between it and the ya'). ﴿The call, when﴾: what is this? It is the realization (tahqiq); ﴿the call, when they turn﴾. The second: softening the second, between it, that is, between the realized hamzah and the ya'; that is: ﴿Nor can you make the deaf hear the call, idha﴾ place it between the hamzah and the ya'. Both readings are among the seven canonical readings.

Then He said: ﴿Nor can you guide the blind out of their straying﴾ [al-Rum 53]. Notice now the transition: the dead, the deaf, the blind.

﴿Nor can you guide the blind out of their straying﴾: ﴿mā﴾ is Hijazi (negating like laysa), ﴿anta﴾ is its subject, the ba' is an extra preposition, and (hadi) is its predicate.

﴿Nor can you [be] a guide﴾: an active participle. ﴿The blind﴾: ﴿al-'umy﴾ is the plural of a'mā, because the plural pattern of af'al is fu'l; Ibn Malik said:

*"fu'l is for such as aḥmar and ḥamrā'..."*

(aḥmar is like a'mā, and ḥamrā' is like 'amyā'), so 'umy is the plural for males and females alike.

﴿Guide the blind out of their straying﴾: what is the meaning of ﴿their straying﴾? That is, from their bewilderment. If they are lost on the road, you cannot guide the blind away from it. Likewise these people who are blind to the truth, may Allah protect us, do not see; they are deaf to it and do not hear; they are dead to it and do not understand. You also cannot guide these people, or can you?

Now reflect on the matter of death and the matter of deafness. He said: ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear, nor can you make the deaf hear﴾, and regarding blindness He said: ﴿Nor can you guide the blind﴾. He did not say "you cannot make the blind hear." The reason: sight is connected with guidance (dalalah), which is guidance, whereas deafness is connected with hearing.

(﴿And you cannot guide the blind out of their straying; you do not make [anyone] hear except those who believe in Our verses, so they are Muslims﴾ [al-Rum 53].)

﴿In﴾: the author said: (mā). What is the meaning of (﴿in﴾ mā)? This "mā" is explanatory (tafsiriyyah), and for this reason it is not assimilated into "in", so one does not say "imma", but rather "in" followed by "mā" in an explicit form, because "mā" explains it; it is the same thing, ﴿in﴾ meaning "mā".

﴿You make hear﴾: the author said: (hearing that comprehends and accepts).

You do not make hear ﴿except those who believe in Our verses﴾: that is, the Qur'an, ﴿so they are Muslims﴾. That is: on the basis of their faith they are Muslims, submissive, because whenever faith is complete, submission is complete. The more a person's faith is strong, the greater his submission. For this reason, faith entails Islam; every believer is a Muslim, but not vice versa. Not every Muslim is a believer; a person may submit outwardly while his heart harbors disbelief, may Allah protect us, unlike faith. For this reason He ordered Islam after faith with the particle fa': ﴿so they are Muslims﴾; they are, because of their faith, Muslims who submit.

His saying ﴿except those who believe in Our verses﴾: the author said it means the Qur'an, even though "āyāt" is plural and not singular. So what is the answer to the author's statement?

The answer to the author's statement is that it is deficient, and the truth is that what is meant by "āyāt" is more general than the Qur'an; it includes all the revealed books, and it also includes the cosmic signs, by believing that this universe was created by Allah, Mighty and Majestic, because some people do not believe in the cosmic signs. See: ﴿And if they see a piece of the sky falling, they say: "Layered clouds"﴾ [al-Tur 44]. What do they say? It is natural; the universe is matter and nature interacting and producing some things from others, and similar things. They did not believe in the signs.

The legal signs likewise: some people do not believe in them; they deny their reports and are arrogant toward their rulings, and this is common.

So the correct view is that what is meant by His saying ﴿Our verses﴾ includes all the legal signs in all the revealed books and all the cosmic signs, because some people deny the cosmic signs, as you know.

If someone says: ﴿You do not make hear except those who believe in Our verses﴾ means that the believer hears, so how can He say "you do not make hear except those who believe," when the believer hears? How would you answer this?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, but whoever believes hears; you make hear those who believe.
* Student: (...) that he is receptive to the call (...).
* Another student: Receptive to hearing and (...).
* Shaykh: The answer to this is one of two ways. Either it is said: ﴿You do not make hear except those who believe﴾ means: except those who were prepared to believe in what you say and who are written with Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as believers. This is a matter not known to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, but he is obliged to make the call so that those whom Allah knows to be believers and prepared for faith hear it. That is one way. Or it is said: religion consists of laws; it is not one thing, but rather laws and multiple rites, and whoever benefits from these rites and applies them is the one who believes in them. This believer, in whom faith has actually occurred, is the one who hears all that the Messenger ﷺ called to from all the laws of the religion. And according to those who establish for religion roots and branches, we say: the roots of religion and its branches.

But Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah said that dividing religion into roots and branches is an innovated statement for which there is no evidence. This is correct; but you do not find in the Qur'an and the Sunnah "roots" and "branches." There is what indicates pillarhood, for example, and that this is a pillar, as in his saying: *"Islam is built upon five."*[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (8), and Muslim (16/20), from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar.]] But as for our saying "roots and branches," Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, rejected this not because it is merely a terminology (there is no dispute over terminology), but because it was used as a means to reach objectionable conclusions. They said, for example, that we do not argue from solitary reports (akhbar al-ahad) in the roots of religion, and they made this a door through which they entered into denying the attributes and denying what has come in reports about the Last Day and similar matters.

In short, what about His saying ﴿except those who believe﴾? What is the answer to it? From one of two ways. The first: except those who were prepared for faith, such that Allah has decreed it for them; these hear and benefit. Or: ﴿except those who believe﴾ means those who are believers now but who hear what they receive afterward of the rites and laws of Islam.

﴿So they are Muslims﴾: is the believer a Muslim outwardly and inwardly?

* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: And the hypocrite?
* Student: Outwardly, not inwardly.
* Shaykh: A Muslim outwardly, not inwardly. And the one who openly declares his disbelief?
* Students: Outwardly and inwardly.
* Shaykh: Outwardly and inwardly; he is not a believer, neither outwardly nor inwardly. People do not go beyond these three categories: one who disbelieves outwardly and inwardly, one who believes outwardly and inwardly, and one who believes outwardly but not inwardly.

There is a fourth division, but it is not possible: one who believes inwardly but not outwardly. This is not possible. It is true that a person may be weak in faith, and you find in him violations outwardly, like the sinful believer. But that he should have no Islam at all, this is not possible.

* Student: It is not applied to him that he (...).
* Shaykh: I do not know.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: He is a Muslim outwardly, but there is an obstacle to displaying it.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: (...) because this is disbelief; because he made it disbelief (...).

* * *

(...) ﴿And if We were to send a wind and they saw it turn yellow, they would surely continue to disbelieve after it﴾: this sentence.

(...) the sight, and it may also mean blindness of insight (baṣīrah). Whichever it is, whether it is sensory or spiritual, and the latter is the apparent meaning of the context, the meaning is that the Messenger ﷺ cannot guide these people, and in it (...).

His saying: ﴿You can only make hear those who believe in Our signs﴾. What is the type of this sentence (...).

* * *

﴿Allah is the One who created you from weakness﴾ [al-Rum 54]. This verse was brought to explain the condition of man and the perfection of the power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

He says: ﴿Allah is the One who created you from weakness﴾. ﴿Allah﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and ﴿the One who﴾ (alladhī) is its predicate (khabar).

﴿created you from weakness﴾ is said with a fatḥah on the ḍād and with a ḍammah on it. The ḍammah is the dialect of the people of the Ḥijāz, and the fatḥah is the dialect of the Banū Tamīm. For this reason it is narrated from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited to me:" ﴿min ḍu'f﴾ [[Narrated by Abu Dawud (3978) and al-Tirmidhi (2936), from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar.]], with a ḍammah on the ḍād; ﴿khalaqakum min ḍu'f﴾. But the hadith is weak. They only mentioned the ḍād with fatḥah and with ḍammah; they are two canonical (sab'iyyah) readings, and the fatḥah is the dialect of the Banū Tamīm, and the ḍammah is the dialect of the people of the Ḥijāz.

* Student: If someone recites it according to the narration of Ḥafs with a ḍammah, do we say it is a mistake, or...?

* The Shaykh: Correct. Any person who recites with any established reading is correct.

﴿Allah is the One who created you from weakness﴾. What is the weakness? It is said: the water (the fluid of "water that is despised" – mā' mahīn). So weakness is taken to be the drop (nuṭfah), because Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿from a despised water﴾ [al-Sajdah 8]. And ﴿min﴾ here indicates the starting point (ibtidā'), like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Man was created of haste﴾ [al-Anbiya' 37]. It is also said: what is meant by weakness is his weakness after the breathing of the spirit into him, since in the state of the drop he is inanimate matter that cannot be described as weak or as strong. Rather, what is meant by weakness is after the breathing of the spirit into him. Have you understood? This is the correct view, for a human being is not a complete creation until after the breathing of the spirit. For this reason Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Then We clothed the bones with flesh, then We produced it as another creation﴾ [al-Mu'minun 14]. This producing is the first point at which a human becomes a human, because a human is a human by his body and his spirit. Based on this we say: what is meant by weakness after the breathing of the spirit into him is the weakness of childhood, and it begins from his being alive in his mother's womb. This is evident and needs no proof: the young human is weak. Then afterwards... And weakness also applies to his sensory powers and his spiritual powers, so he is weak in thinking, which are the spiritual powers, and in reason, and what resembles that.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 30, verses 51–54 (part 1 of 2):

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And if We were to send a wind and they saw it turn yellow, they would surely continue to disbelieve after it﴾ [al-Rum 51].

﴿And if﴾: the lam here is the lam of oath (lam al-qasam), which has entered upon the conditional particle (in), ﴿And if We send﴾. His saying ﴿they would surely [continue]﴾ is the response, but to which of the two is it a response: the condition or the oath? (...) It is indicated by the lam that prepares for the oath, and in it is the conditional (in). The response now belongs to the oath: ﴿they would surely continue to disbelieve after it﴾, and the response of the condition is omitted, indicated by the response of the oath.

﴿And if We send a wind﴾: notice the difference. In the first verse Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿It is Allah who sends the winds﴾, whereas here He says ﴿a wind﴾ in the singular. We have mentioned previously that the plural is used for mercy and the singular for punishment; this is the general rule.

﴿And if We send a wind and they see it turn yellow﴾: the pronoun in ﴿they saw it﴾ does not refer to the wind, but refers to what was brought to life by the water that descended from the sky, because it was mentioned earlier: ﴿how He gives life to the earth after its death﴾. The meaning is: if We send a wind and they see this that was brought to life ﴿turn yellow﴾, that is, dry and crushed by these winds, ﴿they would surely continue to disbelieve after it﴾.

Let us read the author's words: (﴿And if﴾ the lam of oath, ﴿We send a wind﴾ harmful to vegetation, ﴿and they see it﴾: the pronoun refers to what? To the vegetation) ﴿turn yellow, they would [surely]﴾: "they became", the response of the oath; ﴿after it﴾: that is, after its yellowing; ﴿continue to disbelieve﴾: deny the blessing of the rain. ﴿they would surely continue to disbelieve after it﴾: they say, "How can this be? The rain comes and descends, the earth is revived, and then this wind comes and destroys it?" So they disbelieve, may Allah protect us, and forget the blessing of Allah that came before. They forget it, and this is part of the trial, and it falls under the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿And among the people is he who worships Allah on an edge; if good befalls him, he is content with it, but if a trial befalls him, he turns back on his face. He loses this world and the Hereafter﴾ [al-Hajj 11]. So the believer is patient at the time of affliction and thankful at the time of ease.

* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No, on (...).

He, Exalted, says: ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear﴾ [al-Rum 52]. ﴿You﴾ is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, and it is permissible that the address be general to everyone who can be addressed.

﴿You cannot make the dead hear﴾: that is, you cannot make them hear in a way that benefits them, or: you cannot make them hear at the time of invitation. The closer meaning is the first, because it is not reasonable that someone stands over the dead and says, "O people, worship Allah and fear Him." This is not reasonable. But if it were supposed that he invited them, would they hear in a way that benefits them? The answer is no, they do not hear in a way that benefits them.

If someone says: this is a restriction of the verse. The verse is unrestricted, ﴿You cannot make the dead hear﴾, so how is it permissible for you to restrict it by saying "in a way that benefits them"?

We say: this negation of hearing is applied to the negation of beneficial hearing, as in the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿And do not be like those who said, "We hear," while they do not hear﴾ [al-Anfal 21]. They hear with their ears, but they do not hear in a way that benefits them. And we do not take it in its absolute sense, because the hearing of the dead is reported in narrations. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ is established as having "stood over the companions of the well of Badr from among the polytheists and began calling them by their names and the names of their fathers: 'O so-and-so son of so-and-so, O so-and-so son of so-and-so, have you found what your Lord promised to be true? For we have found what our Lord promised us to be true.' Then 'Umar said, 'O Messenger of Allah, do you address people who have decayed?' (meaning: how do you address carcasses, the dead?) He said: 'You are not more hearing of what I say than they are.'"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3976), and Muslim (2875/78), from the hadith of Abu Talhah.]] That is, they hear more intensely than your hearing. So it is established that the dead do hear. Likewise Ibn 'Abd al-Barr declared sound a hadith related from the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, that "No one greets a dead person whom he knew in the world except that Allah returns his soul to him, and he returns the greeting."[[Related by Ibn 'Abd al-Barr in al-Istidhkar (1/185), from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.]] Ibn al-Qayyim mentioned this in his book al-Ruh, and he mentioned Ibn 'Abd al-Barr's authentication of it without objecting to it. Based on this, they do hear, but they do not benefit from this hearing.

Other reports have also come from the Companions on this matter, which Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned at this verse. It is also established in the Sahih that when a person is left by his companions after the burial, to the extent that he hears the sound of their sandals, two angels come to him.[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1338), and Muslim (2870/70), from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik.]] He hears the sound of their sandals on the ground, just as a person walks on the ceiling and we hear his walking on the ceiling. This one also hears the sound of the sandals (...) the sound of the sandals, but Allah, Exalted, makes them hear that.

So the conclusion is that we say: all of this supports that the meaning of ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear﴾ is: hearing in a way that benefits them. It is well known that the Messenger ﷺ did not invite the dead; he did not go to the graves to call them. But those who call on the dead from among the living, the dead do not respond and do not benefit from the call.

He, Exalted, says: ﴿Nor can you make the deaf hear the call﴾. ﴿The deaf﴾ is the first object, and ﴿the call﴾ is the second object. As for ﴿you cannot make the dead hear﴾ in the first instance, the second object has been omitted, because it is a supplementary element (fadlah), and it has already been mentioned to us that it is permissible to omit a supplementary element even without evidence.

And He said: ﴿Nor can you make the deaf hear the call﴾. ﴿The deaf﴾ is the plural of aṣamm, the one who does not hear, the one who does not hear; you cannot make him hear, especially when turning away is joined to it: ﴿when they turn back and flee﴾. This is the strongest form of the absence of hearing from the deaf. The deaf person does not hear even if he is facing you. How much more so when he turns away! (...) For this reason, if the deaf person is in front of you and you call him with some voice, perhaps he will hear. But if he turns away, however much you call him, he will not hear unless you reach him and take hold of him. So the deaf, when they turn back and flee, do not hear. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, restricted the deaf to this state only because it is the state in which they absolutely do not hear, unlike when they are in front of you, for they may hear and infer what you say from the movements of your lips.

﴿Nor can you make the deaf hear the call﴾: the author said: (with the two hamzas realized, and the second softened between it and the ya'). ﴿The call, when﴾: what is this? It is the realization (tahqiq); ﴿the call, when they turn﴾. The second: softening the second, between it, that is, between the realized hamzah and the ya'; that is: ﴿Nor can you make the deaf hear the call, idha﴾ place it between the hamzah and the ya'. Both readings are among the seven canonical readings.

Then He said: ﴿Nor can you guide the blind out of their straying﴾ [al-Rum 53]. Notice now the transition: the dead, the deaf, the blind.

﴿Nor can you guide the blind out of their straying﴾: ﴿mā﴾ is Hijazi (negating like laysa), ﴿anta﴾ is its subject, the ba' is an extra preposition, and (hadi) is its predicate.

﴿Nor can you [be] a guide﴾: an active participle. ﴿The blind﴾: ﴿al-'umy﴾ is the plural of a'mā, because the plural pattern of af'al is fu'l; Ibn Malik said:

*"fu'l is for such as aḥmar and ḥamrā'..."*

(aḥmar is like a'mā, and ḥamrā' is like 'amyā'), so 'umy is the plural for males and females alike.

﴿Guide the blind out of their straying﴾: what is the meaning of ﴿their straying﴾? That is, from their bewilderment. If they are lost on the road, you cannot guide the blind away from it. Likewise these people who are blind to the truth, may Allah protect us, do not see; they are deaf to it and do not hear; they are dead to it and do not understand. You also cannot guide these people, or can you?

Now reflect on the matter of death and the matter of deafness. He said: ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear, nor can you make the deaf hear﴾, and regarding blindness He said: ﴿Nor can you guide the blind﴾. He did not say "you cannot make the blind hear." The reason: sight is connected with guidance (dalalah), which is guidance, whereas deafness is connected with hearing.

(﴿And you cannot guide the blind out of their straying; you do not make [anyone] hear except those who believe in Our verses, so they are Muslims﴾ [al-Rum 53].)

﴿In﴾: the author said: (mā). What is the meaning of (﴿in﴾ mā)? This "mā" is explanatory (tafsiriyyah), and for this reason it is not assimilated into "in", so one does not say "imma", but rather "in" followed by "mā" in an explicit form, because "mā" explains it; it is the same thing, ﴿in﴾ meaning "mā".

﴿You make hear﴾: the author said: (hearing that comprehends and accepts).

You do not make hear ﴿except those who believe in Our verses﴾: that is, the Qur'an, ﴿so they are Muslims﴾. That is: on the basis of their faith they are Muslims, submissive, because whenever faith is complete, submission is complete. The more a person's faith is strong, the greater his submission. For this reason, faith entails Islam; every believer is a Muslim, but not vice versa. Not every Muslim is a believer; a person may submit outwardly while his heart harbors disbelief, may Allah protect us, unlike faith. For this reason He ordered Islam after faith with the particle fa': ﴿so they are Muslims﴾; they are, because of their faith, Muslims who submit.

His saying ﴿except those who believe in Our verses﴾: the author said it means the Qur'an, even though "āyāt" is plural and not singular. So what is the answer to the author's statement?

The answer to the author's statement is that it is deficient, and the truth is that what is meant by "āyāt" is more general than the Qur'an; it includes all the revealed books, and it also includes the cosmic signs, by believing that this universe was created by Allah, Mighty and Majestic, because some people do not believe in the cosmic signs. See: ﴿And if they see a piece of the sky falling, they say: "Layered clouds"﴾ [al-Tur 44]. What do they say? It is natural; the universe is matter and nature interacting and producing some things from others, and similar things. They did not believe in the signs.

The legal signs likewise: some people do not believe in them; they deny their reports and are arrogant toward their rulings, and this is common.

So the correct view is that what is meant by His saying ﴿Our verses﴾ includes all the legal signs in all the revealed books and all the cosmic signs, because some people deny the cosmic signs, as you know.

If someone says: ﴿You do not make hear except those who believe in Our verses﴾ means that the believer hears, so how can He say "you do not make hear except those who believe," when the believer hears? How would you answer this?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, but whoever believes hears; you make hear those who believe.
* Student: (...) that he is receptive to the call (...).
* Another student: Receptive to hearing and (...).
* Shaykh: The answer to this is one of two ways. Either it is said: ﴿You do not make hear except those who believe﴾ means: except those who were prepared to believe in what you say and who are written with Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as believers. This is a matter not known to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, but he is obliged to make the call so that those whom Allah knows to be believers and prepared for faith hear it. That is one way. Or it is said: religion consists of laws; it is not one thing, but rather laws and multiple rites, and whoever benefits from these rites and applies them is the one who believes in them. This believer, in whom faith has actually occurred, is the one who hears all that the Messenger ﷺ called to from all the laws of the religion. And according to those who establish for religion roots and branches, we say: the roots of religion and its branches.

But Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah said that dividing religion into roots and branches is an innovated statement for which there is no evidence. This is correct; but you do not find in the Qur'an and the Sunnah "roots" and "branches." There is what indicates pillarhood, for example, and that this is a pillar, as in his saying: *"Islam is built upon five."*[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (8), and Muslim (16/20), from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar.]] But as for our saying "roots and branches," Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, rejected this not because it is merely a terminology (there is no dispute over terminology), but because it was used as a means to reach objectionable conclusions. They said, for example, that we do not argue from solitary reports (akhbar al-ahad) in the roots of religion, and they made this a door through which they entered into denying the attributes and denying what has come in reports about the Last Day and similar matters.

In short, what about His saying ﴿except those who believe﴾? What is the answer to it? From one of two ways. The first: except those who were prepared for faith, such that Allah has decreed it for them; these hear and benefit. Or: ﴿except those who believe﴾ means those who are believers now but who hear what they receive afterward of the rites and laws of Islam.

﴿So they are Muslims﴾: is the believer a Muslim outwardly and inwardly?

* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: And the hypocrite?
* Student: Outwardly, not inwardly.
* Shaykh: A Muslim outwardly, not inwardly. And the one who openly declares his disbelief?
* Students: Outwardly and inwardly.
* Shaykh: Outwardly and inwardly; he is not a believer, neither outwardly nor inwardly. People do not go beyond these three categories: one who disbelieves outwardly and inwardly, one who believes outwardly and inwardly, and one who believes outwardly but not inwardly.

There is a fourth division, but it is not possible: one who believes inwardly but not outwardly. This is not possible. It is true that a person may be weak in faith, and you find in him violations outwardly, like the sinful believer. But that he should have no Islam at all, this is not possible.

* Student: It is not applied to him that he (...).
* Shaykh: I do not know.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: He is a Muslim outwardly, but there is an obstacle to displaying it.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: (...) because this is disbelief; because he made it disbelief (...).

* * *

(...) ﴿And if We were to send a wind and they saw it turn yellow, they would surely continue to disbelieve after it﴾: this sentence.

(...) the sight, and it may also mean blindness of insight (baṣīrah). Whichever it is, whether it is sensory or spiritual, and the latter is the apparent meaning of the context, the meaning is that the Messenger ﷺ cannot guide these people, and in it (...).

His saying: ﴿You can only make hear those who believe in Our signs﴾. What is the type of this sentence (...).

* * *

﴿Allah is the One who created you from weakness﴾ [al-Rum 54]. This verse was brought to explain the condition of man and the perfection of the power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

He says: ﴿Allah is the One who created you from weakness﴾. ﴿Allah﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and ﴿the One who﴾ (alladhī) is its predicate (khabar).

﴿created you from weakness﴾ is said with a fatḥah on the ḍād and with a ḍammah on it. The ḍammah is the dialect of the people of the Ḥijāz, and the fatḥah is the dialect of the Banū Tamīm. For this reason it is narrated from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited to me:" ﴿min ḍu'f﴾ [[Narrated by Abu Dawud (3978) and al-Tirmidhi (2936), from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar.]], with a ḍammah on the ḍād; ﴿khalaqakum min ḍu'f﴾. But the hadith is weak. They only mentioned the ḍād with fatḥah and with ḍammah; they are two canonical (sab'iyyah) readings, and the fatḥah is the dialect of the Banū Tamīm, and the ḍammah is the dialect of the people of the Ḥijāz.

* Student: If someone recites it according to the narration of Ḥafs with a ḍammah, do we say it is a mistake, or...?

* The Shaykh: Correct. Any person who recites with any established reading is correct.

﴿Allah is the One who created you from weakness﴾. What is the weakness? It is said: the water (the fluid of "water that is despised" – mā' mahīn). So weakness is taken to be the drop (nuṭfah), because Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿from a despised water﴾ [al-Sajdah 8]. And ﴿min﴾ here indicates the starting point (ibtidā'), like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Man was created of haste﴾ [al-Anbiya' 37]. It is also said: what is meant by weakness is his weakness after the breathing of the spirit into him, since in the state of the drop he is inanimate matter that cannot be described as weak or as strong. Rather, what is meant by weakness is after the breathing of the spirit into him. Have you understood? This is the correct view, for a human being is not a complete creation until after the breathing of the spirit. For this reason Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Then We clothed the bones with flesh, then We produced it as another creation﴾ [al-Mu'minun 14]. This producing is the first point at which a human becomes a human, because a human is a human by his body and his spirit. Based on this we say: what is meant by weakness after the breathing of the spirit into him is the weakness of childhood, and it begins from his being alive in his mother's womb. This is evident and needs no proof: the young human is weak. Then afterwards... And weakness also applies to his sensory powers and his spiritual powers, so he is weak in thinking, which are the spiritual powers, and in reason, and what resembles that.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 30, verses 51–54 (part 1 of 2):

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And if We were to send a wind and they saw it turn yellow, they would surely continue to disbelieve after it﴾ [al-Rum 51].

﴿And if﴾: the lam here is the lam of oath (lam al-qasam), which has entered upon the conditional particle (in), ﴿And if We send﴾. His saying ﴿they would surely [continue]﴾ is the response, but to which of the two is it a response: the condition or the oath? It is a response to the oath, because if it were the response to the condition it would not need the lam. The past-tense verb is answered directly without an intermediary. Furthermore, the rule among the scholars of Arabic grammar is that when a condition and an oath are combined, the response of whichever comes later is omitted. Ibn Malik said:

*"When a condition and an oath come together, omit the response of the one that comes later; it is then obligatory."*

(...) It is indicated by the lam that prepares for the oath, and in it is the conditional (in). The response now belongs to the oath: ﴿they would surely continue to disbelieve after it﴾, and the response of the condition is omitted, indicated by the response of the oath.

﴿And if We send a wind﴾: notice the difference. In the first verse Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿It is Allah who sends the winds﴾, whereas here He says ﴿a wind﴾ in the singular. We have mentioned previously that the plural is used for mercy and the singular for punishment; this is the general rule.

﴿And if We send a wind and they see it turn yellow﴾: the pronoun in ﴿they saw it﴾ does not refer to the wind, but refers to what was brought to life by the water that descended from the sky, because it was mentioned earlier: ﴿how He gives life to the earth after its death﴾. The meaning is: if We send a wind and they see this that was brought to life ﴿turn yellow﴾, that is, dry and crushed by these winds, ﴿they would surely continue to disbelieve after it﴾.

Let us read the author's words: (﴿And if﴾ the lam of oath, ﴿We send a wind﴾ harmful to vegetation, ﴿and they see it﴾: the pronoun refers to what? To the vegetation) ﴿turn yellow, they would [surely]﴾: "they became", the response of the oath; ﴿after it﴾: that is, after its yellowing; ﴿continue to disbelieve﴾: deny the blessing of the rain. The meaning is that when Allah, Mighty and Majestic, gives life to the earth after its death and sends upon it a wind so that the vegetation turns yellow, and after its yellowing it is destroyed, as a trial from Him, exalted is He, they would, after this rejoicing and after seeing the signs of mercy, become disbelievers.

﴿they would surely continue to disbelieve after it﴾: they say, "How can this be? The rain comes and descends, the earth is revived, and then this wind comes and destroys it?" So they disbelieve, may Allah protect us, and forget the blessing of Allah that came before. They forget it, and this is part of the trial, and it falls under the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿And among the people is he who worships Allah on an edge; if good befalls him, he is content with it, but if a trial befalls him, he turns back on his face. He loses this world and the Hereafter﴾ [al-Hajj 11]. When Allah sends this wind and the vegetation turns yellow, they should have met that with patience, not disbelief, patience with this affliction, because patience... the patient one is given his reward without reckoning, and perhaps this trial will turn into another blessing, since Allah, Exalted, says: ﴿But if you are patient, it is better for the patient﴾ [al-Nahl 126]; ﴿And if you believe and fear Allah, He will give you your rewards and will not ask you for your wealth﴾ [Muhammad 36]; ﴿And if you are patient and fear Allah, indeed that is of the matters requiring determination﴾ [Al 'Imran 186]. So the believer is patient at the time of affliction and thankful at the time of ease.

* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No, on (...).

He, Exalted, says: ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear﴾ [al-Rum 52]. ﴿You﴾ is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, and it is permissible that the address be general to everyone who can be addressed.

﴿You cannot make the dead hear﴾: that is, you cannot make them hear in a way that benefits them, or: you cannot make them hear at the time of invitation. The closer meaning is the first, because it is not reasonable that someone stands over the dead and says, "O people, worship Allah and fear Him." This is not reasonable. But if it were supposed that he invited them, would they hear in a way that benefits them? The answer is no, they do not hear in a way that benefits them.

If someone says: this is a restriction of the verse. The verse is unrestricted, ﴿You cannot make the dead hear﴾, so how is it permissible for you to restrict it by saying "in a way that benefits them"?

We say: this negation of hearing is applied to the negation of beneficial hearing, as in the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿And do not be like those who said, "We hear," while they do not hear﴾ [al-Anfal 21]. They hear with their ears, but they do not hear in a way that benefits them. And we do not take it in its absolute sense, because the hearing of the dead is reported in narrations. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ is established as having "stood over the companions of the well of Badr from among the polytheists and began calling them by their names and the names of their fathers: 'O so-and-so son of so-and-so, O so-and-so son of so-and-so, have you found what your Lord promised to be true? For we have found what our Lord promised us to be true.' Then 'Umar said, 'O Messenger of Allah, do you address people who have decayed?' (meaning: how do you address carcasses, the dead?) He said: 'You are not more hearing of what I say than they are.'"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3976), and Muslim (2875/78), from the hadith of Abu Talhah.]] That is, they hear more intensely than your hearing. So it is established that the dead do hear. This one also hears the sound of the sandals (...) the sound of the sandals, but Allah, Exalted, makes them hear that.

So the conclusion is that we say: all of this supports that the meaning of ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear﴾ is: hearing in a way that benefits them. It is well known that the Messenger ﷺ did not invite the dead; he did not go to the graves to call them. But those who call on the dead from among the living, the dead do not respond and do not benefit from the call.

This believer, in whom faith has actually occurred, is the one who hears all that the Messenger ﷺ called to from all the laws of the religion. But Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah said that dividing religion into roots and branches is an innovated statement for which there is no evidence. This is correct; but you do not find in the Qur'an and the Sunnah "roots" and "branches." There is what indicates pillarhood, for example, and that this is a pillar, as in his saying: *"Islam is built upon five."*[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (8), and Muslim (16/20), from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar.]] But as for our saying "roots and branches," Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, rejected this not because it is merely a terminology (there is no dispute over terminology), but because it was used as a means to reach objectionable conclusions. They said, for example, that we do not argue from solitary reports (akhbar al-ahad) in the roots of religion, and they made this a door through which they entered into denying the attributes and denying what has come in reports about the Last Day and similar matters.

In short, what about His saying ﴿except those who believe﴾? What is the answer to it? From one of two ways. The first: except those who were prepared for faith, such that Allah has decreed it for them; these hear and benefit. Or: ﴿except those who believe﴾ means those who are believers now but who hear what they receive afterward of the rites and laws of Islam.

﴿So they are Muslims﴾: is the believer a Muslim outwardly and inwardly?

* Shaykh: A Muslim outwardly, not inwardly. And the one who openly declares his disbelief?

There is a fourth division, but it is not possible: one who believes inwardly but not outwardly. This is not possible. It is true that a person may be weak in faith, and you find in him violations outwardly, like the sinful believer. But that he should have no Islam at all, this is not possible.

﴿Allah is the One who created you from weakness﴾ [al-Rum 54]. This verse was brought to explain the condition of man and the perfection of the power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

He says: ﴿Allah is the One who created you from weakness﴾. ﴿Allah﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and ﴿the One who﴾ (alladhī) is its predicate (khabar).

﴿created you from weakness﴾ is said with a fatḥah on the ḍād and with a ḍammah on it. The ḍammah is the dialect of the people of the Ḥijāz, and the fatḥah is the dialect of the Banū Tamīm. For this reason it is narrated from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited to me:" ﴿min ḍu'f﴾ [[Narrated by Abu Dawud (3978) and al-Tirmidhi (2936), from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar.]], with a ḍammah on the ḍād; ﴿khalaqakum min ḍu'f﴾. But the hadith is weak. They only mentioned the ḍād with fatḥah and with ḍammah; they are two canonical (sab'iyyah) readings, and the fatḥah is the dialect of the Banū Tamīm, and the ḍammah is the dialect of the people of the Ḥijāz.

* Student: If someone recites it according to the narration of Ḥafs with a ḍammah, do we say it is a mistake, or...?

* The Shaykh: Correct. Any person who recites with any established reading is correct.

﴿Allah is the One who created you from weakness﴾. What is the weakness? It is said: the water (the fluid of "water that is despised" – mā' mahīn). So weakness is taken to be the drop (nuṭfah), because Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿from a despised water﴾ [al-Sajdah 8]. And ﴿min﴾ here indicates the starting point (ibtidā'), like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Man was created of haste﴾ [al-Anbiya' 37]. It is also said: what is meant by weakness is his weakness after the breathing of the spirit into him, since in the state of the drop he is inanimate matter that cannot be described as weak or as strong. Rather, what is meant by weakness is after the breathing of the spirit into him. Have you understood? This is the correct view, for a human being is not a complete creation until after the breathing of the spirit. For this reason Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Then We clothed the bones with flesh, then We produced it as another creation﴾ [al-Mu'minun 14]. This producing is the first point at which a human becomes a human, because a human is a human by his body and his spirit. Based on this we say: what is meant by weakness after the breathing of the spirit into him is the weakness of childhood, and it begins from his being alive in his mother's womb. This is evident and needs no proof: the young human is weak. Then afterwards... And weakness also applies to his sensory powers and his spiritual powers, so he is weak in thinking, which are the spiritual powers, and in reason, and what resembles that.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 30, verses 51–54 (part 1 of 2):

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And if We were to send a wind and they saw it turn yellow, they would surely continue to disbelieve after it﴾ [al-Rum 51].

﴿And if﴾: the lam here is the lam of oath (lam al-qasam), which has entered upon the conditional particle (in), ﴿And if We send﴾. His saying ﴿they would surely [continue]﴾ is the response, but to which of the two is it a response: the condition or the oath? It is a response to the oath, because if it were the response to the condition it would not need the lam. The past-tense verb is answered directly without an intermediary. Furthermore, the rule among the scholars of Arabic grammar is that when a condition and an oath are combined, the response of whichever comes later is omitted. Ibn Malik said:

*"When a condition and an oath come together, omit the response of the one that comes later; it is then obligatory."*

(...) It is indicated by the lam that prepares for the oath, and in it is the conditional (in). The response now belongs to the oath: ﴿they would surely continue to disbelieve after it﴾, and the response of the condition is omitted, indicated by the response of the oath.

﴿And if We send a wind﴾: notice the difference. In the first verse Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿It is Allah who sends the winds﴾, whereas here He says ﴿a wind﴾ in the singular. We have mentioned previously that the plural is used for mercy and the singular for punishment; this is the general rule.

﴿And if We send a wind and they see it turn yellow﴾: the pronoun in ﴿they saw it﴾ does not refer to the wind, but refers to what was brought to life by the water that descended from the sky, because it was mentioned earlier: ﴿how He gives life to the earth after its death﴾. The meaning is: if We send a wind and they see this that was brought to life ﴿turn yellow﴾, that is, dry and crushed by these winds, ﴿they would surely continue to disbelieve after it﴾.

Let us read the author's words: (﴿And if﴾ the lam of oath, ﴿We send a wind﴾ harmful to vegetation, ﴿and they see it﴾: the pronoun refers to what? To the vegetation) ﴿turn yellow, they would [surely]﴾: "they became", the response of the oath; ﴿after it﴾: that is, after its yellowing; ﴿continue to disbelieve﴾: deny the blessing of the rain. The meaning is that when Allah, Mighty and Majestic, gives life to the earth after its death and sends upon it a wind so that the vegetation turns yellow, and after its yellowing it is destroyed, as a trial from Him, exalted is He, they would, after this rejoicing and after seeing the signs of mercy, become disbelievers.

﴿they would surely continue to disbelieve after it﴾: they say, "How can this be? The rain comes and descends, the earth is revived, and then this wind comes and destroys it?" So they disbelieve, may Allah protect us, and forget the blessing of Allah that came before. They forget it, and this is part of the trial, and it falls under the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿And among the people is he who worships Allah on an edge; if good befalls him, he is content with it, but if a trial befalls him, he turns back on his face. He loses this world and the Hereafter﴾ [al-Hajj 11]. When Allah sends this wind and the vegetation turns yellow, they should have met that with patience, not disbelief, patience with this affliction, because patience... the patient one is given his reward without reckoning, and perhaps this trial will turn into another blessing, since Allah, Exalted, says: ﴿But if you are patient, it is better for the patient﴾ [al-Nahl 126]; ﴿And if you believe and fear Allah, He will give you your rewards and will not ask you for your wealth﴾ [Muhammad 36]; ﴿And if you are patient and fear Allah, indeed that is of the matters requiring determination﴾ [Al 'Imran 186]. So the believer is patient at the time of affliction and thankful at the time of ease.
